greek: Ὀπὴν οὖν τινα ὀλίγην ὑποδείξαντες »τοῖς φιλοθεάμοσι τῆς ἀληθείας« ἐκ τοῦ κατὰ τὰς θυσίας νόμου περί τε Ἰουδαίων τῶν χυδαίων περί τε τῶν αἱρέσεων μυστικῶς διακρινομένων. ὡς ἀκαθάρτων, ἀπὸ τῆς [περὶ καθαρῶν καὶ ἀκαθάρτων ζῴων] θείας ἐκκλησίας, καταπαύσωμεν τὸν λόγον. τὰ μὲν γὰρ διχηλοῦντα καὶ μηρυκισμὸν ἀνάγοντα τῶν ἱερείων καθαρὰ καὶ δεκτὰ τῷ θεῷ παραδίδωσιν ἡ γραφή, ὡς ἂν εἰς πατέρα καὶ εἰς υἱὸν διὰ τῆς πίστεως τῶν δικαίων τὴν πορείαν ποιουμένων (αὕτη γὰρ ἡ τῶν διχηλούντων ἑδραιότης) τῶν »τὰ λόγια τοῦ θεοῦ« »νύκτωρ καὶ μεθ᾿ ἡμέραν μελετώντων« καὶ ἀναπεμπαζομένων ἐν τῷ τῆς ψυχῆς τῶν μαθημάτων δοχείῳ. ἣν * καὶ συνάσκησιν γνωστικὴν ὑπάρχουσαν καθαροῦ ζῴου μηρυκισμὸν ὁ νόμος ἀλληγορεῖ. ὅσα δὲ μήτε ἑκάτερον μήτε τὸ ἕτερον τούτων ἔχει, ὡς ἀκάθαρτα ἀφορίζει. αὐτίκα τὰ ἀνάγοντα μηρυκισμόν, μὴ διχηλοῦντα δέ. τοὺς Ἰουδαίους αἰνίσσεται τοὺς πολλούς, οἳ τὰ μὲν λόγια τοῦ θεοῦ ἀνὰ στόμα ἔχουσιν. τὴν δὲ πίστιν καὶ τὴν βάσιν δι᾿ υἱοῦ πρὸς τὸν πατέρα παραπέμπουσαν οὐκ ἔχουσιν ἐπερειδομένην τῇ ἀληθείᾳ. ὅθεν καὶ ὀλισθηρὸν τὸ γένος τῶν τοιούτων θρεμμάτων, ὡς ἂν μὴ σχιδανοπόδων ὄντων μηδὲ τῇ διπλόῃ τῆς πίστεως ἐπερειδομένων· »οὐδεὶς γάρ«. φησί, »γινώσκει τὸν πατέρα εἰ μὴ ὁ υἱὸς καὶ ᾧ ἂν ὁ υἱὸς ἀποκαλύψῃ.« ἔμπαλίν τε αὖ ἀκάθαρτα ὁμοίως κἀκεῖνα. ὅσα διχηλεῖ μέν. μηρυκισμὸν δὲ οὐκ ἀνάγει. ταυτὶ γὰρ τοὺς αἱρετικοὺς ἐνδείκνυται ὀνόματι μὲν πατρὸς καὶ υἱοῦ ἐπιβεβηκότας. τὴν δὲ τῶν λογίων ἀκριβῆ σαφήνειαν λεπτουργεῖν καὶ καταλεαίνειν ἐξασθενοῦντας, πρὸς δὲ καὶ τὰ ἔργα τῆς δικαιοσύνης ὁλοσχερέστερον. οὐχὶ δὲ ἀκριβέστερον μετερχομένους, εἴ γε καὶ μετέλθοιεν. τοιούτοις τισὶν ὁ κύριος λέγει· »τί με λέγετε ›κύριε κύριε‹ καὶ οὐ ποιεῖτε ἃ λέγω;« ἀκάθαρτοι δὲ πάμπαν οἱ μὴ διχηλοῦντες μηδὲ ἀνάγοντες μηρυκισμόν. ὑμεῖς δ᾿, ὦ Μεγαρεῖς, φησὶν ὁ Φέογνις, οὔτε τρίτοι οὔτε τέταρτοι οὔτε δυωδέκατοι οὔτ᾿ ἐν λόγῳ οὔτ᾿ ἐν ἀριθμῷ, »ἀλλ᾿ ἢ ὡς ὁ χνοῦς, ὃν ἐκρίπτει ὁ ἄνεμος ἀπὸ προσώπου τῆς γῆς« καὶ »ὡς σταγὼν ἀπὸ κάδου«. Τούτων ἡμῖν προδιηνυσμένων καὶ τοῦ ἠθικοῦ τόπου ὡς ἐν κεφαλαίῳ ὑπογραφέντος, σποράδην, ὡς ὑπεσχήμεθα, καὶ διερριμμένως τὰ ζώπυρα τῶν τῆς ἀληθοῦς γνώσεως ἐγκατασπείραντες δογμάτων, ὡς μὴ ῥᾳδίαν εἶναι τῷ περιτυχόντι τῶν ἀμυήτων τὴν τῶν ἁγίων παραδόσεων εὕρεσιν, μετίωμεν ἐπὶ τὴν ὑπόσχεσιν. ἐοίκασι δέ πως οἱ Στρωματεῖς οὐ παραδείσοις ἐξησκημένοις ἐκείνοις τοῖς ἐν στοίχῳ καταπεφυτευμένοις εἰς ἡδονὴν ὄψεως. ὄρει δὲ μᾶλλον συσκίῳ τινὶ καὶ δασεῖ κυπαρίσσοις καὶ πλατάνοις δάφνῃ τε καὶ κισσῷ, μηλέαις τε ὁμοῦ καὶ ἐλαίαις καὶ συκαῖς καταπεφυτευμένῳ, ἐξεπίτηδες ἀναμεμιγμένης τῆς φυτείας καρποφόρων τε ὁμοῦ καὶ ἀκάρπων δένδρων διὰ τοὺς ὑφαιρεῖσθαι καὶ κλέπτειν τολμῶντας τὰ ὥρια, ἐθελούσης λανθάνειν τῆς γραφῆς. ἐξ ὧν δὴ μεταμοσχεύσας καὶ μεταφυτεύσας ὁ γεωργὸς ὡραῖον κατακοσμήσει παράδεισον καὶ ἄλσος ἐπιτερπές. οὔτ᾿ οὖν τῆς τάξεως οὔτε τῆς φράσεως στοχάζονται οἱ Στρωματεῖς, ὅπου γε ἐπίτηδες καὶ τὴν λέξιν οὐχ Ἕλληνες εἶναι βούλονται καὶ τὴν τῶν δογμάτων ἐγκατασπορὰν λεληθότως καὶ οὐ κατὰ τὴν ἀλήθειαν πεποίηνται, φιλοπόνους καὶ εὑρετικοὺς εἶναι τοὺς ἀναγιγνώσκοντας> εἴ τινες τύχοιεν παρασκευάζοντες. πολλὰ γὰρ τὰ δελέατα καὶ ποικίλα διὰ τὰς τῶν ἰχθύων διαφοράς. Καὶ δὴ μετὰ τὸν ἕβδομον τοῦτον ἡμῖν Στρωματέα τῶν ἑξῆς ἀπ᾿ ἄλλης ἀρχῆς ποιησόμεθα τὸν λόγον.

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: We shall shortly examine how the doctrines of the philosophers were seen among the Hebrews; first, however, as is fitting, we must speak of the times of Moses, through which it will be shown beyond dispute that the Hebrew philosophy is the most ancient of all wisdom. Tatian has already treated these matters precisely in his *Address to the Greeks*, and Cassian has done so in the first book of his *Exegetical Works*; nevertheless, the present memorandum also requires us to run through what has been said on the topic.

Apion the grammarian, surnamed Plistonicus, in the fourth book of his *Egyptian Histories* — although he is hostile toward the Hebrews, being Egyptian by birth, and has even composed a work against the Jews — mentions Amosis, king of the Egyptians, and the events of his reign, and cites Ptolemy of Mendes as a witness. Ptolemy's words run thus: Amosis, having become king in the time of Argive Inachus, demolished the city of Avaris, as Ptolemy of Mendes recorded in his *Chronicles*. This Ptolemy was a priest, and in three books he set forth the deeds of the Egyptian kings; he states that during the reign of Amosis, king of Egypt, the Jews, led by Moses, made their journey out of Egypt, from which it follows that Moses flourished in the time of Inachus.

The most ancient of Greek history is the Argolic — that is, the history reckoned from Inachus — as Dionysius of Halicarnassus teaches in his *Chronicles*. The Attic history, reckoned from Cecrops the two-natured and autochthonous, is, as Tatian says word for word, forty generations younger; the Arcadian history, reckoned from Pelasgus, is nine generations younger, and Pelasgus too is said to be autochthonous. The Phthiotic history, reckoned from Deucalion, is younger still by two generations. From Inachus to the time of the Trojan War, twenty or a few more generations are counted, amounting, so to speak, to about four hundred years.

If the Assyrian history is far older than the Greek, as Ctesias says, it will appear that in the four hundred and second year of the Assyrian empire, and in the thirty-second year of the eighth dynasty of Belochus, the migration of Moses out of Egypt took place under Amosis the Egyptian and Inachus the Argive. In Greece, during the time of Phoroneus, who came after Inachus, there occurred the flood of Ogygus and the kingdom in Sicyon — first of Aegialeus, then of Eurypus, then of Telchin — and the kingdom of Crete in Crete. Acusilaus declares that Phoroneus was the first man born; hence the poet of the *Phoroneis* calls him the father of mortal men. Following Acusilaus, Plato writes in the *Timaeus* that, wishing to draw his interlocutors into discourse about ancient things, he undertakes to speak of the most ancient traditions of the city: of Phoroneus, said to be the first, of Niobe, and of the events after the flood.

Under Phorbas came Actaeus, from whom the Attic Actaea takes its name. Under Triopas came Prometheus, Atlas, Epimetheus, the two-natured Cecrops, and Io. Under Crotopus occurred the conflagration in the time of Phaethon and the flood in the time of Deucalion. Under Sthenelus came the kingdom of Amphictyon, the arrival of Danaus in the Peloponnese, and the foundation of Dardania by Dardanus, whom Homer says was the firstborn of cloud-gathering Zeus, together with the carrying off of Europa from Phoenicia to Crete.

greek: Καὶ περὶ μὲν τοῦ παρ’ Ἑβραίων τὰ τῶν φιλοσόφων ἐσκευωρῆσθαι δόγματα μικρὸν ὕστερον διαληψόμεθα, πρότερον δέ, ὅπερ ἀκόλουθον ἦν, περὶ τῶν κατὰ Μωυσέα χρόνων ἤδη λεκτέον, δἰ ὧν δειχθήσεται ἀναμφηρίστως πάσης σοφίας ἀρχαιοτάτη ἡ κατὰ Ἑβραίους φιλοσοφία. εἴρηται μὲν οὖν περὶ τούτων ἀκριβῶς Τατιανῷ ἐν τῷ Πρὸς Ἕλληνας, εἴρηται δὲ καὶ Κασσιανῷ ἐν τῷ πρώτῳ τῶν Ἐξηγητικῶν· ἀπαιτεῖ δὲ ὅμως τὸ ὑπόμνημα καὶ ἡμᾶς ἐπιδραμεῖν τὰ κατὰ τὸν τόπον εἰρημένα. Ἀπίων τοίνυν ὁ γραμματικός, ὁ Πλειστονίκης ἐπικληθείς, ἐν τῇ τετάρτῃ τῶν Αἰγυπτιακῶν ἱστοριῶν, καίτοι φιλαπεχθημόνως πρὸς Ἑβραίους διακείμενος, ἅτε Αἰγύπτιος τὸ γένος, ὡς καὶ κατὰ Ἰουδαίων συντάξασθαι βιβλίον, Ἀμώσιος τοῦ Αἰγυπτίων βασιλέως μεμνημένος καὶ τῶν κατ’ αὐτὸν πράξεων, μάρτυρα παρατίθεται Πτολεμαῖον τὸν Μενδήσιον. καὶ τὰ τῆς λέξεως αὐτοῦ ὧδε ἔχει· κατέσκαψε δὲ τὴν Ἀουαρίαν Ἄμωσις κατὰ τὸν Ἀργεῖον γενόμενος Ἴναχον, ὡς ἐν τοῖς Χρόνοις ἀνέγραφεν ὁ Μενδήσιος Πτολεμαῖος. ὁ δὲ Πτολεμαῖος οὗτος ἱερεὺς μὲν ἦν, τὰς δὲ τῶν Αἰγυπτίων βασιλέων πράξεις ἐν τρισὶν ὅλαις ἐκθέμενος βίβλοις κατὰ Ἄμωσίν φησιν Αἰγύπτου βασιλέα Μωυσέως ἡγουμένου γεγονέναι Ἰουδαίοις τὴν ἐξ Αἰγύπτου πορείαν, ἐξ ὧν συνῶπται κατὰ Ἴναχον ἠκμακέναι τὸν Μωσέα. παλαίτατα δὲ τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν τὰ Ἀργολικά, τὰ ἀπὸ Ἰνάχου λέγω, ὡς Διονύσιος ὁ Ἁλικαρνασσεὺς ἐν τοῖς Χρόνοις διδάσκει, τούτων δὲ † τεσσαράκοντα μὲν γενεαῖς νεώτερα τὰ Ἀττικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Κέκροπος τοῦ διφυοῦς δὴ καὶ αὐτόχθονος, ὥς φησι κατὰ λέξιν ὁ Τατιανός, ἐννέα δὲ τὰ Ἀρκαδικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Πελασγοῦ· λέγεται δὲ καὶ οὗτος αὐτόχθων. τούτων δὲ ἄλλαιν δυοῖν νεώτερα τὰ Φθιωτικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Δευκαλίωνος. εἰς δὲ τὸν χρόνον τῶν Τρωϊκῶν ἀπὸ Ἰνάχου γενεαὶ μὲν εἴκοσι ἢ μιᾷ πλείους διαριθμοῦνται, ἔτη δέ, ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν, τετρακόσια καὶ πρόσω. εἰ δὲ τὰ Ἀσσυρίων πολλοῖς ἔτεσι πρεσβύτερα τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν ἀφ’ ὧν Κτησίας λέγει, φανήσεται τῷ δευτέρῳ καὶ τετρακοσιοστῷ ἔτει τῆς Ἀσσυρίων ἀρχῆς, τῆς δὲ Βηλούχου τοῦ ὀγδόου δυναστείας τῷ δευτέρῳ καὶ τριακοστῷ ἡ Μωυσέως κατὰ Ἄμωσιν τὸν Αἰγύπτιον καὶ κατὰ Ἴναχον τὸν Ἀργεῖον ἐξ Αἰγύπτου κίνησις. ἦν δὲ κατὰ τὴν Ἑλλάδα κατὰ μὲν Φορωνέα τὸν μετὰ Ἴναχον ὁ ἐπὶ Ὠγύγου κατακλυσμὸς καὶ ἡ ἐν Σικυῶνι βασιλεία, πρώτου μὲν Αἰγιαλέως, εἶτα Εὔρωπος, εἶτα Τελχῖνος, καὶ ἡ Κρητὸς ἐν Κρήτῃ. Ἀκουσίλαος γὰρ Φορωνέα πρῶτον ἄνθρωπον γενέσθαι λέγει· ὅθεν καὶ ὁ τῆς Φορωνίδος ποιητὴς εἶναι αὐτὸν ἔφη πατέρα θνητῶν ἀνθρώπων. ἐντεῦθεν ὁ Πλάτων ἐν Τιμαίῳ κατακολουθήσας Ἀκουσιλάῳ γράφει· καί ποτε προαγαγεῖν βουληθεὶς αὐτοὺς περὶ τῶν ἀρχαίων εἰς λόγους τῶν τῇδε τῇ πόλει τὰ ἀρχαιότατα λέγειν ἐπιχειρεῖ, περὶ Φορωνέως τε τοῦ πρώτου λεχθέντος καὶ Νιόβης, καὶ τὰ μετὰ τὸν κατακλυσμόν. κατὰ δὲ Φόρβαντα Ἀκταῖος, ἀφ’ οὗ Ἀκταία ἡ Ἀττική. κατὰ δὲ Τριόπαν Προμηθεὺς καὶ Ἄτλας καὶ Ἐπιμηθεὺς καὶ ὁ διφυὴς Κέκροψ καὶ Ἰώ. κατὰ δὲ Κρότωπον ἡ ἐπὶ Φαέθοντος ἐκπύρωσις καὶ ἡ ἐπὶ Δευκαλίωνος ἐπομβρία. κατὰ δὲ Σθένελον ἥ τε Ἀμφικτυόνος βασιλεία καὶ ἡ εἰς Πελοπόννησον Δαναοῦ παρουσία καὶ ἡ ὑπὸ Δαρδάνου τῆς Δαρδανίας κτίσις, ὃν πρῶτον, φησὶν Ὅμηρος, τέκετο νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς, ἥ τε τῆς Εὐρώπης εἰς Κρήτην ἐκ Φοινίκης ἀνακομιδή.

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: Let the various accounts of the times, narrated by many and presented to us, stand as they are; but the writings — both the Law and the Prophetic books — they say were translated from the Hebrew dialect into the Greek language during the reign of King Ptolemy Lagus, or, as some hold, under the one surnamed Philadelphus, who devoted extraordinary zeal to the project, with Demetrius of Phalerum overseeing the translation work in detail. For while the Macedonians still held Asia, the king, eager to adorn the library he was building in Alexandria with every kind of writing, deemed it worthy to have the Jerusalemites render their prophecies into the Greek tongue (2 Maccabees 2:13).

Since they were still subject to the Macedonians, they chose seventy elders, men skilled in the Scriptures and versed in Greek, and sent them to him together with the sacred books. Each translated every prophecy separately, yet when all the versions were compared they matched in both thought and wording; for it was God's deliberate will that the message reach Greek ears (Deuteronomy 4:6).

It is therefore no wonder that, by the inspiration of the God who gave the prophecy, the translation itself functions as a kind of Greek prophecy; just as in the captivity under Nebuchadnezzar, when the writings had been destroyed in the time of Artaxerxes king of Persia, Ezra the Levite priest, moved by the Spirit, renewed all the ancient Scriptures by prophesying them anew (Ezra 7:10; Nehemiah 8:8).

Aristobulus, in the first of his books addressed to Philometor, writes word for word that Plato followed our legislation and clearly worked through each of its statements. Moreover, the account of the Hebrews' exodus from Egypt — our fellow citizens — and the manifestation and possession of all that befell them, together with the exposition of the whole Law, had been translated by others before Demetrius, before the rise of Alexander and the Persians; hence it is evident that the aforementioned philosopher borrowed much, having become widely learned, just as Pythagoras also transferred many elements from our tradition into his own system (Acts 7:22).

Numenius the Pythagorean philosopher states it outright: "What is Plato but Moses speaking Attic?" This Moses was a theologian and prophet, and, as some say, an interpreter of the sacred laws. The Scriptures themselves, trustworthy witnesses, proclaim his lineage, deeds, and life; yet we too must speak, as concisely as possible (John 5:46).

greek: Καὶ τὰ μὲν περὶ τῶν χρόνων διαφόρως πολλοῖς ἱστορηθέντα καὶ πρὸς ἡμῶν ἐκτεθέντα ὧδε ἐχέτω, ἑρμηνευθῆναι δὲ τὰς γραφὰς τάς τε τοῦ νόμου καὶ τὰς προφητικὰς ἐκ τῆς τῶν Ἑβραίων διαλέκτου εἰς τὴν Ἑλλάδα γλῶττάν φασιν ἐπὶ βασιλέως Πτολεμαίου τοῦ Λάγου ἢ ὥς τινες ἐπὶ τοῦ Φιλαδέλφου ἐπικληθέντος, τὴν μεγίστην φιλοτιμίαν εἰς τοῦτο προσενεγκαμένου, Δημητρίου τοῦ Φαληρέως καὶ τὰ περὶ τὴν ἑρμηνείαν ἀκριβῶς πραγματευσαμένου· ἔτι γὰρ Μακεδόνων τὴν Ἀσίαν κατεχόντων φιλοτιμούμενος ὁ βασιλεὺς τὴν ἐν Ἀλεξανδρείᾳ πρὸς αὐτοῦ γενομένην βιβλιοθήκην πάσαις κατακοσμῆσαι γραφαῖς ἠξίωσε καὶ τοὺς Ἱεροσολυμίτας τὰς παρ’ αὐτοῖς προφητείας εἰς τὴν Ἑλλάδα διάλεκτον ἑρμηνεῦσαι. οἳ δὲ ἅτε ἔτι ὑπακούοντες Μακεδόσι τῶν παρὰ σφίσιν εὐδοκιμωτάτων περὶ τὰς γραφὰς ἐμπείρους καὶ τῆς Ἑλληνικῆς διαλέκτου εἰδήμονας ἑβδομήκοντα πρεσβυτέρους ἐκλεξάμενοι ἀπέστειλαν αὐτῷ μετὰ καὶ τῶν θείων βίβλων. ἑκάστου δὲ ἐν μέρει κατ’ ἰδίαν ἑκάστην ἑρμηνεύσαντος προφητείαν συνέπνευσαν αἱ πᾶσαι ἑρμηνεῖαι συναντιβληθεῖσαι καὶ τὰς διανοίας καὶ τὰς λέξεις· θεοῦ γὰρ ἦν βούλημα μεμελετημένον εἰς Ἑλληνικὰς ἀκοάς. οὐ δὴ ξένον ἐπιπνοίᾳ θεοῦ τοῦ τὴν προφητείαν δεδωκότος καὶ τὴν ἑρμηνείαν οἱονεὶ Ἑλληνικὴν προφητείαν ἐνεργεῖσθαι, ἐπεὶ κἀν τῇ ἐπὶ Ναβουχοδονόσορ αἰχμαλωσίᾳ διαφθαρεισῶν τῶν γραφῶν κατὰ τοὺς Ἀρταξέρξου τοῦ Περσῶν βασιλέως χρόνους ἐπίπνους Ἔσδρας ὁ Λευίτης ὁ ἱερεὺς γενόμενος πάσας τὰς παλαιὰς αὖθις ἀνανεούμενος προεφήτευσε γραφάς. Ἀριστόβουλος δὲ ἐν τῷ πρώτῳ τῶν πρὸς τὸν Φιλομήτορα κατὰ λέξιν γράφει· κατηκολούθηκε δὲ καὶ ὁ Πλάτων τῇ καθ’ ἡμᾶς νομοθεσίᾳ, καὶ φανερός ἐστι περιειργασμένος ἕκαστα τῶν ἐν αὐτῇ λεγομένων. διηρμήνευται δὲ πρὸ Δημητρίου ὑφ’ ἑτέρων, πρὸ τῆς Ἀλεξάνδρου καὶ Περσῶν ἐπικρατήσεως, τά τε κατὰ τὴν ἐξ Αἰγύπτου ἐξαγωγὴν τῶν Ἑβραίων τῶν ἡμετέρων πολιτῶν καὶ ἡ τῶν γεγονότων ἁπάντων αὐτοῖς ἐπιφάνεια καὶ κράτησις τῆς χώρας καὶ τῆς ὅλης νομοθεσίας ἐπεξήγησις· ὥστε εὔδηλον εἶναι τὸν προειρημένον φιλόσοφον εἰληφέναι πολλά (γέγονε γὰρ πολυμαθής), καθὼς καὶ Πυθαγόρας πολλὰ τῶν παρ’ ἡμῖν μετενέγκας εἰς τὴν ἑαυτοῦ δογματοποιίαν. Νουμήνιος δὲ ὁ Πυθαγόρειος φιλόσοφος ἄντικρυς γράφει· τί γάρ ἐστι Πλάτων ἢ Μωυσῆς ἀττικίζων; οὗτος ὁ Μωυσῆς θεολόγος καὶ προφήτης, ὡς δέ τινες νόμων ἱερῶν ἑρμηνεὺς ἦν. τὸ γένος αὐτοῦ καὶ τὰς πράξεις καὶ τὸν βίον ἀξιόπιστοι κηρύσσουσαι αὐταὶ αἱ γραφαί, λεκτέον δὲ ὅμως καὶ ἡμῖν ὡς ὅτι μάλιστα δἰ ὀλίγων.

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: We are commanded to reverence and honor the Word, for we have been persuaded that he is both Savior and Leader, and through him the Father as well; we must do this not only on special days, as some people do, but continuously throughout our entire life and in every possible way. For the chosen race is justified in saying, 'I have praised you seven times a day' (Psalm 119:164), doing so in accordance with the commandment. Therefore the knowledgeable person needs neither a designated place, nor a special temple, nor appointed festivals and days; rather, he honors God in every place and at all times, whether he happens to be alone or among others who believe likewise, which is to say he gives thanks for the knowledge and the way of life he has received. If the presence of a good man always molds the one who meets him toward what is better through shame and respect, how much more will the one who is continually present with God through knowledge, life, and unceasing gratitude become better in every respect — in deeds, words, and disposition? Such a person is convinced that God is present everywhere; he does not suppose that God is confined to specific places, lest he ever imagine himself to be without God and behave recklessly by day and by night. Consequently we conduct our whole life as a festival, persuaded that God is present everywhere; we farm while praising, we sail while singing hymns. We conduct ourselves skillfully according to the rest of our civic duty. The knowledgeable person draws especially near to God, being at once dignified and cheerful in all things: dignified because of his turning toward the divine, and cheerful because of his reckoning of the human goods that God has given us. The prophet displays the excellence of knowledge in these words: 'Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge,' increasing the ruling part of perfection. This one, then, is truly the royal man; this one is the holy priest of God — a priestly race still preserved even now among the most reasonable of the barbarians, who bring the priesthood to the kingdom. Such a man does not surrender himself to the rule of the mob in the theaters; he does not so much as approach in a dream the things said, done, and seen for the sake of dissolute pleasure. He avoids those pleasures of spectacle, and he avoids the varied enjoyments through the other senses — such as the costly fragrance of incense that beguiles the sense of smell, or the elaborate preparations of foods and the diverse enjoyments of wines that entice the sense of taste, or the many-hued and sweet-scented weaves that soften the soul through sensation. Instead, he always directs the dignified enjoyment of all things toward God, and for food and drink and anointing he offers first-fruits of thanksgiving to the Giver of all, acknowledging both the gift and the use of what was given to him through the Word.

greek: Σέβειν δὲ δεῖν ἐγκελευόμεθα καὶ τιμᾶν τὸν [αὐτὸν καὶ] λόγον, σωτῆρά τε αὐτὸν καὶ ἡγεμόνα εἶναι πεισθέντες, καὶ δι᾿ αὐτοῦ τὸν πατέρα, οὐκ ἐν ἐξαιρέτοις ἡμέραις, ὥσπερ ἄλλοι τινές, ἀλλὰ συνεχῶς τὸν ὅλον βίον τοῦτο πράττοντες καὶ κατὰ πάντα τρόπον. ἀμέλει »τὸ γένος τὸ ἐκλεκτὸν« »ἑπτάκις τῆς ἡμέρας ᾔνεσά σοι« φησί, κατ᾿ ἐντολὴν δικαιούμενον. ὅθεν οὔτε ὡρισμένον τόπον * οὔτε ἐξαίρετον ἱερὸν οὐδὲ μὴν ἑορτάς τινας καὶ ἡμέρας ἀποτεταγμένας, ἀλλὰ τὸν πάντα βίον ὁ γνωστικὸς ἐν παντὶ τόπῳ, κἂν καθ᾿ ἑαυτὸν μόνος ὢν τυγχάνῃ καὶ ὅπου τινὰς ἂν τῶν ὁμοίως πεπιστευκότων ἔχῃ, τιμᾷ τὸν θεόν, τουτέστιν χάριν ὁμολογεῖ τῆς γνώσεως καὶ τῆς πολιτείας. εἰ δὲ ἡ παρουσία τινὸς ἀνδρὸς ἀγαθοῦ διὰ τὴν ἐντροπὴν καὶ τὴν αἰδῶ πρὸς τὸ κρεῖττον ἀεὶ σχηματίζει τὸν ἐντυγχάνοντα, πῶς οὐ μᾶλλον ὁ συμπαρὼν ἀεὶ διὰ τῆς γνώσεως καὶ τοῦ βίου καὶ τῆς εὐχαριστίας ἀδιαλείπτως τῷ θεῷ οὐκ εὐλόγως ἂν ἑαυτοῦ παρ᾿ ἕκαστα κρείττων εἴη εἰς πάντα καὶ τὰ ἔργα καὶ τοὺς λόγους καὶ τὴν διάθεσιν; τοιοῦτος ὁ πάντῃ παρεῖναι τὸν θεὸν πεπεισμένος, οὐχὶ δὲ ἐν τόποις τισὶν ὡρισμένοις κατακεκλεισμένον ὑπολαβών, ἵνα δὴ χωρὶς αὐτοῦ ποτε οἰηθεὶς εἶναι καὶ νύκτωρ καὶ μεθ᾿ ἡμέραν ἀκολασταίνῃ. πάντα τοίνυν τὸν βίον ἑορτὴν ἄγοντες, πάντῃ πάντοθεν παρεῖναι τὸν θεὸν πεπεισμένοι, γεωργοῦμεν αἰνοῦντες, πλέομεν ὑμνοῦντες. κατὰ τὴν ἄλλην πολιτείαν ἐντέχνως ἀναστρεφόμεθα. προσεχέστερον δὲ ὁ γνωστικὸς οἰκειοῦται θεῷ σεμνὸς ὢν ἅμα καὶ ἱλαρὸς ἐν πᾶσι. σεμνὸς μὲν διὰ τὴν ἐπὶ τὸ θεῖον ἐπιστροφήν. ἱλαρὸς δὲ διὰ τὸν ἐπιλογισμὸν τῶν ἀνθρωπείων ἀγαθῶν ὧν ἔδωκεν ἡμῖν ὁ θεός. Φαίνεται δὲ τὸ ἔξοχον τῆς γνώσεως ὁ προφήτης ὧδε παριστάς· »χρηστότητα καὶ παιδείαν καὶ γνῶσιν δίδαξόν με·« κατ᾿ ἐπανάβασιν αὐξήσας τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν τῆς τελειότητος. οὗτος ἄρα ὄντως ὁ βασιλικὸς ἄνθρωπος, οὗτος ἱερεὺς ὅσιος τοῦ θεοῦ. ὅπερ ἔτι καὶ νῦν παρὰ τοῖς λογιωτάτοις τῶν βαρβάρων σῴζεται τὸ ἱερατικὸν γένος εἰς βασιλείαν προσαγόντων. οὗτος οὖν οὐδαμῇ μὲν ἑαυτὸν εἰς ὀχλοκρασίαν τὴν τῶν θεάτρων δεσπότιν ἐνδίδωσιν. τὰ λεγόμενα δὲ καὶ πραττόμενα καὶ ὁρώμενα ἡδονῆς ἀσώτου χάριν οὐδὲ ὄναρ προσίεται· οὔτ᾿ οὖν ταύτας τὰς ἡδονὰς τῆς θέας οὔτε τὰς διὰ τῶν ἄλλων ἀπολαυσμάτων ποικιλίας, οἷον θυμιαμάτων πολυτέλειαν τὴν ὄσφρησιν γοητεύουσαν ἢ βρωμάτων συγκαττύσεις καὶ τὰς ἐξ οἴνων διαφόρων ἀπολαύσεις δελεαζούσας τὴν γεῦσιν, οὐδὲ τὰς πολυανθεῖς καὶ εὐώδεις πλοκὰς ἐκθηλυνούσας δι᾿ αἰσθήσεως τὴν ψυχήν· πάντων δὲ τὴν σεμνὴν ἀπόλαυσιν ἐπὶ τὸν θεὸν ἀναγαγὼν ἀεὶ καὶ τῆς βρώσεως καὶ τοῦ πόματος καὶ τοῦ χρίσματος τῷ δοτῆρι τῶν ὅλων ἀπάρχεται, χάριν ὁμολογῶν καὶ [διὰ] τῆς δωρεᾶς καὶ τῆς χρήσεως διὰ λόγου τοῦ δοθέντος αὐτῷ.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: "That's how their fathers treated the prophets," he says. "Oh, you shapeshifter Christ -- now the prophets' destroyer, now their defender! You tore them down as a rival, stealing their disciples for yourself; you propped them up as a friend, shaming the ones who harassed them."

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Christ forbids divorce. He says that a man who dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery, and a man who marries a woman dismissed by her husband is equally an adulterer. By making the marriage of a repudiated woman unlawful, he thereby also prohibits divorce. Moses, however, permits repudiation in Deuteronomy: if a man takes a wife, lives with her, and then finds no favor in her because he has discovered an indecent deed in her, he must write a bill of divorce, hand it to her, and send her from his house (Deuteronomy).

excerpts.author: Origen
english: Our discussion has already turned to the coming judgment and the repayment and punishments for sins, exactly as the holy scriptures threaten and the church's preaching teaches. We are told that at the moment of judgment 'eternal fire' and 'outer darkness,' 'prison' and 'furnace,' and other such things have been prepared for sinners, so we should consider what we ought to think about these realities. To approach them in proper order, it seems right to take up the question of the resurrection first, so that we can understand what it is that will come either to punishment or to rest and blessedness. I have treated this more fully in other books written on the resurrection, showing what appeared to me on the subject; yet because of the present treatise's sequence it is not out of place to repeat a few points here. This is especially necessary because some take offense at the church's faith, claiming we believe in the resurrection foolishly and with complete lack of sense — particularly heretics, to whom I think we must answer as follows.

If they admit that there is a resurrection of the dead, let them tell us: what is it that has died, if not the body? The resurrection of the body will therefore take place. Then let them say whether they think we are to make use of bodies or not. When the apostle Paul declares that 'the body is sown as an animal body, it will rise as a spiritual body' (1 Cor 15:42-44), I do not see how they can deny that the body rises or that we shall use bodies in the resurrection. Now, if it is certain that we must use bodies, and the bodies that have fallen are said to 'rise' — for nothing properly 'rises' except what has previously fallen — then there is no doubt that these bodies rise precisely so that we may be clothed with them again after the resurrection. One point follows from another: if bodies rise, they rise without doubt to serve as our clothing; and if it is necessary for us to be in bodies (as it certainly is), we ought not to be in any bodies other than our own. If it is true that bodies rise and that spirits rise, there can be no doubt that they are said to rise from the dead after casting off corruption and laying aside mortality; otherwise rising from the dead would appear vain and superfluous, only to die again. This becomes clearer when someone carefully considers the quality of the animal body which, once sown in the earth, will produce the quality of a spiritual body. For from the animal body itself, the power of the resurrection and the grace of the spiritual body bring forth that spiritual body, when it is transformed from lowliness to glory (1 Cor 15:42-44).

Since the heretics consider themselves extremely learned and wise, we will question them: does every body have some shape — that is, is it formed by some habit? If they say there is a body not formed by any habit, they will show themselves the most unlearned and foolish of all; no one would deny this unless completely alien to all learning. But if, following the logical consequence, they admit that every body is indeed formed by some definite habit, we will ask them to demonstrate and describe the habit of the spiritual body — which they certainly cannot do. We will also ask about the differences among those who rise. How will they prove true the statement that 'one is the flesh of birds, another of fish; and there are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies; but one is the glory of the heavenly bodies, another of the earthly bodies; one is the glory of the sun, another of the moon, another of the stars, for star differs from star in glory; so also is the resurrection of the dead'? Following that logic, let them show us the differences of glory among the heavenly bodies of those who rise. If they attempt in any way to devise an explanation based on the differences of heavenly bodies, we will then ask them to assign the differences of the resurrection also by comparison with earthly bodies. We, however, understand it this way: the apostle, wishing to describe how great the difference is among those who will rise 'in glory' — that is, the saints — took a comparison from heavenly bodies, saying: 'One is the glory of the sun, another of the moon, another of the stars.' And again, wishing to teach the differences of those who in this life have not been purified and will come to the resurrection — that is, sinners — he takes an example from earthly things, saying: 'One is the flesh of birds, another of fish.' For it is fitting that heavenly things are compared to the saints, and earthly things to sinners. These points have been made against those who deny the resurrection of the dead, that is, the resurrection of bodies.

Now we turn our discussion to some of our own people who, either from narrowness of understanding or poverty of explanation, introduce a very base and degraded sense of the resurrection of the body. We ask them: how do they understand the animal body to be changed by the grace of the resurrection and to become spiritual? How do they think that what is sown 'in weakness' will rise 'in power,' and what is sown 'in lowliness' will rise 'in glory'? And how will what is sown 'in corruption' be transferred to 'incorruption'? If they believe the apostle that the body rising 'in glory and in power and in incorruption' has already been made spiritual (1 Cor 15:42-44), it seems absurd and contrary to the apostle's meaning to say that it is again entangled in the passions of 'flesh and blood,' when the apostle clearly says: 'For flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God, nor can corruption possess incorruption' (1 Cor 15:50). How, too, do they accept what the apostle says, that 'we will all be changed'? That change, according to the order we mentioned above, is to be expected, and in it we rightly hope for something worthy of divine grace — something we believe will come to pass in this order: just as the apostle describes when 'a naked grain of wheat or some other seed' is sown in the earth, to which 'God gives a body as he wills,' after the grain itself has first died. So also our bodies are to be thought of as falling to the earth like a grain; in them a principle is implanted that contains the bodily substance, and although the bodies have died and been corrupted and scattered, the word of God — that same principle, always preserved in the substance of the body — raises them from the earth and restores and repairs them, just as the power within the grain of wheat, after its corruption and death, repairs and restores the grain into the body of the stalk and the ear. And so, for those who will deserve to inherit the heavenly kingdom, that principle of repairing the body, which we spoke of above, by God's command repairs the 'spiritual body' from the earthly and animal body, so that it can dwell in the heavens; but for those of lower merit, or more base, or even the lowest and most hidden, the glory and dignity of the body will be given according to the dignity of each one's life and soul — yet in such a way that even for those destined for 'eternal fire' or 'punishments,' through the very transformation of the resurrection the body that rises is incorrupt, so that it cannot be corrupted or dissolved even by punishments.

If, therefore, the quality of the body that rises from the dead is such, let us now see what the threat of 'eternal fire' means. For we find in the prophet Isaiah that the 'fire' by which each one is punished is designated as their own; he says: 'Walk in the light of your fire and in the flame that you have kindled for yourselves' (Isa 50:11). Through these words it seems to be indicated that each sinner kindles his own 'flame' of his own 'fire,' and does not sink into some fire previously kindled by another or already standing before him. The fuel and material of this fire are our sins, which the apostle Paul calls 'wood and hay and stubble.' I think that just as in the body an abundance and quality or quantity of food contrary to health generates fevers, and fevers of different kinds or durations according to the measure in which the imbalance has collected the material and supplied fuel for the fevers (the quality of that material, gathered from diverse imbalance, being the cause of a more bitter or longer disease): so also the soul, when it has gathered a multitude of evil works and an abundance of sins in itself, at the fitting time all that congregation of evils boils over into punishment and is inflamed into penalties; since also the mind itself or conscience, through divine power, receiving all things into memory — of which it impressed certain signs and forms on itself when it sinned — will see a certain history of its own crimes, whether foully or shamefully committed or even impiously done, laid out before its eyes. Then the conscience itself is stirred and pricked by its own goads and becomes its own accuser and witness. I think the apostle Paul understood this when he says: 'For they will accuse or even defend one another in their thoughts on the day when God will judge the hidden things of men according to my gospel through Jesus Christ' (Rom 2:16). From this it is understood that certain torments are generated around the very substance of the soul from the harmful affections of sins.

excerpts.author: Origen
english: Let us now briefly consider what we should think about the promises as well. It is certain that no animal at all can be entirely idle and immobile; rather, it strives to be moved and to act in every way, always willing to do something. I think it is clear that this nature belongs to all living things. Therefore, the rational animal — that is, human nature — must always be moving or doing something. If someone is forgetful of himself and ignores what befits him, his whole intention is directed toward bodily uses, and through all his movements he is occupied with the body's pleasures and desires. If, however, he is the sort who strives to care for or provide something in common — whether advising for the republic, supporting the magistrates, or exercising whatever certainly seems to benefit the common good — he pursues that. Now, if someone is such that he understands something better than these bodily things and devotes himself to wisdom and knowledge, without doubt he will direct all his industry toward such studies, so that he may come to know the causes and reason of things investigated. Just as, then, in this life one person judges the body's greatest good to be pleasure, another strives to consult for the common good, and another devotes himself to studies and intelligence: so we ask that in that true life, which is called "hidden with Christ in God" — that is, in that eternal life — such a way of living or state might exist for us. (Colossians 3:3)

latin: Videamus nune breviter quid etiam de repromissionibus sentiendum sit. Certum est quia nullum animal omnimodis otiosum atque immobile esse potest, sed omni genere moveri et agere semper et velle aliquid gestit; et hanc inesse naturam omnibus animantibus manifestum puto. Multo ergo magis rationabile animal, id est hominis naturam necesse est semper aliquid movere vel agere. Et si quidem immemor sui sit eb quid se deceat ignoret, circa usus corporales omnis sua movetur intentio et per omnes motus suos erga voluptates ac libidines corporis oecupatur; si vero talis sit, qui in commune aliquid curare vel providere studeat, aut rei publicae consulens aut magistratibus parens aut quidquid illud est, quod in commune certe prodesse videatur, exercet. Jam vero si qui talis sit, ut aliquid melius quam haee, quae corporea videntur, intellegat et sapientiae ac scientiae operam navet, sine dubio erga huiuscemodi studia omnem sui declinabit industriam, quo possit inquisita veritate rerum causas rationemque cognoscere. Nicut ergo in hae vita alius quidem summum bonum corporis iudicat voluptatem, alius vero in commune consulere, alius studus et intellegentiae operam dare: ita requirimus in illa “vitae quae vera est, quae “abscondita essedicitur -cum Christo in deo’, id est in illa aeterna vita, si aliqui talis erii nobis vivendi ordo vel status.

excerpts.author: Origen
english: We must now ask whether there was another world before this present one, and if so, whether it was like this one, or slightly different or inferior; or whether there was no world at all, but rather something of the kind we understand the 'end' to be after all things, 'when the kingdom is handed over to God and the Father' (1 Corinthians 15:24) — an end that would nonetheless belong to another world, namely the one after which this world began, the varied fall of intellectual natures having provoked God into this varied and diverse condition of the world.

I think we must similarly inquire whether after this world there will be some cure and correction, harsher and full of pain for those who refused to obey the word of God, but through rational instruction and reasonable training by which those who in the present life have already devoted themselves to these studies and have been made purer in mind have advanced to a richer understanding of truth, and whether the end of all things will follow immediately after this; or whether, for the correction and amendment of those who need such things, another world will come again, either similar to this present one, or better than this one, or even much worse; and whatever kind that world after this one may be, how long it will last, or whether it will exist at all; and whether there will ever be a time when no world exists anywhere, or whether there was ever a time when no world existed at all; or whether there were many worlds or will be many, or whether it might happen that one world is equal and similar to another in every respect and indistinguishable.

excerpts.author: Origen
english: But since human senses and common understanding are not enough to commit the sum of the matter when discussing such great and important things -- so to speak, to pronounce visibly about invisible things -- we must also take up testimonies of divine Scripture for the proof of what we say. And so that these testimonies may have certain and undoubted faith, whether in the things that are to be said by us or in those already said, it seems necessary first to show that the divine Scriptures themselves are of God, that is, inspired by the Spirit of God.

excerpts.author: Origen
english: We have arrived at the moment to return to the incarnation of the Lord and our Savior, to consider how he became man and lived among men. We have weighed the matter as best our meager powers allow, drawing more from the contemplation of his works than from our own perception; we have looked to the visible creation and, by faith, to the invisible, because human frailty cannot see all things with the eye or grasp them by reason—we are, after all, the weakest and most fragile of all rational animals (for beings in heaven or above the heavens are more excellent). It remains, then, for us to seek the mediator between all these creatures and God, the one Paul the apostle proclaims as "firstborn of all creation" (Colossians 1:15). We also see what the holy Scriptures say of his majesty: that he is called "the image of the invisible God" and "firstborn of all creation," that "all things visible and invisible—thrones, dominions, principalities, powers—were created in him and through him and for him; he is before all things, and in him all things hold together" (Colossians 1:16). He is the head of all, having only God the Father as his head, as Scripture says: "The head of Christ is God." We perceive, too, that "no one knows the Father except the Son, and no one knows the Son except the Father"—for who can know Wisdom except the one who begot it? Who can know Truth except the Father of Truth? Who can fathom the nature of the Word, which is from God, except God alone, with whom the Word was? We must hold it certain that this Word (or Reason) knows this Wisdom, this Truth, and no one else except the Father alone—he of whom it is written, "I do not think the world itself could contain the books that would be written" of the glory and majesty of the Son of God. It is impossible to commit to writing the things that pertain to the Savior's glory. Having weighed such great and wonderful things about the nature of the Son of God, we stand astonished with overwhelming wonder that this supreme nature emptied itself of its majesty, became man, and lived among men—as the grace poured upon his lips testifies, as the heavenly Father bears witness to him, and as signs, wonders, and varied mighty works confirm. Even before the presence he showed in the body, he sent prophets as forerunners and messengers of his coming; and after his ascension into the heavens, he filled holy apostles with the power of his divinity and sent them—uneducated and ignorant men, drawn from tax collectors and fishermen—to circle the earth, that they might gather from every nation and people a company of the godly who believe in him.

english: 1. The order of our arrangement now requires us, after the discussion of the preceding subjects, to institute a general inquiry regarding the soul ; and, beginning with points of inferior importance, to ascend to those that are of greater. Now, that there are souls in all living things, even in those which live in the waters, is, I suppose, doubted by no one. For the general opinion of all men maintains this; and confirmation from the authority of holy Scripture is added, when it is said that God made great whales, and every living creature that moves which the waters brought forth after their kind. It is confirmed also from the common intelligence of reason, by those who lay down in certain words a definition of soul . For soul is defined as follows: a substance φανταστική and ὁρμητική , which may be rendered into Latin, although not so appropriately, sensibilis et mobilis . This certainly may be said appropriately of all living beings, even of those which abide in the waters; and of winged creatures too, this same definition of anima may be shown to hold good. Scripture also has added its authority to a second opinion, when it says, You shall not eat the blood, because the life of all flesh is its blood; and you shall not eat the life with the flesh; in which it intimates most clearly that the blood of every animal is its life. And if any one now were to ask how it can be said with respect to bees, wasps, and ants, and those other things which are in the waters, oysters…

2. But the nature of the incarnation will render unnecessary any inquiry into the soul of Christ . For as He truly possessed flesh, so also He truly possessed a soul . It is difficult indeed both to feel and to state how that which is called in Scripture the soul of God is to be understood; for we acknowledge that nature to be simple, and without any intermixture or addition. In whatever way, however, it is to be understood, it seems, meanwhile, to be named the soul of God ; whereas regarding Christ there is no doubt . And therefore there seems to me no absurdity in either understanding or asserting some such thing regarding the holy angels and the other heavenly powers, since that definition of soul appears applicable also to them. For who can rationally deny that they are sensible and moveable? But if that definition appear to be correct, according to which a soul is said to be a substance rationally sensible and moveable, the same definition would seem also to apply to angels . For what else is in them than rational feeling and motion? Now those beings who are comprehended under the same definition have undoubtedly the same substance. Paul indeed intimates that there is a kind of animal-man who, he says, cannot receive the things of the Spirit of God , but declares that the doctrine of the Holy Spirit seems to him foolish, and that he cannot understand what is to be spiritually discerned. In another passage he says it is sown an animal body, and arises a spiritual body,…

3. But perhaps this question is asked, If it be the understanding which prays and sings with the spirit, and if it be the same which receives both perfection and salvation , how is it that Peter says, Receiving the end of your faith , even the salvation of your souls ? If the soul neither prays nor sings with the spirit, how shall it hope for salvation ? Or when it attains to blessedness, shall it be no longer called a soul ? Let us see if perhaps an answer may be given in this way, that as the Saviour came to save what was lost, that which formerly was said to be lost is not lost when it is saved; so also, perhaps, this which is saved is called a soul , and when it has been placed in a state of salvation will receive a name from the Word that denotes its more perfect condition. But it appears to some that this also may be added, that as the thing which was lost undoubtedly existed before it was lost, at which time it was something else than destroyed, so also will be the case when it is no longer in a ruined condition. In like manner also, the soul which is said to have perished will appear to have been something at one time, when as yet it had not perished, and on that account would be termed soul , and being again freed from destruction, it may become a second time what it was before it perished, and be called a soul . But from the very signification of the name soul which the Greek word conveys, it has appeared to a few curious inquirers that a meaning of no small…

4. Now, if this be the case, it seems to me that this very decay and falling away of the understanding is not the same in all, but that this conversion into a soul is carried to a greater or less degree in different instances, and that certain understandings retain something even of their former vigour, and others again either nothing or a very small amount. Whence some are found from the very commencement of their lives to be of more active intellect , others again of a slower habit of mind , and some are born wholly obtuse, and altogether incapable of instruction. Our statement, however, that the understanding is converted into a soul , or whatever else seems to have such a meaning, the reader must carefully consider and settle for himself, as these views are not be regarded as advanced by us in a dogmatic manner, but simply as opinions, treated in the style of investigation and discussion. Let the reader take this also into consideration, that it is observed with regard to the soul of the Saviour , that of those things which are written in the Gospel , some are ascribed to it under the name of soul , and others under that of spirit. For when it wishes to indicate any suffering or perturbation affecting Him, it indicates it under the name of soul ; as when it says, Now is My soul troubled; and, My soul is sorrowful, even unto death; and, No man takes My soul from Me, but I lay it down of Myself. Into the hands of His Father He commends not His soul , but His spirit; and…

excerpts.author: Origen
english: Everyone who believes and is certain that grace and truth came through Jesus Christ, and who knows that Christ is the Truth — just as he said, "I am the Truth" (John 14:6) — receives the knowledge that moves people to live well and happily from nowhere else but the very words and teaching of Christ. When we speak of Christ's words, we do not mean only what he taught after becoming man and living in the flesh; Christ was already the Word of God in Moses and the prophets. Without the Word of God, how could they have prophesied about Christ? To prove this point it would not be hard to show from the divine Scriptures how both Moses and the prophets, filled with the Spirit of Christ, spoke and did everything they did. But my aim is to finish this present work with all possible brevity, so I judge it sufficient to cite just this one testimony of Paul from the letter he wrote to the Hebrews. There he says: "By faith Moses, when he had grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter, choosing rather to be mistreated with the people of God than to enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin. He considered the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt" (Hebrews 11:24-26). And Paul also indicates that Christ spoke in him after his ascension into heaven, asking: "Or are you seeking proof of the Christ who speaks in me?" (2 Corinthians 13:3).

Since many who profess to believe in Christ disagree not only in small and minor matters but also in great and major ones — that is, about God, or about the Lord Jesus Christ, or about the Holy Spirit, and not only about these but also about other creatures, such as dominions or holy powers — it seems necessary first to lay down a sure and clear rule concerning each of these, and then to investigate the rest. Just as we stopped looking for truth among all those who claimed it with false opinions once we believed that the Son of God, Christ, is the Truth and convinced ourselves that we must learn it from him, so now, though many think they hold the mind of Christ and some of them differ from the earlier ones, the only truth to be believed is the ecclesiastical preaching that has been preserved through the succession of the apostles and remains in the churches to this day — the truth that in nothing disagrees with the ecclesiastical and apostolic tradition.

We must know that the holy apostles, when they preached the faith of Christ, handed down to all believers — even to those who seemed slower in inquiring into divine knowledge — the things they judged necessary, manifestly and plainly, while leaving the reasons for their assertions to be investigated by those who would merit the Spirit's excellent gifts, especially the grace of speech, wisdom, and knowledge through the Holy Spirit. They said that certain things exist, but they kept silent about how or from where they exist, so that the more studious among their successors, lovers of wisdom, might have an exercise in which to show the fruit of their genius — those, namely, who prepared themselves to be worthy and capable of receiving wisdom.

The items explicitly handed down by apostolic preaching are these. First, there is one God, who created and ordered all things, and who, when nothing existed, brought all things into being: the God of the first creation and ordering of the world, the God of all the just — Adam, Abel, Seth, Enos, Enoch, Noah, Shem, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, the twelve patriarchs, Moses, and the prophets. This same God, in the last days, as he had promised through his prophets, sent the Lord Jesus Christ, first to call Israel, and then also the Gentiles after the unfaithfulness of the people of Israel. This God is just and good, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ; he gave the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospels, and he is the God of the apostles and of both the Old and the New Testaments. Next, Jesus Christ, who came, was born before all creation from the Father. Having served the Father in the ordering of all things — "for through him all things were made" (John 1:3) — in the last times he emptied himself, became man, was incarnate, and, being God, remained what he was, God. He took on a body like ours, differing only in that he was born of the Virgin and the Holy Spirit. And because this Jesus Christ was born and suffered in truth, not in appearance, he truly died this common death; for he truly rose from the dead, and after his resurrection conversed with his disciples and was taken up. Then they handed down that the Holy Spirit is associated with the Father and the Son in honor and dignity. Here it is not yet clearly discerned whether he is begotten or unbegotten, or whether he should be counted as the Son of God; but these things must be investigated from Holy Scripture and searched out with sagacity. What is preached most plainly in the Church is that the one Holy Spirit inspired every saint, prophet, and apostle, and that there is not one Spirit in the Old Testament and another in those inspired at the advent of Christ.

After these points, it is already established that the soul, having its own substance and life, when it departs from this world will be dealt with according to its merits: either to inherit eternal life and blessedness, if its deeds have earned it, or to be handed over to eternal fire and torments, if the guilt of sins has turned it away. There will also be a time of the resurrection of the dead, and this body, which is now "sown in corruption, will rise in incorruption, and that which is sown in dishonor, will rise in glory" (1 Corinthians 15:42-43). It is also defined in ecclesiastical preaching that every rational soul possesses free will and its own volition; and that it has a struggle against the devil and his angels and contrary powers, because they try to burden it with sins, while we, if we live rightly and wisely, strive to free ourselves from such stain. From this it follows that we are not subject to necessity, forced to do either evil or good even against our will; for if we are our own masters, perhaps some powers can attack us toward sin and others help us toward salvation, but we are not compelled by necessity to act rightly or wrongly. This is what those think who say that the course and movements of the stars are the cause of human actions — not only of those that happen outside the freedom of our will, but also of those that lie within our power. About the soul, however — whether it is derived from the seed, so that its reason or substance is inserted into the bodily seeds, or whether it has another origin, and if this origin is generated or ungenerated, or whether it is imposed on the body from outside — the preaching does not clearly distinguish.

The ecclesiastical preaching also taught about the devil and his angels and contrary powers that they exist, but it did not clearly explain what they are or how they are. Among many, however, the opinion is held that the devil was an angel who, becoming apostate, persuaded many angels to fall away with him, and these are now called his angels.

There is also in ecclesiastical preaching that this world was made and had a beginning at a certain time, and that it will be dissolved because of its own corruption. But what existed before this world, or what will exist after it, is not clearly known to many; for the teaching on these matters is not evident in ecclesiastical preaching.

Then, that the Scriptures were written through the Spirit of God and have a meaning not only the one that is manifest but also another, hidden one, is preached in the Church. For the things described are forms of certain sacraments and images of divine things. On this the whole Church holds one opinion: that the whole Law is spiritual, yet not all that the Law breathes is known to everyone, but only to those to whom the grace of the Holy Spirit is given in the word of wisdom and knowledge. The term "incorporeal" is not only unusual among many others but also unknown in our Scriptures. If someone tries to bring forward a passage from the book called the Doctrine of Peter, where the Savior seems to say to the disciples, "I am not an incorporeal demon," one must first reply that this book is not among the ecclesiastical books, and must show that this writing is neither Peter's nor that of any other who was inspired by the Spirit of God. Even if this were conceded, the sense indicated in that passage is not the same as the one discussed by Greek or Gentile authors concerning the incorporeal nature of philosophers. In that book, "incorporeal demon" was said because the shape or outline of the demonic body is not like our gross and visible body; but according to the mind of the one who composed that writing, it must be understood that he said he does not have the kind of body demons have — which is naturally subtle and like a thin air, and for that reason is considered or called incorporeal by many — but that he has a solid and palpable body. In human usage, everything that is not such a body is called incorporeal by the simpler or more ignorant; just as someone might call the air we breathe incorporeal, because it is not a body that can be grasped, held, or resisted.

We inquire, however, whether the thing itself that Greek philosophers call "incorporeal" is found in Holy Scripture under another name. How God himself should be understood must also be asked: whether as corporeal and deformed according to some shape, or of another nature than bodies — which is not clearly designated in our preaching. The same things must be inquired about Christ and the Holy Spirit, and also about every soul and every rational nature. There is also in ecclesiastical preaching that there are angels of God and good powers who minister to him for the salvation of men; but when these were created, or what they are, or how they are, is not clearly distinguished. About the sun, moon, and stars, whether they are animate or inanimate, is not clearly handed down. Therefore we must use such things as elements and foundations, according to the commandment that says, "Illuminate for yourselves the light of knowledge" (cf. Psalm 36:9), so that anyone who wishes may complete a certain ordered body of knowledge from the reason of all these things, investigating what is true about each, and may construct one coherent body of examples and affirmations — either those found in Holy Scripture or those discovered through the investigation and right course of the thing itself.

latin: Omnes qui eredunt et certi sunt quod gratia et veritas per lesum Christum facta sit, et Christum esse veritatem norunt, secundum quod ipse dixit: “Ego sum veritas”, scientiam quae provocat homines ad bene beateque vivendum non aliunde quam ab ipsis Christi verbis doetrinaque suscipiunt. Christi autem verbis dieimus non his solum, quae homo factus atque in carne positus docuit; et prius namque Christus dei verbum in Moyse atque in prophetis erat. Nam sine verbo dei quomodo poterant prophetare de Christo? Ad cuius rei probationem non esset difficile ex divinis seripturis ostendere, quomodo vel Moyses vel prophetae spiritu Christi repleti vel locuti sunt vel gesserunt omnia quae gesserunt, nisi studii nobis esset, praesens hoc opus omni qua possumus brevitate suecingere. Unde sufficere aestimo uno hoc Pauli testimonio debere nos uti ex epistula, quam ad Hebraeos scribit, in qua ita ait: “Fide magnus factus Moyses negavit se dici filium filiae Pharaonis, magis eligens afflietari cum populo dei quam temporalem habere peccati iueunditatem, maiores divitias aestimans Aegyptiorum thesauris inproperium Christi”. Sed et post adsumptionem eius in caelos quod in apostolis suis loeutus sit, hoc modo indicat Paulus: “Aut numquid probamentum quaeritis eius, qui in me loquitur Christus?” 2. Quoniam ergo multi ex his, qui Christo se credere profitentur, non solum in parvis et minimis discordant, verum etiam in magnis et maximis, id est vel de deo vel de ipso domino lesu Christo vel de spiritu sancto, non solum autem de his, sed et de alus creaturis, id est vel de dominationibus vel de virtutibus sanctis: propter hoc necessarium videtur prius de his singulis certam lineam manifestamque regulam ponere, tum deinde etiam de ceteris quaerere. Sicut enim, multis apud Graecos et barbaros pollicentibus veritatem, desivimus apud omnes eam quaerere, qui eam falsis opinionibus asserebant, posteaquam eredidimus fihum esse dei Christum et ab ipso nobis hane discendam esse persuasimus: ita eum multi sint, qui se putant sentire quae Christi sunt, et nonnulh eorum diversa a prioribus sentiant, servetur vero ecclesiastica praedicatio per successionis ordinem ab apostolis tradita et usque ad praesens in ecclesiis permanens, illa sola credenda est veritas, quae in nullo ab ecclesiastica et apostolica traditione discordat. 3. Illud autem scire oportet, quoniam sancti apostoli fidem Christi praedieantes de quibusdam quidem, quaecumque necessaria crediderunt, p omnibus eredentibus, etiam his, qui pigriores erga inquisitionem divinae scientiae videbantur, manifestissime tradiderunt, rationem seilicet assertioms eorum relinquentes ab his inquirendam, qui spiritus dona excellentia mererentur et praecipue sermonis, sapientiae et scientiae gratiam per ipsum sanctum spiritum percepissent; de aliis vero dixerunt quidem quia sint, quomodo autem aut unde sint, siluerunt, profecto ut studiosiores quique ex posteris suis, qui amatores essent sapientiae, exercitium habere possent, in quo ingenii sui fructum ostenderent, hi videlicet, qui dignos se et capaces ad recipiendam sapientiam praepararent. 4. Species vero eorum, quae per praedicationem apostolicam manifeste traduntur, istae sunt. Primo, quod unus est deus, qui omnia creavit atque composuit, quique, cum nihil esset, esse fecit universa, deus a prima creatura et conditione mundi, omnium iustorum deus, Adam Abel Seth Enos Enoch No? Sem Abraham Isaac lacob duodecim patriarcharum Moysei et prophetarum; et quod hie deus in novissimis diebus, sicut per prophetas suos ante promiserat, misit dominum lesum Christum, primo quidem vocaturum Israhel, secundo vero etiam gentes post perfidiam populi Israhel. Hie deus iustus et bonus, pater domini nostri lesu Christi, legem et prophetas et evangelia ipse dedit, qui et apostolorum deus est et veteris ac novi testamenti. Tum deinde quia Christus lesus, ipse qui venit, ante omnem creaturam natus ex patre est. Qui cum in omnium conditione patri ministrasset, “per ipsum” namque “omnia facta sunt”, novissimis temporibus se ipsum exinaniens homo factus est, incarnatus est, cum deus esset, et homo factus mansit quod erat, deus. Corpus assumsit nostro corpori simile, eo solo differens, quod natum ex virgine et spiritu sancto est. Et quoniam hie lesus Christus natus et passus est in veritate, et non per phantasiam, communem hanc mortem vere mortuus; vere enim et a mortuis resurrexit et post resurrectionem conversatus cum diseipulis suis assumtus est. Tum deinde honore ac dignitate patri ac filio sociatum tradiderunt spiritum sanctum. In hoe non iam manifeste discernitur, utrum natus aut innatus, vel filius etiam ipse dei habendus sit, neene; sed inquirenda iam ista pro viribus sunt de sancta scriptura et sagaci perquisitione investiganda. Sane quod iste spiritus sanctus unumquemque sanctorum vel prophetarum vel apostolorum inspiraverit, et non alius spiritus in veteribus, alius vero in his, qui in adventu Christi inspirati sunt, fuerit, manifestissime in ecclesia praedicatur. 9. Post haec iam quod anima substantiam vitamque habens propriam, cum ex hoe mundo discesserit, pro suis meritis dispensabitur, sive vitae aeternae ac beatitudinis hereditate potitura, si hoc ei sua gesta praestiterint, sive igni aeterno ac supplieus mancipanda, si in hoc eam scelerum culpa detorserit; sed et quia erit tempus resurrectionis mortuorum, eum corpus hoc, quod nune “in corruptione seminatur, surget in incorruptionec, et quod “seminatur in ignominia, surget in gloria”. Est et illud definitum in eeclesiastica praedicatione, omnem animam rationabilem esse liberi arbitru et voluntatis; esse quoque ei certamen adversum diabolum et angelos eius contrariasque virtutes, ex eo quod ili peccatis eam onerare contendant, nos vero si recte consulteque vivamus, ab huiuscemodi labe exuere nos conemur. Unde et consequens est intellegere, non nos necessitati esse subiectos, ut omni modo, etiamsi nolimus, vel mala vel bona agere cogamur. Si enim nostri arbitri! sumus, inpugnare nos fortasse possint aliquae virtutes ad peccatum et aliae iuvare ad salutem, non tamen necessitate cogimur vel recte agere vel male; quod fieri arbitrantur hi, qui stellarum cursum et motus causam dieunt humanorum esse gestorum, non solum eorum, quae extra arbitrii accidunt libertatem, sed et eorum, quae in nostra sunt posita potestate. De anima vero utrum ex seminis traduce ducatur, ita ut ratio ipsius vel substantia inserta ipsis corporalibus seminibus habeatur, an vero aliud habeat initium, et hoc ipsum initium si genitum est aut non genitum, vel certe si extrinsecus corpori inditur, necne: non satis manifesta praedicatione distinguitur. 6. De diabolo quoque et angelis eius contrarüsque virtutibus ecelesiastica praedicatio docuit quoniam sint quidem haec, quae autem sint vel quomodo sint, non satis clare exposuit. Apud plurimos tamen ista habetur opinio, quod angelus fuerit iste diabolus, et apostata effectus quam plurimos angelorum secum declinare persuaserit, qui et nune usque angel ipsius nuncupantur. 7. Est praeterea et illud in eeclesiastiea praedicatione, quod mundus iste factus sit et a certo tempore coeperit et sit pro 1psa sui corruptione solvendus. Quid tamen ante hunc mundum fuerit, aut quid post mundum erit, jam non pro manifesto multis innotuit. Non enim evidens de his in ecclesiastica praedicatione sermo profertur. 8. Tum deinde quod per spiritum dei seripturae conscriptae sint et sensum habeant non eum solum, qui in manifesto est, sed et alium quendam latentem quam plurimos. Formae enim sunt haec quae descripta sunt sacramentorum quorundam et divinarum rerum imagines. De quo totius eeclesiae una sententia est, esse quidem omnem legem spiritalem, non tamen ea, quae spirat lex, esse omnibus nota nisi his solis, quibus gratia spiritus sancti in verbo sapientiae ac scientiae condonatur. Appellatio autem (id est incorporei) non solum apud multos alios, verum etiam apud nostras scripturas inusitata est et incognita. Si vero quis velt nobis proferre ex illo libello, qui Petri Doctrina appellatur, ubi salvator videtur ad discipulos dieere: “Non sum daemonium incorporeum”, primo respondendum est ei quoniam liber ipse inter libros eeclesiasticos non habetur, et ostendendum quia neque Petri est ipsa scriptura neque alterius cuiusquam, qui spiritu dei fuerit inspiratus. Quod etiamsi ipsum concederetur, non idem sensus inibi ex isto sermone indicatur, qui a graecis vel gentilibus auctoribus ostenditur, eum de incorporea natura a philosophis disputatur. In hoc enim libello -incorporeum daemonium: dixit pro eo, quod ipse ille quicumque est habitus vel eircumscriptio daemoniei corporis non est similis huie nostro crassiori et visibili corpori; sed secundum sensum eius, qui composuit illam scripturam, intellegendum est quod dixit, id est non se habere tale corpus quale habent daemones (quod est naturaliter subtile quoddam et velut aura tenue, et propter hoe vel putatur a multis vel dicitur incorporeum), sed habere se corpus solidum et palpabile. In consuetudine vero hominum omne, quod tale non fuerit, incorporeum a simplicioribus vel imperitioribus nominatur; velut si quis aérem istum quo fruimur incorporeum dieat, quoniam quidem non est tale corpus, ut conprehendi ac teneri possit urgentique resistere. 9. Quaeremus tamen si vel alio nomine res ipsa, quam graeci philosophi (id est ineorporeum) dicunt, in sanctis scripturis invenitur. Deus quoque ipse quomodo intellegi debeat requirendum est, corporeus et secundum aliquem habitum deformatus, an alterius naturae quam corpora sunt, quod utique in praedicatione nostra manifeste non designatur. Eadem quoque etiam de Christo et de saneto spiritu requirenda sunt, sed et de omni anima atque omni rationabili natura nihilominus requirendum est. Est etiam illud in eeclesiastica praedicatione, esse angelos dei quosdam et virtutes bonas, qui ei ministrant ad salutem hominum con- "^" summandam; sed quando isti creati sint, vel quales, aut quomodo sint, non satis in manifesto distinguitur. De sole autem et luna et stellis, utrum animantia sint an sine anima, manifeste non traditur. Oportet igitur velut elementis ac fundamentis huiusmodi uti secundum mandatum, quod dicit: “Inluminate vobis lumen scientiae”, omnem qui eupit seriem quandam et corpus ex horum omnium ratione perficere, ut manifestis et necessarüs assertionibus de singulis quibusque quid sit in vero rimetur, et unum, ut diximus, corpus efficiat exemplis et affirmationibus, vel his, quas in sanctis scripturis invenerit, vel quas ex consequentiae ipsius indagine ac recti tenore reppererit.

excerpts.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus
excerpts.locus: Argument 10.— Hence the Mere Word-Sages are Conf
english: I ask this of the philosophers now living—those I knew myself and those I heard about from others—and of everyone else: receive what I am about to say without bias. Let no one assume I speak from friendship toward the man, or because I still cling to the other philosophers (whom, if anyone else does, I myself—being a lover of the word—wish to honor, and I want to speak well of them and hear others speak well of them). But these philosophers are so utterly despised by almost everyone that the very name of philosophy is scorned; I would rather choose a private life than learn anything from men who, because of their conduct, seemed unworthy even to approach—though I may have judged that wrongly. Still, let no one suppose I say this from some ambition, whether from praise for the man or from rivalry toward outside philosophers. Nor let us appear to flatter by saying less than their deeds deserve, nor let us offer up words, names, and crafted phrases that they themselves invent for self-praise. For even as a youth I was not taught the common rhetoric of the rhetorician—to praise and deliver an encomium for something untrue—and I willingly endured that lack. So now, when I am about to praise, I do not think it right to exalt him merely by censuring others, or to speak ill of the man because of others' faults so that I might have something greater to say about him, disparaging his blessed life. That is not how we think; rather, I will simply acknowledge what I have experienced, without comparison or verbal artifice.

greek: ᾿Ἐξαιτοῦμαι δὲ παρά τε φιλοσόφων τῶν νῦν ὄντων, σοὺυς αὐτὸς ἔγνων καὶ ὃσους ἄλλων διηγουμένων ἤκουσα, καὶ παρὰ τῶν ἄλλων δὲ ἀνθρώπων, ἀνεμεσήτως ἔχειν πρὸς τὰ νῦν ἡμῖν λεγόμενα. μηδέ μέ τις ἢ φιλίᾳ τῇ πρὸς τὸν ἄνδρα ἢ καὶ ἀπτεχϑανόμενον ἔτι τοῖς λοιποῖς φιλοσόφοις (ὧν, εἴπτερ τις ἄλλος, καὶ αὐτὸς ἐραστής ve διὰ τοὺς λόγους εἶναι ϑέλω, καὶ εὐφημεῖν αὐτοὺς βούλομαι αὐτός τε καὶ ἑτέρων τὰ κάλλιστα λεγόντων περὶ αὐτῶν ἀκούεξιν᾽ ἀλλὰ γὰρ τοιαῦτά ἐστιν, ὡς εἰς ἔσχατον περιϊβρίζεσϑαι μὲν ὑπὸ πάντων σχεδὸν καὶ τοὔνομα τῆς φιλοσοφίας, ἐμὲ δὲ μικροῦ δεῖν ἰδιωτεύειν ἑλέσϑαι πτάντη, ἤπερ τι μαϑεῖν ὧν οὗτοι ἀπαγγέλλουσιν, οἷς διὰ τὸν λοιττὸν βίον οὐδὲ προσιέναι ἄξιον εἶναι ἐδόκουν, ἴσως οὐκ ὀρϑῶς τοῦτο φρονῶν), πλὴν μή μέ τις φιλοτιμίᾳ τινὶ ἤτοι τῶν εἰς τὸν ἄνδρα ἐπαίνων ἢ τῇ πρὸς τοὺς ἔξω φιλοσόφους ἄλλῃ ταύτῃ φιλο- τὸ τιμίᾳ ταῦτα λέγειν ὑπονοησάτω" ἀλλὰ καὶ μικρότερα ἡμᾶς τῶν αὐτοῖ: ἔργων, μὴ κολακεύειν δοχοίημεν, λέγειν τεεττείσϑω οὐχὲ ῥήματα καὶ ὀνόματα καὶ ἀφορμὰς ἐντέχνους ἐγχωμίων ἑαυτοῖς ἐχποριζομένοις" ὃς οὐδ᾽ ὕτε μειράκιον ὧν τὴν δημώδη ῥητορικὴν ἔχ. ῥήτορος ἐδιδασκόμην, ἐπαινεῖν καὶ τὸ λέγειν περί του ἐγκώμιον, ὃ τι μὴ ἀληϑὲς ἦν, ἑκὼν ὑπέμενον. οὐ τοίνυν οὐδὲ νῦν ἐπαινεῖν ττροϑέμενος, ἁπλῶς τοῖς ἑτέρων ψόγοις τοῦτον ἐξαίρειν οἶμαι δεῖν" ἢ κακῶς ἂν ἔλεγον τὸν ἄνδρα, τοῖς ἄλλων πταίσμασιν, ἵνα τι ττερὶ αὐτοῦ μεῖζον δὴ λέγειν ἔχοιμι, τταραβαλὼν τὸν μακάριον αὐτοῦ βίον" οὐχ οὕτως ἀφραίνομεν᾽ ἀλλ᾽ αὐτὸ ὃ πέπονθα δίχα τινὸς παραβολῆς χαὶ τεανουργίας τῆς ἐν λόγοις ὁμολογήσω.

excerpts.author: Origen
english: If he had been well-disposed toward the accusation, he ought to have set out the prophecies in their own words — whether those in which God Almighty promised to be the speaker, or those in which the Son of God was the speaker, or even those in which the Holy Spirit was believed to be speaking. For in this way he also struggled to dismantle what had been said and to show that the words were not inspired, even though they contain a turning away from sins, a rebuke of what once was, and a foreknowledge of what is to come. That is why those who copied down the prophecies of the prophets also preserved them, so that later readers might marvel at them as words of God and be benefited not only by the reproachful and corrective passages but also by the predictive ones. By the outcomes they are persuaded concerning the divine Spirit, and so they continue practicing piety according to the word, persuaded by the law and the prophets. The prophets spoke whatever was useful for hearers to understand and that contributed to the correction of character, without any concealment, according to the will of God. But whatever was more mystical, more contemplative, and belonged to a theory beyond common hearing, they declared through riddles, allegories, what are called dark sayings, and the so-called parables or proverbs — so that those who do not shirk labor but accept every toil for the sake of virtue and truth, after examining, might find, and having found, might manage as reason directs. But the foolish Celsus, as if enraged because he did not grasp such words of the prophets, insulted them. He said that, stretching these things out, they add in sequence unknown, absurd, and completely unclear things, of which no one with a mind could find the meaning. For they are unclear and meaningless, and they give any foolish or deceitful person an opportunity to interpret whatever they want, wherever they want. And it seemed to me he said these things cunningly, wishing to prevent those who encounter the prophecies from testing and examining their meaning, as far as he is able. He suffered something similar to those who spoke about a certain prophet: when a prophet entered someone's presence and foretold the future to him, they said, "Why did this epileptic enter to you?"

greek: Ἐχρῆν δὲ αὐτὸν, εἴπερ εὐγνωμόνει πρὸς τὴν κατηγορίαν, ἐκθέσθαι αὐταῖς λέξεσι τὰς προφητείας, εἴτ᾿ ἐν αἷς θεὸς παντοκράτωρ ἐπηγγέλλετο εἶναι ὁ λέγων, εἴτ᾿ ἐν αἷς ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ, εἴτε καὶ ἐν αἷς τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον λέγον εἶναι ἐπιστεύετο· οὕτω γὰρ καὶ ἠγωνίασεν ἀνασκευάσαι τὰ εἰρημένα καὶ δεῖξαι ὅτι οὐκ ἔνθεοι ἦσαν οἱ λόγοι, περιέχοντες ἐπιστροφὴν ἀπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτημάτων καὶ ἔλεγχον τῶν ποτε ὄντων καὶ πρόγνωσιν περὶ τῶν μελλόντων. διὸ καὶ οἱ κατ᾿ αὐτοὺς ἀπογραψάμενοι τὰς προφητείας αὐτῶν ἐφύλαξαν, ἵνα καὶ οἱ μεταγενέστεροι ἀναγινώσκοντες θαυμάζωσιν ὡς λόγους θεοῦ καὶ ὠφελούμενοι οὐ μόνον ἀπὸ τῶν ἐπιπληκτικῶν καὶ ἐπιστρεπτικῶν ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν προγνωστικῶν ταῖς ἐκβάσεσι πειθόμενοι περὶ τοῦ θεῖον εἶναι πνεῦμα τὸ προειρηκὸς τὴν κατὰ τὸν λόγον εὐσέβειαν ἀσκοῦντες διατελῶσι, πειθόμενοι τῷ νόμῳ καὶ τοῖς προφήταις. οἱ μὲν ουν προφῆται ὅσα ἦν αὐτόθεν νοηθῆναι τοῖς ἀκούουσι χρήσιμα καὶ συμβαλλόμενα τῇ τῶν ἠθῶν ἐπανορθώσει χωρὶς πάσης ἐπικρύψεως κατὰ τὸ βούλημα τοῦ θεοῦ εἰρήκασιν, ὅσα δὲ μυστικώτερα ἦν καὶ ἐποπτικώτερα καὶ ἐχόμενα θεωρίας τῆς ὑπὲρ τὴν πάνδημον ἀκοὴν, ταῦτα „δι᾿ αἰνιγμάτων“ καὶ ἀλληγοριῶν καὶ τῶν καλουμένων σκοτεινῶν λόγων καὶ τῶν ὀνομαζομένων παραβολῶν ἢ παροιμιῶν ἀπεφήναντο· ἵν᾿ οἱ μὴ φυγοπονοῦντες ἀλλὰ πάντα πόνον ὑπὲρ ἀρετῆς καὶ ἀληθείας ἀναδεχόμενοι ἐξετάσαντες εὕρωσι καὶ εὑρόντες, ὡς λόγος αἱρεῖ, οἰκονομήσωσιν. ὁ δὲ γεννάδας Κέλσος ὡσπερεὶ θυμωθεὶς ἐπὶ τῷ μὴ νενοηκέναι τοὺς τῶν προφητῶν τοιούτους λόγους ἐλοιδόρησεν αὐτοὺς, εἰπὼν ὅτι ταῦτα ἐπανατεινάμενοι προστιθέασιν ἐφεξῆς ἄγνωστα καὶ πάροιστρα καὶ πάντῃ ἄδηλα, ὧν τὸ μὲν γνῶμα οὐδεὶς ἂν νοῦν ἔχων εὑρεῖν δύναιτο· ἀσαφῆ γὰρ καὶ τὸ μηδὲν, ἀνοήτῳ δὲ ἢ γόητι παντὶ περὶ παντὸς ἀφορμὴν ἐνδίδωσιν, ὅπῃ βούλεται, τὸ λεχθὲν σφετερίζεσθαι. καὶ πανούργως μοι ἔδοξε ταῦτ᾿ εἰρηκέναι, κωλύειν τὸ ὅσον ἐφ᾿ ἑαυτῷ βουλόμενος τοὺς ἐντυγχάνοντας ταῖς προφητείαις βασανίζειν καὶ ἐξετάζειν αὐτῶν τὸν νοῦν· καὶ πέπονθέ τι πρᾶγμα παραπλήσιον τοῖς εἰποῦσι περί τινος προφήτου, εἰσελθόντος πρός τινα καὶ τὰ μέλλοντα προειπόντος αὐτῷ· „τί εἰσῆλθεν ὁ ἐπίληπτος οὗτος πρός σε;“

excerpts.author: Origen
english: He goes on to say that the pronouncements once delivered by the Pythia, the Dodonian priests, the Clarian oracle, the shrine at Branchidae, the oracle of Ammon, and by countless other prophets — prophets through whom the whole earth was settled in a gentle way — are not even taken into account. Yet the utterances of those in Judea, whether spoken in the same manner or not, and the sort of thing still customary among the peoples around Phoenicia and Palestine, these are treated as wonderfully reliable and unchangeable. Let us therefore speak about the oracles that have been handed down. It is possible for us to collect from Aristotle and from those who philosophized in the Peripatetic tradition no small number of arguments to overturn the case for the Pythia and the other oracles. It is also possible to cite the words of Epicurus and of those who embrace his teaching on the same matters, and to show that some Greeks themselves reject the divinations believed and marveled at throughout all Greece. But let us grant that the matters concerning the Pythia and the other oracles are neither fabrications nor human pretenses about divine inspiration. Even so, let us see whether it can be demonstrated to those who examine things in a love of truth that, even if one accepts these as genuine oracles, it is not necessary to conclude that gods are present in them. Rather, they are evil demons and hostile spirits, enemies of the human race, who hinder the soul's ascent and the journey through virtue and the restoration of true piety toward God. Now, it is reported about the Pythia — who appears to be the most renowned of the other oracles — that the prophetess of Apollo, sitting over the mouth of the Castalian spring, receives a spirit through the female organs; and when she has been filled with it, she utters the things regarded as solemn and divine prophecies. Observe, then, through these facts whether the impurity and profanity of that spirit are not revealed. It does not enter the soul of the prophetess through pure and invisible channels, but through those parts which it was not even lawful for a sane and human person to see, let alone touch. And this is done not merely once or twice — for perhaps such a thing might seem more tolerable — but as many times as she is believed to prophesy from Apollo. Moreover, the fact that it drives the supposed prophetess into a state of ecstasy and madness, so that she does not follow herself, is not the work of a divine spirit. For the one possessed by the divine spirit ought to have been benefited far earlier by all that is taught from the oracles concerning the middle and natural life — whether for what is useful or for what is advantageous — and ought to be more discerning, especially at the very time when the divine is present to him.

greek: Φησὶν οὖν· τὰ μὲν ὑπὸ τῆς Πυθίας ἢ Δωδωνίδων ἢ Κλαρίου ἢ ἐν Βραγχίδαις ἢ ἐν Ἄμμωνος ὑπὸ μυρίων τε ἄλλων θεοπρόπων προειρημένα, ὑφ᾿ ὧν ἐπιεικῶς πᾶσα γῆ κατῳκίσθη, ταῦτα μὲν (ἐν) οὐδενὶ λόγῳ τίθενται· τὰ δὲ ὑπο τῶν ἐν Ἰουδαίᾳ τῷ ἐκείνων τρόπῳ λεχθέντα ἢ μὴ λεχθέντα, καὶ ὥσπερ εἰώθασιν ἔτι νῦν οἱ περὶ Φοινίκην τε καὶ Παλαιστίνην, ταῦτά γε θαυμαστὰ καὶ ἀπαράλλακτα ἡγοῦνται. λέγωμεν οὖν περὶ τῶν κατειλεγμένων χρηστηρίων ὅτι δυνατὸν μὲν ἡμῖν συνάγουσιν ἀπὸ Ἀριστοτέλους καὶ τῶν τὰ τοῦ Περιπάτου φιλοσοφησάντων οὐκ ὀλίγα εἰπεῖν εἰς ἀνατροπὴν τοῦ περὶ τῆς Πυθίας καὶ τῶν λοιπῶν χρηστηρίων λόγου· δυνατὸν δὲ καὶ τὰ λελεγμένα τῷ Ἐπικούρῳ καὶ τοῖς ἀσπαζομένοις αὐτοῦ τὸν λόγον περὶ τῶν αὐτῶν παραθέμενον δεῖξαι ὅτι καὶ Ἑλλήνων τινὲς ἀνατρέπουσι τὰς νομιζομένας καὶ τεθαυμασμένας ἐν πάσῃ Ἑλλάδι θεοπροπίας. ἀλλὰ γὰρ δεδόσθω μὴ εἶναι πλάσματα μηδὲ προσποιήσεις ἀνθρώπων περὶ θεοφορίας τὰ περὶ τὴν Πυθίαν καὶ τὰ λοιπὰ χρηστήρια· ἴδωμεν οὖν εἰ μὴ καὶ οὕτως δύναται τοῖς φιλαλήθως ἐξετάζουσι τὰ πράγματα ἀποδείκνυσθαι ὅτι καὶ τῷ παραδεχομένῳ εἶναι ταῦτα τὰ μαντεῖα οὐκ ἀναγκαῖον προσέσθαι ὅτι θεοί τινες εἰσὶ παρ᾿ αὐτοῖς, ἀλλ᾿ ἐκ τοῦ ἐναντίου δαίμονές τινες φαῦλοι καὶ πνεύματα ἐχθρὰ τῷ γένει τῶν ἀνθρώπων καὶ κωλύοντα τὴν τῆς ψυχῆς ἄνοδον καὶ δι᾿ ἀρετῆς πορείαν καὶ τῆς ἀληθινῆς εὐσεβείας ἀποκατάστασιν πρὸς τὸν θεόν. ἱστόρηται τοίνυν περὶ τῆς Πυθίας, ὅπερ δοκεῖ τῶν ἄλλων μαντείων λαμπρότερον τυγχάνειν. ὅτι περικαθεζομένη τὸ τῆς Κασταλίας στόμιον ἡ τοῦ Ἀπόλλωνος προφῆτις δέχεται πνεῦμα διὰ τῶν γυναικείων κόλπων· οὗ πληρωθεῖσα ἀποφθέγγεται τὰ νομιζόμενα εἶναι σεμνὰ καὶ θεῖα μαντεύματα. ὅρα δὴ διὰ τούτων εἰ μὴ τὸ τοῦ πνεύματος ἐκείνου ἀκάθαρτον καὶ βέβηλον ἐμφαίνεται, μὴ διὰ μανῶν καὶ ἀφανῶν πόρων καὶ πολλῷ γυναικείων κόλπων καθαρωτέρων ἐπεισιὸν τῇ ψυχῇ τῆς θεσπιζούσης ἀλλὰ διὰ τούτων, ἃ οὐδὲ θέμις ἦν τῷ σώφρονι καὶ ἀνθρώπῳ βλέπειν, οὔπω λέγεσθαι ἢ καὶ ἅπτεσθαι· καὶ τοῦτο ποιεῖν οὐχ ἅπαξ που οὐδὲ δὶς (ἴσως γὰρ ἔδοξεν ἀνεκτότερον τὸ τοιοῦτο τυγχάνειν), ἀλλὰ τοσαυτάκις, ὁσάκις προφητεύειν ἐκείνη ἀπὸ τοῦ Ἀπόλλωνος πεπίστευται. ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ εἰς ἔκστασιν καὶ μανικὴν ἄγειν κατάστασιν τὴν δῆθεν προφητεύουσαν, ὡς μηδαμῶς αυτὴν ἑαυτῇ παρακολουθεῖν, οὐ θείου πνεύματος ἔργον ἐστίν· ἐχρῆν γὰρ τὸν κάτοχον τῷ θείῳ πνεύματι πολλῷ πρότερον παντὸς οὑτινοσοῦν τοῦ ἀπὸ τῶν χρησμῶν διδασκομένου τὸ συμβαλλόμενον εἰς τὸν μέσον καὶ κατὰ φύσιν βίον ἢ πρὸς τὸ λυσιτελὲς ἢ πρὸς τὸ συμφέρον ὠφεληθῆναι καὶ διορατικώτερον παρ᾿ ἐκεῖνο μάλιστα καιροῦ τυγχάνειν, ὅτε σύνεστιν αὐτῷ τὸ θεῖον.

excerpts.author: Origen
english: Now that we have turned to the subject of the prophets, what follows will prove useful not only for Jews, who hold that the prophets spoke by the divine Spirit, but also for well-disposed Greeks. We will tell these readers that they must accept that the Jews possessed prophets as well. Otherwise, the Jews could not have continued in the law given to them, maintained their faith in the Creator as they had received it, or resisted any impulse to abandon their heritage for the polytheism of the nations. We will demonstrate this necessity as follows. Scripture says, 'The nations will listen to soothsayers and diviners' (Deuteronomy 18:14). Yet to Israel God declared, 'The Lord your God has not given this to you' (Deuteronomy 18:14). He adds, 'The Lord your God will raise up a prophet for you from among your brothers' (Deuteronomy 18:15). Now the nations practice divination through soothsayers, the flight of birds, the reading of entrails, ventriloquists, those who promise sacrificial rites, and Chaldean astrologers who cast nativities—all of which were forbidden to the Jews. If the Jews had lacked any divinely given consolation for knowing the future, mere human curiosity about what is to come would have driven them to despise their own institutions as devoid of the divine. They would never have accepted another prophet after Moses, nor preserved the prophets' words. Instead, they would have defected to the divinations and oracles of the nations, or attempted to establish such practices among themselves. Therefore, it is not at all absurd that their prophets spoke beforehand to comfort those who long for such knowledge—so that even Samuel prophesied about lost donkeys, and the prophet recorded in the third book of Kings spoke concerning the illness of a royal child (2 Kings 1:2-3). How else would the Jewish elders who administer the law have rebuked anyone who sought divination from idols? Just as Elijah rebuked Ahaziah: 'Is it because there is no God in Israel that you are going to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron?' (2 Kings 1:3).
