greek: Ἐπεὶ δ᾿ ἅπαξ εἰς τὸν περὶ τῶν προφητῶν ἤλθομεν λόγον, Ἰουδαίοις μὲν, τοῖς πιστεύουσι θείῳ πνεύματι αὐτοὺς λελαληκέναι, οὐ μόνον οὐκ ἔσται ἀχρήσιμα τὰ ἐποισθησόμενα (ἀλλὰ) καὶ τοῖς εὐγνωμονοῦσι δὲ τῶν Ἑλλήνων. πρὸς οὓς ἐροῦμεν ὅτι ἀναγκαῖον παραδέξασθαι ὅτι καὶ Ἰουδαῖοι προφήτας εἶχον, εἴπερ ἔμελλον συνέχεσθαι ἐν τῇ δοθείσῃ αὐτοῖς νομοθεσίᾳ καὶ πιστεύειν τῷ δημιουργῷ, καθάπερ εἰλήφεισαν, καὶ ὅσον ἐπὶ τῷ νόμῳ μὴ ἔχειν ἀφορμὰς ἀποστῆναι εἰς τὴν τῶν ἐθνῶν πολυθεότητα. τὸ δ᾿ ἀναγκαῖον οὕτω παραστήσομεν. „τὰ ἔθνη,“ ὡς γέγραπται καὶ ἐν αὐτῷ τῷ τῶν Ἰουδαίων νόμῳ, „κληδόνων καὶ μαντειῶν ἀκούσονται“· τῷ δὲ λαῷ ἐκείνῳ εἴρηται· „σοὶ δὲ οὐχ οὕτως ἔδωκε κύριος ὁ θεός σου.“ καὶ ἐπιφέρεται τούτῳ τὸ „προφήτην ἐκ τῶν ἀδελφῶν σου ἀναστήσει σοι κύριος ὁ θεός σου.“ εἴπερ οὖν τῶν ἐθνῶν χρωμένων μαντείαις εἴτε διὰ „κληδόνων“ εἴτε δι᾿ οἰωνῶν εἴτε δι᾿ ὀρνίθων εἴτε δι᾿ ἐγγαστριμύθων εἴτε καὶ διὰ τῶν τὴν θυτικὴν ἐπαγγελλομένων εἴτε καὶ διὰ Χαλδαίων γενεθλιαλογούντων, ἅπερ πάντα Ἰουδαίοις ἀπείρητο. Ἰουδαῖοι εἰ μηδεμίαν εἶχον παραμυθίαν γνώσεως τῶν μελλόντων, ὑπ᾿ αὐτῆς ἂν τῆς ἀνθρωπίνης περὶ τὴν γνῶσιν λιχνείας τῶν ἐσομένων ἀγόμενοι κατεφρόνησαν μὲν ἂν τῶν ἰδίων ὡς οὐδὲν ἐχόντων θεῖον ἐν ἑαυτοῖς καὶ οὐκ ἂν μετὰ Μω(??)σέα προφήτην προσήκαντο οὐδ᾿ ἀνέγραψαν αὐτῶν τοὺς λόγους, αὐτόμολοι δὲ ἐπὶ τὸ τῶν ἐθνῶν μαντεῖα καὶ χρηστήρια μετέστησαν ἢ ἐπεχείρησαν ἂν ἱδρῦσαί τι τοιοῦτον καὶ παρ᾿ ἑαυτοῖς. ὥστ᾿ οὐδὲν ἄτοπόν ἐστι καὶ περὶ τῶν τυχόντων τοὺς παρ᾿ αὐτοῖς προφήτας εἰς παραμυθίαν τῶν τὰ τοιαῦτα ποθούντων προειρηκέναι, ὥστε καὶ „περὶ ὄνων ἀπολωλυιῶν“ προφητεύειν τὸν Σαμουὴλ καὶ περὶ νόσου παιδὸς βασιλικοῦ τὸν ἐν τῇ τρίτῃ τῶν Βασιλειῶν ἀναγεγραμμένον. πῶς δ᾿ ἂν τῷ βουλομένῳ ἀπὸ τῶν εἰδώλων μαντείαν λαβεῖν ἐπέπλησσον οἱ τὰ τοῦ νόμου Ἰουδαίων πρεσβεύοντες; ὥσπερ εὑρίσκεται Ἠλίας τῷ Ὀχοζίᾳ ἐπιπλήσσων καὶ λέγων· „εἰ παρὰ τὸ μὴ εἶναι θεὸν ἐν Ἰσραὴλ ὑμεῖς πορεύεσθε ἐκζητῆσαι ἐν τῇ Βαὰλ μυῖαν θεὸν Ἀκκαρῶν.“

excerpts.author: Origen
english: The question of which ancient leaders and holy men we ought to follow, so that we are not left perplexed, demands careful thought. Celsus directs us toward inspired poets, wise men, and philosophers, yet he refuses to name them; he merely promises to reveal guides while vaguely designating those very poets, sages, and philosophers. Had he supplied their names, it would have been reasonable for us to engage with his proposal, since he is handing us blind guides concerning the truth, so that we stumble, or—even if they are not entirely blind—guides who have gone astray on many doctrines of the truth. Whether he has in mind Orpheus as an inspired poet, or Parmenides, or Empedocles, or even Homer or Hesiod himself, let him demonstrate how those who follow such guides will fare better and gain greater benefit for living than those who have abandoned every idol and temple, along with all Jewish superstition, and who look only to the Father of the Word, God, through the Word of God. And who, exactly, are the wise men and philosophers from whom Celsus wants us to hear many divine teachings—after we have left behind Moses, the servant of God, and the prophets of the Creator of all, who spoke countless inspired truths, who shed light on the human race and proclaimed the way of godliness, who withheld none of their own mysteries but instead made theology available to the more intelligent, theology that can lift the soul above earthly concerns? Yet they also condescended to the humbler capacities of ordinary men, simple women, slaves, and, in short, everyone who had been helped by no one—or by Jesus alone—so that, as far as possible, they might live better with doctrines about God that they could grasp.

greek: Τίνι δὲ καὶ ἕπεσθαι ἡμᾶς ὁ Κέλσος βούλεται ὡς οὐκ ἀπορήσοντας παλαιῶν ἡγεμόνων καὶ ἱερῶν ἀνδρῶν κατανοητέον. ἀναπέμπει ἡμᾶς ἐπὶ ἐνθέους, ὡς λέγει, ποιητὰς καὶ σοφοὺς (καὶ) φιλοσόφους, μὴ τιθεὶς αὐτοῖς ὀνόματα, καὶ τοὺς ὁδηγοὺς δείξειν ἐπαγγελλόμενος ἀορίστως ἀποφαίνεται τοὺς ἐνθέους ποιητὰς καὶ σοφοὺς καὶ φιλοσόφους. εἰ δ᾿ ἐτίθει τὰ ὀνόματα ἑκάστου τούτων, κἂν ἀγωνίζεσθαι εὔλογον ἡμῖν ἐφαίνετο, ὅτι τυφλώττοντας περὶ τὴν ἀλήθειαν ὁδηγοὺς ἡμῖν δίδωσιν, ἵνα σφάλωμεν, ἢ εἰ καὶ μὴ πάνυ τυφλώττοντας, περὶ πολλά γε τῆς ἀληθείας δόγματα ἐσφαλμένους. εἴτ᾿ οὖν Ὀρφέα βούλεται ἔνθεον εἶναι ποιητὴν εἴτε Παρμενίδην εἴτ᾿ Ἐμπεδοκλέα εἴτε καὶ αὐτὸν Ὀμηρον ἢ καὶ Ἡσίοδον, δεικνύτω ὁ βουλόμενος, πῶς βέλτιον ὁδεύσουσιν οἱ τοιούτοις ὁδηγοῖς χρώμενοι καὶ ὠφέληνται περὶ τῶν κατὰ τὸν βίον παρὰ τοὺς καταλιπόντας διὰ τὴν Ἰησοῦ τοῦ Χριστοῦ διδασκαλίαν πάντα ἀγάλματα καὶ ἱδρύματα ἀλλὰ καὶ πᾶσαν Ἰουδαϊκὴν δεισιδαιμονίαν καὶ πρὸς μόνον ἀναβλέποντας διὰ τοῦ λόγου τοῦ θεοῦ τὸν πατέρα τοῦ λόγου θεόν. τίνες δὲ καὶ οἱ σοφοὶ ἢ οἱ φιλόσοφοι, παρ᾿ ὧν βούλεται πολλὰ καὶ θεῖα ἀκοῦσαι ἡμᾶς ὁ Κέλσος, καταλιπόντας θεράποντα θεοῦ Μωϋσέα καὶ προφήτας τοῦ τῶν ὅλων δημιουργοῦ, ἀληθῶς ἐνθέως μυρία ὅσα εἰρηκότας, καὶ αὐτὸν ἐπιλάμψαντα τῷ γένει τῶν ἀνθρώπων καὶ καταγγείλαντα ὁδὸν θεοσεβείας καὶ μηδένα τὸ ὅσον ἐφ᾿ ἑαυτῷ ἄγευστον καταλιπόντα τῶν ἰδίων μυστηρίων, ἀλλὰ δι᾿ ὑπερβάλλουσαν φιλανθρωπίαν ἔχοντα μὲν διδόναι τοῖς συνετωτέροις θεολογίαν, ἐπᾶραι τὴν ψυχὴν ἀπὸ τῶν τῇδε πραγμάτων δυναμένην. οὐδὲν (δ᾿) ἧττον συγκαταβαίνοντα καὶ ταῖς ὑποδεεστέραις ἕξεσιν ἰδιωτῶν ἀνδρῶν καὶ ἁπλουστέρων γυναικῶν οἰκετῶν τε καὶ ἁπαξαπλῶς τῶν ὑπὸ μηδενὸς ἢ Ἰησοῦ μόνου βεβοηθημένων πρὸς τὸ, ὡς ἐνεχώρει, βέλτιον αὐτοὺς βιοῦν μετὰ δογμάτων ὧν ἐδύναντο περὶ θεοῦ χωρεῖν;

excerpts.author: Origen
english: Among the Jewish prophets, some were wise before they ever received prophecy or divine inspiration, while others were enlightened through the very act of prophesying and became that kind of person. They were chosen by providence to trust the divine Spirit and the words that come from it, because their manner of life is disagreeable, extremely demanding, and free—utterly undaunted by death and danger in every respect. For the Word chooses just such people to serve as prophets of the God over all.

These prophets made a mockery of the famed endurance of Antisthenes, Crates, and Diogenes. Because they spoke the truth and freely rebuked sinners, they were stoned, sawn in two, tempted, and killed by the sword. They wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, afflicted, and mistreated—roaming deserts and mountains, hiding in caves and holes in the ground. The world was not worthy of them (Hebrews 11:37-38). They kept their eyes fixed on God and on the invisible realities of God—things not perceived by the senses—and for that reason those realities are eternal.

The life of each prophet is recorded, but for our present purpose it is enough to set forth the life of Moses (since his prophecies are also preserved, written in the Law), the life of Jeremiah (preserved in the prophecy that bears his name), and the life of Isaiah, who surpassed all asceticism by going naked and barefoot for three years. Consider also the vigorous life of the youths—Daniel and his companions—by reading of their abstinence from wine and the fact that their food was vegetables, since they avoided meat. If you are able, look further back at those who came before: Noah prophesying, Isaac praying prophetically over his son, and Jacob addressing each of his twelve sons: 'Come, that I may tell you what will happen in the last days.' These, and many thousands of others, prophesied to God and also foretold the things concerning Jesus the Christ.

Therefore we give no credence whatever to the words spoken by the Pythia, the Dodonian oracles, the Clarian oracle, the shrine at Branchidae, the oracle of Ammon, or by the myriads of other so-called prophets. But we do set forth the words spoken by those who prophesied in Judaea, because we see that their strenuous, free, and dignified life—empowered by the Spirit of God—was worthy of them. They prophesied in a new way that bears no resemblance whatever to the divinations that come from demons.

greek: Τῶν δ᾿ ἐν Ἰουδαίοις προφητῶν οἱ μὲν πρὸ τῆς προφητείας καὶ τῆς θείας κατακωχῆς ἦσαν σοφοὶ, οἱ δ᾿ ἀπ᾿ αὐτῆς τῆς προφητείας φωτισθέντες τὸν νοῦν τοιοῦτοι γεγόνασιν, αἱρεθέντες ὑπὸ τῆς προνοίας εἰς τὸ πιστευθῆναι τὸ θεῖον πνεῦμα καὶ τοὺς ἀπὸ τούτου λόγους διὰ τὸ τοῦ βίου δυσμίμητον καὶ σφόδρα εὔτονον καὶ ἐλευθέριον καὶ πάντῃ πρὸς θάνατον καὶ κινδύνους ἀκατάπληκτον. τοιούτους γὰρ καὶ ὁ λόγος αἱρεῖ δεῖν εἶναι τοὺς τοῦ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεοῦ προφήτας. οἵτινες παίγνιον ἀπέφηναν τὴν Ἀντισθένους καὶ Κράτητος καὶ Διογένους εὐτονίαν. δι᾿ ἀλήθειαν γοῦν καὶ τὸ ἐλευθερίως ἐλέγχειν τοὺς ἁμαρτάνοντας „ἐλιθάσθησαν, ἐπρίσθησαν, ἐπειράσθησαν, ἐν φόνῳ μαχαίρας ἀπέθανον· περιῆλθον γὰρ ἐν μηλωταῖς, ἐν αἰγείοις δέρμασιν, ὑστερούμενοι, κακουχούμενοι, ἐν ἐρημίαις πλανώμενοι καὶ ὄρεσι καὶ σπηλαίοις καὶ ταῖς ὀπαῖς τῆς γῆς, ὧν οὐκ ην ἄξιος ὁ ἐπὶ γῆς κόσμος“· ἀεὶ ἐνορῶντες τῷ θεῷ καὶ τοῖς ἀοράτοις τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ μὴ βλεπομένοις αἰσθητῶς καὶ διὰ τοῦτο οὖσιν αἰωνίοις. ὁ δὲ βίος ἑκάστου τῶν προφητῶν ἀναγέγραπται· ἀρκεῖ δὲ ἐπὶ τοῦ παρόντος παραθέσθαι τὸν Μωϋσέως βίον (καὶ γὰρ αὐτοῦ φέρονται προφητεῖαι, ἀναγεγραμμέναι ἐν τῷ νόμῳ) καὶ τὸν Ἱερεμἰου, φερόμενον ἐν τῇ ὁμωνύμῳ αὐτοῦ προφητείᾳ, καὶ τὸν Ἡσαΐου, ὃς ἐπορεύθη ὑπερτείνων πᾶσαν ἄσκησιν „γυμνὸς καὶ ἀνυπόδετος“ ἔτεσι τρισίν. ἴδε δὲ καὶ παιδαρίων, τοῦ Δανιὴλ καὶ τῶν σὺν αὐτῷ, τὸν ἐῤῥωμένον βίον, ἀναγνοὺς τὴν ὑδροποσίαν αὐτῶν καὶ ὅτι ἡ τροφὴ ἦν αὐτοῖς ὄσπριον, ἐμψύχων ἀπεχομένοις. εἰ δὲ δύνασαι, καὶ τὰ πρὸ τούτων θέασαι, Νῶε προφητεύσαντος καὶ Ἰσαὰκ τῷ υἱῷ ἐπευξαμένου προφητικῶς καὶ τοῦ Ἰακὼβ λέγοντος ἑκάστῳ τῶν δώδεκα· „δεῦτε, ἵνα ἀναγγείλω ὑμῖν, τί ἔσται ἐπ᾿ ἐσχάτων τῶν ἡμερῶν.“ οὗτοι δὴ καὶ ἄλλοι μυρίοι προφητεύσαντες τῷ θεῷ καὶ τὰ περὶ Ἰησοῦ τοῦ Χριστοῦ προεῖπον. διόπερ ἐν οὐδενὶ μὲν τιθέμεθα λόγῳ τὰ ὑπὸ τῆς Πυθίας ἢ Δωδωνίδων ἢ Κλαρίου ἢ ἐν Βραγχίδαις ἢ ἐν Ἄμμωνος ἢ ὑπὸ μυρίων ἄλλων λεγομένων θεοπρόπων προειρημένα· τὰ δ᾿ ὑπὸ τῶν ἐν Ἰουδαίᾳ προφητευσάντων τεθήπαμεν, ὁρῶντες ὅτι ἄξιος ἦν αὐτῶν ὁ ἐῤῥωμένος καὶ εὔτονος καὶ σεμνὸς βίος πνεύματος θεοῦ, τρόπῳ προφητεύοντος καινῷ καὶ οὐδὲν ἔχοντι παραπλήσιον ταῖς ἀπὸ δαιμόνων μαντείαις.

english: Preface In the name of the Father , and the Son , and the Holy Spirit , one God. This is a transcript of the excellent law. But before beginning to give the transcript of the book of the law, it will be worth while to instruct you, O brother, as to its excellence, and the dignity of its disposition. Its first excellence is, that God delivered it by the hand of our most blessed ruler, the chief of the prophets , and first of the apostles , or those who were sent to the children of Israel , viz. Moses the son of Amram, the son of Kohath, of the sons of Levi. Now he was adorned with all manner of wisdom, and endowed with the best genius. Illustrious in dignity, remarkable for the integrity of his disposition, distinguished for power of reason, he talked with God . And He chose him as an instrument of value. By His leader and prophet , God Most High sent it clown to us, and committed it to us (blessed be His name) in the Syriac tongue of the Targum, which the Seventy translated into the Hebrew tongue, to wit, into the tongue of the nation, and the idiom of the common people. Moses . therefore, received it from the eternal Lord, and was the first to whom it was entrusted, and who obeyed its rules and ordinances. Then he taught it to the children of Israel , who also embraced it. And he explained to them its profound mysteries and dark places. And he expounded to them those things which were less easy, as God permitted him, and concealed from them those secrets of the law, as God…

6. Hippolytus, the Syrian expositor of the Targum, has said: We find in an ancient Hebrew copy that God commanded Noah to range the wild beasts in order in the lower floor or storey, and to separate the males from the females by putting wooden stakes between them. And thus, too, he did with all the cattle, and also with the birds in the middle storey. And God ordered the males thus to be separated from the females for the sake of decency and purity, lest they should perchance get intermingled with each other. Moreover, God said to Moses : Provide victuals for yourself and your children. And let them be of wheat, ground, pounded, kneaded with water, and dried. And Noah there and then bade his wife, and his sons' wives, diligently attend to kneading dough and laying it in the oven. They kneaded dough accordingly, and prepared just about as much as might be sufficient for them, so that nothing should remain over but the very least. And God charged Noah , saying to him: Whosoever shall first announce to you the approach of the deluge, him you shall destroy that very moment. In the meantime, moreover, the wife of Cham was standing by, about to put a large piece of bread into the oven. And suddenly, according to the word of the Lord, water rushed forth from the oven, and the flow of water penetrated and destroyed the bread. Therefore the wife of Cham exclaimed, addressing herself to Noah : Oh, sir, the word of God has come good: that which God foretold has come to pass; execute,…

english: First fragment (Preface) As I wish to give an accurate account of the times of the captivity of the children of Israel in Babylon , and to discuss the prophecies contained in the visions of the blessed Daniel, (as well as) his manner of life from his boyhood in Babylon , I too shall proceed to bear my testimony to that holy and righteous man, a prophet and witness of Christ , who not only declared the visions of Nebuchadnezzar the king in those times, but also trained youths of like mind with himself, and raised up faithful witnesses in the world. He is horn, then, in the time of the prophetic ministry of the blessed Jeremiah, and in the reign of Jehoiakim or Eliakim. Along with the other captives, he is carried off a prisoner to Babylon . Now there are born to the blessed Josiah these five sons — Jehoahaz, Eliakim, Johanan, Zedekiah, or Jeconiah, and Sadum. And on his father's death, Jehoahaz is anointed as king by the people at the age of twenty-three years. Against him comes up Pharaoh -Necho, in the third month of his reign; and he takes him (Jehoahaz) prisoner, and carries him into Egypt , and imposes tribute on the land to the extent of one hundred talents of silver and ten talents of gold. And in his stead he sets up his brother Eliakim as king over the land, whose name also he changed to Jehoiakim, and who was then eleven years old. Against him came up Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon , and carries him off prisoner to Babylon , taking with him also some of the vessels…

1. In speaking of a lioness from the sea, he meant the rising of the kingdom of Babylon , and that this was the golden head of the image. And in speaking of its eagle wings, be meant that king Nebuchadnezzar was exalted and that his glory was lifted up against God. Then he says its wings were plucked off, i.e., that his glory was destroyed; for he was driven out of his kingdom. And the words, A man's heart was given it, and it was made stand upon the feet of a man , mean that he came to himself again, and recognised that he was but a man , and gave the glory to God . Then after the lioness he sees a second beast, like a bear, which signified the Persians. For after the Babylonians the Persians obtained the power. And in saying that it had three ribs in its mouth, he pointed to the three nations, Persians , Medes, and Babylonians , which were expressed in the image by the silver after the gold. Then comes the third beast, a leopard, which means the Greeks; for after the Persians , Alexander of Macedon had the power, when Darius was overthrown, which was also indicated by the brass in the image. And in saying that the beast had four wings of a fowl, and four heads, he showed most clearly how the kingdom of Alexander was parted into four divisions. For in speaking of four heads, he meant the four kings that arose out of it. For Alexander, when dying, divided his kingdom into four parts. Then he says, The fourth beast (was) dreadful and terrible: it had iron teeth, and claws of…

2. After this, then, what remains, beloved, but the toes of the feet of the image, in which part shall be of iron and part of clay mixed together? By the toes of the feet he meant, mystically , the ten kings that rise out of that kingdom. As Daniel says, I considered the beast; and, lo, (there were) ten horns behind, among which shall come up another little horn springing from them; by which none other is meant than the antichrist that is to rise; and he shall set up the kingdom of Judah. And in saying that three horns were plucked up by the roots by this one, he indicates the three kings of Egypt , Libya, and Ethiopia , whom this one will slay in the array of war . And when he has conquered all, he will prove himself a terrible and savage tyrant, and will cause tribulation and persecution to the saints , exalting himself against them. And after him, it remains that the stone shall come from heaven which smote the image and shivered it, and subverted all the kingdoms, and gave the kingdom to the saints of the Most High. This became a great mountain, and filled the whole earth.

3. As these things, then, are destined to come to pass, and as the toes of the image turn out to be democracies, and the ten horns of the beast are distributed among ten kings, let us look at what is before us more carefully, and scan it, as it were, with open eye. The golden head of the image is identical with the lioness, by which the Babylonians were represented. The golden shoulders and the arms of silver are the same with the bear, by which the Persians and Medes are meant. The belly and thighs of brass are the leopard, by which the Greeks who ruled from Alexander onwards are intended. The legs of iron are the dreadful and terrible beast, by which the Romans who hold the empire now are meant. The toes of clay and iron are the ten horns which are to be. The one other little horn springing up in their midst is the antichrist. The stone that smites the image and breaks it in pieces, and that filled the whole earth, is Christ, who comes from heaven and brings judgment on the world.

excerpts.author: Hippolytus
english: The first people, the ones from circumcision, were my strength and the beginning of my endeavors, just as God promised to Abraham and to his seed (Genesis). Yet they have become hard to endure, since the people hardened themselves against obedience to God. They are stubborn and self-willed, not only resisting God's obedience but also becoming self-willed enough to lay hands on the Lord. You have insulted, because the people insulted the Father through our Lord Jesus Christ. "Do not become completely hardened," the Spirit says encouragingly, so that by becoming completely hardened you may not be poured out and lost, but instead receive hope of salvation; for whoever becomes hardened and is poured out perishes. Scripture says, "You went up onto your father's bed" (Genesis), and first it recounts what happened: in the last days the people will plot against the Father's bed -- that is, the bride, the Church -- intending to corrupt her, and they continue doing so even today, plotting against her through blasphemies.

excerpts.author: Hippolytus
english: The Book of Psalms contains new teaching that comes after Joshua's legislation. In fact, it counts as the second instructional book after Joshua's writing. After Moses and Joshua died, David arose after the period of the judges. He was deemed worthy to be called the father of the Savior, and he first handed down to the Hebrews a new way of singing psalms. Through this way he abolishes the sacrificial regulations that Moses legislated, and he introduces a new way of worshiping God through hymns and shouts. He also teaches many other things that repeat the law of Joshua, drawing from the material of his own work.

excerpts.author: Cyprian
english: When the Lord warns us, saying, "You are the salt of the earth" (Matt 5:13), and commands us to be simple in innocence yet prudent in that very simplicity, what else should we do, beloved brothers, but take thought for ourselves and watch with anxious hearts so that we may both understand and guard against the crafty enemy’s hidden plots? Lest we who have put on Christ, the wisdom of God the Father, appear less than wise in protecting our salvation. For persecution alone is not the only danger, nor only those open attacks that rage against God’s servants to overthrow and cast them down. Caution is easier when fear is manifest, and the mind readies itself for battle when the adversary shows himself. The enemy is far more to be feared and avoided when he creeps in secretly, deceiving by a false appearance of peace and slipping in by hidden approaches — hence he has received the name of serpent. This is his constant cunning, this the blind and concealed deceit with which he entraps mankind. From the world’s beginning he deceived, flattering with lying words and leading artless souls astray by their unguarded credulity. He even attempted to tempt the Lord Himself, approaching stealthily as if to creep in again and deceive; yet he was recognized and repulsed, and so cast down because he was detected. From this an example has been given us: we must flee the way of the old man and walk in the footsteps of the living Christ, lest, being off guard, we fall once more into the snare of death, but, foreseeing the danger, we may lay hold of immortality. And how can we lay hold of immortality unless we keep the commandments of Christ, by which death is assaulted and conquered, Christ Himself warning and saying, "If you wish to enter life, keep the commandments"? And again, "If you do what I command you, I no longer call you servants, but friends" (John 15:14). These, finally, He calls strong and stable, founded upon a rock with a massive structure, solidified by an immovable and unshaken firmness against every tempest and whirlwind of this world. "Everyone who hears these words of mine and does them," He says, "I will compare to a wise man who built his house upon the rock. The rain fell, the floods came, the winds blew and beat against that house, and it did not fall, because it had been founded on the rock" (Matt 7:24–25). We must therefore cling to His words, learning and doing whatever He taught and commanded. But how can anyone believe he is in Christ if he does not do what Christ commanded? Or whence will he reach the reward of faith who refuses to keep the faith of the commandment? He must waver and wander, seized by a spirit of error and blown about like dust driven by the wind; nor will he make progress toward salvation who does not hold fast the truth of the way that saves. Yet, beloved brothers, we must beware not only of open and manifest dangers, but also of those that deceive by the subtle craft of cunning deceit. What could be more cunning or subtle than this: that the enemy, detected and cast down by the advent of Christ, after light has come to the Gentiles and the saving light has shone for mankind’s salvation — that the deaf might receive hearing of spiritual grace, the blind open their eyes to God, the weak recover by eternal health, the lame run to the Church, the mute pray with clear voices and prayers — seeing idols abandoned and his own seats and temples deserted by the multitude of believers, he has devised a new fraud to deceive the unwary under the very title of the Christian name? He has invented heresies and schisms by which to subvert the faith, corrupt the truth, and divide unity. Those whom he cannot hold in the blindness of the old way, he entraps and deceives by the error of a new way. He snatches men from the very Church; and while they think they have drawn near to the light and escaped the world’s darkness, he pours fresh darkness upon them, unknown to them, so that, not standing with the Gospel of Christ and its observance and law, they call themselves Christians, and walking in darkness believe they possess the light — the adversary flattering and deceiving, who, according to the Apostle’s word, transforms himself into an angel of light, and his ministers into ministers of righteousness, calling night day, destruction salvation, despair by the pretext of hope, perfidy by the pretext of faith, antichrist by the name of Christ; so that, while they speak what is plausible, they may frustrate the truth by subtlety. This happens, beloved brothers, when we do not return to the origin of truth, nor seek the head, nor preserve the doctrine of the heavenly Master.

latin: CUM moneat Dominus et dicat: Vos estis sal terrae, cumque esse nos jubeat ad innocentiam simplices, et tamen cum simplicitate prudentes, quid aliud, fratres dilectissimi, quam providere nos convenit, et sollicito corde vigilantes, subdoli hostis insidias intelligere pariter et cavere ne qui Christum sapientiam Dei Patris induimus, minus sapere in tuenda salute videamur? Neque enim persecutio sola metuenda est et ea quae subruendis ac dejiciendis Dei servis aperta impugnatione grassantur. Facilior cautio est ubi manifesta formido est, et ad certamen animus ante praestruitur quando se adversarius confitetur. Plus metuendus est et cavendus inimicus cum latenter obrepit, cum, per pacis imaginem fallens, occultis accessibus serpit; unde et nomen serpentis accepit. Ea est ejus semper astutia, ea est circumveniendi hominis caeca et latebrosa fallacia. Sic ab initio statim mundi fefellit, et, verbis mendacibus blandiens, rudes animas incauta credulitate decepit. Dominum ipsum tentare conatus, quasi obreperet rursus et falleret, latenter accessit. Intellectus tamen est et retusus; et ideo prostratus, quia agnitus atque detectus. Unde nobis exemplum datum est veteris hominis viam fugere, vestigiis Christi viventis insistere; ne denuo incauti in mortis laqueum revolvamur, sed, ad periculum providi, accepta immortalitate potiamur. Immortalitate autem potiri quomodo possumus, nisi ea quibus mors expugnatur et vincitur, Christi mandata servemus, ipso monente et dicente: Si vis ad vitam venire, serva mandata. Et iterum: Si feceritis quae mando vobis, jam non dico vos servos, sed amicos. Hos denique fortes dicit et stabiles, hos super petram robusta mole fundatos, hos contra omnes tempestates et turbines saeculi immobili et inconcussa firmitate solidatos. Qui audit, inquit, verba mea et facit ea, similabo eum viro sapienti qui aedificavit domum suam supra petram. Descendit pluvia, venerunt flumina, flaverunt venti et impegerunt in domum illam, et non cecidit; fundata enim fuit super petram. Verbis igitur ejus insistere, quaecumque et docuit et fecit discere et facere debemus. Caeterum credere se in Christum, quomodo dicit qui non facit quod Christus facere praecepit? Aut unde perveniet ad praemium fidei, qui fidem non vult servare mandati? Nutet necesse est et vagetur, et, spiritu erroris abreptus, velut pulvis quem ventus excutit ventiletur; nec ambulando proficiet ad salutem, qui salutaris viae non tenet veritatem. Cavenda sunt autem, fratres dilectissimi, non solum quae sunt aperta atque manifesta, sed et astutae fraudis subtilitate fallentia. Quid vero astutius, quidve subtilius, quam ut Christi adventu detectus ac prostratus inimicus, postquam lux Gentibus venit et sospitandis hominibus salutare lumen effulsit, ut surdi auditum gratiae spiritalis admitterent, aperirent ad Deum oculos suos caeci, infirmi aeterna sanitate revalescerent, claudi ad Ecclesiam currerent, muti claris vocibus et precibus orarent, videns ille idola derelicta et per nimium credentium populum sedes suas ac templa deserta, excogitaverit novam fraudem, ut sub ipso christiani nominis titulo fallat incautos? Haereses invenit et schismata, quibus subverteret fidem, veritatem corrumperet, scinderet unitatem. Quos detinere non potest in viae veteris caecitate, circumscribit et decipit novi itineris errore. Rapit de ipsa Ecclesia homines; et, dum sibi appropinquasse jam lumini atque evasisse saeculi noctem videntur, alias nescientibus tenebras rursus infundit, ut cum Evangelio Christi et cum observatione ejus et lege non stantes, Christianos se vocent, et ambulantes in tenebris habere se lumen existiment, blandiente adversario atque fallente, qui, secundum Apostoli vocem, transfigurat se velut angelum lucis, et ministros suos subornat velut ministros justitiae, asserentes noctem pro die, interitum pro salute, desperationem sub obtentu spei, perfidiam sub praetextu fidei, antichristum sub vocabulo Christi; ut, dum verisimilia mentiuntur, veritatem subtilitate frustrentur. Hoc eo fit, fratres dilectissimi, dum ad veritatis originem non reditur, nec caput quaeritur, nec magistri coelestis doctrina servatur.

excerpts.author: Cyprian
english: Behold, most beloved brothers, peace has been restored to the Church, and what once seemed impossible to the unbelieving and the faithless — our security — has been repaired by divine aid and vengeance; minds are turning back to joy, the storm of oppression and the cloud have been dispersed, and tranquility and serenity now shine forth. Praises must be given to God, and His benefits and gifts celebrated with thanksgiving, for our voice never ceased giving thanks even in the midst of persecution. Indeed, the enemy cannot be so powerful that we, who love the Lord with our whole heart, soul, and strength, would fail to proclaim His blessings and praises always and everywhere with glory.

The day longed for by all has arrived, and after the horrible, dark night the world has shone radiant with the Lord's light. We gaze upon the confessors with joyful faces, clinging to them with holy kisses and embracing those we have yearned for with an insatiable desire. The white cohort of Christ's soldiers stands before us, having broken the fierce fury of persecution through a steadfast confrontation, prepared for the patience of prison and armed for the tolerance of death. You have resisted the world mightily, offered a glorious spectacle to God, and become an example for the brothers who will follow.

The religious voice has spoken of Christ, confessing that it once believed in Him. Illustrious hands, accustomed only to divine works, have refused sacrilegious sacrifices. Mouths sanctified by the heavenly food of the Lord's body and blood have rejected profane contagions and the remnants of idols. Your head, freed from the impious and wicked veil that covered the heads of those who sacrificed, remains free; your forehead, marked with the sign of God, could not bear the devil's crown but has reserved itself for the Lord's crown. How joyfully the mother Church receives you, returning from battle, into her bosom! How blessed and joyful she opens her gates so that you may enter with assembled troops, bearing trophies from the defeated enemy! With the triumphant men come women who, fighting the world, have also conquered their own sex; virgins arrive with a double glory of their warfare, and children surpass their years through virtue. The multitude of the rest who stand follows your glory, tracing your footsteps with insignia of praise closely joined. The same sincerity of heart and the same tenacity of faith dwell in them. Rooted in the unshaken roots of heavenly precepts and strengthened by evangelical traditions, they were not terrified by prescribed exiles, destined torments, loss of family, or bodily punishments. Days were appointed to test their faith, yet whoever remembers that he has renounced the world knows no day of the world, and he who hopes for eternity from God no longer calculates earthly times.

No one, most beloved brothers, should mutilate this glory, nor should anyone weaken the incorrupt firmness of those who stand with malignant detraction. When the day appointed for those who deny has passed, whoever has not professed within that day has confessed to being a Christian. The first title of victory is to confess the Lord, seized by the hands of the Gentiles; the second step toward glory is to be reserved for the Lord by a cautious withdrawal. The former is a public confession, the latter a private one. The public confession conquers the judge of the world, while the private confession, content with God as its judge, preserves a pure conscience through integrity of heart. In the public confession fortitude is more prompt; in the private confession solicitude is more secure. The public confessor, with his hour approaching, has already been found mature; the private confessor, perhaps delayed, who abandoned his patrimony and withdrew because he would not deny, would certainly have confessed if he had also been detained.

latin: PAX ecce, dilectissimi fratres, Ecclesiae reddita est et, quod difficile nuper incredulis ac perfidis impossibile videbatur, ope atque ultione divina securitas nostra reparata est. In laetitiam mentes redeunt, et, tempestate pressurae ac nube discussa, tranquillitas ac serenitas refulserunt. Dandae laudes Deo, et beneficia ejus ac munera cum gratiarum actione celebranda, quamvis agere gratias nostra vox nec in persecutione cessaverit. Neque enim tantum inimico licere potest ut non, qui Dominum toto corde et anima et virtute diligimus, benedictiones ejus et laudes semper et ubique cum gloria praedicemus. Exoptatus votis omnium dies venit, et, post longae noctis horribilem tetramque caliginem, Domini luce radiatus mundus eluxit. Confessores, praeconio boni nominis claros et virtutis ac fidei laudibus gloriosos, laetis conspectibus intuemur, sanctis osculis adhaerentes, desideratos diu inexplebili cupiditate complectimur. Adest militum Christi cohors candida, qui persecutionis urgentus ferociam turbulentam stabili congressione fregerunt, parati ad patientiam carceris, armati ad tolerantiam mortis. Repugnastis fortiter saeculo, spectaculum gloriosum praebuistis Deo, secuturis fratribus fuistis exemplo. Religiosa vox Christum locuta est, in quem se semel credidisse confessa est. Illustres manus, quae non nisi divinis operibus assueverant, sacrificiis sacrilegis restiterunt. Sanctificata ora coelestibus cibis, post corpus et sanguinem Domini, profana contagia et idolorum reliquias respuerunt. Ab impio sceleratoque velamine, quo illic velabantur sacrificantium capita captiva, caput vestrum liberum mansit. Frons cum signo Dei pura, diaboli coronam ferre non potuit, coronae se Domini reservavit. Quam vos laete sinu suo excipit mater Ecclesia de praelio revertentes! quam beata, quam gaudens portas suas aperit, ut adunatis agminibus intretis, de hoste prostrato trophaea referentes! Cum triumphantibus viris et feminae veniunt, quae cum saeculo dimicantes, sexum quoque vicerunt. Veniunt et geminata militiae suae gloria virgines, et pueri annos suos virtutibus transeuntes. Necnon et caetera stantium multitudo vestram gloriam sequitur, proximis et pene conjunctis laudis insignibus vestigia vestra comitatur. Eadem et in illis sinceritas cordis, eadem fidei tenacis integritas. Inconcussis praeceptorum coelestium radicibus nixos et evangelicis traditionibus roboratos, non praescripta exilia, non destinata tormenta, non rei familiaris damna, non corporis supplicia terruerunt. Explorandae fidei praefiniebantur dies. Sed qui saeculo renuntiasse se meminit, nullum saeculi diem novit; nec tempora terrena jam computat qui aeternitatem de Deo sperat. Nemo, fratres dilectissimi, nemo hanc gloriam mutilet, nemo incorruptam stantium firmitatem maligna obtrectatione debilitet. Cum dies negantibus praestitutus excessit, quisquis professus intra diem non est, Christianum se esse confessus est. Primus est victoriae titulus, gentilium manibus apprehensum Dominum confiteri: secundus ad gloriam gradus est cauta secessione subtractum Domino reservari. Illa publica, haec privata confessio est. Ille judicem saeculi vincit, hic contentus Deo suo judice conscientiam puram cordis integritate custodit. Illic, fortitudo promptior, hic sollicitudo securior. Ille appropinquante hora sua, jam maturus inventus est; hic fortasse dilatus est qui, patrimonio derelicto, idcirco secessit quia non erat negaturus: confiteretur utique si fuisset et ipse detentus.

excerpts.author: Cyprian
english: Dear brothers, the Gospel's teachings are divine lessons: they lay the foundations of our hope, shore up our faith, feed our hearts, steer our journey, and defend our salvation. While they instruct willing minds here on earth, they lead us to the heavenly kingdoms. God chose to speak and be heard through his servants the prophets many times, yet the words of the Son are far greater. The Word of God, who spoke in the prophets, now testifies with his own voice. He no longer commands that a way be prepared for the One who is coming; he comes himself, opens the way, and shows it to us. Once we wandered in the darkness of death, foolish and blind; now, enlightened by the light of grace, we walk the path of life with the Lord as our guide and ruler.

Among his other saving instructions and divine precepts given for his people's salvation, he himself gave us the very form of prayer, teaching us what to ask for. The One who gave us life taught us to pray, out of the same kindness by which he deigned to grant every other gift. His purpose is that when we speak to the Father with the prayer and petition the Son taught, we may be heard more readily. He had already foretold the hour when true worshipers would worship the Father in spirit and truth (John 4:23), and he fulfilled that promise. Because we have received the Spirit and truth from his sanctification, we can now worship him truly and spiritually, following his own tradition. What prayer could be more spiritual than the one Christ gave us, since he also sent us the Holy Spirit? What prayer could be truer before the Father than the one spoken by the Son, who is Truth itself? To pray differently than he taught is not merely ignorance; it is a fault. He himself said, "You reject the commandment of God, that you may establish your own tradition."

Let us pray, then, dear brothers, just as God our Teacher taught us. It is a friendly, intimate prayer to ask God for what is his own, letting Christ's prayer rise to the Father's ears. May the Father recognize his Son's words when we pray. May the One who dwells within our hearts also be on our lips. Since we have him as our Advocate with the Father for our sins, when we plead as sinners for our offenses, let us speak our Advocate's own words. He said that whatever we ask the Father in his name, he will give us (John 14:13-14); how much more effectively, then, do we obtain what we seek in Christ's name if we ask using his own prayer?

latin: EVANGELICA praecepta, fratres dilectissimi, nihil aliud sunt quam magisteria divina, fundamenta aedificandae spei, firmamenta corroborandae fidei, nutrimenta fovendi cordis, gubernacula dirigendi itineris, praesidia obtinendae salutis; quae, dum dociles credentium mentes in terris instruunt, ad coelestia regna perducunt. Multa et per Prophetas servos suos dici Deus voluit et audiri; sed quanto majora quae Filius loquitur, quae Dei sermo qui in Prophetis fuit propria voce testatur, non jam mandans ut paretur venienti via, sed ipse veniens, et viam nobis aperiens et ostendens; ut qui, in tenebris mortis errantes, improvidi et caeci prius fuimus, luce gratiae luminati, iter vitae duce et rectore Domino teneremus. Qui inter caetera salutaria sua monita et praecepta divina quibus populo suo consulit ad salutem, etiam orandi ipse formam dedit, ipse quid precaremur monuit et instruxit. Qui fecit vivere, docuit et orare, benignitate ea scilicet qua et caetera dare et conferre dignatus est; ut, dum prece et oratione quam Filius docuit apud Patrem loquimur, facilius audiamur. Jam praedixerat horam venire quando veri adoratores adorarent Patrem in spiritu et veritate, et implevit quod ante promisit; ut qui spiritum et veritatem de ejus sanctificatione percepimus, de traditione quoque ejus vere et spiritaliter adoremus. Quae enim potest esse magis spiritalis oratio quam quae a Christo nobis data est, a quo nobis et Spiritus sanctus missus est? Quae vera magis apud Patrem precatio quam quae a Filio, qui est Veritas, de ejus ore prolata est? ut aliter orare quam docuit non ignorantia sola sit, sed et culpa, quando ipse posuerit et dixerit: Rejicitis mandatum Dei, ut traditionem vestram statuatis. Oremus itaque, fratres dilectissimi, sicut magister Deus docuit. Amica et familiaris oratio est Deum de suo rogare, ad aures ejus ascendere Christi oratione. Agnoscat Pater Filii sui verba cum precem facimus. Qui habitat intus in pectore, ipse sit et in voce. Et cum ipsum habeamus apud Patrem advocatum pro peccatis nostris, quando peccatores pro delictis nostris petimus, advocati nostri verba promamus. Nam, cum dicat quia quodcumque petierimus a Patre in nomine ejus dabit nobis,, quanto efficacius impetramus quod petimus in Christi nomine, si petamus ipsius oratione?

excerpts.author: Cyprian
english: Many and great are the divine benefits by which the Father and Christ have worked, and continue to work, for our salvation. The Father sent the Son to preserve us and give us life, and the Son chose to be sent and to become the Son of Man so that He might make us sons of God. He humbled Himself in order to raise up the people who lay prostrate; He was wounded in order to heal our wounds; He took the form of a servant in order to lead servants into freedom; He endured death in order to bestow immortality on mortals. These are many and great gifts of divine mercy.

But consider further: what kind of providence, and how great a clemency, provides us with a plan of salvation so that the redeemed person may be more fully cared for? When the Lord came, He healed the wounds Adam had borne and cured the ancient poison of the serpent. He gave a law to the restored and commanded them not to sin again, lest something worse befall the sinner. We were confined, shut up in a narrow prescription of innocence. Human frailty and weakness would have had no recourse unless divine pity came to our aid once more. By displaying works of justice and mercy, God opened a way to preserve our salvation, so that we might wash away whatever filth we contract afterward through alms.

The Holy Spirit speaks in the divine Scriptures and says: "Sins are purged by alms and by faith" (cf. Prov. 16:6). Not the sins contracted before, for those are purged by the blood and sanctification of Christ. Again He says: "Just as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin" (Sir. 3:30). Here it is also shown and proven that, just as the fire of Gehenna is quenched by the bath of saving water, so the flame of sins is calmed by alms and just works. Because the remission of sins is given once in Baptism, a constant and continual operation that imitates Baptism obtains God's indulgence again.

The Lord teaches this in the Gospel as well. When His disciples were denounced for eating without first washing their hands, He answered: "The One who made the inside also made the outside. But give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you" (Luke 11:40–41). He was teaching and showing that it is not the hands that need washing, but the heart, and that the filth inside must be removed rather than the outside. The One who purifies the inside also purifies the outside, and with a purified mind, the skin and body also begin to be clean. Furthermore, warning us and showing from what source we can be clean and purified, He added that alms must be given. The Merciful One teaches and urges us to practice mercy, and because He seeks to preserve those He redeemed at a great price, He teaches that those who have been defiled after the grace of Baptism can be purified once more.

Let us therefore recognize, dearest brothers, the wholesome gift of divine indulgence. Since we cannot exist without some wound of conscience, let us cure our wounds with spiritual remedies. Let no one flatter himself on the purity of his heart, trusting in his own innocence to decide that medicine need not be applied to his wounds. For it is written: "Who can boast, 'My heart is pure; I am clean from my sin'?" (Prov. 20:9). And again John says in his Epistle: "If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us" (1 John 1:8). If no one can be without sin, and whoever claims to be blameless is either proud or foolish, how necessary and kind is divine clemency! Knowing that the healed still bear some wounds afterward, God has given remedies to heal and save those wounds again.

Finally, dearest brothers, divine admonition has never ceased or been silent. In the holy Scriptures, both Old and New, the people of God are always and everywhere urged to works of mercy. With the Holy Spirit singing and exhorting, whoever is instructed in the hope of the heavenly kingdom is commanded to give alms. God commands and orders through Isaiah: "Cry out with strength, do not hold back; lift up your voice like a trumpet, and declare to My people their transgression, to the house of Jacob their sins" (Isaiah 58:1). When He had commanded that their sins be reproached to them, and their wicked deeds be proclaimed with a full impulse of indignation, and had said that they could not satisfy for their offenses even with prayers, supplications, and fasts, nor appease God's wrath even by lying in sackcloth and ashes, nonetheless, in the final passage He showed that God can be appeased only by alms. He added: "Share your bread with the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house; when you see the naked, cover him, and do not hide yourself from your own flesh" (Isaiah 58:7). Then your light shall break forth like the dawn, your healing shall spring up quickly, your righteousness shall go before you, and the glory of the Lord shall be your rear guard. Then you shall call, and the Lord will answer; you shall cry, and He will say, 'Here I am' (Isaiah 58:8–9).

latin: MULTA et magna sunt, fratres charissimi beneficia divina quibus in salutem nostram Dei Patris et Christi larga et copiosa clementia et operata sit et semper operetur, quod conservandis ac vivificandis nobis Pater Filium misit, ut reparare nos posset, quodque Filius missus esse et hominis filius fieri voluit ut nos Dei filios faceret. Humiliavit se, ut populum qui prius jacebat erigeret: vulneratus est, ut vulnera nostra curaret: servivit, ut ad libertatem servientes extraheret: mori sustinuit, ut immortalitatem mortalibus exhiberet. Multa haec sunt et magna divinae misericordiae munera. Sed adhuc, qualis providentia illa et quanta clementia est quod nobis salutari ratione prospicitur, ut homini qui redemptus est reservando plenius consulatur! Nam, cum Dominus adveniens sanasset illa quae Adam portaverat vulnera, et venena serpentis antiqua curasset, legem dedit sano, et praecepit ne ultra jam peccaret, ne quid peccanti gravius eveniret. Coarctati eramus et in angustum innocentiae praescriptione conclusi. Nec haberet quid fragilitatis humanae infirmitas atque imbecillitas faceret, nisi iterum pietas divina subveniens, justitiae et misericordiae operibus ostensis, viam quamdam tuendae salutis aperiret, ut sordes postmodum, quascumque contrahimus, eleemosynis abluamus. Loquitur in Scripturis divinis Spiritus sanctus et dicit: Eleemosynis et fide delicta purgantur. Non utique illa delicta quae fuerant ante contracta, nam illa Christi sanguine et sanctificatione purgantur. Item denuo dicit: Sicut aqua extinguit ignem, sic eleemosyna extinguit peccatum. Hic quoque ostenditur et probatur quia, sicut lavacro aquae salutaris gehennae ignis extinguitur, ita et eleemosynis atque operationibus justis delictorum flamma sopitur. Et quia semel in Baptismo remissa peccatorum datur, assidua et jugis operatio Baptismi instar imitata, Dei rursus indulgentiam largitur. Hoc et in Evangelio Dominus docet. Nam cum denotarentur discipuli ejus quod ederent, nec prius manus abluissent, respondit et dixit: Qui fecit quod intus est, fecit et quod foris est. Verum date eleemosynam, et ecce vobis munda omnia: docens scilicet et ostendens non manus lavandas esse, sed pectus, et sordes intrinsecus potius quam extrinsecus detrahendas; verum qui purgaverit quod est intus, eum quoque id quod foris est repurgasse, et emundata mente, cute quoque et corpore mundum esse coepisse. Porro autem, monens et ostendens unde mundi et purgati esse possimus, addidit eleemosynas esse faciendas. Misericors docet et monet misericordiam fieri; et quia servare quaerit quos magno pretio redemit, post Baptismi gratiam sordidatos docet denuo posse purgari. Agnoscamus itaque, fratres charissimi, divinae indulgentiae munus salubre, et emundandis purgandisque peccatis nostris, qui sine aliquo conscientiae vulnere esse non possumus, medelis spiritalibus vulnera nostra curemus. Nec quisquam sic sibi de puro atque immaculato pectore blandiatur, ut, innocentia sua fretus, medicinam non putet adhibendam esse vulneribus, cum scriptum sit: Quis gloriabitur castum se habere cor, aut quis gloriabitur mundum se esse a peccatis? et iterum in Epistola sua Joannes ponat et dicat: Si dixerimus quia peccatum non habemus, nos ipsos decipimus, et veritas in nobis non est. Si autem nemo esse sine peccato potest, et quisquis inculpatum se esse dixerit, aut superbus aut stultus est, quam necessaria, quam benigna est divina clementia, quae, cum sciat non deesse sanatis quaedam postmodum vulnera, dedit curandis denuo sanandisque vulneribus remedia salutaria! Numquam denique, fratres dilectissimi, admonitio divina cessavit et tacuit quominus in Scripturis sanctis tam veteribus quam novis semper et ubique ad misericordiae opera Dei populus provocaretur; et canente atque exhortante Spiritu sancto, quisquis ad spem regni coelestis instruitur, facere eleemosynas jubetur. Mandat et praecipit Esaiae Deus: Exclama, inquit, in fortitudine, et noli parcere. Sicut tuba exalta vocem tuam, et annuntia plebi meae peccata ipsorum et domui Jacob facinora eorum. Et cum peccata eis sua exprobrari praecepisset, cumque eorum facinora pleno indignationis impetu protulisset, dixissetque eos nec, si orationibus et precibus et jejuniis uterentur, satisfacere pro delictis posse, nec, si in cilicio et cinere volverentur, iram Dei posse lenire, in novissima tamen parte, demonstrans solis eleemosynis Deum posse placari, addidit dicens: Frange esurienti panem tuum, et egenos sine tecto induc in domum tuam. Si videris nudum, vesti eum, et domesticos seminis tui non despicias. Tunc erumpet temporaneum lumen tuum, et vestimenta tua cito orientur, et praeibit ante te justitia, et claritas Dei circumdabit te. Tunc exclamabis, et Deus exaudiet te. Dum adhuc loqueris dicet: Ecce adsum.

excerpts.author: Novatian
english: Consider another passage where we similarly read of God, an angel being presented. When Jacob was complaining to his wives Leah and Rachel about their father's injustice, and when he reported that he already desired to return and go back to his own land, he also brought forward the authority of his dream. At that time he relates that the angel of God said to him through a dream: 'Jacob.' And he says, 'I answered.' 'What is it?' He says, 'Look with your eyes and see the he-goats and rams mounting the ewes and she-goats — streaked, white, varied, ash-colored, and spotted.' (Genesis 31:10-13) 'For I have seen everything Laban has done to you. I am the God who appeared to you in the place of God, where you anointed a standing stone for me and vowed a vow to me there. Now therefore arise, depart from this land, go to the land of your birth, and I will be with you.' If the angel of God speaks these words to Jacob, and the angel himself adds, saying, 'I am the God who appeared to you in the place of God,' we perceive not only this angel but God presented without any hesitation. For he reports that a vow from Jacob was destined for the place of God, and he does not say, 'in my place.' Therefore there is a place of God, and here God is present as well. But there the place of God is simply presented; for it was not said, 'in the place of the angel and of God,' but only 'of God.' Here, however, the one who promises these things is declared to be both God and angel; so that a proper distinction exists between the one who is called only God, and the one who is not called simply God but also angel. From this it follows that if no other angel can possess such great authority as to confess himself God and testify that a vow was made to him — except only Christ, to whom a vow can be vowed not because he is an angel but because he is God — then it is clear that the Father cannot be accepted here, but the Son, God and angel. But if this one is Christ, as he is, then whoever calls Christ either a mere man or only an angel is in grave danger, stripping him of the power of the divine name which he frequently received from the faith of the heavenly scriptures, which frequently call him both angel and God. To all these points this is added: just as divine scripture frequently presents him as both angel and God, so it presents him as both man and God, expressing what he was going to be, and depicting even then in an image what he had to be in the truth of substance. For Jacob was left alone, and a man wrestled with him until morning.

excerpts.author: Novatian
english: I must also address the section where the heretic thinks he sees clearly but has actually lost all truth and light, so that he may finally recognize the total blindness of his error. He repeatedly throws up the words: "I have been with you for a long time, and still you do not know me? Philip, whoever has seen me has seen the Father" (John 14:9). He needs to learn what he fails to understand. Philip is rebuked, and justly so, because he said, "Lord, show us the Father, and that will be enough for us." When had Philip ever heard or learned from Christ that Christ was the Father? On the contrary, he had heard and learned far more often that He was the Son, not the Father. When the Lord said, "If you had known me, you would have known my Father also; from now on you know him and have seen him" (John 14:7), He did not mean to be understood as the Father Himself. He meant that whoever approaches the Son of God with total faith and total devotion will come to the Father through the Son in whom he believes, and will see Him. Jesus said, "No one comes to the Father except through me" (John 14:6). Therefore, the one who comes to God the Father will not only come to know Him, but ought also to hold fast in mind and heart as if he already knows and sees the Father. Divine Scripture often announces things not yet done as if they were already accomplished, because they are certain to happen. It does not merely predict them as future; it narrates them as already fulfilled. Long before Christ was born in Isaiah's time, it was said, "A child is born to us" (Isaiah 9:6). Before He came to Mary, the prophet was told, "Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son" (Isaiah 7:14). Before Christ revealed the Father's heart, it was said, "His name shall be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God" (Isaiah 9:6). Before He suffered, it was proclaimed, "He was led like a lamb to the slaughter" (Isaiah 53:7). Before the cross existed, God said, "All day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient people" (Isaiah 65:2; Romans 10:21). Before He was given vinegar, it was written, "They gave me vinegar for my thirst" (Psalm 69:21). Before He was stripped, it was said, "They cast lots for my garment" (Psalm 22:18), "They numbered my bones" (Psalm 22:17), "They pierced my hands and feet" (Psalm 22:16). Divine Scripture speaks of future events as accomplished, and of future perfections as already perfect, because their coming is beyond doubt. That is why the Lord said in this passage, "From now on you know him and have seen him" (John 14:7). He declared that the Father would be seen by anyone who followed the Son — not that the Son Himself was the Father seen, but that the reward for following Him and becoming His disciple would be the vision of the Father. The Son is the image of God the Father (John 14:9; Colossians 1:15), so that, just as the Father works, so also the Son works, and the Son imitates all the Father's works (John 5:19). Thus each person may have it as if he had already seen the Father, while seeing the One who always imitates the invisible Father in every work. But if Christ Himself were the Father, how could He immediately add, "Whoever believes in me will do the works I do, and greater works than these will he do, because I am going to the Father" (John 14:12)? And He goes on: "If you love me, keep my commandments. And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Advocate" (John 14:15–16). Then: "If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him" (John 14:23). And: "The Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things and remind you of everything I have said" (John 14:26). He anticipates this passage to show He is the Son, and rightly adds: "If you loved me, you would rejoice that I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I" (John 14:28). What about when He also says: "I am the true vine, and my Father is the gardener. Every branch in me that bears no fruit he takes away, and every branch that does bear fruit he prunes, that it may bear more fruit" (John 15:1–2)? He insists: "As the Father has loved me, so have I loved you. Abide in my love. If you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love, just as I have kept my Father's commandments and abide in his love" (John 15:9–10). He also says: "I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you" (John 15:15). And He adds: "They will do all these things to you on account of my name, because they do not know the one who sent me" (John 15:21). The Lord would never have appended these words, which plainly testify that He is not the Father but the Son, if He had thought of Himself as the Father or wanted to be understood as the Father — unless He meant to express that each believer ought to possess, as if he had already seen the Father, the vision of God's image through the Son. For everyone who believes in the Son is exercised in contemplating that image, so that, growing accustomed to seeing the divine through the image, he may advance and grow until he reaches the perfect contemplation of God the Father Almighty. Since the one who embraces this with mind and heart, believing all this will come to pass, already possesses in a real sense the Father he will one day see, and already holds as certain what he knows he will obtain. But if Christ were the Father, what future reward would He promise that He had already given and bestowed? He says, "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God" (Matthew 5:8). He thereby promises the contemplation and vision of the Father. So He had not yet given it; why promise what is already given? If He were the Father, He would have been seen and touched. Yet while Christ was being touched and seen, He still promised that the pure in heart would see God. This proves He is not the Father — the One who, though present and visible, promised that the pure in heart would see the Father. Therefore, it was the Son, not the Father, who made this promise. As the Son, He promised what He had yet to be seen: a promise that would have been pointless if He were not the Son. Why promise the pure in heart that they would see the Father, if those present were already seeing Christ as the Father? But because He was the Son, not the Father, and the Son is the image of God, He was seen then, while the Father — being invisible — is promised to the pure in heart as the one they will see. This is enough said against this heretic, though it is only a few points out of many. A broad and extensive field would open if we wished to engage him more fully. Deprived of the light from these two passages, he is completely overcome by the blindness of his own doctrine.

latin: Adhuc adiciam illam quoque partem in qua dum haereticus quasi oculo quodam gaudet proprio, ueritatis et luminis amisso, totam caecitatem sui agnoscat erroris. identidem enim et frequenter opponit quia dictum sit: sano tempore uobiscum sum, et non agnoscitis me? Philippe, qui uidit me, uidit et patrem. sed quod non intellegit, discat. culpatur Philippus, et iure quidem meritoque, quia dixerit: domine, ostende nobis patrem, et sufficit nobis. quando enim ex Christo aut audierat istud aut didicerat, quasi esset pater Christus, cum contra magis, quod filius esset, non quia pater, frequenter audisset, et saepe didicisset? quod enim dixit dominus, s me cognouistis, et patrem meum cognouistis, et a modo nostis illum, et uidistis illum, non sic dixerat ut se patrem uellet intellegi, sed quoniam qui penitus et plene et cum tota fide et tota religione accessit ad dei filium, omnibus modis per ipsum filium, in quem sic credit, ad patrem peruenturus sit, eundemque uisurus. nemo enim, inquit, potest uenire ad patrem nisi per me, et ideo ad patrem deum non tantum uenturus est, et cogniturus ipsum patrem, sed etiam sic tenere debet, atque ita animo ac mente praesumere, quasi iam nouerit patrem pariter et uiderit. Saepe enim scriptura diuina, quae nondum facta pro factis annuntiat, quia sic futura sunt, et quae omnibus modis fieri habent, non quasi futura sint, praedicat, sed quasi facta sint, narrat. denique cum nondum temporibus Isaiae prophetae Christus natus fuisset, quia puer, aiebat, natus est nobis; et cum nondum accessum esset ad Mariam, e accessit ad propheten, dicebat, e concepit, et peperit filium. et cum nondum sinum patris Christus exposuisset, referebat: e uocabitur nomen eius magni consili angelus. et cum nondum fuisset passus, guas? outs, pronuntiabat, ad iugulationem adductus est. et cum adhuc crux nusquam esset, aiebat: Tota die expandi manus meas ad populum non credentem., et cum nondum iniuriose potatus fuisset, s7fz, ait, mea potauerunt me aceto. et cum spoliatus adhuc non fuisset, dicebat, super uestem meam miserunt sortem: et dinumerauerunt ossa mea: effoderunt manus meas et pedes. prouidens enim scriptura diuina pro factis dicit, quae futura scit, et pro perfectis dicit, quae futura habet, quae sine dubitatione uentura sunt. et ideo dominus in praesenti loco dicebat: a modo nostis illum, et uidistis. dicebat enim uisum iri ab eo patrem, quisquis filium secutus fuisset; non quasi filius ipse esset pater uisus, sed quod praemium consecuturus esset, quisquis illum sequi et discipulus eius esse uoluisset, ut uidere patrem posset. nam et imago est dei patris, ut his etiam illud accedat, quoniam sicut pater operatur, ita operatur et filius, et imitator est filius omnium operum paternorum; ut perinde habeat unusquisque, quasi iam uiderit patrem, dum eum uidet qui inuisibilem patrem in omnibus operibus semper imitatur. Ceterum si ipse pater est Christus, quomodo confestim adicit et dicit: gud credit in me, opera quae ego facio et ipse Faciet, et maiora his faciet, quia ego ad patrem uado? et adhuc subnectit: si diligitis me, praecepta mea seruate: et ego rogabo patrem, et alium aduocatum dabit uobis. post quae etiam illud subnectit: s quis me diligit, sermonem meum custodiet: et pater meus diliget illum, et ad eum ueniemus, et mansionem apud illum Jaciemus. nec non etiam subdidit illud quoque: aduocatus autem ille spiritus sanctus, quem missurus est pater, ille uos docebit et commemorabit- omnia quaecumque dixero. praemittit adhuc istum locum, quo ostendat se esse filium, et merito subdidit, et dicit: s me diligeretis, gauderetis, quia eo ad patrem: quia pater maior me est. quid autem cum etiam ila subnectit: ego sum uitis uera, et pater meus agricola: omne sarmentum in me non afferens fructum tollit illud, et omne fructtSerum purgat, ut fructum ampliorem ferat? instat adhuc et adicit: sicut dilexit me pater, et ego dilexi uos; manete in mea caritate; si mandata mea seruaueritis, manebitis in mea caritale, sicut ego patris mandata seruaui, et maneo in eius caritate. adhuc ingerit, et dicit: dixi autem uos amicos, quia omnia quae audiui a patre meo, nota uobis feci. aggregat etiam hoc: sed haec omnia facient uobis propter nomen meum, quia ignorant eum qui me misit. Haec ergo numquam post illa euidenter illum non patrem sed filium esse testantia dominus subdidisset, si aut patrem se esse meminisset, aut patrem se uellet intellegi. nisi quoniam ut illud exprimeret, perinde unumquemque iam habere debere, dum imaginem dei patris per filium uidet, atque si uiderit patrem—quandoquidem unusquisque credens in filium exerceatur in imaginis contemplatione, ut assuefactus ad diuinitatem uidendam imagine proficere possit et crescere usque ad dei patris omnipotentis perfectam contemplationem,—et quoniam, qui hoc animo ac mentecombiberit et de omnibus sic futurum esse crediderit, patrem, quem uisurus sit, quasi iam quodammodo uiderit et hic iam sic habeat, quasi teneat, quod habiturum se pro certo sciat. Ceterum, si ipse pater fuisset, quid quasi futurum praemium repromittebat, quod iam praestiterat et dederat? nam quoniam dicit: beati mundo corde, quia ipsi deum uidebunt, polliceri deprehenditur contemplationem et aspectum patris. ergo nondum dederat: cur enim repromitteret, si iam dedisset? dederat enim, si pater esset; uidebatur enim, et contingebatur. quando autem, dum contingitur ipse Christus et uidetur, repromittit tamen et dicit, quoniam qui mundo fuerit corde, deum uidebit, hoc ipso probat patrem se non esse, qui tunc praesens cum uideretur repromittebat, quod patrem uisurus esset quisquis mundo corde fuisset. erat ergo repromittens haec non pater sed filius; quia qui filius erat, quod uideri habebat repromittebat: cuius repromissio superuacua fuisset, nisi filius fuisset. cur enim repromittebat mundis ut uiderent patrem, Si iam tunc qui praesentes erant, patrem Christum uidebant? sed quia filius erat, non pater, merito et filius, quia imago dei, tunc uidebatur, et pater, quia inuisibilis, mundis corde, ut uideretur, repromittitur et notatur. Haec igitur satis sit etiam aduersus istum haereticum dictasse, pauca de multis. campus enim, et quidem latus ac fusus, aperietur, plenius haereticum istum si agitare uoluerimus; quandoquidem duobus istis locis quibusdam effossis luminibus orbatus, totus sit in doctrinae suae caecitate superatus.

excerpts.author: Methodius of Olympus
english: I. From the Discourse on the Resurrection. I. Read the Book on the Resurrection by St. Methodius, Bishop and Martyr, of which that which follows is a selection, that the body is not the fetter of the soul , as Origen thought, nor are souls called by the prophet Jeremiah fettered on account of their being within bodies. For he lays down the principle that the body does not hinder the energies of the soul , but that rather the body is carried about with it, and cooperates in whatever the soul commits to it. But how are we to understand the opinion of Gregory the theologian, and many Others? II. That Origen said that the body was given to the soul as a fetter after the fall, and that previously it lived without a body; but that this body which we wear is the cause of our sins ; wherefore also he called it a fetter, as it can hinder the soul from good works. III. That if the body was given to the soul after the fall as a fetter, it must have been given as a fetter upon the evil or the good. Now it is impossible that it should be upon the good; for no physician or artificer gives to that which has gone wrong a remedy to cause further error , much less would God do so. It remains, then, that it was a fetter upon evil . But surely we see that, at the beginning, Cain, clad in this body, committed murder ; and it is evident into what wickedness those who succeeded him ran. The body is not, then, a fetter upon evil , nor indeed a fetter at all; nor was the soul clothed in it for the…

1. Read a compendious interpretation of some apostolic words from the same discourse. Let us see, then, what it is that we have endeavoured to say respecting the apostle. For this saying of his, I was alive without the law once, Romans 7:9 refers to the life which was lived in paradise before the law, not without a body, but with a body, by our first parents , as we have shown above; for we lived without concupiscence, being altogether ignorant of its assaults. For not to have a law according to which we ought to live, nor a power of establishing what manner of life we ought to adopt, so that we might justly be approved or blamed, is considered to exempt a person from accusation. Because one cannot lust after those things from which he is not restrained, and even if he lusted after them, he would not be blamed. For lust is not directed to things which are before us, and subject to our power, but to those which are before us, and not in our power. For how should one care for a thing which is neither forbidden nor necessary to him? And for this reason it is said, I had not known lust , except the law had said, You shall not covet . Romans 7:7 For when (our first parents ) heard, Of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil , you shall not eat of it; for in the day you eat thereof you shall surely die, Genesis 2:17 then they conceived lust , and gathered it. excerpts.citation: Arnobius — Against the Nations Against the Heathen (Book I)
excerpts.author: Arnobius
english: I have learned that certain people, convinced of their own superior wisdom, are raving like frenzied prophets. They claim that ever since the Christian religion appeared in the world, the earth has gone to ruin and the human race has been overwhelmed by every kind of disaster; even the heavenly powers, they say, have abandoned their solemn watch over human affairs and have been driven from the regions of the earth. I have therefore decided, as best my ability and my modest style allow, to answer this envious slander and refute its false charges. I must do so lest these accusers imagine that their popular rhetoric actually proves something weighty, or lest, if we keep silence, they suppose they have won the case — a case lost by its own merit, not by any failure of its defenders. I will not deny that the accusation sounds formidable, and that we deserve hostile hatred, if it can be shown that our presence caused the world to stray from its laws, drove the gods far away, and imported such vast miseries upon the ages. Let us then examine the mind behind this opinion and test the truth of its claims. Setting aside all partisan zeal that usually obscures a clear view of reality, let us weigh the matter on an even balance. The connected force of the following arguments will certainly prove that we are not the impious ones; rather, those who boast of serving the gods and clinging to ancient rites will be found guilty of the very crime they charge against us.

First, in a calm and friendly tone, we ask them: since the Christian name began to exist on earth, what has nature — the very order of things — experienced or suffered that is new, unknown, or contrary to the fundamental laws established from the beginning? Have the primary elements, out of which all things are composed, been altered into opposite qualities? Has any part of the vast machine and structure of the universe, which encloses and sustains us, been loosened or dissolved? Has the world's rotation, exceeding its primordial motion, begun to creep more slowly or to spin with precipitous speed? Have the stars started to rise in the west and set in the east? Has the sun, prince of the stars, by whose light all things are clothed and by whose heat they are animated, flared up or grown cold, corrupting the tempered moderation of its course? Has the moon ceased to renew itself and return to its ancient phases through the constant succession of the new? Have cold, heat, and the moderate temperatures of the seasons perished in confusion? Has winter begun to have long days and summer to recall the latest dawns of night? Have the winds breathed their last? Have the lightning flashes died out, so that the sky is no longer driven into clouds and the fields, moistened by rain, no longer flourish? Does the earth refuse the seed entrusted to it? Do the trees refuse to bud? Has the flavor of edible fruit and the juice of the vine been changed? Does the oil pressed from olives yield a foul gore and fail to feed the lamp? Do land animals and sea creatures no longer conceive or give birth? Do fetuses in the womb no longer follow their natural development and law? Finally, do human beings — scattered by the first navigation over the earth's uninhabitable shores — no longer contract marriages with proper solemnities? Do they not beget children, conduct public and private business, manage their households? Do they not, each as he pleases, direct their talents through various arts and disciplines and reap the fruits of their studies? Do they not rule and command, those to whom the lot of such things has fallen? Do they not grow daily in dignity and power? Do they not preside over courts, interpret laws and rights? Do they not observe in every nation the ancestral moral institutions that sustain and contain human life? Since all this remains exactly as it was, and no novelty has broken in to disrupt the perpetual course of things, what is this claim that a stain has come upon the earth since the Christian religion entered the world and revealed the hidden mysteries of truth?

They reply that pestilences, droughts, wars, crop failures, locusts, mice, hail, and other scourges that afflict human affairs are sent by the gods, enraged by our injuries and offenses. If it were not foolish to linger over matters so clear they need no defense, I would certainly demonstrate, by reviewing earlier ages, that these evils are neither unknown nor sudden; they did not burst upon the world only after our people was deemed worthy of the happiness of this name. If we are the cause, and these plagues were devised as punishment for our crime, how did antiquity know the names of these miseries? How did it have words for war, pestilence, and hail — by what concept could it name them, or take them into its vocabulary? If these evils are new and spring from recent offenses, who could have coined words for things it had never experienced and never learned of from its ancestors? 'Crop failure and grain shortages press us hard,' they say. Were the ancient and most ancient ages never acquainted with this necessity? Do not the very names by which these evils are called testify and proclaim that no mortal has ever been immune from them? If that is hard to believe, I can cite authors who record how many and how great nations have felt the horror of famine and perished in vast numbers. Hailstrikes are frequent and have struck everywhere. Do we not read in ancient writings that stone rains have often devastated whole regions? Excessive rains ruin crops and signal sterility. Was antiquity exempt from these evils? We know that even great rivers have dried up in the mud. Pestilences have burned through the human race. Run through the annals written in many languages and you will learn that all nations have often been desolated and stripped of their inhabitants. Locusts and mice attack and gnaw every kind of crop. Consult your own histories and learn from these plagues how often earlier ages were afflicted and reduced to misery. Cities tremble, shaken by the most violent earthquakes, until they stand in danger. Did earlier times not see cities swallowed by great chasms, or did they enjoy security from such disasters? When was the human race destroyed by a flood? Not before us? When was the world burned and dissolved into ashes? Not before us? When were the greatest cities covered by the waves of the sea? Not before us? When were wars waged with wild beasts and battles fought with lions? Not before us? When did poisonous snakes bring destruction upon peoples? Not before us? As for the frequent wars, city devastations, and the incursions of Germans and Scythians that you habitually throw at us — I say this with your leave and goodwill — you do not see what you are saying, blinded by the lust for calumny. Were we the cause when, as Plato demonstrates, a vast host erupted from the island of Atlantis ten thousand years ago and wiped out innumerable nations from their foundations? Was it our envy that, among the Assyrians and Bactrians under Ninus and Zoroaster, they fought not only with iron and strength but also with magical and Chaldaean arts from hidden teachings? Was the rape of Helen, led on by the gods themselves and a dire fate for her and future ages, a crime of our religion? Was it the effect of our name that Xerxes poured the sea onto the land and marched across the waters? Did we make and stir up the causes that let a single youth from the borders of Macedonia subjugate the kingdoms and peoples of the East to captivity and servitude?
