latin: Age nunc, omnes erraverint; deceptus sit Apostolus de testimonio reddendo quibusdam; nullam respexerit Spiritus Sanctus, uti eam in veritatem deduceret, ad hoc missus a Christo, ad hoc postulatus de Patre, ut esset doctor veritatis; neglexerit officium Dei villicus, Christi vicarius, sinens Ecclesias aliter interim intelligere, aliter credere, quam ipse per Apostolos praedicabat: ecquid verisimile est, ut tot ac tantae in unam fidem erraverint? Nullus inter multos eventus unus est exitus: variasse debuerat error doctrinae Ecclesiarum. Caeterum, quod apud multos unum invenitur, non est erratum, sed traditum. Audeat ergo aliquis dicere illos errasse qui tradiderunt?

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Where was Marcion then, the Pontic shipowner and Stoic enthusiast? Where was Valentinus, the Platonist disciple? The record shows they were not around even earlier, back under Antoninus; at first they actually believed the catholic teaching in the Roman church, under Bishop Eleutherius. But their restless curiosity — the kind that made even fellow Christians avoid them — got them thrown out once, then twice. Finally Marcion was cut off for good, taking his two hundred sestertii with him, and the pair scattered the poison of their doctrines. Later Marcion confessed repentance and tried to meet the condition set for his return: he would be readmitted only if he brought back to the church the others he had schooled for destruction. Death beat him to it. Heresies had to exist, yes; but that does not make heresies good, as if evil were not also necessary. The Lord had to be betrayed; still, woe to the betrayer — lest anyone use that as a defense of heresy. Even Apelles' pedigree needs examining: he is no more ancient than Marcion, his founder and forerunner. He fell for a woman, abandoned Marcionite continence, and slipped away from the eyes of the most holy teacher Alexander to Alexandria. Years later he came back no better, except that he was no longer a Marcionite; he stumbled into another woman, the virgin Philumene (mentioned above), who later became a monstrous prostitute. Deceived by her power, he wrote down the revelations he learned from her. People still alive remember them — their own disciples and successors — so they cannot deny being later arrivals. Though they are also refuted by their own works, as the Lord said. If Marcion split the New Testament from the Old, he comes after what he split; he could not split what was not already united. United first, then separated — that proves the splitter is later. Valentinus, explaining differently and 'correcting,' only shows that whatever he corrects was previously flawed. These are the most notorious and frequent adulterers of the truth. And what about Nigidius, whoever he is, and Hermogenes, and the rest still walking around perverting God's ways? Let them show me their authorization. If they preach another God, how do they use that God's own things, letters, and names against the God they preach? If they preach the same God, how do they do it differently? Let them prove they are new apostles: let them say Christ descended again, taught again, was crucified again, died again, rose again — because that is how apostles operate, receiving power to work the same signs he did. I want to see their powers produced; unless I acknowledge their greatest power, by which they perversely imitate the apostles: the apostles made the dead live; these men make the living dead.

latin: Ubi tunc Marcion, ponticus nauclerus, stoicae studiosus? Ubi Valentinus platonicae sectator? Nam constat illos, neque adeo olim fuisse, Antonini fere principatu, et in catholicae primo doctrinam credidisse apud Ecclesiam romanensem, sub episcopatu Eleutherii benedicti, donec ob inquietam semper eorum curiositatem, qua fratres quoque vitabant semel et iterum ejecti, Marcion quidem cum ducentis sestertiis quae Ecclesiae intulerat, novissime in perpetuum discidium relegati, venena doctrinarum suarum disseminaverunt. Postmodum idem Marcion, poenitentiam confessus cum conditioni datae sibi occurrit, ita pacem recepturus, si caeteros quos perditioni erudisset, Ecclesiae restitueret, morte praeventus est. Oportebat enim haereses esse. Nec tamen ideo bonum haereses, quia eas oportebat, quasi non et malum oportuerit esse. Nam et Dominum tradi oportebat; sed vae traditori? ne quis etiam hinc haereses defendat. Si et Apellis stemma retractandum est, tam non vetus et ipse quam Marcion institutor et praeformator ejus: sed lapsus in foeminam desertor continentiae marcionensis, ab oculis sanctissimi magistri Alexandriam secessit; inde post annos regressus non melior, nisi tantum qua jam non marcionites, in alteram foeminam impegit, illam virginem Philumenen, quam supra edidimus, postea vero immane prostibulum et ipsam, cujus energemate circumventus, quas ab ea didicit phaneroseis scripsit. Adhuc in saeculo supersunt qui meminerint eorum, etiam proprii discentes et successores ipsorum, ne se posteriores negare possint. Quanquam et de operibus suis, ut dixit Dominus, revincuntur. Si enim Marcion Novum Testamentum a Vetere separavit, posterior est eo quod separavit; quia separare non posset, nisi quod unitum fuit. Unitum ergo ante quam separaretur, postea separatum, posteriorem ostendit separatorem. Item Valentinus, aliter exponens, et sine dubio emendans, hoc omnino quicquid emendat, ut mendosum retro, anterius fuisse demonstrat. Hos ut insigniores et frequentiores adulteros veritatis nominamus. Caeterum et Nigidius nescio quis, et Hermogenes, et multi alii qui adhuc ambulant pervertentes vias Dei, ostendant mihi ex qua auctoritate prodierunt. Si alium Deum praedicant, quomodo ejus Dei rebus et litteris et nominibus utuntur adversus quem praedicant? si eumdem, quomodo aliter? Probent se novos apostolos esse: dicant Christum iterum descendisse, iterum ipsum docuisse, iterum crucifixum, iterum mortuum, iterum resuscitatum: sic enim Apostolos solet facere, dare illis praeterea virtutem eadem signa edendi, quae et ipse. Volo igitur et virtutes eorum proferri; nisi quod agnosco maximam virtutem eorum, qua Apostolos in perversum aemulantur: illi enim de mortuis vivos faciebant, isti de vivis mortuos faciunt.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Still, if anyone dares to slot themselves into the apostolic age so they can claim the apostles handed them down—since they were 'under the apostles'—we can say: Let them produce the origins of their churches. Let them lay out the succession of their bishops, running unbroken from the start, so that their first bishop can show an apostle, or an apostolic man who stuck with the apostles, as his author and predecessor. That is how apostolic churches present their credentials: the church of Smyrna reports Polycarp was appointed by John; Rome produces Clement, ordained by Peter; likewise every other church exhibits bishops the apostles installed, as bearers of apostolic seed. Let the heretics fabricate a pedigree like that. What is forbidden them after blasphemy? But even if they forge one, they gain nothing. Their own doctrine, set beside the apostolic, will expose by its variety and contradiction that they have no apostolic author and are not apostolic; because just as the apostles never taught conflicting things among themselves, so apostolic men never proclaimed anything contrary to the apostles—unless those who learned from the apostles preached otherwise. Therefore, they will be tested against those churches which, though they cannot name an apostle or apostolic man as their founder because they are much later, indeed established daily, nevertheless conspire in the same faith and are reckoned no less apostolic by reason of doctrinal kinship. Thus all heresies, challenged by our churches to meet either standard, let them prove themselves apostolic as they imagine. But they are not, they cannot prove what they are not, and they are not received into peace and communion by churches that are in any way apostolic—precisely because of a sacramental difference that is in no way apostolic.

latin: Caeterum, si quae audent interserere se aetati apostolicae, ut ideo videantur ab Apostolis traditae, quia sub Apostolis fuerunt, possumus dicere: Edant ergo origines Ecclesiarum suarum: evolvant ordinem episcoporum suorum, ita per successiones ab initio decurrentem, ut primus ille episcopus aliquem ex Apostolis, vel apostolicis viris, qui tamen cum Apostolis perseveraverit, habuerit auctorem et antecessorem. Hoc enim modo Ecclesiae apostolicae census suos deferunt: sicut Smyrnaeorum Ecclesia Polycarpum ab Joanne conlocatum refert: sicut Romanorum, Clementem a Petro ordinatum edit; proinde utique et caeterae exhibent quos ab Apostolis in episcopatum constitutos apostolici seminis traduces habeant. Confingant tale aliquid Haeretici. Quid enim illis post blasphemiam inlicitum est? Sed etsi confinxerint, nihil promovebunt. Ipsa enim doctrina eorum cum apostolica comparata, ex diversitate et contrarietate sua pronuntiabit, neque apostoli alicujus auctoris esse, neque apostolici; quia sicut Apostoli non diversa inter se docuissent, ita et apostolici non contraria Apostolis edidissent, nisi illi qui ab Apostolis didicerunt aliter praedicaverunt. Ad hanc itaque formam probabuntur ab illis ecclesiis, quae licet nullum ex Apostolis, vel apostolicis, auctorem suum proferant, ut multo posteriores, quae denique quotidie instituuntur; tamen in eadem fide conspirantes, non minus apostolicae deputantur, pro consanguinitate doctrinae. Ita omnes haereses ad utramque formam nostris Ecclesiis provocatae, probent se quaqua putant apostolicas. Sed adeo nec sunt, nec probare possunt quod non sunt, nec recipiuntur in pacem et communicationem ab Ecclesiis quoquo modo apostolicis, scilicet ob diversitatem sacramenti nullo modo apostolicae.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: If you want to put your curiosity to better use for your own salvation, then make the rounds of the apostolic churches. In those churches the very chairs of the apostles still preside in their original places, and their authentic letters are read aloud, echoing each apostle's voice and preserving his likeness. Is Achaia nearby? You have Corinth. Not far from Macedonia? You have Philippi and the Thessalonians. Able to reach Asia? You have Ephesus. If you border Italy, you have Rome, from which authority is also close at hand for us. What a blessed church! The apostles poured out their entire teaching there with their own blood; Peter matched the Lord's passion there; Paul was crowned with John's death there; and the apostle John, after being plunged into boiling oil and suffering no harm, was exiled to an island. Let us see what he learned and taught when he contended with the African churches as well. He acknowledges one God, the Creator of all, and Christ Jesus, the Son of God the Creator, born of the Virgin Mary, and the resurrection of the flesh. He blends the Law and the Prophets with the gospel and apostolic writings, draws his faith from them, seals it with water, clothes it with the Holy Spirit, feeds it with the Eucharist, urges it toward martyrdom, and on that basis admits no one who opposes this rule. This is the rule — not merely one that foretold future heresies, but the one from which heresies actually sprang. Yet they did not come from it, because they were formed against it. Even from the kernel of the olive a wild, bitter oleaster springs up; even from the poppy a most pleasing and sweet fig, a windy and empty caprifig, arises. So heresies come from our fruit, not our stock — from the grain of truth, but growing wild with falsehood.

latin: Age jam, qui voles curiositatem melius exercere in negotio salutis tuae, percurre Ecclesias apostolicas, apud quas ipsae adhuc cathedrae Apostolorum suis locis praesident; apud quas ipsae authenticae litterae eorum recitantur, sonantes vocem et repraesentantes faciem uniuscujusque. Proxima est tibi Achaia? habes Corinthum. Si non longe es a Macedonia, habes Philippos, habes Thessalonicenses. Si potes in Asiam tendere, habes Ephesum. Si autem Italiae adjaces, habes Romam, unde nobis quoque auctoritas praesto est. Ista quam felix Ecclesia! cui totam doctrinam Apostoli cum sanguine suo profuderunt; ubi Petrus passioni Dominicae adaequatur; ubi Paulus Joannis exitu coronatur; ubi Apostolus Joannes, posteaquam, in oleum igneum demersus, nihil passus est, in insulam relegatur; videamus quid didicerit, quid docuerit, cum Africanis quoque Ecclesiis contesserarit. Unum Deum novit, creatorem universitatis, et Christum Jesum ex virgine Maria Filium Dei creatoris, et carnis resurrectionem; Legem et Prophetas cum evangelicis et apostolicis litteris miscet, et inde potat fidem; eam aqua signat, Sancto Spiritu vestit, eucharistia pascit, ad martyrium exhortatur, et ita adversus hanc institutionem neminem recipit. Haec est institutio, non dico jam quae futuras haereses praenuntiabat, sed de qua haereses prodierunt. Sed non fuerunt ex illa, ex quo factae sunt adversus illam. Etiam de olivae nucleo mitis et optimae et necessariae asper oleaster oritur; etiam de papavere ficus gratissimae et suavissimae ventosa et vana caprificus exsurgit. Ita et haereses de nostro frutice, non nostro genere; veritatis grano, sed mendacio sylvestres.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: If things stand this way—if the truth is awarded to us, who follow the rule that the Church received from the Apostles, the Apostles from Christ, Christ from God—then the logic of our position is settled: heretics must not be admitted to a contest over Scripture, because we prove, even without Scripture, that they have no claim on it. If they are heretics, they cannot be Christians; they possess nothing from Christ, having chosen to follow their own preference and taken the name 'heretic.' Not being Christians, they hold no right to Christian writings. We are therefore justified in demanding: Who are you? When and where did you come from? What are you doing on my property—property that is not yours? By what right, Marcion, do you cut down my forest? By what license, Valentine, do you divert my springs? By what authority, Apelles, do you move my boundary markers? What are the rest of you sowing and grazing here at your own pleasure? This possession is mine; I have held it for a long time. My title is firm, traced back to the very authors to whom the truth belonged. I am the heir of the Apostles. Just as they safeguarded it in their testament, entrusted it to the faith, and bound it with an oath, so I hold it. You, on the other hand, have always been disinherited and renounced—strangers, enemies. And how else could heretics be strangers and enemies to the Apostles except through a divergence in doctrine, which each one either invented or adopted on his own authority against the Apostles?

latin: Si haec ita se habent, ut veritas nobis adjudicetur, quicumque in ea regula incedimus quam Ecclesia ab Apostolis, Apostoli a Christo, Christus a Deo tradidit, constat ratio propositi nostri, definientis non esse admittendos haereticos ad ineundam de Scripturis provocationem, quos sine Scripturis probamus ad Scripturas non pertinere. Si enim haeretici sunt, christiani esse non possunt, non a Christo habendo quod de sua electione sectati haereticorum nomine admittunt. Ita non christiani, nullum jus capiunt christianarum litterarum. Ad quos merito dicendum est: Qui estis? quando, et unde venistis? quid in meo agitis, non mei? quo denique, Marcion, jure sylvam meam caedis? qua licentia, Valentine, fontes meos transvertis? qua potestate, Apelles, limites meos commoves? Quid hic caeteri ad voluntatem vestram seminatis et pascitis? Mea est possessio; olim possideo: habeo origines firmas, ab ipsis auctoribus quorum fuit res. Ego sum haeres Apostolorum. Sicut caverunt testamento suo, sicut fidei commiserunt, sicut adjuraverunt, ita teneo. Vos certe exhaeredaverunt semper et abdicaverunt, ut extraneos, ut inimicos. Unde autem extranei et inimici Apostolis haeretici, nisi ex diversitate doctrinae, quam unusquisque de suo arbitrio adversus Apostolos, aut protulit, aut recepit?

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: So that is where you have to locate the corruption of Scripture and its interpretation -- right where divergent doctrine shows up. People who set out to teach something different were forced to retool the instruments of doctrine, because they could not teach differently unless they had different tools to teach with. Just as their doctrinal corruption could not have succeeded without corrupting its instruments, so our doctrinal integrity would not be possible without the integrity of the means through which doctrine is handled.

What exactly is the case against us in our own writings? What private material have we ever introduced to fix something contrary to Scripture by subtracting, adding, or transposing? The Scriptures are what we are from their very beginning; we come from them, before anything was otherwise, before you interpolated them. Since every interpolation is by definition later, springing from rivalry -- a rivalry that is neither prior nor native to the thing it rivals -- it is absurd to any wise person that we, who are first and derived from Scripture, should be accused of foisting an adulterated style onto it, while they, who are later and opposed, are not.

One man corrupts Scripture with his hand, another corrupts its sense with his explanation. Even if Valentinus appears to use an intact text, he did not lay hands on the truth with any less cunning than Marcion. Marcion wielded a butcher's cleaver openly, not a pen, because he slaughtered Scripture to supply his own material. Valentinus spared the text, but only because he did not devise Scripture for his material; he devised his material for Scripture. Yet he subtracted more and added more, stripping away the proper force of each word and inserting arrangements of things that do not compare.

latin: Illic igitur et Scripturarum et expositionum adulteratio deputanda est, ubi diversitas doctrinae invenitur. Quibus fuit propositum aliter docendi, eos necessitas coegit aliter disponendi instrumenta doctrinae. Alias enim non potuissent aliter docere, nisi aliter haberent per quae docerent. Sicut illis non potuisset succedere corruptela doctrinae sine corruptela instrumentorum ejus; ita et nobis integritas doctrinae non competisset sine integritate eorum, per quae doctrina tractatur. Etenim quid contrarium nobis in nostris? quid de proprio intulimus, ut aliquid contrarium ei quod esset in Scripturis deprehensum, detractione, vel adjectione, vel transmutatione remediaremus? Quod sumus, hoc sunt Scripturae ab initio suo; ex illis sumus, antequam aliter fuit, antequam a vobis interpolarentur. Cum autem omnis interpolatio posterior credenda sit, veniens utique ex caussa aemulationis, quae neque prior, neque domestica unquam est ejus quod aemulatur, tam incredibile est sapienti cuique, ut nos adulterum stylum intulisse videamur Scripturis, qui sumus et primi et ex ipsis, quam illos non intulisse, qui sunt et posteri et adversi. Alius manu Scripturas, alius sensus expositione intervertit. Neque enim si Valentinus integro instrumento uti videtur, non callidiore ingenio, quam Marcion, manus intulit veritati. Marcion enim exerte et palam machaera, non stylo usus est; quoniam ad materiam suam caedem Scripturarum confecit. Valentinus autem pepercit; quoniam non ad materiam Scripturas, sed materiam ad Scripturas excogitavit: et tamen plus abstulit, et plus adjecit, auferens proprietates singulorum quoque verborum, et adjiciens dispositiones non comparentium rerum.

excerpts.author: Origen
english: All who believe and are certain that grace and truth came through Jesus Christ, and who know that Christ himself is the truth — just as he said, "I am the truth" (John 14:6) — receive the knowledge that moves people to live well and blessedly from nowhere else than Christ's own words and teaching. When we speak of Christ's words, we do not mean only what he taught as a man in the flesh; for Christ was the Word of God in Moses and the prophets long before. Without the Word of God, how could they have prophesied about Christ? To prove this point it would not be hard to show from the divine Scriptures how Moses and the prophets, filled with the Spirit of Christ, spoke and did everything they did — but our aim is to finish this present work with all possible brevity. So I judge that this single testimony from Paul in his letter to the Hebrews is enough: "By faith Moses, when he grew up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter, choosing rather to be mistreated with the people of God than to enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin. He considered the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt" (Heb 11:24–26). And even after his assumption into heaven, Paul shows that Christ spoke in him, saying, "Or do you seek proof that Christ is speaking in me?" (2 Cor 13:3).

Since many who profess faith in Christ disagree not only in small and minor matters but also in great and major ones — whether about God, or about the Lord Jesus Christ, or about the Holy Spirit, and not only about these but also about other creatures, that is, about dominions or holy virtues — it seems necessary first to lay down a certain and clear rule concerning each of these, and only then to investigate the rest. Just as, when many among Greeks and barbarians promised the truth, we stopped seeking it among all who asserted it with false opinions, once we believed that the Son of God, Christ, is the truth and convinced ourselves that we must learn it from him — so also now, when many think they hold the mind of Christ and some of them differ from their predecessors, the ecclesiastical preaching that has been preserved through the succession of the apostles and remains in the churches to the present is the only truth to be believed, the one that in nothing disagrees with the ecclesiastical and apostolic tradition.

One must know that the holy apostles, when they preached the faith of Christ, handed down as clearly as possible the things they believed necessary for all believers — even for those who seemed slower in the pursuit of divine knowledge — leaving the reasoning behind their assertions to be investigated by those who would merit the excellent gifts of the Spirit, and especially the grace of speech, wisdom, and knowledge through the Holy Spirit. But about other matters they said only that they exist; they were silent on how or from where they exist. This they did so that the more studious among their successors, lovers of wisdom, might have an exercise in which to show the fruit of their genius — those, namely, who prepared themselves to be worthy and capable of receiving wisdom.

The things that are plainly handed down through apostolic preaching are these. First, that there is one God who created and ordered all things, and who, when nothing existed, brought the universe into being — the God of the first creation and ordering of the world, the God of all the righteous from Adam, Abel, Seth, Enos, Enoch, Noah, Shem, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, the twelve patriarchs, Moses, and the prophets. And that this God, in the last days, as he had promised through his prophets, sent the Lord Jesus Christ — first to call Israel, and then also the Gentiles after the unfaithfulness of the people of Israel. This God is just and good, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who gave the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospels, and who is the God of the apostles and of both the Old and New Testaments.

Then, that Jesus Christ, who came, was born from the Father before all creation. Having served the Father in the ordering of all things — "for through him all things were made" (John 1:3) — in the last times he emptied himself, became man, was incarnate, and, though he was God, remained what he was: God. He assumed a body like our own, differing only in that he was born of a virgin and the Holy Spirit. And because this Jesus Christ was born and suffered in truth, and not in appearance, he truly died this common death; for he truly rose from the dead, and after his resurrection he conversed with his disciples and was taken up.

Then they handed down that the Holy Spirit is associated with the Father and the Son in honor and dignity. Here it is not yet clearly discerned whether he is begotten or unbegotten, or whether he should be reckoned as the Son of God; but these things must be investigated from Holy Scripture and sought out with careful inquiry. Certainly it is preached most clearly in the church that the same Holy Spirit inspired each of the saints, whether prophets or apostles — and that there is not one Spirit in the Old Testament and another in those who were inspired at the advent of Christ.

After this, the church preaches that the soul, having its own substance and life, when it departs from this world will be dispensed according to its merits: either to inherit eternal life and blessedness, if its deeds have earned it, or to be handed over to eternal fire and torments, if the guilt of its sins has led it there. And also that there will be a time of the resurrection of the dead, and this body, which now "is sown in corruption, will rise in incorruption, and what is sown in dishonor will rise in glory" (1 Cor 15:42–43). It is also defined in the ecclesiastical preaching that every rational soul has free will and its own volition; and that it has a struggle against the devil and his angels and contrary powers, because they try to burden it with sins, while we, if we live rightly and wisely, strive to strip off that kind of stain. From this it follows that we are not subject to necessity, forced to do either good or evil even against our will; for if we are masters of our own choice, perhaps some powers may attack us toward sin and others help us toward salvation, but we are not compelled by necessity to act rightly or wrongly. That is what those think who make the course and motion of the stars the cause of human actions — not only of those things that fall outside the freedom of choice, but even of those that lie within our own power.

The church's preaching does not clearly distinguish whether the soul is derived from the seed by traducianism, so that its reason or substance is held to be inserted in the bodily seeds themselves, or whether it has another origin — and whether that origin is begotten or unbegotten, or certainly whether it is infused into the body from outside or not. About the devil also, and his angels and contrary powers, the ecclesiastical preaching teaches that they exist, but it has not clearly explained what they are or how they are. Among many, however, the opinion prevails that this devil was an angel who, having apostatized, persuaded very many angels to desert with him — and they are now called his angels.

There is also this in the ecclesiastical preaching: that this world was made and began at a certain time, and that it will be dissolved because of its own corruption. But what was before this world, or what will be after it, has not been made clearly known to many. For no clear sermon on these things is put forward in the ecclesiastical preaching.

Then also, that the Scriptures were written by the Spirit of God and have a sense not only the one that is on the surface, but also another, hidden, sense for very many. For these are the forms that describe certain sacraments and images of divine things. The whole church agrees on this: that the whole Law is spiritual, yet what the Law breathes is not known to all, but only to those to whom the grace of the Holy Spirit is granted in the word of wisdom and knowledge. The term "incorporeal" is unusual and unknown not only among many others, but even in our own Scriptures. If someone should try to bring against us a passage from the little book called The Teaching of Peter, where the Savior seems to say to the disciples, "I am not an incorporeal demon," one must first answer that the book itself is not counted among the ecclesiastical books, and must show that neither is the writing Peter's nor that of anyone else inspired by the Spirit of God. Even if that were granted, the sense indicated there by this saying is not the same as the one exhibited by Greek or Gentile authors when they dispute the incorporeal nature in philosophy. For in that little book — "incorporeal demon" — he said it because that being, whoever it is, does not have a body like our grosser and visible body; but according to the sense of the one who composed that writing, it must be understood that he meant: he does not have the kind of body demons have (which is naturally a certain subtle, almost airy body, and therefore is thought or called incorporeal by many), but he has a solid and tangible body. For in human usage, anything that is not such a body is called incorporeal by simpler or less instructed people — just as if someone called this air we breathe incorporeal, because it is not a body that can be grasped, held, or resisted when pressed.

Still we will inquire whether the very thing that Greek philosophers call "incorporeal" is found in Holy Scripture under another name. How God himself is to be understood must also be investigated: whether he is corporeal and has some deformed shape, or of another nature than bodies — which is certainly not explicitly designated in our preaching. The same must be inquired also about Christ and about the Holy Spirit, and no less about every soul and every rational nature. There is also this in the ecclesiastical preaching: that there are certain angels of God and good powers who serve him for the accomplishment of human salvation; but when they were created, or of what kind, or how they are, is not clearly distinguished. About the sun, moon, and stars, whether they are animate or soulless, nothing is plainly handed down. Therefore we must use such things as elements and foundations, according to the command that says, "Illuminate for yourselves the light of knowledge" (cf. Ps 36:10), so that anyone who wishes may complete a system and a body of doctrine from the reasoning of all these things, and, as we said, may make one coherent whole with clear and necessary assertions, investigating what is true about each thing — either from the examples and affirmations found in Holy Scripture, or from those discovered through investigation of the consequences and their right tenor.

latin: Omnes qui eredunt et certi sunt quod gratia et veritas per lesum Christum facta sit, et Christum esse veritatem norunt, secundum quod ipse dixit: “Ego sum veritas”, scientiam quae provocat homines ad bene beateque vivendum non aliunde quam ab ipsis Christi verbis doetrinaque suscipiunt. Christi autem verbis dieimus non his solum, quae homo factus atque in carne positus docuit; et prius namque Christus dei verbum in Moyse atque in prophetis erat. Nam sine verbo dei quomodo poterant prophetare de Christo? Ad cuius rei probationem non esset difficile ex divinis seripturis ostendere, quomodo vel Moyses vel prophetae spiritu Christi repleti vel locuti sunt vel gesserunt omnia quae gesserunt, nisi studii nobis esset, praesens hoc opus omni qua possumus brevitate suecingere. Unde sufficere aestimo uno hoc Pauli testimonio debere nos uti ex epistula, quam ad Hebraeos scribit, in qua ita ait: “Fide magnus factus Moyses negavit se dici filium filiae Pharaonis, magis eligens afflietari cum populo dei quam temporalem habere peccati iueunditatem, maiores divitias aestimans Aegyptiorum thesauris inproperium Christi”. Sed et post adsumptionem eius in caelos quod in apostolis suis loeutus sit, hoc modo indicat Paulus: “Aut numquid probamentum quaeritis eius, qui in me loquitur Christus?” 2. Quoniam ergo multi ex his, qui Christo se credere profitentur, non solum in parvis et minimis discordant, verum etiam in magnis et maximis, id est vel de deo vel de ipso domino lesu Christo vel de spiritu sancto, non solum autem de his, sed et de alus creaturis, id est vel de dominationibus vel de virtutibus sanctis: propter hoc necessarium videtur prius de his singulis certam lineam manifestamque regulam ponere, tum deinde etiam de ceteris quaerere. Sicut enim, multis apud Graecos et barbaros pollicentibus veritatem, desivimus apud omnes eam quaerere, qui eam falsis opinionibus asserebant, posteaquam eredidimus fihum esse dei Christum et ab ipso nobis hane discendam esse persuasimus: ita eum multi sint, qui se putant sentire quae Christi sunt, et nonnulh eorum diversa a prioribus sentiant, servetur vero ecclesiastica praedicatio per successionis ordinem ab apostolis tradita et usque ad praesens in ecclesiis permanens, illa sola credenda est veritas, quae in nullo ab ecclesiastica et apostolica traditione discordat. 3. Illud autem scire oportet, quoniam sancti apostoli fidem Christi praedieantes de quibusdam quidem, quaecumque necessaria crediderunt, p omnibus eredentibus, etiam his, qui pigriores erga inquisitionem divinae scientiae videbantur, manifestissime tradiderunt, rationem seilicet assertioms eorum relinquentes ab his inquirendam, qui spiritus dona excellentia mererentur et praecipue sermonis, sapientiae et scientiae gratiam per ipsum sanctum spiritum percepissent; de aliis vero dixerunt quidem quia sint, quomodo autem aut unde sint, siluerunt, profecto ut studiosiores quique ex posteris suis, qui amatores essent sapientiae, exercitium habere possent, in quo ingenii sui fructum ostenderent, hi videlicet, qui dignos se et capaces ad recipiendam sapientiam praepararent. 4. Species vero eorum, quae per praedicationem apostolicam manifeste traduntur, istae sunt. Primo, quod unus est deus, qui omnia creavit atque composuit, quique, cum nihil esset, esse fecit universa, deus a prima creatura et conditione mundi, omnium iustorum deus, Adam Abel Seth Enos Enoch No? Sem Abraham Isaac lacob duodecim patriarcharum Moysei et prophetarum; et quod hie deus in novissimis diebus, sicut per prophetas suos ante promiserat, misit dominum lesum Christum, primo quidem vocaturum Israhel, secundo vero etiam gentes post perfidiam populi Israhel. Hie deus iustus et bonus, pater domini nostri lesu Christi, legem et prophetas et evangelia ipse dedit, qui et apostolorum deus est et veteris ac novi testamenti. Tum deinde quia Christus lesus, ipse qui venit, ante omnem creaturam natus ex patre est. Qui cum in omnium conditione patri ministrasset, “per ipsum” namque “omnia facta sunt”, novissimis temporibus se ipsum exinaniens homo factus est, incarnatus est, cum deus esset, et homo factus mansit quod erat, deus. Corpus assumsit nostro corpori simile, eo solo differens, quod natum ex virgine et spiritu sancto est. Et quoniam hie lesus Christus natus et passus est in veritate, et non per phantasiam, communem hanc mortem vere mortuus; vere enim et a mortuis resurrexit et post resurrectionem conversatus cum diseipulis suis assumtus est. Tum deinde honore ac dignitate patri ac filio sociatum tradiderunt spiritum sanctum. In hoe non iam manifeste discernitur, utrum natus aut innatus, vel filius etiam ipse dei habendus sit, neene; sed inquirenda iam ista pro viribus sunt de sancta scriptura et sagaci perquisitione investiganda. Sane quod iste spiritus sanctus unumquemque sanctorum vel prophetarum vel apostolorum inspiraverit, et non alius spiritus in veteribus, alius vero in his, qui in adventu Christi inspirati sunt, fuerit, manifestissime in ecclesia praedicatur. 9. Post haec iam quod anima substantiam vitamque habens propriam, cum ex hoe mundo discesserit, pro suis meritis dispensabitur, sive vitae aeternae ac beatitudinis hereditate potitura, si hoc ei sua gesta praestiterint, sive igni aeterno ac supplieus mancipanda, si in hoc eam scelerum culpa detorserit; sed et quia erit tempus resurrectionis mortuorum, eum corpus hoc, quod nune “in corruptione seminatur, surget in incorruptionec, et quod “seminatur in ignominia, surget in gloria”. Est et illud definitum in eeclesiastica praedicatione, omnem animam rationabilem esse liberi arbitru et voluntatis; esse quoque ei certamen adversum diabolum et angelos eius contrariasque virtutes, ex eo quod ili peccatis eam onerare contendant, nos vero si recte consulteque vivamus, ab huiuscemodi labe exuere nos conemur. Unde et consequens est intellegere, non nos necessitati esse subiectos, ut omni modo, etiamsi nolimus, vel mala vel bona agere cogamur. Si enim nostri arbitri! sumus, inpugnare nos fortasse possint aliquae virtutes ad peccatum et aliae iuvare ad salutem, non tamen necessitate cogimur vel recte agere vel male; quod fieri arbitrantur hi, qui stellarum cursum et motus causam dieunt humanorum esse gestorum, non solum eorum, quae extra arbitrii accidunt libertatem, sed et eorum, quae in nostra sunt posita potestate. De anima vero utrum ex seminis traduce ducatur, ita ut ratio ipsius vel substantia inserta ipsis corporalibus seminibus habeatur, an vero aliud habeat initium, et hoc ipsum initium si genitum est aut non genitum, vel certe si extrinsecus corpori inditur, necne: non satis manifesta praedicatione distinguitur. 6. De diabolo quoque et angelis eius contrarüsque virtutibus ecelesiastica praedicatio docuit quoniam sint quidem haec, quae autem sint vel quomodo sint, non satis clare exposuit. Apud plurimos tamen ista habetur opinio, quod angelus fuerit iste diabolus, et apostata effectus quam plurimos angelorum secum declinare persuaserit, qui et nune usque angel ipsius nuncupantur. 7. Est praeterea et illud in eeclesiastiea praedicatione, quod mundus iste factus sit et a certo tempore coeperit et sit pro 1psa sui corruptione solvendus. Quid tamen ante hunc mundum fuerit, aut quid post mundum erit, jam non pro manifesto multis innotuit. Non enim evidens de his in ecclesiastica praedicatione sermo profertur. 8. Tum deinde quod per spiritum dei seripturae conscriptae sint et sensum habeant non eum solum, qui in manifesto est, sed et alium quendam latentem quam plurimos. Formae enim sunt haec quae descripta sunt sacramentorum quorundam et divinarum rerum imagines. De quo totius eeclesiae una sententia est, esse quidem omnem legem spiritalem, non tamen ea, quae spirat lex, esse omnibus nota nisi his solis, quibus gratia spiritus sancti in verbo sapientiae ac scientiae condonatur. Appellatio autem (id est incorporei) non solum apud multos alios, verum etiam apud nostras scripturas inusitata est et incognita. Si vero quis velt nobis proferre ex illo libello, qui Petri Doctrina appellatur, ubi salvator videtur ad discipulos dieere: “Non sum daemonium incorporeum”, primo respondendum est ei quoniam liber ipse inter libros eeclesiasticos non habetur, et ostendendum quia neque Petri est ipsa scriptura neque alterius cuiusquam, qui spiritu dei fuerit inspiratus. Quod etiamsi ipsum concederetur, non idem sensus inibi ex isto sermone indicatur, qui a graecis vel gentilibus auctoribus ostenditur, eum de incorporea natura a philosophis disputatur. In hoc enim libello -incorporeum daemonium: dixit pro eo, quod ipse ille quicumque est habitus vel eircumscriptio daemoniei corporis non est similis huie nostro crassiori et visibili corpori; sed secundum sensum eius, qui composuit illam scripturam, intellegendum est quod dixit, id est non se habere tale corpus quale habent daemones (quod est naturaliter subtile quoddam et velut aura tenue, et propter hoe vel putatur a multis vel dicitur incorporeum), sed habere se corpus solidum et palpabile. In consuetudine vero hominum omne, quod tale non fuerit, incorporeum a simplicioribus vel imperitioribus nominatur; velut si quis aérem istum quo fruimur incorporeum dieat, quoniam quidem non est tale corpus, ut conprehendi ac teneri possit urgentique resistere. 9. Quaeremus tamen si vel alio nomine res ipsa, quam graeci philosophi (id est ineorporeum) dicunt, in sanctis scripturis invenitur. Deus quoque ipse quomodo intellegi debeat requirendum est, corporeus et secundum aliquem habitum deformatus, an alterius naturae quam corpora sunt, quod utique in praedicatione nostra manifeste non designatur. Eadem quoque etiam de Christo et de saneto spiritu requirenda sunt, sed et de omni anima atque omni rationabili natura nihilominus requirendum est. Est etiam illud in eeclesiastica praedicatione, esse angelos dei quosdam et virtutes bonas, qui ei ministrant ad salutem hominum con- "^" summandam; sed quando isti creati sint, vel quales, aut quomodo sint, non satis in manifesto distinguitur. De sole autem et luna et stellis, utrum animantia sint an sine anima, manifeste non traditur. Oportet igitur velut elementis ac fundamentis huiusmodi uti secundum mandatum, quod dicit: “Inluminate vobis lumen scientiae”, omnem qui eupit seriem quandam et corpus ex horum omnium ratione perficere, ut manifestis et necessarüs assertionibus de singulis quibusque quid sit in vero rimetur, et unum, ut diximus, corpus efficiat exemplis et affirmationibus, vel his, quas in sanctis scripturis invenerit, vel quas ex consequentiae ipsius indagine ac recti tenore reppererit.

excerpts.author: Cyprian
english: When the Lord warns us, 'You are the salt of the earth' (Matt 5:13), and commands us to be simple in innocence yet prudent in that same simplicity, what else should we do, beloved brothers, than take care? We must watch with anxious hearts, discerning and guarding against the cunning enemy's treacherous plots, lest we who have put on Christ, the wisdom of God the Father, appear less wise in protecting our salvation. It is not only open persecution that threatens, nor only those assaults that attack God's servants plainly and throw them down. Caution comes easily when danger is visible, and the mind readies itself for battle when the adversary shows his face. The enemy is far more to be feared and avoided when he steals in secretly, disguising himself with a façade of peace and slipping in by hidden approaches — which is why he bears the name of the serpent. This is his constant craft: a blind, concealed deceit that entraps mankind. From the very beginning of the world he deceived, coaxing simple souls with lying words and catching them in unsuspecting credulity. He even dared to tempt the Lord Himself, stealing close in another attempt to deceive; but he was recognized and repulsed, thrown down because he had been detected. This gives us our pattern: flee the way of the old man, plant our feet in the steps of the living Christ, so that we do not fall unawares again into death's snare, but, foreseeing the danger, may lay hold of immortality.

And how can we lay hold of immortality unless we keep the commandments of Christ, by which death is overcome and conquered? He Himself warns and says, 'If you wish to enter life, keep the commandments,' and again, 'If you do what I command you, I no longer call you servants, but friends' (John 15:14-15). These, finally, He calls strong and stable, founded on a massive rock, set fast with immovable, unshakable firmness against every tempest and whirlwind of the world. 'Whoever hears my words and does them,' He says, 'I will liken to a wise man who built his house on rock. The rain fell, the rivers rose, the winds blew and beat against that house, and it did not fall, because it had been founded on rock' (Matt 7:24-27). We must therefore stand firm on His words, learning and doing whatever He taught and commanded. How can someone claim to believe in Christ while refusing to do what Christ commanded? Where will such a one find the reward of faith who will not keep the faith of the commandment? He must waver and wander, seized by a spirit of error and blown about like dust before the wind; he will never advance toward salvation who does not hold to the truth of the saving way.

But we must be on guard, beloved brothers, not only against what is open and plain, but also against what deceives with the subtlety of cunning fraud. What could be more cunning, more subtle, than this: the enemy, detected and thrown down by Christ's advent, after the light has come to the Gentiles and the saving light has shone for mankind — so that the deaf receive the hearing of spiritual grace, the blind open their eyes to God, the weak recover eternal health, the lame run to the Church, the mute pray with clear voices — seeing idols abandoned and his own seats and temples deserted by the multitude of believers, he devises a new fraud to deceive the unwary under the very title of the Christian name? He invents heresies and schisms to subvert faith, corrupt truth, and tear apart unity. Those he cannot hold in the blindness of the old way, he encircles and deceives by the error of a new way. He snatches men from the very Church; and while they think they have approached the light and escaped the world's darkness, he pours fresh darkness upon them, unknown to them, so that — not standing with the Gospel of Christ, its observance, and its law — they still call themselves Christians, and walking in darkness believe they possess the light. The adversary flatters and deceives, transforming himself, as the Apostle says, into an angel of light, and disguising his ministers as ministers of righteousness. They declare night to be day, destruction to be salvation, despair under the pretext of hope, perfidy under the pretext of faith, antichrist under the name of Christ — so that, by speaking what sounds plausible, they frustrate the truth with subtlety. This happens, beloved brothers, when we do not return to the source of truth, nor seek the Head, nor preserve the doctrine of the heavenly Master.

latin: CUM moneat Dominus et dicat: Vos estis sal terrae, cumque esse nos jubeat ad innocentiam simplices, et tamen cum simplicitate prudentes, quid aliud, fratres dilectissimi, quam providere nos convenit, et sollicito corde vigilantes, subdoli hostis insidias intelligere pariter et cavere ne qui Christum sapientiam Dei Patris induimus, minus sapere in tuenda salute videamur? Neque enim persecutio sola metuenda est et ea quae subruendis ac dejiciendis Dei servis aperta impugnatione grassantur. Facilior cautio est ubi manifesta formido est, et ad certamen animus ante praestruitur quando se adversarius confitetur. Plus metuendus est et cavendus inimicus cum latenter obrepit, cum, per pacis imaginem fallens, occultis accessibus serpit; unde et nomen serpentis accepit. Ea est ejus semper astutia, ea est circumveniendi hominis caeca et latebrosa fallacia. Sic ab initio statim mundi fefellit, et, verbis mendacibus blandiens, rudes animas incauta credulitate decepit. Dominum ipsum tentare conatus, quasi obreperet rursus et falleret, latenter accessit. Intellectus tamen est et retusus; et ideo prostratus, quia agnitus atque detectus. Unde nobis exemplum datum est veteris hominis viam fugere, vestigiis Christi viventis insistere; ne denuo incauti in mortis laqueum revolvamur, sed, ad periculum providi, accepta immortalitate potiamur. Immortalitate autem potiri quomodo possumus, nisi ea quibus mors expugnatur et vincitur, Christi mandata servemus, ipso monente et dicente: Si vis ad vitam venire, serva mandata. Et iterum: Si feceritis quae mando vobis, jam non dico vos servos, sed amicos. Hos denique fortes dicit et stabiles, hos super petram robusta mole fundatos, hos contra omnes tempestates et turbines saeculi immobili et inconcussa firmitate solidatos. Qui audit, inquit, verba mea et facit ea, similabo eum viro sapienti qui aedificavit domum suam supra petram. Descendit pluvia, venerunt flumina, flaverunt venti et impegerunt in domum illam, et non cecidit; fundata enim fuit super petram. Verbis igitur ejus insistere, quaecumque et docuit et fecit discere et facere debemus. Caeterum credere se in Christum, quomodo dicit qui non facit quod Christus facere praecepit? Aut unde perveniet ad praemium fidei, qui fidem non vult servare mandati? Nutet necesse est et vagetur, et, spiritu erroris abreptus, velut pulvis quem ventus excutit ventiletur; nec ambulando proficiet ad salutem, qui salutaris viae non tenet veritatem. Cavenda sunt autem, fratres dilectissimi, non solum quae sunt aperta atque manifesta, sed et astutae fraudis subtilitate fallentia. Quid vero astutius, quidve subtilius, quam ut Christi adventu detectus ac prostratus inimicus, postquam lux Gentibus venit et sospitandis hominibus salutare lumen effulsit, ut surdi auditum gratiae spiritalis admitterent, aperirent ad Deum oculos suos caeci, infirmi aeterna sanitate revalescerent, claudi ad Ecclesiam currerent, muti claris vocibus et precibus orarent, videns ille idola derelicta et per nimium credentium populum sedes suas ac templa deserta, excogitaverit novam fraudem, ut sub ipso christiani nominis titulo fallat incautos? Haereses invenit et schismata, quibus subverteret fidem, veritatem corrumperet, scinderet unitatem. Quos detinere non potest in viae veteris caecitate, circumscribit et decipit novi itineris errore. Rapit de ipsa Ecclesia homines; et, dum sibi appropinquasse jam lumini atque evasisse saeculi noctem videntur, alias nescientibus tenebras rursus infundit, ut cum Evangelio Christi et cum observatione ejus et lege non stantes, Christianos se vocent, et ambulantes in tenebris habere se lumen existiment, blandiente adversario atque fallente, qui, secundum Apostoli vocem, transfigurat se velut angelum lucis, et ministros suos subornat velut ministros justitiae, asserentes noctem pro die, interitum pro salute, desperationem sub obtentu spei, perfidiam sub praetextu fidei, antichristum sub vocabulo Christi; ut, dum verisimilia mentiuntur, veritatem subtilitate frustrentur. Hoc eo fit, fratres dilectissimi, dum ad veritatis originem non reditur, nec caput quaeritur, nec magistri coelestis doctrina servatur.

excerpts.author: Eusebius of Caesarea
english: He has left us a great many notes that show a well‑educated mind diligently applied to divine matters, and they are full of every kind of help; we will direct eager learners to them, having usefully recorded what has come to our knowledge.

One of his works is an address to Antoninus — the one so named — and to his children and the Roman Senate, speaking on behalf of our doctrines; another is a second apology for our faith, addressed to the successor and namesake of that emperor, Aurelian Verus, whose deeds we will discuss in due course.

There is also a treatise to the Greeks in which he develops a long argument on many questions debated among us and the Greek philosophers, especially the nature of demons; we need not set that one out now.

Yet another writing of his addressed to the Greeks has reached us, titled "Refutation," and still another on the monarchy of God, which he establishes not only from our own Scriptures but also from Greek books.

On these works a certain "Psalter" was composed, and there is also a scholastic treatise "On the Soul" in which, after laying out various opinions on the problem at hand, he presents the views of the Greek philosophers; he promises to answer those views and to set forth his own opinion in another work.

greek: Πλεῖστα δὲ οὗτος καταλέλοιπεν ἡμῖν πεπαιδευμένης διανοίας καὶ περὶ τὰ θεῖα ἐσπουδακυίας ὑπομνήματα, πάσης ὠφελείας ἔμπλεα· ἐφ’ ἃ τοὺς φιλομαθεῖς ἀναπέμψομεν, τὰ εἰς ἡμετέραν γνῶσιν ἐλθόντα χρησίμως παρασημηνάμενοι. ὁ μέν τίς ἐστιν αὐτῷ λόγος πρὸς ’ Αντωνῖνον τὸν προσαγορευθέντα καὶ τοὺς τούτου παῖδας τήν τε Ῥωμαίων σύγκλητον προσφωνητικὸς ὑπὲρ τῶν καθ’ ἡμᾶς δογμάτων, ὁ δὲ δευτέραν περιέχων ὑπὲρ τῆς ἡμετέρας πίστεως ἀπολογίαν, ἢν πρὸς τὸν τοῦ δεδηλωμένου αὐτοκράτορος διάδοχόν τε καὶ ὁμώνυμον Ἀωτωνῖνον Οὐῆρον, οὗ τὰ κατὰ τοὺς χρόνους ἐπὶ τοῦ παρόντος διέξιμεν· καὶ ἄλλος ὁ πρὸς Ἕλληνας, ἐν ᾧ μακρὸν περὶ πλείστων παρ’ ἡμῖν τε καὶ τοῖς Ἑλλήνων φιλοσόφοις ζητουμένων κατατείνας λόγον, περὶ τῆς τῶν δαιμόνων διαλαμβάνει φύσεως· ἃ οὐδὲν ἄν ἐπείγοι τὰ νῦν παρατίθεσθαι. καὶ αὖθις ἕτερον πρὸς Ἕλληνας εἰς ἡμᾶς ἐλήλυθεν αὐτοῦ σύγγραμμα, δ’ καὶ ἐπέγραφεν Ἕλεγχον, καὶ παρὰ τούτους ἄλλο περὶ θεοῦ μοναρχίας, ἢν οὐ μόνον ἐκ τῶν παρ’ ἡμῖν γραφῶν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν συνίστησιν βιβλίων· ἐπὶ τούτοις ἐπιγεγραμμένον Ψάλτης, καὶ ἄλλο σχολικὸν Περὶ ψυχῆς, ἐν ᾧ διαφόρους πεύσεις προτείνας περὶ τοῦ κατὰ τὴν ὑπόθεσιν προβλήματος , τῶν παρ’ Ἕλλησιν Φιλοσόφων παρατίοθεται τὰς δόξας, αἷς καὶ ἀντιλέξειν ὑπισχνεῖται τήν τε αὐτὸς αὐτοῦ δόξαν ἐν ἑτέρῳ παραθήσεσθαι συγγράμματι.

excerpts.author: Eusebius of Caesarea
english: During this period, Hegesippus—whom we know from earlier accounts—was thriving in the church, along with Dionysius, bishop of Corinth; Pinytus, another bishop in Crete; Philippus; Apollinarius; Melito; Musanus; Modestus; and above all, Irenaeus. It is from them that the orthodox written tradition of the apostolic teaching, or of the sound faith, has reached us.

greek: XXI. Ἥκμαζον δ’ ἐν τούτοις ἐπὶ τῆς ἐκκλησίας Ἡγήσιππόσ τε, ὅν ἵσμεν ἐκ τῶν προτέρων, καὶ Διονύσιος Κορινθίων ἐπίσκοπος Πινυτός τ’ ἑ ἄλλος τῶν ἐπὶ Κρήτης ἐπίσκοπος Φίλιππός τε ἐπὶ τούτοις καὶ Ἀπολινάριος καὶ Μελίτων Μουσανός τε καὶ Μόδεστος καὶ ἐπὶ πᾶσιν Εἰρήναιος, ὧν καὶ εἰς ἡμᾶς τῆς ἀποστολικῆς παραδόσεως ἢ τῆς ὑγιοῦς πίστεως ἔγγραφος κατῆλθεν ὀρθοδοξία.

excerpts.author: Eusebius of Caesarea
english: At this time, Melito, bishop of the parish in Sardis, and Apollinarius of the parish in Hierapolis were flourishing. Each of them presented an apology concerning the faith to the aforementioned Roman emperor. The following works of theirs have come to our knowledge: of Melito, the two books On the Passover; On the Commonwealth and the Prophets; On the Church; the discourse On the Lord's Day; On the Faith of Man; On Creation; On the Obedience of Faith; On the Senses; in addition to these, On the Soul and the Body; On Baptism; On Truth; On Faith and the Birth of Christ; his prophetic discourse; On the Soul and the Body (again); On Hospitality; the Key; On the Devil and the Revelation of John; On the Indwelling God; and above all, the little book To Antoninus.

In his work On the Passover, Melito indicates the time at which he was writing by beginning with these words: 'When Servillius Paulus was proconsul of Asia, at which time Sagaris bore witness as a martyr, a great dispute arose in Laodicea concerning the Passover, which had fallen at that time, and these things were recorded.' Clement of Alexandria mentions this discourse in his own work On the Passover, saying that he composed it because of Melito's writing.

greek: Ἐπὶ τῶνδε καὶ Μελίτων τῆς ἐν Σάρδεσιν παροικίας ἐπίσκοπος Ἀπολινάριός τε τῆς ἐν Ἱεραπόλει διαπρεπῶς ἤκμαζον, οἳ καὶ τῷ δηλω- θέντι κατὰ τοὺς χρόνους ‘ Ρωμαίων βασιλεῖ λόγους ὑπὲρ τῆς πίστεως ἰδίως ἑκάτερος ἀπολογίας προσεφώνησαν. τούτων εἰς ἡμετέραν γνῶσιν ἀφῖκται τὰ ὑποτεταγμένα· Μελίτωνος, τὰ Περὶ τοῦ πάσχα δύο καὶ τὸ Περὶ πολιτείας καὶ προφητῶν καὶ ὁ Περὶ ἐκκλησίας καὶ ὁ Περὶ κυριακῆς λόγος, ἔτι δὲ ὁ Περὶ πίστεως ἀνθρώπου καὶ ὁ Περὶ πλάσεως, καὶ ὁ Περὶ ὑπακοῆς πίστεως καὶ Περὶ] αἰσθητηρίων καὶ πρὸς τούτοις ὁ Περὶ ψυχῆς καὶ σώματος [ ηνενοισ] καὶ ὁ Περὶ λουτροῦ καὶ Περὶ ἀληθείας καὶ Περὶ πίστεως καὶ γενέσεως χριστοῦ καὶ λόγος αὐτοῦ προφητείας καὶ Περὶ ψυχῆς καὶ σώματος καὶ ὁ Περὶ φιλοξενίας καὶ ἡ Κλεὶς καὶ τὰ Περὶ τοῦ διαβόλου καὶ τῆς Ἀποκαλύψεως Ἰωάννου καὶ ὁ Περὶ ἐνσωμάτου θεοῦ, ἐπὶ πᾶσι καὶ τὸ Πρὸς Ἀντωνῖνον βιβλίδιον. Ἐν μὲν οὖν τῷ Περὶ τοῦ πάσχα τὸν χρόνον καθ’ ὅν συνέταττεν, ἀρχόμενος σημαίνει ἐν τούτοις· “ ἐπὶ Σερουιλλίου Παύλου ἀνθυπάτου τῆς Ἀσίας, ᾧ Σάγαρις καιρῷ ἐμαρτύρησεν, ἐγένετο ζήτησις πολλὴ ἐν Λαοδικείᾳ περὶ τοῦ πάσχα, ἐμπεσόντος κατὰ καιρὸν ἐν ἐκείναις ταῖς ἡμέραις, καὶ ἐγράφη παῦτα.” τούτου δὲ τοῦ λόγου μέμνηται Κλήμης ὁ Ἀλεξανδρεὺς ἐν ἰδίῳ Περὶ τοῦ πάσχα λόγῳ, ὃν ὡς ἐξ αἰτίας τῆς τοῦ Μελίτωνος γραφῆς φησιν ἑαυτὸν συντάξαι.

excerpts.author: Barnabas
english: Let us see whether this people or the first one inherits, and whether the covenant belongs to us or to them. Listen, then, to what the Scripture says about the people: Isaac prayed to the Lord for his wife Rebekah because she was barren, and she conceived (Genesis 25:21). Then Rebekah went to inquire of the Lord, and the Lord said to her, "Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples from within you will be separated; one people will be stronger than the other, and the older will serve the younger" (Genesis 25:23). You ought to understand who Isaac is and who Rebekah is, and on whose behalf he showed that this people is greater than that one. In another prophecy Jacob speaks more clearly to his son Joseph, saying, "Behold, the Lord has not deprived me of seeing your face; bring me your sons so that I may bless them" (Genesis 48:11). And he brought Ephraim and Manasseh, wanting Manasseh to be blessed because he was the older; for Joseph brought him to his father Jacob's right hand. But Jacob saw a type by the Spirit of the people in between, and what did he say? He crossed his hands and put his right hand on the head of Ephraim, the second and younger, and blessed him (Genesis 48:14). Joseph said to Jacob, "Put your right hand on the head of Manasseh, for he is my firstborn son" (Genesis 48:18). Jacob said to Joseph, "I know, my son, I know; but the greater shall serve the lesser, and this one also shall be blessed" (Genesis 48:19). See on whom he has placed his hand, making this people first and heir of the covenant. If then we are still reminded through Abraham, we lack the perfect knowledge of ours. What then does he say to Abraham when he was counted righteous through faith while still alone? "Behold, I have made you, Abraham, father of the nations who believe through uncircumcision in God" (Genesis 17:5).

greek: Ἴδωμεν δὲ εἰ οὗτος ὁ λαὸς κληρονομεῖ ἡ ὁ πρῶτος, καὶ εἰ ἡ διαθήκη εἰς ἡμᾶς ἢ εἰς ἐκείνους. ἀκούσατε οὖν περὶ τοῦ λαοῦ τί λέγει ἡ γραφή: Ἐδεῖτο δὲ Ἰσαὰκ περὶ Ῥεβέκκας τῆς γυναικὸς αὐτοῦ, ὅτι στεῖρα ἦν: καὶ συνέλαβεν. εἶτα ἐξῆλθεν Ῥεβέκκα πυθέσθαι παρὰ κυρίου, καὶ εἶπεν κύριος πρὸς αὐτήν: Δύο ἔθνη ἐν τῇ γαστρί σου καὶ δύο λαοὶ ἐν τῇ κοιλίᾳ σου, καὶ ὑπερέξει λαὸς λαοῦ καὶ ὁ μείζων δουλεύσει τῷ ἐλάσσονι. αἰσθάνεσθαι ὀφείλετε, τίς ὁ Ἰσαὰκ καὶ τίς ἡ Ῥεβέκκα. καὶ ἐπὶ τίνων δέδειχεν, ὅτι μείζων ὁ λαὸς οὗτος ἢ ἐκεῖνος. καὶ ἐν ἄλλῃ προφητείᾳ λέγει φανερώτερον ὁ Ἰακὼβ πρὸς Ἰωσὴφ τὸν υἱὸν αὐτοῦ, λέγων: Ἰδού, οὐκ ἐστέρησέν με κύριος τοῦ προσώπου σου: προσάγαγέ μοι τοὺς υἱούς σου, ἵνα εὐλογήσω αὐτούς. καὶ προσήγαγεν Ἐφραὶμ καὶ Μανασσῆ, τὸν Μανασσῆ θέλων ἵνα εὐλογηθῇ, ὅτι πρεσβύτερος ἦν: ὁ γὰρ Ἰωσὴφ προσήγαγεν εἰς τὴν δεξιὰν χεῖρα τοῦ πατρὸς Ἰακώβ. εἶδεν δὲ Ἰακὼβ τύπον τῷ πνεύματι τοῦ λαοῦ τοῦ μεταξύ: καὶ τί λέγει; Καὶ ἐποίησεν Ἰακὼβ ἐναλλὰξ τὰς χεῖρας αὐτοῦ καὶ ἐπέθηκεν τὴν δεξιὰν ἐπὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν Ἐφραίμ, τοῦ δευτέρου καὶ νεωτέρου, καὶ εὐλόγησεν αὐτόν. καὶ εἶπεν Ἰωσὴφ πρὸς Ἰακώβ: Μετάθες σου τὴν δεξιὰν ἐπὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν Μανασσῆ, ὅτι πρωτότοκός μου υἱός ἐστιν. καὶ εἶπεν Ἰακὼβ πρὸς Ἰωσήφ: Οἰδα, τέκνον, οἶδα: ἀλλ’ ὁ μείζων δουλεύσει τῷ ἐλάσσονι, καὶ οὗτος δὲ εὐλογηθήσεται. βλέπετε, ἐπὶ τίνων τέθεικεν, τὸν λαὸν τοῦτον εἶναι πρῶτον καὶ τῆς διαθήκης κληρονόμον. εἰ οὖν ἔτι καὶ διὰ τοῦ Ἀβραὰμ ἐμνήσθη, ἀπέχομεν τὸ τέλειον τῆς γνώσεως ἡμῶν. τί οὖν λέγει τῷ Ἀβραάμ, ὅτε μόνος πιστεύσας ἐτέθη εἰς δικαιοσύνην; Ἰδού, τέθεικά σε, Ἀβραάμ, πατέρα ἐθνῶν τῶν πιστευόντων δἰ ἀκροβυστίας τῷ θεῷ.

excerpts.author: Barnabas
english: Yes, but let us see whether the covenant God swore to give the people was actually given. It was given, but the people themselves were not worthy to receive it because of their sins. The prophet says that Moses fasted on Mount Sinai for forty days and forty nights to receive the Lord's covenant for the people. Moses received the two tablets, written by the finger of the Lord's own hand in the Spirit, and brought them down to give to the people. Then the Lord said to Moses, "Moses, Moses, come down quickly, because your people, whom you led out of Egypt, have acted lawlessly" (Exod 32:7). Moses understood they had made molten idols for themselves again, so he threw the tablets from his hands and they shattered. Moses received the covenant, but the people proved unworthy.

So how did we receive it? Learn this: Moses received it as a servant, but the Lord Himself gave it to us as a people of inheritance, having endured suffering for our sake. He was revealed so that they might be completed in their sins, and so that we, through the heir of the Lord's covenant, Jesus, might receive it. He was prepared for this very purpose: that by appearing He might redeem our hearts—hearts already spent on death and handed over to the lawlessness of error—from darkness, and might establish a covenant with us in word. Scripture says this is how the Father commands Him: having redeemed us from darkness, He is to prepare a holy people for Himself (Isaiah 42:6-7). The prophet declares, "I am the Lord your God; I called you in righteousness, I will hold your hand and strengthen you. I gave you as a covenant to the nation, a light to the nations, to open blind eyes and bring out those bound in chains from prison, those sitting in darkness."

We know, then, from what we were redeemed. Again the prophet says: "Behold, I have set you as a light to the nations, to be salvation to the end of the earth," says the Lord who redeemed you, God (Isaiah 49:6). And again the prophet says: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because He anointed me to preach good news to the poor; He sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to proclaim release to captives and sight to the blind, to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of recompense, to comfort all who mourn" (Isaiah 61:1-2).

greek: Ναί. ἀλλὰ ἴδωμεν, εἰ ἡ διαθήκη, ἣν ὤμοσεν τοῖς πατράσιν δοῦναι τῷ λαῷ, εἰ δέδωκεν. δέδωκεν: αὐτοὶ δὲ οὐκ ἐγένοντο ἄξιοι λαβεῖν διὰ τὰς ἁμαρτίας αὐτῶν. λέγει γὰρ ὁ προφήτης: Καὶ ἦν Μωϋσῆς νηστεύων ἐν ὄρει Σινᾶ, τοῦ λαβεῖν τὴν διαθήκην κυρίου πρὸς τὸν λαόν, ἡμέρας τεσσεράκοντα καὶ νύκτας τεσσεράκοντα. καὶ ἔλαβεν Μωϋσῆς παρὰ κυρίου τὰς δύο πλάκας τὰς γεγραμμένας τῷ δακτύλῳ τῆς χειρὸς κυρίου ἐν πνεύματι: καὶ λαβὼν Μωϋσῆς κατέφερεν πρὸς τὸν λαὸν δοῦναι. καὶ εἶπεν κύριος πρὸς Μωϋσῆν. Μωϋσῆ Μωϋσῆ, κατάβηθι τὸ τάχος, ὅτι ὁ λαός σου, ὃν ἐξήγαγες ἐκ γῆς Αἰγύπτου. ἠνόμησεν. καὶ συνῆκεν Μωϋσῆς, ὅτι ἐποίησαν ἑαυτοῖς πάλιν χωνεύματα, καὶ ἔρριψεν ἐκ τῶν χειρῶν, καὶ συνετρίβησαν αἱ πλάκες τῆς διαθήκης κυρίου. Μωϋσῆς μὲν ἔλαβεν, αὐτοὶ δὲ οὐκ ἐγένοντο ἄξιοι. πῶς δὲ ἡμεῖς ἐλάβομεν, μάθετε. Μωϋσῆς θεράπων ὢν ἔλαβεν, αὐτὸς δὲ κύριος ἡμῖν ἔδωκεν εἰς λαὸν κληρονομίας, δἰ ἡμᾶς ὑπομείνας. ἐφανερώθη δέ. ἵνα κἀκεῖνοι τελειωθῶσιν τοῖς ἁμαρτήμασιν, καὶ ἡμεῖς διὰ τοῦ κληρονομοῦντος διαθήκην κυρίου Ἰησοῦ λάβωμεν, ὃς εἰς τοῦτο ἡτοιμάσθη, ἵνα αὐτὸς φανείς, τὰς ἤδη δεδαπανημένας ἡμῶν καρδίας τῷ θανάτῳ καὶ παραδεδομένας τῇ τῆς πλάνης ἀνομίᾳ λυτρωσάμενος ἐκ τοῦ σκότους, διάθηται ἐν ἡμῖν διαθήκην λόγῳ. γέγραπται γάρ, πῶς αὐτῷ ὁ πατὴρ ἐντέλλεται, λυτρωσάμενον ἡμᾶς ἐκ τοῦ σκότους ἑτοιμάσαι ἑαυτῷ λαὸν ἅγιον. λέγει οὖν ὁ προφήτης: Ἐγὼ κύριος, ὁ θεός σου, ἐκάλεσά σε ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ καὶ κρατήσω τῆς χειρός σου καὶ ἐνισχύσω σε, καὶ ἔδωκά σε εἰς διαθήκην γένους, εἰς φῶς ἐθνῶν ἀνοῖξαι ὀφθαλμοὺς τυφλῶν καὶ ἐξαγαγεῖν ἐκ δεσμῶν πεπεδημένους καὶ ἐξ οἴκου φυλακῆς καθημένους ἐν σκότει. γινώσκομεν οὖν, πόθεν ἐλυτρώθημεν. πάλιν ὁ προφήτης λέγει: Ἰδού, τέθεικά σε εἰς φῶς ἐθνῶν, τοῦ εἶναί σε εἰς σωτηρίαν ἕως ἐσχάτου τῆς γῆς, οὕτως λέγει κύριος ὁ λυτρωσάμενός σε θεός. καὶ πάλιν ὁ προφήτης λέγει: Πνεῦμα κυρίου ἐπ’ ἐμέ, οὖ εἵνεκεν ἔχρισέν με εὐαγγελίσασθαι ταπεινοῖς χάριν, ἀπέσταλκέν με ἰάσασθαι τοὺς συντετριμμένους τὴν καρδίαν, κηρῦξαι αἰχμαλώτοις ἄφεσιν καὶ τυφλοῖς ἀνάβλεψιν, καλέσαι ἐνιαυτὸν κυρίου δεκτὸν καὶ ἡμέραν ἀνταποδόσεως, παρακαλέσαι πάντας τοὺς πενθοῦντας.

excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english: John, the Lord's disciple, proclaims this faith because he wants to tear out the error that Cerinthus sowed in human hearts — and earlier still, the error that the so-called Nicolaitans planted. They are a counterfeit offshoot, wrongly named, whose purpose is to confuse people and to persuade them that one God made everything through his Word. The heretics deny this. They claim there is one creator and another, different Father of the Lord; one son of the creator, and another Christ from above who, they say, stayed impassible, descended into Jesus the creator's son, and then flew back to his Pleroma. They call the Trinity "the Only-begotten," and the Logos "the true son of the Only-begotten." They insist that our material condition was not made by the first God but by some power far below, cut off from the invisible, ineffable realm above. Therefore the Lord's disciple, wanting to enclose all such teachings and to establish the rule of truth in the Church — because there is one almighty God who made all things, visible and invisible, through his Word — also signals that through the Word, by which God perfected the creation, he has provided salvation for people who live in that creation. So he begins his Gospel teaching: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God (John 1:1). He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made. What was made held life in him, and that life was the light of humanity; the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it. "All things," he says, "were made through him"; therefore this creation of ours is included among those all things. The heretics cannot claim that everything they name exists only below their Pleroma. If their Pleroma contains these things, then this creation is not outside it — as we showed in the previous book. But if these things lie outside the Pleroma, which is impossible, then their Pleroma is not "all things"; so this creation cannot be outside it either. John himself has removed every dissension from us by declaring: He was in the world, and the world was made through him, yet the world did not know him. He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him. But according to Marcion and those like him, the world was not made through him, nor did he come to his own — he came to what is alien. According to certain Gnostics, angels made this world, not the Word of God. According to the Valentinians, the world was not made through him but through the Demiurge. They say the Demiurge fashioned the creation by forming likenesses that imitate the realities above. They claim the Lord and the Demiurge were sent by the Mother, through whom they want the world to have been made — yet the Gospel plainly says that all things were made through the Word who was in the beginning with God, and that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). According to them, neither the Word nor Christ nor the Savior (whom they say was composed from all things) became flesh. They refuse to let the Word and Christ enter this world; they say the Savior did not become incarnate or suffer, but descended like a dove into Jesus — who came from their "disposition" — announced the unknown Father, and then ascended back to the Pleroma. Some say Jesus from the disposition was incarnate and suffered, passing through Mary like water through a pipe. Others say the Demiurge's son received the Jesus from the disposition. Others say Jesus was born of Joseph and Mary, and the impassible, fleshless Christ from above descended into him. By no heretical opinion did the Word of God become flesh. If anyone examines all their systems, he will find that every one of them presents the Word of God and the Christ from above as fleshless and impassible. Some think he merely appeared, like a transfigured man, yet they deny he was born or became incarnate. Others say he did not even assume human form, but descended like a dove into the Jesus born of Mary. Thus the Lord's disciple, exposing all these as false witnesses, declares: The Word became flesh and dwelt among us. And so that we do not ask whose Word became flesh, he himself teaches further: There was a man sent from God, named John; he came as a witness to testify about the light. He was not the light, but came to testify about the light. So John the forerunner, who testifies to the light — by which God was he sent? Surely by the God whose angel is Gabriel, who also announced his birth; who promised through the prophets to send his angel before the face of his Son to prepare his way — that is, to testify about the light — in the spirit and power of Elijah. And Elijah was the servant and prophet of which God? The God who made heaven and earth, as Elijah himself confesses. Therefore John was sent by the founder and creator of this world. How else could he testify about the light that descended from the invisible, ineffable realm? All heretics have decreed that the Demiurge is ignorant of the power above him, yet John is found to be the witness and revealer of that power. That is why the Lord said John was more than a prophet. All the other prophets announced the coming of the Father's light; they longed to see the one they preached. But John not only announced him like the rest — he saw him coming, pointed him out, and persuaded many to believe in him, so that he holds the place of both prophet and apostle.

latin: Hane fidem annuntians Johannes Domini discipulus, volens per Evangelii annuntiationem auferre eum, qui a Cerintho inseminatus erat hominibus errorem, et multo prius ab his qui dicuntur Nicolaite, qui sunt vulsio ejus quee falso cognominatur ut confunderet eos, et suaderet quoniam unus Deus qui omnia fecit per Verbum suum ; et non, quemadmodum illi dicunt, alterum quidem fabricatorem, alium autem Patrem Domini: et alium quidem fabricatoris filium, alterum vero ®de superioribus Christum, quem et impassibilem perseverasse, descendentem in Jesum filium fabricatoris, et iterum revolasse in suum Pleroma: et Tinitium quidem esse monogenem; Logon autem verum filium unigeniti: et eam conditionem quze est secundum nos, non a primo Deo factam, sed a virtute aliqua valde deorsum subjecta, et abscissa ab eorum communicatione quze sunt invisibilia et innominabilia. Omnia igitur talia cireumscribere volens discipulus Domini, et ' regulam veritatis constituere in Ecclesia, quia est unus Deus omnipotens, qui per Verbum suum omnia fecit, et visibilia et invisibilia; significans quoque, quoniam per Verbum, per quod Deus perfecit conditionem, in hoe et salutem his qui in conditione sunt preestitit hominibus; sic inchoavit in ea que est secundum Evangelium doctrina: Jn principio erat Verbum, et Verbum erat apud Deum, et Deus erat Verbum: hoc erat in principio apud Deum. Omnia per ipsum facta sunt, et sine ipso factum est nihil. Quod factum est, in ipso vita erat, et vita erat lua hominum, et lux in tenebris lucet, et tenebre eam non comprehenderunt. Omnia, inquit, per ipsum facta sunt ; in omnibus ergo est et hzee quae secundum nos est conditio: non enim concedetur eis, omnia dici ea que sunt infra Pleroma ipsorum. Si enim et hee Pleroma ipsorum continet, non extra est tanta ista conditio, quemadmodum ostendimus in eo libro qui ante hune est ; si autem extra Pleroma sunt heec, quod quidem impossibile visum est, jam non est omnia Pleroma ipsorum: non est ergo extra heee tanta conditio. Abstulit autem a nobis dissensiones omnes ipse Johannes, dicens: In hoc mundo erat, et mundus per ipsum factus est, et mundus eum non cognovit. In sua propria venit, et sui eum non receperunt. Secundum autem Marcionem et eos qui similes sunt ei, neque mundus per eum factus est ; neque in sua venit, sed in aliena, Secundum autem quosdam Gnosticorum, ¢ab angelis factus est iste mundus, et non per Verbum Dei. Secundum autem eos qui sunt a Valentino, iterum non per eum factus est, sed per Demiurgum. Hic enim operabatur similitudines tales fieri, ad imitationem eorum que sunt sursum, quemadmodum dicunt: Demiurgus autem perficiebat fabricationem conditionis. Emissum enim dicunt eum a matre Dominum et Demiurgum ejus dispositionis quee est secundum conditionem, per quem hune mundum factum volunt: cum Evangelium manifeste dicat, quoniam per Verbum, quod in principio erat apud Deum, omnia sunt facta: quod Verbum, inquit, caro factum est, et habitavit in nobis. 8. Secundum autem illos, neque Verbum caro factum est, neque Christus, neque qui ex omnibus factus est Salvator. Htenim Verbum et Christum nec advenisse in hune mundum volunt: Salvatorem vero non incarnatum neque passum; descendisse autem quasi columbam in eum Jesum qui factus est ex dispositione, et cum annuntiasset incognitum Patrem, iterum ascendisse in Pleroma. Incarnatum autem et passum quidam quidem eum qui ex dispositione sit dicunt Jesum, quem per Mariam dicunt pertransisse, quasi aquam per tubum: alii vero ° Demiurgi filium, in quem descendisse eum Jesum qui ex dispositione sit: alii rursum Jesum quidem ex Joseph et Maria natum dicunt, et in hune descendisse Christum qui de superioribus sit, sine carne et impassibilem exsistentem. Secundum autem nullam sententiam heereticorum, Verbum Dei caro factum est. Si enim quis regulas ipsorum omnium perscrutetur, inveniet quoniam sine carne et impassibilis ab omnibus illis inducitur Dei Verbum, et qui est in superioribus Christus. Alii enim putant manifestatum eum, quemadmodum hominem transfiguratum; neque autem natum, neque incarnatum dicunt illum: alii vero neque figuram eum assumsisse hominis; sed quemadmodum columbam descendisse in eum Jesum, qui natus est ex Maria. Omnes igitur illos falsos testes ostendens discipulus Domini, ait: Ht Verbum caro factum est, et habitavit in nobis. Et ut non inquiramus, cujus Dei Verbum caro factum est, ipse insuper docet, dicens : Fuit homo missus a Deo, erat ei nomen Johannes: hic venit in testimonium, ut testaretur de lumine. Non erat ipse lumen, sed ut testaretur de lumine. Preecursor igitur Johannes, qui testatur de lumine, a quo Deo missus est? Utique ab eo cujus Gabriel est angelus, qui etiam evangelisavit generationem ejus; qui et per prophetas promisit angelum suum missurum ante faciem Filii sui, et preeparaturum viam ejus, hoc est, testificaturum de lumine, i spiritw et virtute Helie. Helias autem rursus cujus Dei servus et propheta fuit? Ejus qui fecit coelum et terram, quemadmodum et ipse confitetur. A conditore igitur et fabricatore hujus mundi missus Johannes, quemadmodum poterat testificari de eo lumine, quod ex his que sunt innominabilia et invisibilia descenderit ? Omnes enim heeretici decreverunt, Demiurgum ignorare eam que sit super eum virtutem, cujus testis et ostensor invenitur Johannes. Propter hoc Dominus plus quam prophetam dixit eum habuisse. Reliqui enim omnes prophetze annuntiaverunt adventum paterni luminis; concupierunt autem digni esse videre eum quem preedicabant: Johannes autem et preenuntiavit similiter sicut alii, et advenientem vidit et demonstravit, et credere in eum suasit multis, ita ut ipse et prophete et apostoli locum habuerit.

excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english: Therefore, since these demonstrations stand, there is no need to go searching for the truth among others, when it is so easy to receive it from the Church. The Apostles, like men entrusting a treasure to a rich repository, deposited the fullness of truth in her, so that anyone who wishes may draw from her the drink of life. This is the entrance to life; all the rest, however, are thieves and robbers. For this reason we must avoid them, but we must love the things that belong to the Church with the greatest diligence and lay hold of the tradition of truth.

What if a dispute arose over some minor question? Would it not be necessary to turn to the most ancient churches, where the Apostles conversed, and learn from them what is certain and clear regarding the present issue? What if the Apostles had not even left us the Scriptures? Would it not then be necessary to follow the order of tradition, which they handed down to those to whom they entrusted the churches?

Many nations of barbarians who believe in Christ assent to this order. They possess salvation written in their hearts by the Spirit, without paper or ink, carefully preserving the ancient tradition. They believe in one God, the maker of heaven and earth and all that is in them, through Christ Jesus, the Son of God. Because of his surpassing love for his creation, he endured his birth from the Virgin, himself uniting man to God. He suffered under Pontius Pilate, rose again, was received in glory, and will come in glory as the Savior of those who are saved and the Judge of those who are judged. He will send into eternal fire the transgressors of truth and the despisers of his Father and his coming.

Those who have believed this faith without written documents are, in respect to our speech, barbarians; but in respect to judgment, custom, and conduct, they are supremely wise because of their faith, and they please God, living in all justice, chastity, and wisdom. If anyone announces to them the inventions of the heretics, speaking in the heretics' own tongue, they immediately stop their ears and flee far away, refusing even to endure such blasphemous talk. Thus, through that ancient tradition of the elders, they do not admit the heretics' portentous speech even into the conception of their minds, for there was no assembly among them and no instituted doctrine.

Before Valentinus came, those who are from Valentinus did not exist; nor did those who are from Marcion exist before Marcion; nor did any of the other malignant opinions enumerated above exist to become the authors of their perversity. Valentinus came to Rome under Hyginus, flourished under Pius, and remained until Anicetus. Cerdon, Marcion's predecessor, also came to Rome under Hyginus, the eighth bishop, frequently entering the Church and making confession. He ended this way: sometimes teaching secretly, sometimes making confession, sometimes corrected by others for his bad teaching, and he kept away from the gathering of the devout. Marcion succeeded him and grew strong under Anicetus, who held the tenth place in the episcopate. The rest who are called Gnostics received their start from Menander, Simon's disciple, as we have shown; each one, having shared in a particular opinion, became its father and high priest. All these men arose much later, in the midst of the Church's times, to launch their apostasy.
