Hee est enim vitze introitus; omnes autem reliqui fures sunt et latrones. Propter quod oportet devitare quidem illos; que autem sunt Ecclesiz, cum summa diligentia diligere, et apprehendere veritatis traditionem. Quid enim? Et si de aliqua modica queestione disceptatio esset, nonne oporteret in antiquissimas recurrere ecclesias, in quibus Apostoli conversati sunt, et ab eis de presenti quastione sumere quod certum et re liquidum est? Quid autem si neque Apostoli quidem Scripturas reliquissent nobis, nonne oportebat ordinem sequi_ traditionis, quam tradiderunt iis quibus committebant ecclesias? Cui ordinationi assentiunt multze gentes barbarorum eorum qui in Christum credunt, sine charta vel atramento scriptam habentes per Spiritum in cordibus suis salutem, et veterem traditionem diligenter custodientes, in unum Deum credentes fabricatorem cceli et terree, et omnium quz in eis sunt, per Christum Jesum Dei Filium. Qui propter eminentissimam erga figmentum suum dilectionem, eam que esset ex Virgine generationem sustinuit, ipse per se hominem adunans Deo, et passus sub Pontio Pilato, et resurgens, et in claritate receptus, in gloria venturus Salvator eorum qui salvantur, et judex eorum qui judicantur, et mittens in ignem sternum transfiguratores veritatis, et contemtores Patris sui et adventus ejus. Hane fidem qui sine literis crediderunt, quantum ad sermonem nostrum, barbari sunt: quantum autem ad sententiam, et consuetudinem, et conversationem, propter fidem perquam sapientissimi sunt, et placent Deo, conversantes in omni justitia et castitate et sapientia. Quibus si aliquis annuntiaverit ea que ab hereticis adinventa sunt, proprio sermone eorum colloquens, statim concludentes aures longo longius fugient, ne audire quidem sustinentes blasphemum colloquium. | Sie per illam veterem stolorum traditionem, ne in conceptionem quidem mentis admittunt, quodcunque eorum portentiloquium est, neque enim congregatio fuit apud eos, neque doctrina instituta. 2. Ante Valentinum enim non fuerunt, qui sunt a Valentino; neque ante Marcionem erant, qui sunt a Marcione; neque omnino erant reliqui sensus maligni, quos supra enumeravimus, initiatores et inventores perversitatis eorum fierent. Valentinus enim venit Romam sub Hygino; Pio, et prorogavit tempus usque ad Anicetum. Oerdon autem qui ante Marcionem, et hic sub Hygino, qui fuit octavus episcopus, seepe in ecclesiam veniens, et exhomologesin faciens, sic consummavit, modo quidem latenter docens, modo vero exhomologesin faciens, modo vero ab aliquibus traductus in his que docebat male, et abstentus est a religiosorum hominum conventu. 3. Marcion autem illi succedens invaluit sub Aniceto, !}decimum locum episcopatus continente. Reliqui vero qui vocantur Gnostici, a Menandro Simonis discipulo, quemadmodum ostendimus, accipientes initia, unusquisque eorum, cujus participatus est sententiz, ejus et pater, et antistes apparuit. Omnes autem hi multo posterius, mediantibus jam Ecclesize temporibus, insurrexerunt in suam apostasiam.

excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english: Many prophets and righteous men, knowing through the Holy Spirit that He would come, prayed to live in the time when they might see their Lord face to face and hear His words. In response, the Lord made this plain to His disciples: "Many prophets and righteous men desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it" (Matt. 13:17). How could they have longed to see and hear unless they had foreknown His coming? And how could they have foreknown it unless they had received that foreknowledge from Him? How could the Scriptures testify about Him unless all things had always been revealed and shown to believers through the Word by one and the same God? At one time He spoke with His creature; at another He gave the law; at another He rebuked; at another He exhorted; and then He freed the servant, adopted him as a son, and at the appointed time granted an incorruptible inheritance for man's perfection. For He says this to him for increase and growth, just as Scripture says: "Grow and multiply" (Gen. 1:28).

This is how God differs from man: God acts, but man is acted upon. The One who acts is always the same; but what is acted upon — having beginning, middle, addition, and increase — must receive these things. God does good, and He does good to man. God is perfect in all things, equal and like to Himself; He is wholly light, wholly mind, wholly substance, the fountain of all good things. But man, receiving progress and increase, moves toward God. Just as God is always the same, so also man, found in God, will always advance toward God. For God never ceases to do good and enrich man, and man never ceases to receive benefit and be enriched by God. As the receptacle of His goodness and the instrument of His manifestation, man is grateful to the One who made him; but as the receptacle of His just judgment, man — ungrateful and despising his Maker, disobedient to His Word — receives judgment. To those always bearing much fruit, having more of the Lord's money, He promised to give Himself. "Well done, good and faithful servant," He says; "because you were faithful in a little, I will set you over much; enter into the joy of your Lord" — the Lord Himself promising much.

Just as He now promises to give much to those bearing fruit, according to the gift of His grace and not according to a change of knowledge — for the Lord endures, and the same Father is revealed — so also to those who came later, the same Lord through His coming attributed a greater gift of grace than what was in the Old Testament. The former people heard through servants that the King was coming, and they rejoiced moderately, according to what they hoped; but those who saw Him present, who obtained liberty and possessed His gift, have greater grace and more abundant exultation, rejoicing at the King's coming, just as David says: "My soul will exult in the Lord; it will rejoice in His salvation" (Psalm 35:9 LXX). And for this reason, when He entered Jerusalem, all who were on the road — the people of David — in the sorrow of their souls recognized their King, spread their garments under Him, adorned the way with green branches, and cried out with great joy and exultation: "Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!" But the evil stewards, who went about among the lesser ones and those whose reason was not settled — and therefore did not want the King to come — said to Him, "Do You hear what these are saying?" The Lord answered, "Have you never read, 'Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies You have perfected praise'?" (Ps. 8:2). This was spoken by David concerning the Son of God, showing it was fulfilled in Himself, and signifying that they indeed possess the power of Scripture and the disposition of God; but He is the Christ announced by the prophets, whose name is praised in all the earth, perfecting praise from the mouth of infants and nursing babies to His Father. Therefore His magnificence was also exalted on high.

If, then, He Himself is present — the One predicted by the prophets, our Lord Jesus Christ — and His coming attributes a fuller grace and greater gift to those who received Him, it is manifest that the Father is also the same One announced by the prophets. The Son did not make known a different Father, but the same One who was proclaimed from the beginning. From Him He brought liberty to those who serve Him lawfully, with a willing soul and whole heart. But to those who despise Him and are not subject to God, who pursue external purities for the glory of men — which were handed down as figures of future things, as a kind of shadow and outline of the Law, sketching eternal things from temporal ones and heavenly things from earthly ones — feigning to observe more than what was commanded, as if they preferred their own diligence even to God, while inwardly full of hypocrisy, lust, and all malice — He brought eternal perdition, cutting them off from life.

QuonramM autem non solum prophetze et justi multi, preescientes per Spiritum sanctum adventum ejus, orayerunt in illud tempus venire, in quo facie ad faciem viderent Dominum suum, et sermones audirent ejus, Dominus fecit manifestum, dicens discipulis: Multi prophet et justi cupierunt videre que videtis, et non viderunt, et audire que auditis, et non audierunt. Quemadmodum igitur concupierunt et audire, et videre, nisi preescissent futurum ejus adventum? Quomodo autem prescire potuerunt, nisi ab ipso preescientiam ante accepissent? Quomodo autem Scripture testificantur de eo, nisi ab uno et eodem Deo omnia semper per Verbum revelata et ostensa fuissent credentibus ; aliquando quidem colloquente eo cum suo plasmate, aliquando autem dante legem, aliquando vero exprobrante, aliquando vero exhortante, ac deinceps liberante servum, et adoptante in filium, et apto tempore incorruptele heereditatem prestante, ad perfectionem hominis? enim eum in augmentum et incrementum, quemadmodum et Scriptura dicit: Crescite et multiplicamini. 2. Et hoe Deus ab homine differt, quoniam Deus quidem facit, homo autem fit: et quidem qui facit, semper idem est: quod autem fit, et initium, et medietatem, et adjectionem, et augmentum accipere debet. Et Deus quidem bene facit, bene autem homini. Et Deus°quidem perfectus in omnibus, ipse sibi eequalis et similis; totus cum sit lumen, et totus mens, et totus substantia, et fons omnium bonorum: homo vero profectum percipiens et augmentum ad Deum. Quemadmodum enim Deus semper idem est; sic et homo in Deo inventus, semper proficiet Deum. Neque enim Deus cessat aliquando in benefaciendo, et locupletando hominem: neque homo cessat beneficium accipere, et ditari a Deo. excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english: We do not know God by his magnitude; it is impossible to measure the Father. But we are led to God through his Word by his love, and by obeying him we always learn how great God is. He himself establishes, chooses, and adorns all things through himself — he who is present to us. And so we have been made together with everything he contains. This is what Scripture says: God formed man from the dust of the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life (Genesis 2:7). Therefore angels did not make us; they did not form us, nor could angels fashion the image of God. No one else could do it except the Word of the Lord — no power far removed from the Father. God did not need such agents to accomplish what he had predetermined, as if he lacked his own hands. The Word and Wisdom, the Son and the Spirit, are always present to him; through them and in them he freely and willingly made all things. To them he speaks, saying, "Let us make man in our image and likeness"; he himself takes from himself the substance of creatures, the pattern of things made, and the design of the world's ornaments.

excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english: All things are of one and the same substance — that is, they come from one and the same God — just as the Lord says to the disciples: "Therefore every scribe who has been trained for the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings out of his treasure what is new and what is old" (Matt 13:52). He did not teach that one person brings out the old and another the new; it is one and the same householder. The Lord is that householder, who rules the whole household of God paternally: to the servants and those still undisciplined he gives a law worthy of them, but to the children, justified by faith, he gives fitting precepts, and to the sons he opens his inheritance. He calls his disciples scribes and teachers of the kingdom of heaven, and of them he also says elsewhere to the Jews: "I send you prophets and wise men and scribes... and you will kill some of them and persecute them from town to town" (Matt 23:34). Thus the new and old brought out of the treasure speak, without contradiction, of the two testaments: the old, which was the former legislation, and the new, which is the way of life according to the Gospel. Of this David says: "Sing to the Lord a new song" (Ps 96:1), and Isaiah: "Sing to the Lord a new hymn" (Isa 42:10). "From the ends of the earth his name is praised; his deeds are proclaimed in the islands" (Isa 24:16; 42:12). And Jeremiah says: "Behold, the days are coming, declares the Lord, when I will make a new covenant... not like the covenant I made with their fathers at Mount Horeb" (Jer 31:31). Both testaments, however, are produced by one and the same householder — the Word of God, our Lord Jesus Christ — who spoke with Abraham and Moses, who restored liberty to us in newness and multiplied it, which comes from him.

For he says: "Something greater than the temple is here" (Matt 12:6), and "greater than Solomon... greater than Jonah" (Matt 12:41-42), for he gives to men his presence and resurrection from the dead. But he does not change God, nor does he proclaim another Father; he proclaims the same One who always has more for his household, and as their love for God progresses, he gives more and greater gifts — just as the Lord told the disciples: "You will see greater things than these" (John 1:50), and Paul says: "Not that I have already obtained this or am already perfect... For we know in part and we prophesy in part, but when the perfect comes, the partial will pass away" (1 Cor 13:9-10). So when the perfect comes, we will not see another Father, but this One whom we now long to see, for "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God" (Matt 5:8). We will not wait for another Christ and Son of God, but for this One who was born of the Virgin Mary, who suffered, in whom we believe and whom we love — just as Isaiah says: "They will say in that day: 'Behold, this is our God; we have waited for him, that he might save us. This is the Lord; we have waited for him; let us be glad and rejoice in his salvation'" (Isa 25:9). And Peter says in his epistle: "Though you have not seen him, you love him. Though you do not now see him, you believe in him and rejoice with joy that is inexpressible" (1 Pet 1:8). We will not receive another Holy Spirit, except this One who is with us and cries, "Abba, Father" (Rom 8:15; Gal 4:6). And in these very things we will have increase and progress, so that we may now enjoy the gifts of God not through a mirror and in riddles, but face to face (1 Cor 13:12). Thus also now, perceiving more than Solomon — which is the advent of the Son of God — we have not learned another God besides the Creator and Maker of all things, who was shown to us from the beginning, nor another Christ, Son of God, except the one who was foretold by the prophets.

For with the New Testament known and foretold by the prophets, the One who was to establish it according to the Father's will was also foretold, and he was manifested to men as God willed, so that believers in him may always progress. And through the testaments there is one salvation and one God. The precepts that form a human being are many, and not few are those who lead a human being to God. To an earthly and temporal king, since he is a man, it is permitted to grant greater advancement to those subject to him; but to God, since he is the same and always wills to bestow greater grace on the human race and to honor with more gifts those who please him — is this not progress? To find another Father besides the One announced from the beginning, and then, besides the one thought to have been found a second time, to find a third — and the same progress from a third to a fourth, and from that another and another — so that, always thinking to progress, such a mind will never stand in God. For it is expelled from the One who is, and turning back it seeks but never finds God; it will always swim in the depth of incomprehensibility, unless, converted through repentance, it returns from where it was cast out, confessing and believing in one God, the Father, the Creator, who was announced by the Law and the prophets, who was testified to by Christ — just as he himself says to those who accused his disciples of not keeping the tradition of the elders: "Why do you break the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition? For God commanded, 'Honor your father and your mother,' and, 'Whoever reviles father or mother must surely die.' ... So for the sake of your tradition you have made void the word of God" (Matt 15:3-6). Clearly confessing the Father and God, Christ acknowledges the One who said in the Law: "Honor your father and your mother, that it may go well with you" (Deut 5:16). For the Word of God confessed the precept of the Law; the true God did not call another God except his own Father.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Where was Marcion then, that Pontic shipowner and student of Stoicism? Where was Valentinus, the follower of Platonism? The record shows they were not always what they became; they appeared around the reign of Antoninus, and at first they accepted Catholic teaching in the Roman church under the blessed bishop Eleutherius. Their restless curiosity drove them on, a curiosity that even made their fellow believers avoid them, until they were expelled not once but twice. Marcion, who had brought two hundred sestertii to the church, was finally consigned to permanent separation, and the pair proceeded to spread the poison of their doctrines.

Later Marcion confessed repentance and, meeting the condition imposed on him, was to receive peace if he restored to the church the others he had taught for destruction; but death cut him off first. It was necessary for heresies to exist. That does not make heresies good, as if evil were not also necessary. The Lord had to be betrayed, yet woe to the betrayer; let no one cite this necessity to defend heresy.

If we must trace the line of Apelles, he is no more ancient than Marcion, his founder and forerunner. Apelles fell for a woman, abandoned Marcionite continence, and fled from the eyes of the most holy master Alexander to Alexandria. Years later he returned, no better, except that he was no longer a Marcionite, and he fastened onto another woman, the virgin Philumene, whom I mentioned earlier. She turned out to be a monstrous prostitute, and, caught in her spell, he wrote the phaneroseis he learned from her.

People still alive remember these men, including their own disciples and successors, so they cannot deny being their heirs. Even their own works convict them, as the Lord said. If Marcion separated the New Testament from the Old, he is later than what he separated; he could not separate them unless they had first been united. United before, separated after, the separator is shown to be the later party. Likewise Valentinus, by expounding differently and 'correcting,' proves that whatever he corrects was flawed beforehand. These are the most prominent and frequent adulterers of the truth.

Then there are Nigidius, whoever he is, Hermogenes, and many others still walking about perverting God's ways. Let them show me from what authority they sprang. If they preach another god, how do they use that god's own things, letters, and names against the very one they preach? If they preach the same God, how do they do it differently? Let them prove they are new apostles: let them say Christ descended again, taught again, was crucified again, died again, rose again. That is how the apostles operated, and they received power to work the same signs he did. I want to see their powers produced; unless, of course, you count their supreme power, by which they perversely imitate the apostles: the apostles made the dead live, these men make the living dead.

latin: Ubi tunc Marcion, ponticus nauclerus, stoicae studiosus? Ubi Valentinus platonicae sectator? Nam constat illos, neque adeo olim fuisse, Antonini fere principatu, et in catholicae primo doctrinam credidisse apud Ecclesiam romanensem, sub episcopatu Eleutherii benedicti, donec ob inquietam semper eorum curiositatem, qua fratres quoque vitabant semel et iterum ejecti, Marcion quidem cum ducentis sestertiis quae Ecclesiae intulerat, novissime in perpetuum discidium relegati, venena doctrinarum suarum disseminaverunt. Postmodum idem Marcion, poenitentiam confessus cum conditioni datae sibi occurrit, ita pacem recepturus, si caeteros quos perditioni erudisset, Ecclesiae restitueret, morte praeventus est. Oportebat enim haereses esse. Nec tamen ideo bonum haereses, quia eas oportebat, quasi non et malum oportuerit esse. Nam et Dominum tradi oportebat; sed vae traditori? ne quis etiam hinc haereses defendat. Si et Apellis stemma retractandum est, tam non vetus et ipse quam Marcion institutor et praeformator ejus: sed lapsus in foeminam desertor continentiae marcionensis, ab oculis sanctissimi magistri Alexandriam secessit; inde post annos regressus non melior, nisi tantum qua jam non marcionites, in alteram foeminam impegit, illam virginem Philumenen, quam supra edidimus, postea vero immane prostibulum et ipsam, cujus energemate circumventus, quas ab ea didicit phaneroseis scripsit. Adhuc in saeculo supersunt qui meminerint eorum, etiam proprii discentes et successores ipsorum, ne se posteriores negare possint. Quanquam et de operibus suis, ut dixit Dominus, revincuntur. Si enim Marcion Novum Testamentum a Vetere separavit, posterior est eo quod separavit; quia separare non posset, nisi quod unitum fuit. Unitum ergo ante quam separaretur, postea separatum, posteriorem ostendit separatorem. Item Valentinus, aliter exponens, et sine dubio emendans, hoc omnino quicquid emendat, ut mendosum retro, anterius fuisse demonstrat. Hos ut insigniores et frequentiores adulteros veritatis nominamus. Caeterum et Nigidius nescio quis, et Hermogenes, et multi alii qui adhuc ambulant pervertentes vias Dei, ostendant mihi ex qua auctoritate prodierunt. Si alium Deum praedicant, quomodo ejus Dei rebus et litteris et nominibus utuntur adversus quem praedicant? si eumdem, quomodo aliter? Probent se novos apostolos esse: dicant Christum iterum descendisse, iterum ipsum docuisse, iterum crucifixum, iterum mortuum, iterum resuscitatum: sic enim Apostolos solet facere, dare illis praeterea virtutem eadem signa edendi, quae et ipse. Volo igitur et virtutes eorum proferri; nisi quod agnosco maximam virtutem eorum, qua Apostolos in perversum aemulantur: illi enim de mortuis vivos faciebant, isti de vivis mortuos faciunt.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: If we have done anything against Marcion before, let the record show it from this point on. We are launching a new work from an old foundation. I first withdrew a hasty little treatise, later replacing it with a fuller composition. I lost that one too, before it could be copied, thanks to the fraud of a brother who then turned apostate — he had copied certain passages very badly and circulated them publicly. The need for correction became an opportunity for innovation, and that occasion persuaded me to add more. So this pen, now third after the second, and now first after the third, must preface the outcome of this little work, so that its scattered variety may not confuse anyone.

Pontus, denied by nature the name Euxine, is mocked by it instead. But do not judge hospitable Pontus by its location; it has withdrawn from our more humane shores as if in shame of its own barbarity. The most ferocious nations inhabit it — if you can call it inhabited, given they live in wagons. Their dwellings are uncertain, life is crude, lust promiscuous and mostly naked; even when they hide, they are marked by quivers suspended from their yokes, so that no one may intervene. Thus they do not blush at their own arms. They devour the corpses of their parents alongside slaughtered beasts at a feast. Death is cursed if they do not die so as to be eaten. Women are not softened by their sex according to modesty; they bind their breasts, make a burden for their axes, and prefer to wage war rather than marry.

Harshness comes from heaven as well: the day is never open, the sun never smiles, the air is one unbroken cloud, the whole year is winter, and everything that blows is the north wind. Liquids freeze back into snow, rivers are stopped by ice, mountains are heaped with frost. Everything is numb, everything stiff; nothing there is warm except savagery — the savagery that gave the stage its stories of Tauric sacrifices, Colchian loves, and Caucasian crosses. But nothing in Pontus is as barbarous and sad as the fact that Marcion was born there: worse than a Scythian, more unstable than a Hamaxobian, more inhuman than a Massagete, more daring than an Amazon, darker than a cloud, colder than winter, more fragile than frost, more deceitful than the Hister, more abrupt than the Caucasus. Why not? For with him the true Prometheus, God Almighty, is torn apart by blasphemies.

Now Marcion is even more troublesome to the beasts of that barbarity. For who is as much a castrator of flesh as the man who abolished marriage? Who is as much a devourer of the Pontic mouse as the man who gnawed away the Gospels? Did you, Euxine, produce a more probable beast for philosophers than for Christians? That cynic Diogenes sought to find a human being, carrying a lantern at midday. Marcion, having found God, lost Him with the extinguished light of his faith.

His disciples will not deny that his first faith was with us, as his own letters testify, so that from this point it can already be determined: a heretic is one who, having deserted what he previously was, later chooses for himself what he was not before. For to such an extent will heresy be reckoned as what is introduced later, inasmuch as truth will be held to be what was handed down before and from the beginning.

But another little book will sustain this level against the heretics, even without a re-examination of doctrines, to be overcome. This is what they know about the prescription of novelty. Now, insofar as a confrontation is to be admitted from time to time, lest the summary of the prescription be deemed everywhere to be advocated out of diffidence, I will first weave the rule of the adversary, lest it be hidden from anyone, in which the principal question will be fought.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: For indeed, as the Creator of all things, He was from the beginning discovered equally with them, they having been themselves manifested that He might become known as God . For although Moses , some long while afterwards, seems to have been the first to introduce the knowledge of the God of the universe in the temple of his writings, yet the birthday of that knowledge must not on that account be reckoned from the Pentateuch. For the volume of Moses does not at all initiate the knowledge of the Creator, but from the first gives out that it is to be traced from Paradise and Adam, not from Egypt and Moses .

The greater part, therefore, of the human race , although they knew not even the name of Moses , much less his writings, yet knew the God of Moses ; and even when idolatry overshadowed the world with its extreme prevalence, men still spoke of Him separately by His own name as God , and the God of gods, and said, If God grant, and, As God pleases, and, I commend you to God . Reflect, then, whether they knew Him, of whom they testify that He can do all things. To none of the writings of Moses do they owe this. The soul was before prophecy . From the beginning the knowledge of God is the dowry of the soul , one and the same among the Egyptians , and the Syrians, and the tribes of Pontus . For their souls call the God of the Jews their God. Do not, O barbarian heretic , put Abraham before the world.

Even if the Creator had been the God of one family , He was yet not later than your god; even in Pontus was He known before him. Take then your standard from Him who came first: from the Certain (must be judged) the uncertain; from the Known the unknown. Never shall God be hidden, never shall God be wanting. Always shall He be understood, always be heard, nay even seen, in whatsoever way He shall wish. God has for His witnesses this whole being of ours, and this universe wherein we dwell. He is thus, because not unknown, proved to be both God and the only One, although another still tries hard to make out his claim.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: They say it's justified. After all, who isn't as well known to their own people as to strangers? Nobody. I'll hold to that line of reasoning too. What kind of situation would it be for something to be foreign to God? If anyone existed to whom nothing was foreign — because it's God's nature that all things are His and all things pertain to Him — then He'd immediately hear from us: 'What business does He have with foreigners?' He'll hear that more fully in due course. For now, it's enough that no one is approved when nothing about them is approved. Just as the Creator is God and an undisputed God because all things are His and nothing is foreign to Him, so another is not God because not all things are His and therefore they're foreign. Finally, if the universe belongs to the Creator, I don't even see a place for another God. Everything is full and occupied by its Author. If some space lies vacant in creation for some divinity, it'll be a false vacancy. Truth lies open to falsehood. What great power do idols have that they won't receive Marcion's God somewhere? So I demand this too from the Creator's pattern: God should have been recognized from His works — from His own world, His own man, His own age — since even the world's error has presumed gods, which people sometimes acknowledge, because something from each seems useful and convenient for life's utilities and conveniences. So this too is believed to be divine: to establish or demonstrate what's suitable and necessary for human affairs. So much so that if authority is accommodated to a false divinity from which the true one preceded, Marcion's God ought to have produced at least one little circle of His own, so that some new Triptolemus might be proclaimed. Or produce a reason worthy of God for why He created nothing, if He exists; because He would have created if He had been God, by that very prejudice by which our God is made manifest in no other way than that He created all this. For once the rule stands firm — that they can't confess the Creator as God and also want the other to be believed as God equally without proving Him according to the pattern of Him whom they themselves and everyone acknowledge as God — then, when no one doubts the Creator is God because He created all this, no one ought to believe that the one who created nothing is also God, unless some reason is perhaps brought forward. This necessity appears to be twofold: either He didn't want to create anything, or He wasn't able. The third option is absent, but inability is unworthy of God. Whether unwillingness is worthy, I want to investigate. Tell me, Marcion: did your God want to be recognized at some time or not? Did He come down and preach and suffer and rise again with some other purpose than to be recognized? But without doubt, if He is recognized, He wanted to be. For nothing happens around Him unless He willed it. So He who procured knowledge of Himself so assiduously that He was exhibited in the shame of the flesh — and even greater shame if it's false, for it's more shameful if He also lied about the substance of the body — who also took the Creator's curse upon Himself, hanging on the tree — how much more honestly would He have established knowledge of Himself through some indications of His own creation! Especially against Him, having knowledge, among whom from the beginning He was not recognized by His works. For what kind of thing is it that the Creator, indeed not knowing there is another God above Himself as the Marcionites want — who swore and asserted He is alone — armed knowledge of Himself with such great works, as much as He could not have neglected according to the presumption of His singularity, while the other, more exalted one, knowing the inferior God to be so instructed, provided no preparation for Himself to be recognized? When He ought to have created more remarkable and superior works, so that God might be recognized from His works according to the Creator, and from more honorable works, a more powerful and noble Creator.

latin: Et merito, inquiunt. quis enim non tam suis notus est quam extraneis? nemo. teneo et hanc uocem. quale est enim, ut aliquid extraneum deo sit? cui nihil extraneum esset, si quis esset, — quia dei hoc est, omnia illius esse et omnia ad illum pertinere — uel ne statim audiret a nobis: quid ergo illi cum extraneis? quod plenius suo loco audiet. at nunc satis est nullum probari cuius nihil probatur. sicut enim creator ex hoc et deus et indubitatus deus, quia omnia ipsius et nihil extraneum illi, ita et alius idcirco non deus, quia omnia non eius ideoque et extranea. denique si uniuersitas «rpatoris est, iam nec locum uideo dei alterius. plena et occupata sunt omnia suo auctore. si uacat aliquid spatii alicuius diuinitati in creaturis, plane falsae uacabit. patet mendacio ueritas. tanta uis idolorum cur non recipiat alicubi deum Marcionis? igitur et hoc ex forma creatoris expostulo, deum (eius) ex operibus cognosci debuisse alicuius proprii sui mundi et hominis et saeculi, quando etiam error orbis propterea deos praesumpserit, quos homines interdum confitetur. quoniam aliquid ab unoquoque prospectum uidetur utilitatibus et commodis uitae. ita et hoc ex forma dei creditum est diuinum esse, instituere uel demonstrare quid aptum et necessarium rebus humanis. adeo inde auctoritas accommodata si falsae diuinitati, unde praecesserat uerae, unam saltim cicerculam deus Marcionis propriam protulisse debuerat, ut nouus aliqui Triptolemus praedicaretur. aut exhibe rationem deo dignam, cur nihil condiderit, si est; quia condidisset, si fuisset, illo scilicet praeiudicio, quo et nostrum deum non alias manifestum est esse quam quia totum condidit hoc., semel enim praescriptio stabit non posse illos et deum confiteri creatorem et eum, quem uolunt aeque deum credi, non ad eius formam probare, quem et ipsi et omnes deum (agnoscunt,) ut, quando hoc ipso nemo creatorem deum dubitet. quia totum hoc condidit, hoc ipso nemo debeat credere deum et illum, qui nihil condidit, nisi ratio forte proferatur. duplex ista uideatur necesse est, ut aut noluerit condere quid aut non potuerit. tertium cessat sed non potuisse indignum deo est. noluisse an dignum, uolo inquirere. dic mihi, Marcion, uoluit deus tuus cognosci se quocumque in tempore an non? alio proposito et descendit et praedicauit et passus resurrexit quam uti cognosceretur? at sine dubio, si cognitus est, uoluit. nihil enim circa eum fieret, nisi uoluisset. qui ergo tantopere notitiam sui procuranit, ut in dedecore carnis exhiberetur, et quidem maiore, si falsae, - nam hoc turpius, si et mentitus est substantiam corporis — qui et maledictum in se creatoris admisit ligno suspensus, quanto honestius per aliqua propriae molitionis indicia cognitionem sui praestruxisset! maxime aduersus eum cognosci habens, apud quem ex operibus ab initio cognitus non erat. nam et quale est, ut creator quidem ignorans esse alium super se deum, ut uolunt Marcionitae, qui solum se etiam iurans adseuerabat, tantis operibus notitiam sui armauerit, quam potuerat non ita curasse secundum singularitatis suae praesumptionem, ille autem sublimior, sciens inferiorem deum tam instructum, nullam sibi prospexerit agnoscendo paraturam? quando etiam insigniora et superbiora opera debuisset condidisse, ut et deus ex operibus cognosceretur secundum creatorem et ex honestioribus potior et generosior creatore.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Even if we could admit He exists, we would still have to argue that He exists without cause. Anything without cause lacks a thing, because every thing is a cause — it exists so that there is someone whose thing it is. Since nothing ought to be without cause, that is, without a thing — for if it is without cause, it might as well not exist — lacking the cause of a thing means lacking the thing itself. To that extent, I judge it more fitting for God not to exist than to exist without cause. He is without cause who, by not having a thing, has no cause. But God ought not to exist without cause, that is, without a thing. So every time I demonstrate that He exists without cause, as if He exists, I prove He does not exist — because if He had existed, He would not have existed without cause at all.

Thus I also say that faith seizes Him without cause from man. Normally one believes in God shaped by the authority of works. But He foresaw nothing of the kind through which man might learn of God. Even though many believe in Him, they do not believe by reason straightaway. They lack God's pledge, His works worthy of God. And so, under this name of cessation and defection of works, of impudence and malice, He is kin to impudence — which snatches faith not owed to Him, for whom He foresaw nothing to be laid out — and to malice — which made many guilty of unbelief, securing nothing for faith.

latin: Ceterum et si esse eum possemus confiteri, sine causa esse eum deberemus argumentari. sine causa enim esset qui rem non haberet, quia res omnis causa est, ut sit aliquis, cuius res sit. porro in quantum nihil oportet esse sine causa, [id est sine re] quia si sine causa sit, proinde est atque si non sit. [non habens rei causam rem ipsam] in tantum deum dignius credam non esse quam esse sine causa. sine causa est enim qui rem non habendo non habet causam. deus autem sine causa, id est sine re, esse non debet. ita quotiens ostendo eum sine causa esse, tamquam sit, hoc constituo, non esse illum, quia si fuisset, omnino sine causa non fuisset. sic et ipsam fidem dico illum sine causa ab homine captare. aliter solito deum credere ex operum auctoritate formatum. quia nihil tale prospexit, per quod homo deum didicit. nam etsi credunt plerique in illum, non statim ratione credunt. non habentes dei pignus, opera eius deo digna. itaque hoc nomine cessationis et defectionis operum et impudentiae et malignitatis adfinis est: impudentiae, qua fidem non debitam sibi captat, cui praestruendae nihil prospexit. malignitatis. qua plures incredulitatis reos fecit, nihil fidei procurando.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: When we push God to this extreme—to the One for whom nothing is more proper or worthy than the testimony that marks Him as Creator—the most shameless Marcionites, recoiling in disgust, turn to demolishing the Creator’s works.

‘Certainly,’ they say, ‘the world is a great work and worthy of God!’ Is the Creator then not God? Clearly He is God. Therefore the world is not unworthy of God: for God would not have made anything unworthy of Himself, even if He made the world for humanity, not for Himself, though every work is inferior to its maker. And yet, if it is unworthy of God to have made something, how much more unworthy is it that He made nothing at all! Or is it unworthy, so that one could even hope for a more worthy author.

So let me speak of something even from this supposedly unworthy world, which even among the Greeks bears the name of ornament and cultivation, not filth. The very substances that the self‑styled professors of wisdom—whose minds animate every heresy—have declared to be gods: Thales called water a god, Heraclitus fire, Anaximenes air, Anaximander all heavenly bodies, Strato heaven and earth, Zeno air and ether, Plato the stars, which he calls the fiery kind of gods. When they considered the world—its magnitude, power, authority, honor, beauty, and the help, faith, and law of the individual elements that conspire to bring forth, nourish, complete, and restore all things—most physicists feared that the world’s substances, so vast, would be deemed less than God, the very substances worshipped by Persian magi, Egyptian hierophants, and Indian gymnosophists.

Even common, vulgar idolatry, ashamed of the names and myths of ancient dead men in its images, flees to a naturalistic interpretation and masks its disgrace with cleverness: it portrays Jupiter as a fiery substance, Juno as an airy one, following the sound of Greek words; Vesta as fire, the Camenae as water, the Great Mother as earth sown with seed, plowed by oxen, watered by baths. Thus Osiris, who is always buried, sought among the living, and found with joy, testifies to the faith of recurring crops, living elements, and the returning year, just as the rites of dry and burning nature philosophize about the lions of Mithras. And indeed, substances that are higher in position or status are more easily regarded as gods than as unworthy of God. Shall I descend to humble things? A single tiny flower from the hedges—not from the meadows—a single shell from any sea—not from the Red Sea—a single feather of a partridge, I say nothing of the peacock—will declare to you a sordid craftsman, the Creator.

latin: Cum deum hoc gradu expellimus, cui nulla conditio\' tam propria et deo digna quam creatoris testimonium praesignarit, narem contrahentes impudentissimi Marcionitae conuertuntur ad destructionem operum creatoris. \'nimirum\', inquiunt. \'grande opus et dignum deo mundus\'! numquid ergo ereator minime deus? plane deus. ergo nec mundus deo indignus: nihil etenim deus indignum se fecisset, etsi mundum homini.\' non sibi fecit, etsi omne opus inferius est suo artifice. et tamen, si quale quid fecisse indignum est deo, quanto indignius deo est nihil eum omnino fecisse! ** uel indignum, quo posset etiam digniorum auctor sperari. ut ergo aliquid + et de isto huius mundi indigno loquar, cui et apud Graecos ornamenti et cultus, non sordium, nomen est, indignas uidelicet substantias ipsi illi sapientiae professores, de quorum ingeniis omnis haeresis animatur. deos pronuntiauerunt, ut Thales aquam, ut Heraclitus ignem, ut Anaximenes aerem. ut Anaximander uniuersa caelestia, ut Strato caelum et terram, ut Zeno aerem et aetherem, ut Plato sidera, quae genus deorum igneum appellat, cum de mundo, considerando scilicet et magnitudinem et uim et potestatem et honorem et decorem, opem fidem legem singulorum elementorum, quae omnibus gignendis alendis conficiendis reficiendisque conspirant, ut plerique physicorum, formidauerint, [initium ac finem mundo constare] ne substantiae eius, tantae scilicet, minus dei haberentur, quas colunt et Persarum magi et Aegyptiorum hierophantae et Indorum gymnosophistae. ipsa quoque uulgaris superstitio communis idolatriae, cum in simulacris de nominibus et fabulis ueterum mortuorum pudet, ad interpretationem naturalium refugit et dedecus suum ingenio obumbrat, figurans Iouem in substantiam feruidam et Iunonem eius in aeream secundum sonum Graecorum uocabulorum. item Vestam in ignem et Camenas in aquam et Magnam Matrem in terram seminalia demessam, lacertis aratam, lauacris rigatam. sic et, Osiris quod semper sepelitur et in uiuido quaeritur et cum gaudio inuenitur, reciprocarum frugum et uiuidorum elementorum et recidiui anni fidem argumentantur, sicut aridae et ardentis naturae sacramenta leones Mithrae philosophantur. et superiores quidem situ aut statu substantias sufficit facilius deos habitas quam deo indignas. ad humilia deficiam? unus, opinor, de sepibus flosculus, non dico de pratis, una cuiuslibet maris conchula, non dico de rubro, una tetraonis pinnula, taceo de pauo, sordidum artificem pronuntiabit tibi creatorem?

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: You mock the smaller animals, too — the ones the greatest Artisan deliberately enlarged through their own talents or strengths — thereby teaching that greatness proves itself in moderation, just as virtue does in weakness, as the apostle says (1 Corinthians 12:22). Imitate the bees' architecture if you can, the ants' dwellings, the spiders' webs, the silkworms' threads; endure the very beasts of your bed and cloak if you can — the beetles' poisons, the flies' stings, the mosquitoes' trumpets and lances. What will the greater things be like, when such tiny things either help or harm you, so that you do not despise the Creator even in the smallest things?

Finally, walk yourself around and examine the human being inside and out: will this work of our God please you, the work your Lord — that better God — admired, for whose sake he labored to descend from the third heaven into these poor elements, for whose sake he was even crucified in this cell of the Creator?

But that God, at any rate, has not rejected up to now the Creator's water, with which he washes his own, nor the oil with which he anoints his own, nor the fellowship of honey and milk, with which he nurtures his infants, nor the bread, with which he represents his own body even in his own sacraments, though he stands in need of the Creator's alms. You, however — a disciple above the master, a servant above the Lord — you presume to be wiser than he, destroying what he desires.

I want to examine whether, at least from faith, you do not also desire what you destroy. You oppose heaven, yet you capture heaven's freedom inside dwellings; you despise the earth — now plainly the mother of your enemy, the flesh — and you wring out all its marrow for food; you reject the sea, but only up to its resources, which you count as holier food. If I offered you a rose, you would not despise the Creator. Hypocrite: so that you may prove yourself a Marcionite — that is, a rejecter of the Creator — for this ought to have been pursued as martyrdom among you, if the world displeased you — into whatever material you resolve, you use the Creator's substance. How great is the obstinacy of your hardness! You devalue the very things in which you both live and die.

latin: At cum et animalia inrides minutiora, quae maximus artifex de industria ingeniis aut uiribus ampliauit, sic magnitu-i dinem in mediocritate probari docens quemadmodum uirtutem ; in infirmitate secundum apostolum, imitare, si potes, apis aedificia, formicae stabula, aranei retia, bombycis stamina, sustine, si potes, illas ipsas lectuli et tegetis tuae bestias,I cantharidis uenena, muscae spicula, culicis et tubam et lanceam. qualia erunt maiora, cum tam modicis aut iuuaris aut laederis, ut nec in modicis despicias creatorem? postremo te tibi circumfer, intus ac foris considera hominem: placebit tibi uel hoc opus dei nostri, quod tuus dominus, ille deus melior, adamauit, propter quem in haec paupertina elementa de tertio caelo descendere laborauit, cuius causa in hac cellula creatoris etiam crucifixus est? sed ille quidem usque nunc nec aquam reprobauit creatoris, qua suos abluit, nec oleum, quo suos ungit, nec mellis et lactis societatem, qua suos infantat, nec panem, quo ipsum corpus suum repraesentat etiam in sacramentis propriis egens mendicitatibus creatoris. at tu, super magistrum discipulus et seruus super dominum. I, sublimius illo sapis, destruens quae ille desiderat. uolo inspicere, si ex fide saltim, ut non et ipse quae destruis adpetas. I aduersaris caelum, et libertatem caeli in habitationibus captas:I despicis terram — plane inimicae iam tuae, carnis, matricem — et, omnes medullas eius uictui extorques; reprobus et mare, sed usque ad copias eius, quas sanctiorem cibum deputas. rosam tibi si obtulero, non fastidies creatorem. hypocrita, ut apocarteresi probes te Marcionitam, id est repudiatorem creatoris, — nam haec apud uos pro martyrio adfectari debuisset, si uobis mundus displiceret — in quamcumque materiam resolueris, substantiam creatoris uteris. quanta obstinatio duritiae tuae! depretias in quibus et uiuis et moreris.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Whether before or after these points, once you claim that Marcion's god has his own condition, his own world, and his own heaven — we will examine that third heaven later, if we ever get around to discussing your apostle — but in the meantime, whatever his substance may be, it ought to have appeared alongside his own god. Yet here we are: the Lord was revealed in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, while the substance remains entirely undiscovered in the fifteenth year of Emperor Severus. This substance, which supposedly outdoes the creator's trivialities, should have stayed hidden — not while its own Lord and author remained hidden. So if the substance itself could not be revealed in this world, how did the Lord obey it in this world? If this world seized the Lord, why could it not seize the substance — unless the Lord is perhaps greater?

Now the question turns to place, and it touches both that upper world and its god. Consider: if that god also has his world beneath him, above the creator, he made it in a place — specifically, the vacant space between his own feet and the creator's head. Therefore the god himself was in a place, and he made the world in a place, and that place will be greater than both god and world. Nothing that contains something else fails to be greater than what it contains. And we must check whether any vacant spaces still remain there, where a third god might station himself with his own world. So start counting gods now. Place will be a god — not only because it surpasses god, but because it is innate, ungenerated, and therefore eternal and equal to god, the place in which god has always existed.

Next, if that god also fashioned the world from some underlying material — innate, ungenerated, and contemporary with god, as Marcion supposes of the creator — you drag this too into the majesty of place, which encloses both god and material: two gods. For material is also a god according to the form of divinity — namely innate, ungenerated, and eternal. Or if he made the world from nothing, this same conclusion will be forced on the creator, to whom material is subjected in the substance of the world. But he, too, ought to have made it from material, since the same reasoning applies to the god opposed to the creator, making him equally god. And so Marcion gives me three gods for now: the maker, the place, and the material.

Accordingly, he also puts the creator in a place, judging by the same condition, and subjects material to him — innate, ungenerated, and eternal by that same name, just like the Lord. Further, by assigning evil to material — innate to the innate, ungenerated to the ungenerated, eternal to the eternal — he has now produced a fourth god. You therefore have, in the upper realm, three substances of divinity; in the lower, four. When their own Christs are added to these — one who appeared under Tiberius, another promised by the creator — Marcion suffers obvious fraud at the hands of those who suppose he introduces two gods, when he actually assigns nine, albeit unknowingly.

latin: Post haec, uel ante haec, cum dixeris esse et illi conditionem suam et suum mundum et suum caelum, — de caelo quidem illo tertio uidebimus, si et ad apostolum uestrum discutiendum peruenerimus — interim, quaecumque substantia eius est, cum suo utique deo apparuisse debuerat. at nunc quale est, ut dominus anno quinto* decimo Tiberii Caesaris reuelatus sit, substantia uero anno quinto decimo iam Seueri imperatoris nulla omnino comperta sit? quae friuolis creatoris praecellens utique latere desisset, non latente iam domino suo et auctore. et ideo, si ipsa non potuit manifestari in hoc mundo, quomodo dominus paruit eius in hoc mundo? si dominum cepit hic mundus, cur substantiam capere non potuit, nisi domino fortasse maiorem? iam nunc de loco quaestio est, pertinens et ad mundum illum superiorem et ad ipsum deum eius. ecce enim, si et ille habet mundum suum infra se, super creatorem, in loco utique fecit eum, cuius spatium uacabat inter pedes suos et caput creatoris. ergo et deus ipse in loco erat et mundum in loco faciebat, et erit iam locus ille maior et deo et mundo. nihil enim non maius est id quod capit eo quod capitur. et uidendum, ne qua adhuc illic uacent subsiciua. in quibus et tertius aliqui stipare deus se cum mundo suo possit. ergo iam incipe deos computare. erit enim et locus deus, non tantum qua deo maior, sed et qua innatus et infectus ac per hoc aeternus et deo par, in quo semper deus fuerit. dehinc si et ille mundum ex aliqua materia subiacente molitus est innata et infecta et contemporali deo, quemadmodum de creatore Marcion sentit, redigis et hoc ad maiestatem loci, qui et deum et materiam, duos deos, clusit. et materia enim deus secundum formam diuinitatis, innata scilicet et infecta et aeterna, aut si de nihilo molitus est mundum, hoc et de creatore sentire cogetur, cui materiam subicit in substantiam mundi. sed ex, materia et ille fecisse debebit. eadem ratione occurrente illi quoque, [deo] quae opponitur creatori, ut aeque deo. atque ita tres interim mihi deos numera Marcionis, factorem et locum et materiam. proinde et creatorem in loco facit, utique eadem condicione censendo, et materiam ei subicit, utique innatam et infectam et hoc nomine aeternam, ut dominum. amplius; I et malum materiae deputans, innatum innatae, infectum infectae et aeternum aeternae, quartum iam hinc deum fecit. habes igitur in superioribus tres substantias diuinitatis, in inferioribus quat- i tuor. his cum accedunt et sui Christi, alter qui apparuit sub Tiberio alter qui a creatore promittitur. manifestam iam fraudem Marcion patitur ab eis, qui duos illum deos inferre : praesumunt, cum nouem adsignet, licet nesciens,

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Since there is no other world, neither is there another god for it. It follows, then, that they split the two kinds of things—visible and invisible—between two gods as authors, and so they reserve the invisible things for their own god. Who, except a heretical spirit, could even entertain the idea that the invisible things belong to a god who has produced not a single visible thing? They belong far more properly to the one who has actually worked visible things and thereby grounded faith in the invisible as well; it is much more just to trust some exemplars than none at all. We will also see to which author the apostle assigns the invisible things, once we have examined him. For now we are relying on the plainest common sense and sound reasoning, preparing the ground for the appeal to Scripture, confirming that this diversity of visible and invisible things must be credited to the Creator God. His entire operation consists of diversities: corporeal and incorporeal, animate and inanimate, vocal and mute, mobile and stationary, fertile and sterile, dry and moist, hot and cold. That same diversity has tempered man himself, both in body and in senses: some members strong, others weak; some honorable, others dishonorable; some paired, others single; some alike, others unalike. And so also in the inner senses: now joy, now anxiety; now love, now hatred; now anger, now gentleness. If the whole universe is thus modulated as a rivalry of conditions, then the invisible things are owed to the visible things—not to be assigned to a different author than the one to whom their rivals belong. They themselves point out the Creator as diverse: commanding what he forbids and forbidding what he commands, striking and healing. So why do they take him as uniform in this one respect, as only the founder of visible things, when it should be believed that he created both visible and invisible, just as he created both life and death, both evil and peace? And certainly, if those invisible things are greater than the visible things in their own place, then it is also fitting that the greater things belong to him whose are the great things, because neither great things nor, still less, greater things can belong to him to whom not even moderate things are comparable.

latin: Non comparente igitur mundo alio sicut nec deo eius. consequens est, ut duas species rerum, uisibilia et inuisibilia. duobus auctoribus deis diuidant et ita suo deo inuisibilia defendant. quis autem poterit inducere in animum, nisi spiritus haereticus, eius esse inuisibilia. qui nihil uisibile praemiserit. quam eius, qui uisibilia operatus inuisibilium quoque fidem fecerit, cum iustius multo sit aliquibus exemplariis adnuere quam nullis? uidebimus et apostolus cui auctori inuisibilia deputet, cum et illum explorauerimus. nunc enim communibus plurimum sensibus et argumentationibus iustis secuturae scripturarum quoque aduocationi fidem sternimus, confirmantes diuersitatem hanc uisibilium et inuisibilium deo creatori deputandam, sicuti tota operatio eius ex diuersitatibus constat, ex corporalibus et incorporalibus, ex animalibus et inanimalibus, ex uocalibus et mutis, ex mobilibus et statiuis, ex genitalibus et sterilibus, ex aridis et sucidis, ex calidis et frigidis. sic et hominem ipsum diuersitas temperauit, tam in corpore quam in sensu. alia membra fortia alia infirma, alia honesta alia inhonesta. alia gemina alia unica, alia comparia alia disparia. proinde et in sensu nunc laetitia nunc anxietas nunc amor nunc odium nunc ira nunc lenitas. quod si ita est, ut aemula inter se conditionis uniuersitas ista modulata sit, iam igitur et uisibilibus inuisibilia debentur, non alteri auctori deputanda quam cui et aemula eorum. (qui) ipsum creatorem diuersum notant, iubentem quae prohibuit et prohibentem quae iussit, percutientem et sanantem, cur in hac sola specie uniformem eum capiunt, uisibilium solummodo conditorem, quem proinde credendum sit et uisibilia et inuisibilia condidisse quemadmodum et uitam et mortem, et mala et pacem? et utique, si illa inuisibilia maiora sunt uisibilibus creatoris suo loco magnis, sic quoque congruit eius esse maiora, cuius et magna, quia nec magna, nedum maiora, ei competant, cuius nec modica comparent.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: They burst out of their corner and say: "One single work is enough for our God: He freed humanity by His supreme, paramount goodness — a work to be preferred to all places." (The manuscript actually reads 'locusts', but the absurdity is theirs.) Oh, a greater God! — whose work is so great it cannot be found anywhere except in the man of the lesser God! But the order of proof is backwards. First you have to prove He is God through the standard — His works — then, and only then, through His benefits. First you ask whether He exists, and then what kind of God He is. Existence is settled by works; character by benefits. You don't establish His existence simply because He is said to have freed humanity; you establish His existence first, and then you can say He freed humanity — so that it also becomes established whether He actually did free anyone, since He was capable both of existing and of not freeing. How, then, can He be believed to exist just because He is said to have freed, when He was capable both of existing and of not freeing?

Now, in this very article — drawn away from the question of the unknown God — if it is sufficiently established that He neither created anything nor ought to have created, so that He might be known through His works (because if He had existed, He ought to have been known, and certainly from the beginning of things — for it was not fitting for God to have stayed hidden) — we must go back to the origin of the question of the unknown God so that I can shake off its other branches as well. First it will be necessary to ask: He who presented Himself to knowledge only later, why later and not from the beginning of things, for which He was certainly necessary, since He is God, and indeed all the more necessary, because the better He is, the less He ought to have been hidden? It cannot be said that there was neither material nor cause for knowing God, since both humanity was in the world from the beginning — the very humanity He now assists — and the malice of the Creator, against which, as good, He assists. Therefore, either He ignored both the cause and the material of His necessary revelation, or He doubted, or He was unable, or He was unwilling. All of these are unworthy of God, especially the best God. But we will fill out this point elsewhere with the reproach of His late revelation, just as now we settle it with sheer demonstration.

latin: His compressi erumpunt dicere: (sufficit unicum hoc opus deo nostro, quod hominem liberauit summa et praecipua bonitate sua et omnibus locustis anteponenda\'. o deum maiorem, cuius tam magnum opus non potuit inueniri quam in homine dei minoris! enimuero prius est, ut eum probes esse per quae deum probari oportet, per opera, tunc deinde per beneficia. primo enim quaeritur, an sit, et ita, qualis sit. alterum de operibus, alterum de beneficiis dinoscetur. ceterum non quia liberasse dicitur hominem, ideo esse eum constat, sed si esse constiterit, tunc et liberasse dicetur, ut et an liberauerit constet, quia potuerit et esse et non liberasse. quomodo ergo, quia liberasse dicetur, etiam esse credetur, cum potuerit et esse et non liberasse? . Nunc, in isto articulo ab ignoti dei quaestione deducto si satis constitit tam nihil illum condidisse quam debuisse condidisse, uti cognosceretur ex operibus, quia si fuisset, cognosci debuisset, et utique a primordio rerum, — deum enim non decuisset latuisse — regrediar necesse est ad originem quaestionis dei ignoti, ut ceteros quoque ramulos eius excutiam. primo enim quaeri oportebit, qui postea se protulerit in notitiam cur postea et non a primordio rerum quibus utique necessarius, qua deus, et quidem necessarior quo melior latere non debuit. non enim potest dici non fuisse aut materiam aut causam cognoscendi deum, cum et homo a primordio esset in saeculo, cui nunc subuenit, et malitia creatoris, aduersus quam ut bonus subuenit. igitur aut ignorauit et causam et materiam suae reuelationis necessariae aut dubitanit ++ aut non potuit aut noluit. omnia haec deo indigna, maxime optimo. sed et hunc locum alibi implebimus exprobratione serae reuelationis, sicut nunc sola demonstratione.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Let him proceed, then, into recognition — when he wished, when he could, when the fatal hour arrived. Perhaps the ascending node blocked him, or some baleful influence, or Saturn in square, or Mars in trine. After all, the mathematicians are mostly Marcionites, and they don't blush to admit it; they live by the very stars of the Creator.

Here we must test the quality of the revelation: whether he was revealed worthily, so that it holds together; whether truly, so that he may be believed to be what he was worthily revealed to be. Things worthy of God will prove God.

We define God as first to be known by nature, then recognized by doctrine — nature from his works, doctrine from his preachings. But where there is no nature, natural instruments fail. So he ought to have effected his own revelation through preachings, especially against the one who needed revealing — the one who, despite works of creation and preaching so many and so great, had barely managed to fill man with faith.

How, then, was he known? If by human conjecture, I deny that God can be known except by himself — and not merely to the form of the Creator, but to the condition of such divine greatness and human mediocrity, lest man appear greater than God. God did not will to be known; he was dragged into public recognition by his own powers. Human mediocrity finds it easier to fabricate gods for itself, based on the experiments of all time, than to follow the truth that nature already grasps.

Otherwise, if man presumes to comment on God this way, then let others do as Romulus did with Consus, Tatius with Cloacina, Hostilius with Pavor, Metellus with Alburnus, and some before this time with Antinous. We know Marcion as a shipowner, not a king or emperor.

latin: Processerit, age, iam in notitiam quando uoluit, quando potuit, quando hora fatalis aduenit. fortasse enim anabibazon ei obstabat aut aliquae maleficae aut Saturnus quadratus aut Mars trigonus. nam et mathematici plurimum Marcionitae, nec hoc erubescentes, de ipsis etiam stellis uiuere creatoris. tractandum est hic de reuelationis qualitate, an digne reuelatus sit, ut constet, an uere, et ita credatur esse quem digne constiterit reuelatum. digna enim deo probabunt deum. nos definimus deum primo natura cognoscendum, dehinc doctrina recognoscendum, natura ex operibus, doctrina ex praedicationibus. sed cui nulla natura est naturalia instrumenta non suppetunt. ergo uel praedicationibus reuelationem sui debuerat operari, maxime aduersus eum reuelandus, qui et conditionis et praedicationis operibus tot ac tantis uix tamen hominem fide impleuerat. quomodo itaque cognitus est? si per humanam coniecturam, nego deum alias cognosci posse quam per semetipsum, nec tantum ad formam prouocans creatoris uerum et ad condicionem tam diuinae magnitudinis quam humanae mediocritatis, ne maior deo homo uideri possit, qui eum non ultro uolentem cognosci suis uiribus quodammodo in publicum agnitionis extraxerit, cum humana mediocritas facilius deos fingere sibi norit secundum totius aeui experimenta quam uerum sectari, quem natura iam intellegunt. alioquin, si sic homo d.-\'um commentabitur, quomodo Romulus Consum et Tatius Cloacinam et Hostilius Pauorem et Metellus Alburnum et quidam ante hoc tempus Antinoum, hoc aliis licebit; nos Marciouem nauclerum nouimus, non regem nec imperatorem.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: The Marcionites shoot back: 'Our God, even if not from the beginning, even if not by arrangement, still revealed Himself in Christ Jesus — by His own initiative?' Fine. A book on Christ covering every phase of His career will come later — we must separate the topics so each gets fuller, more orderly treatment — but for now a few words will suffice to show that Christ fulfilled the laws not of some other God but of the Creator.

In the fifteenth year of Tiberius, Christ Jesus deigned to descend from heaven. As for the saving Spirit of Marcion — who willed it so — I never bothered to investigate in which year of Antoninus the Greater he exhaled his dog-star breath from Pontus, though the fact itself is agreed. The Antoninian heretic is impious under Pius. From Tiberius to Antoninus runs about one hundred fifteen and a half years plus half a month. They put the same span between Christ and Marcion. So when Marcion first introduced this God under Antoninus, as we have proven, the case is clear to anyone with sense: the timeline condemns what first appeared under Antoninus as never having appeared under Tiberius — which means the God of the Antoninian empire was not the God of the Tiberian, and therefore was not revealed by Christ, whom all agree Marcion first preached.

I will now prove this consensus from the adversaries themselves. The separation of Law and Gospel is Marcion's proper and principal work, and his disciples cannot deny what they possess in their supreme instrument, by which they are initiated and hardened into this heresy. These are Marcion's 'Antitheses' — opposing contradictions — which try to force a breach between Gospel and Law, so that from the diversity of pronouncements in each instrument they can argue a diversity of gods. Since that very separation of Law and Gospel is what insinuated another God of the Gospel against the God of the Law, it follows that before this separation that God was not in knowledge — He was made known only by the argument of separation — and thus was not revealed by Christ, who preceded the separation, but was invented by Marcion, who established the separation against the peace of Gospel and Law, a peace that reason itself preserved unharmed and unshaken from Christ's appearance to Marcion's audacity, a peace that acknowledged no other God of both Law and Gospel except the Creator, against whom the separation was launched by the Pontic after so much time.

[salutis] qui ita uoluit quoto quidem anno Antonini maioris de Ponto suo exhalauerit aura canicularis, non curaui inuestigare. de quo tamen constat. Antoninianus haereticus est, sub Pio impius. a Tiberio autem usque ad Antoninum anni fere centum quindecim et dimidium anni cum dimidio mensis. tantundem temporis ponunt inter Christum et Marcionem. cum igitur sub Antonino primus: Marcion hunc deum induxerit, sicut probauimus, statim. qui sapis, plana res est: praeiudicant tempora quod sub Antonino primum processit sub Tiberio non processisse, id est deum Antoniniani imperii Tiberiani non fuisse, atque ita non a Christo reuelatum quem constat a Marcione primo praedicatum. hoc nunc ut probem constare. quod superest ab ipsis aduersariis sumam. separatio legis et euangelii proprium et principale opus est Marcionis, nec poterant negare discipuli eius quod in summo instrumento habent, quo denique initiantur et indurantur in hanc haeresim. nam hae sunt \'Antithesis\' Marcionis, id est contrariae oppositiones. quae conantur discordiam euangelii cum lege committere. ut ex diuersitate sententiarum utriusque instrumenti diuersitatem quoque argumententur deorum. igitur cum ea separatio legis et euangelii ipsa sit, quae alium deum euangelii insinuauerit aduersus deum legis, apparet ante eam separationem deum in notitia non fuisse, qui ab argumento separationis innotuit, atque ita non a Christo reuelatum qui fuit ante separationem, sed a Marcione commentatum, qui instituit separationem aduersus euangelii legisque pacem, quam retro inlaesam et inconcussam ab apparentia Christi usque ad audaciam Marcionis illa utique ratio seruauit, quae non alium deum et legis et euangelii tuebatur praeter creatorem, aduersus quem tanto post tempore separatio a Pontico inmissa est.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Ponticus drags out two gods like the twin Symplegades that wrecked his ship: the Creator, our God, whom he cannot deny, and his own deity, whom he will never prove. He suffered this catastrophe, poor wretch, because he let a single, simple passage from the Lord's teaching — the parable of the good and bad tree, applied to human beings, not gods — drive him to the presumption that a good tree cannot bear bad fruit nor a bad tree good fruit; in other words, a good mind or faith cannot produce evil works, nor an evil mind good works. He stumbled, as many do now, especially heretics, over the problem of evil — where does it come from? — and, senses dulled by the sheer bulk of his own curiosity, he latched onto the Creator's declaration: "I am the one who creates evil." The more he had already presumed the Creator to be the author of evil, and the more other arguments that seduce every perverse mind reinforced that view, the more he read the bad tree bearing bad fruit — clearly evil fruit — into the Creator, and concluded there simply had to be another god to serve as the good tree bearing good fruit. Spotting in Christ what looked like an entirely different disposition, one of sheer, unmixed kindness that contrasted with the Creator's, he easily argued a new, alien divinity revealed in his Christ, and with that pinch of leaven he soured the entire batch of faith with heretical bitterness. He also had a certain Cerdo as the instigator of this scandal: two blind men thought they could more easily perceive two gods than one, because they had never seen the one God whole; even to the bleary-eyed, a single lamp looks like many. So he demolished the God he was forced to confess by slandering evil, and built up the god he tried to invent by exalting the good. We will expose the natures he has assigned to these articles through our own responses.

latin: Duos Ponticus deos adfert, tamquam duas Symplegadas naufragii sui, quem negare non potuit, id est creatorem, id est nostrum, et quem probare non poterit, id est suum, passus, infelix, huius praesumptionis instinctum de simplici capitulo dominicae pronuntiationis, in homines non in deos disponentis exempla illa bonae et malae arboris, quod neque bona malos neque mala bonos proferat fructus, id est neque mens uel fides bona malas edat operas neque mala bonas. languens enim — quod et nunc multi, et maxime haeretici — circa mali quaestionem, unde malum, et obtusis sensibus ipsa enormitate curiositatis inueniens creatorem pronuntiantem: ego sum, qui condo mala, quanto ipsum praesumpserat mali auctorem et ex aliis argumentis, quae ita persuadent peruerso cuique, tanto in creatorem interpretatus malam arborem malos fructus condentem, scilicet mala, alium deum praesumpsit esse debere in partem bonae arboris bonos fructus. et ita in Christo quasi aliam inueniens dispositionem solius et purae benignitatis, ut diuersae a creatoris, facile nouam et hospitam argumentatus est diuinitatem in Christo suo reuelatam modicoque exinde fermento totam fidei massam haeretico acore desipuit. habuit et Cerdonem quendam informatorem scandali huius: duo facilius duos deos caeci perspexisse se existimauerunt. unum enim non integre uiderant. lippientibus etiam singularis lucerna numerosa est. alterum igitur deum, quem confiteri cogebatur, de malo infamando destruxit, alterum, quem commentari conitebatur, de bono praeferendo construxit. has naturas quibus disposuerit articulis, per ipsas responsiones nostras ostendemus.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: We also need to defend that very clear proof against the clamor of the opposing side. They claim Marcion didn't so much innovate the rule by separating Law and Gospel as revert to a rule previously adulterated. Oh Christ, most patient Lord, you endured the perversion of your preaching for so many years, until Marcion finally came to your rescue! They even pit Peter and the other pillars of the apostleship against Paul, because Paul rebuked them for not walking straight toward the truth of the Gospel. This is the same Paul who was still raw in grace and trembling lest he had run or would run in vain when he first conferred with the earlier apostles. So if, while still burning with zeal like a new convert, he judged something in their conduct reprehensible toward Judaism, then—once convinced—he would later become all things to all men to win them all: to Jews as a Jew, to those under the Law as under the Law. You want that rebuke of mere conduct—a rebuke that would please his future accuser—to be suspected as a falsification of his preaching toward God. But on the contrary, concerning the unity of preaching we read above, they joined right hands and agreed on a division of duties in the fellowship of the Gospel. As Paul says elsewhere: "Whether I or they, so we preach." Even when he describes certain false brothers who slipped in to divert the Galatians to a different gospel, he shows that this adulteration of the Gospel did not aim at transferring faith to another God and Christ, but at preserving the discipline of the Law—detecting those who insisted on circumcision and on observing times, days, months, and years of Jewish ceremonies. They should have known these were already excluded, according to the renewed disposition of the Creator, who had long before preached this very thing through his prophets. Through Isaiah: "The old things have passed away; behold, I am doing new things" (Isaiah 43:19). And through Jeremiah: "I will make a covenant, not like the one I made with your fathers when I led them out of Egypt" (Jeremiah 31:32). And elsewhere: "Renew a newness for yourselves, and be circumcised to your God, and circumcise the foreskins of your hearts." Therefore the apostle, now establishing this circumcision and this newness, was also dissuading those old ceremonies—ceremonies whose own Creator had once declared would cease. Through Hosea: "I will turn away all her delights, her feast days, new moons, sabbaths, and all her ceremonies" (Hosea 2:13). For so also through Isaiah: "I do not endure your new moons and sabbaths and great days; your festivals and fasts and feast days my soul hates." But if the Creator had already rejected all these things long ago, and the apostle now pronounced them rejected, the apostle's own verdict—consistent with the Creator's decrees—proves he did not preach another God than the one whose decrees he wanted recognized. He brands as false both the apostles and the brothers in this cause who would transfer the Gospel of Christ the Creator from the newness foretold by the Creator to the antiquity rejected by the Creator.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: If Marcion preaches a new God while trying to shut out the old God's law, why does he lay down not a single rule about this new deity, but only about the old law — unless it's because faith stayed put in the Creator, so that only the Creator's law could still be acknowledged? That very Psalm saw it coming: "Let us break their chains and throw off their yoke" (Psalm 2:3); and sure enough, the nations erupted, the peoples plotted emptiness, earth's kings took their stand, and rulers gathered as one against the Lord and against his Christ.

If Paul had been proclaiming a different God, there would have been zero debate over whether to keep the law — since that law wouldn't pertain to the new Lord and rival of the law in the first place. The sheer novelty and otherness of such a God would have erased not just the question of the old, alien law, but every mention of it. But that wasn't the issue. The whole dispute was this: when the very same God of the law is preached in Christ, why is his law being whittled away? Faith never budged from the Creator and his Christ; what wavered was conduct and discipline.

Some argued over eating idol-meat, some over women's veils, some over marriage or divorce, a few even over the hope of resurrection — but no one argued over God. If that question had been in play, it would have surfaced with the apostle, and how much more urgently. But if truth suffered adultery regarding God's rule after the apostles' time, then the apostolic tradition suffered no such corruption in its own day, and no other apostolic tradition will be recognized than the one published today in their churches.

You will not find a single church on the apostolic roll that does not Christianize in the Creator. And if those churches were corrupted from the start, which ones remain intact? Obviously, the ones opposed to the Creator. So produce one from your apostolic roll, and you'll be refuted. Since it's now established on every front that from Christ to Marcion no other God stood in the rule of this sacrament but the Creator, our proof stands fortified: we've shown the heretic's 'knowledge of God' began by severing Gospel from law, and the definition above holds — you must not believe in a God a man has cobbled together from his own senses, unless he's a prophet; that is, not from his own senses. If Marcion can claim that, he must prove it; nothing will be retracted. For by this wedge of truth all heresy is expelled, once Christ is shown to be the circumciser not of some other God, but of the Creator.
