excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: How can Antichrist be utterly overthrown unless we are also given ground to demolish his other injections, now that the defense of prescriptions has been relaxed? Let us move on, then, to the very person of God — or rather, to the shadow and phantom that passes for Christ. He must be examined by the very standard by which he is preferred to the Creator. There will certainly be fixed rules for testing the goodness of God. But first I must find and seize that goodness, and only then bring it to the rules. For when I scan the timeline, it is nowhere to be found from the beginning of matter and the entrance of causes. It ought to have been present with them, acting from that point onward, since it had the obligation to act. Already there were death and the sting of death, transgression, and the Creator's own malice (Gen 2:17). Against these the goodness of another God ought to have rushed to help, presenting itself as the first rule of divine goodness — if it proved natural, it would have assisted immediately, right when the cause began. Everything in God ought to be natural and innate, so that it may be eternal, in keeping with his own state; otherwise it would be judged adventitious and alien, and therefore temporal and foreign to eternity. So too a perpetual, constant goodness is demanded in God — one stored and ready in the treasury of natural properties, preceding its own causes and materials, embracing each first occasion, not despising or abandoning it, if indeed it came first. Finally I must also ask here: why did his goodness not operate from the beginning, just as we asked why he himself was not revealed from the beginning? Why not? The one who was to be revealed through goodness, if he existed at all. It is impossible for God to be unable to do anything, much less to fail to exercise his own natural properties. If those properties are held in check, why do they not run? Then they would not be natural. For even inactivity is unknown to his nature; hence the verdict: if he acts. Thus it will not appear that he was unwilling to exercise goodness, meanwhile sheltering behind the name of nature. Nature cannot be unwilling — it directs itself so that if it ceases, it ceases to be. But the goodness in Marcion's God once ceased from work; therefore it was not natural goodness, which could have ceased at some point, something natural things are not permitted to do. And if it is not natural, it is no longer to be believed eternal or equal to God. Because it is not eternal, since it is not natural — a thing that finally guarantees no perpetuity for itself, neither from the past nor promised for the future. For just as it did not exist from the beginning, it certainly will not exist at the end. It is able not to be at some time, just as it once was not. Therefore, since it is established that the goodness of that God ceased from the beginning — for it did not free man from the beginning — and it ceased by will rather than weakness, the will that suppressed that goodness will be exposed as the end of malice. What is more malicious than refusing to benefit when you can, than torturing utility, than allowing injury? The whole eulogy of the Creator will be rewritten onto the one who abetted the Creator's savagery by delaying his own goodness. For whatever is not done lies in whose hand? It is already charged to him when it is done. Man is condemned to death for tasting one little tree; from then on transgressions advance with punishments, and all who never knew a blade of grass in paradise already perish (Gen 2:17). And does some better God either not know or tolerate this? If the purpose was that he might be found better by contrast, how much worse must the Creator be judged? It is enough that he is malicious in this scheme, who also willed that the Creator be burdened, admitted his operations, and held the world in vexation. What verdict will you pass on a doctor who feeds the disease by delaying aid and stretches out the danger by prolonging the remedy, so that he may cure more precious or famous cases? Such a sentence must also be pronounced on Marcion's God: the permitter of evil, the favorer of injury, the pimp of grace, the betrayer of benignity — which he did not immediately display for his cause. He would have displayed it if he were good by nature and not by acquisition, if he were optimal by genius and not by discipline, if he were God from eternity and not from Tiberius — indeed, what is truer, from Cerdo and Marcion. Now that God has outdone Tiberius, so that divine goodness might be dedicated on earth by his empire.

latin: Sed quomodo funditus euertetur antichristus, nisi ceteris quoque iniectionibus eius elidendis locus detur. relaxata praescriptionum defensione? accedamus igitur iam hinc ad ipsam dei personam, uel potius umbram et phantasma secundum Christum ipsius. per idque examinetur, per quod creatori praefertur. et utique erunt regulae certae ad examinandam dei bonitatem. sed prius est, ut inueniam illam et adprehendam. et ita ad regulas perducam. cum enim circumspicio tempora, nusquam est a primordio materiarum et introitu causarum. cum quibus debuerat inueniri, exinde agens, quo agere habuit. erat enim iam et mors et aculeus mortis, delictum, et ipsa malitia creatoris. aduersus quam subuenire deberet alterius dei bonitas, t primae huic regulae diuinae bonitatis occurrens, si se naturalem probaret, statim succurrens, ut causa coepit. omnia enim in deo naturalia et ingenita esse debebunt, ut sint aeterna, secundum statum ipsius, ne obuenticia et extranea reputentur ac per hoc temporalia et aeternitatis aliena. ita et bonitas perennis et iugis exigetur in deo, quae in thesauris naturalium proprietatum reposita et parata antecederet causas et materias suas, et primam quamque susciperet, non despiceret et destitueret, si antecedebat. denique non minus et hic quaeram, cur non a primordio operata sit bonitas eius, quam de ipso quaesiuimus, cur non a primordio sit reuelatus? quidni? qui per bonitatem reuelari haberet, si qui fuisset. non posse quid deo non licet, nedum naturalibus suis fungi. quae si continentur, quo minus currant, naturalia non erunt. et otium enim sui natura non nouit; hinc censetur, si agat. sic nec noluisse uidebitur exercere bonitatem, interim naturae nomine. natura enim se non potest nolle, quae se ita dirigit, ut, si cessauerit, non sit. sed cessauit aliquando in deo Marcionis de opere bonitas: ergo non fuit naturalis bonitas, quae potuit aliquando cessasse, quod naturalibus non licet. et si non erit naturalis, iam nec aeterna credenda nec deo par. quia non aeterna, dum non naturalis, quae denique nullam sui perpetuitatem aut de praeterito constituat aut de futuro repromittat. nam ut a primordio non fuit, et in finem sine dubio non erit. potest enim et non esse quandoque, sicut non fuit aliquando. igitur cum constet in primordio cessasse bonitatem dei illius — (non) enim a primordio liberauit hominem — et uoluntate potius eam quam infirmitate cessasse, iam uoluntas subpressae bonitatis finis inuenietur malignitatis. quid enim tam malignum quam nolle prodesse cum possis,, quam utilitatem cruciare, quam iniuriam sinere? totum denique creatoris elogium in illum rescribetur, qui saeuitias eius i bonitatis suae mora iuuit. nam in cuius manu est quid ne fiat, eius iam deputatur, cum fit. homo damnatur in mortem ob unius arbusculae delibationem, et exinde proficiunt delicta cum poenis et pereunt iam omnes, qui paradisi nullum caespitem norunt. et hoc melior aliqui deus aut nescit aut sustinet? si ut ex hoc melior inueniretur, quanto creator deterior haberetur. satis et in isto consilio malitiosus, qui et illum uoluit oneratum, operationibus eius admissis, et saeculum in uexatione detinuit. quid de tali medico iudicabis, qui nutriat morbum mora praesidii et periculum extendat dilatione remedii, quo pretiosius aut famosius curet? talis et in deum Marcionis dicenda sententia est, mali permissorem, iniuriae fautorem, gratiae lenocinatorem, benignitatis praeuaricatorem, quam non statim causae suae exhibuit; plane exhibiturus, si natura bonus et non accessione, si ingenio optimus et non disciplina, si ab aeuo deus et non a Tiberio, immo, quod uerius, a Cerdone et Marcione. Tiberio nunc deus ille praestiterit, ut imperio eius diuina bonitas in terris dedicaretur,

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: I am setting another rule before him: just as natural things are rational, so everything in God must be rational. I demand a reason for goodness, because nothing else can count as good unless it is rationally good, let alone that goodness itself should be caught being irrational. It is easier for evil with some reason attached to pass for good than for good, deserted by reason, to escape being judged evil. I deny rational goodness to Marcion's God—first of all, because he proceeded to save a foreign man. I know they will claim this is the principal and perfect goodness, since it is poured out voluntarily and freely on foreigners without any debt of familiarity—according to which we are commanded to love even our enemies, who are already foreigners by that very name. Why, then, did he not regard man from the beginning, a foreigner from the beginning? By holding back, he prejudged that he had nothing to do with the foreigner. Moreover, the discipline of loving a foreigner or enemy came before the command to love your neighbor as yourself. Even though that command comes from the Creator's law, you must accept it too, so that it is not destroyed by Christ but rather built upon. For the more you love your neighbor, the more you are commanded to love your enemy and the foreigner. Exacting what is owed is an exaggeration of owed goodness. But owed goodness comes before unowed goodness—as principal, as more worthy, as minister and companion to its own, that is, unowed goodness, which is prior. So when the first reason for goodness is to show it to one's own out of justice, and the second is to show it to a foreigner out of the overflow of justice, what kind of second reason can be assigned to one who lacks the first, who does not have his own man, and is therefore deficient even in the lesser? Furthermore, how did what is deficient, which never had its own, overflow into a foreigner? Produce the principal reason, and only then vindicate the subsequent one. Nothing can be vindicated without rational order; so much so that reason itself never loses order in anything. Let the reason for goodness now begin from the second degree, that is, toward a foreigner: nor will that second degree of goodness hold together with reason, having been destroyed in another way. For only then will the second goodness toward a foreigner be considered rational if it operates without injury to him whose property it is. Whatever goodness justice first produces is rational. Just as in the principal degree, when it is shown to one's own, it will be rational if it is just, so also toward a foreigner it can appear rational if it is not unjust. But what kind of goodness consists through injury, and that for a foreigner? Perhaps injurious goodness might be considered rational for a household member. But for a foreigner, to whom not even legitimate goodness is owed, by what reason can such unjust goodness be defended? What is more unjust, more iniquitous, more wicked than to benefit a foreign servant in such a way that he is taken from his master, vindicated to another, suborned against his master's head—and what is more outrageous—right in the master's own house, living off the master's own stores, trembling under the master's own blows? Such a defender would be condemned even in the world, let alone the plagiarist. Marcion's God acts no differently: bursting into a foreign world, snatching man from God, son from father, pupil from educator, servant from master, so that he makes him impious toward God, irreligious toward his father, ungrateful toward his educator, wicked toward his master. I ask you: if rational goodness produces such a person, what would irrational goodness produce? I cannot imagine anyone more shameless than the one who is baptized in another's water for another god, who expands toward another god in another's heaven, who is laid out on another's earth for another god, who offers thanksgiving over another's bread to another god, who works with another's goods in the name of alms and love for another god. What kind of god is so good that man becomes evil through him, so favorable that he makes another god—indeed, that god's own master—angry?

cessando praeiudicauit cum extraneo nihil sibi esse. ceterum disciplinam diligendi extraneum uel inimicum antecessit praeceptum diligendi proximum tamquam te ipsum. quod etsi ex lege creatoris, et tu quoque illud excipere debebis, ut a Christo non destructum, sed potius exstructum. nam quo magis proximum diligas, diligere iuberis inimicum et extraneum. exaggeratio est debitae bonitatis exactio indebitae. antecedit autem debita indebitam, ut principalis, ut dignior, ut ministra et comite sua [id est indebita] prior. igitur cum prima bonitatis ratio sit in rem suam exhiberi ex iustitia, secunda autem in alienam ex redundantia iustitiae super scribarum et Pharisaeorum, quale est secundam ei rationem referri, cui deficit prima, non habenti proprium hominem ac per hoc quoque exiguae? porro exigua, quae suum non habuit, quomodo in alienum redundauit? exhibe principalem rationem, et tunc uindica sequentem. nulla res sine ordine rationalis potest uindicari; tanto abest, ut ratio ipsa in aliquo ordinem amittat. sit nunc et a secundo gradu incipiens ratio bonitatis, in extraneum scilicet: nec secundus illi gradus ratione constabit, alio modo destructus. tunc enim rationalis habebitur uel secunda in extraneum bonitas, si sine iniuria eius operetur, cuius est res. quamcumque bonitatem iustitia prima efficit rationalem. sicut in principali gradu, cum in rem suam exhibetur, rationalis erit si iusta sit, sic et in extraneum rationalis uideri poterit, si non sit iniusta. ceterum qualis bonitas quae per iniuriam constat, et quidem pro extraneo? fortasse enim pro domestico aliquatenus rationalis habeatur bonitas iniuriosa. pro extraneo uero, cui nec proba legitime deberetur, qua ratione tam iniusta rationalis defendetur? quid enim iniustius, quid iniquius et improbius quam ita alieno benefacere seruo, ut domino eripiatur, ut alii uindicetur, ut aduersus caput domini subornetur, et quidem, quod indignius, in ipsa adhuc domo domini, de ipsius adhuc horreis uiuens, sub ipsius adhuc plagis tremens? talis adsertor etiam damnaretur in saeculo, nedum plagiator. non aliter ** deus Marcionis, inrumpens in alienum mundum, eripiens deo hominem, patri filium, educatori aluminum, domino famulum, ut eum efficiat deo impium, patri inreligiosum, educatori ingratum, domino nequam. oro te, si rationalis bonitas talem facit, qualem faceret inrationalis? non putem impudentiorem quam qui in aliena aqua alii deo tingitur, ad alienum caelum alii deo expanditur, in aliena terra alii deo sternitur, super alienum panem alii deo gratiarum actionibus fungitur, de alienis bonis ob alium deum nomine elemosynae et dilectionis operatur. quis iste deus tam bonus, ut homo ab illo malus fiat, tam propitius, ut alium illi deum, et dominum quidem ipsius, faciat iratum?

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: God is eternal and rational, yes — but I say He is also perfect in every respect: 'You will be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect' (Matthew 5:48). So demonstrate this perfect goodness of yours, even though the imperfect version is already well enough attested — a goodness that is neither natural nor rational.

Now the argument shifts: Marcion's goodness is not merely imperfect, but positively defective, scanty, and exhausted. It operates with a smaller stock of raw material and fails to show itself in all cases. Not everyone is saved — fewer than all, whether Jews or Christians of the Creator. With the majority perishing, how can you defend a 'perfect' goodness that fails in the greater part, yields to destruction, and is partial in its reach — doing something for a few, nothing for many, surrendering the rest to ruin? If the majority are not saved, then it is not goodness but malice that turns out perfect. The operation of goodness saves; the operation of malice does not. And a goodness that fails to save the many while saving only a few is more perfect in its failure to help than in its help.

You cannot pin this universal defection of goodness on the Creator. What judge do you acknowledge — a dispenser, perhaps, of goodness to be understood, not a lavish giver, which is what you claim for your god? You prefer him to the Creator on this single count: goodness. But if he alone possesses it in full, no one ought to lack it. I will not press the charge of imperfect goodness against Marcion's god based on the majority perishing; it is enough that those he does save exhibit an imperfect salvation, proving his imperfect goodness — saved in soul, lost in flesh, which does not rise again in his scheme. Where does this halving of salvation come from, if not from a defection of goodness? What would perfect goodness have done but bring the whole person into salvation — the whole person condemned by the Creator, the whole person summoned by the best God?

As far as I can see, even the flesh is stained in his system, the flesh is excluded from marriage, the flesh is punished in the confession of the Name. Even if sins are charged to the flesh, the soul's guilt comes first, and the principality of fault belongs rather to the soul — the flesh merely serves as its minister. A flesh without a soul does not sin at all. So here too the goodness is unjust and therefore imperfect: it abandons the more innocent substance to destruction, though that substance offends by obedience, not by choice. Christ, even if he did not assume the reality of flesh as your heresy claims, still deigned to undergo its likeness. And that very likeness, which he feigned, he owed something to. What is a human being, after all, but flesh? The name 'human' denotes a bodily, material thing, not an animating principle, assigned by the Author. 'God made man from the clay of the earth' — not the soul; the soul comes from the breath — 'and man became a living soul' (Genesis 2:7). Who? The one made from clay. 'God put man in the garden' — the thing he formed, not the thing he breathed into: the one who is now flesh, not the one who is soul.

So if that is the case, with what mouth do you contend for the title of perfect goodness — a goodness that fails not only in the special task of liberating the human person, but in the general property of humanity itself? If grace is full and mercy solid, yet they avail only for the soul, then this present life provides more, since we enjoy it whole and entire. To rise again in part is not liberation but punishment. It would have been the mark of perfect goodness for a human, once liberated into faith in the best God, to be immediately removed from the dwelling and dominion of the harsh God. But now, Marcionite, you still endure fevers, thorns, the pain of your flesh — not only the Creator's thunderbolts, wars, plagues, and other scourges, but even his scorpions. You are cast into the very realm you think you have escaped from his kingdom, where his flies still trample you. If you have been torn free from the future, why not from the present as well, so that the liberation might be perfect?

Our condition is different — with the Author, with the Judge, with the offended Prince of the race. You merely prefer a good God. But you cannot show that God to be perfect, when you are not perfectly liberated from him.

quodsi plures salui non erunt, erit iam non bonitas, sed malitia perfectior. sicut enim bonitatis operatio est, quae facit saluos, ita malignitatis, quae non facit saluos. magis autem non faciens saluos, dum paucos facit, perfectior erit in non iuuando quam (in) iuuan lo. non poteris et in creatorem referre bonitatis in omnes defectionem. quem enim iudicem tenes, dispensatorem, si forte, bonitatis ostendis intellegendum, non profusorem, quod tuo deo uindicas. usque adeo hac sola eum praefers bonitate creatori. quam si solam profitetur et totam, nulli deesse debuerat. sed nolo iam de parte maiore pereuntium imperfectae bonitatis arguere deum Marcionis: sufficit ipsos, quos saluos facit, imperfectae salutis inuentos imperfectam bonitatem eius ostendere, scilicet anima tenus saluos, carne deperditos, quae apud illum non resurgit. unde haec dimidiatio salutis nisi ex defectione bonitatis? quid erat perfectae bonitatis quam totum hominem redigere in salutem, totum damnatum a creatore, totum a deo optimo adlectum? quod sciam, et caro tingitur apud illum, et caro de nuptiis tollitur, et caro in confessione nominis desaeuitur. sed et si carni delicta reputantur, praecedit animae reatus et culpae principatus animae potius adscribendus. cui caro ministri nomine occurrit. carens denique anima caro hactenus peccat. ita et in hoc iniusta bonitas et sic quoque imperfecta, innocentiorem substantiam relinquens in exitium, obsequio, non arbitrio delinquentem. cuius Christus etsi non induit ueritatem. ut tuae haeresi uisum est, imaginem tamen eius subire dignatus est. ipsum quod mentitus est illam, aliquid ei t debuit debuisse quid est autem homo aliud quam caro, siquidem nomen hominis materia corporalis, non animalis, ab auctore sortita est? et fecit hominem deus, inquit, limum de terra, non animam; anima enim de afflatu: et factus est homo in animam uiuam; quis? utique qui de limo: et posuit deus hominem in paradiso; quod finxit, non quod flauit: qui caro nunc, non qui anima. itaque si ita est. quo ore contendes perfectum bonitatis titulum, quae non iam a partitione speciali hominis liberandi defecit, sed a proprietate generali? si plena est gratia et solida misericordia, quae soli animae salutaris est, plus praestat haec uita, qua toti et integri fruimur. ceterum ex parte resurgere multari erit, non liberari. erat et illud perfectae bonitatis, ut homo, liberatus in fidem dei optimi, statim eximeretur de domicilio atque dominatu dei saeui. at nunc et febriculas, o Marcionita, et ceteros tribulos et spinas dolor carnis tuae tibi edit; nec fulminibus tantum aut bellis et pestibus aliisque plagis creatoris sed et scorpiis eius obiectus, in quo te putas liberatum de regno eius, cuius te muscae adhuc calcant? si de futuro erutus es, cur non et de praesenti, ut perfecte? alia est nostra condicio apud auctorem, apud iudicem, apud offensum principem generis. tu tantummodo bonum deum praefers. non potes autem perfecte bonum ostendere a quo non perfecte liberaris.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: On the question of goodness, we have traced the argument this far: Marcion's 'goodness' does not measure up to God at all. It is neither innate, nor rational, nor perfect; it is wicked, unjust, and unworthy of the very name of goodness. The logic is inescapable: to the degree this 'goodness' suits God, it disqualifies Him from being God, since He is exalted on the strength of such a counterfeit goodness, and cannot be true or unique in that mode. This forces the further question: should God be defined by goodness alone, once senses and affections — those so-called 'appendages' — are stripped away? The Marcionites shunt those faculties off their God and dump them on the Creator. We, by contrast, recognize those same faculties in the Creator as worthy of God, and on that ground we refuse to call any being 'God' if it lacks the full complement of divine attributes. Suppose some Epicurean tries to baptize a god with the name of Christ, picturing a blessed, incorruptible being who causes no trouble to himself or anyone else — Marcion chewed over this very view and stripped his god of severity and judicial power. He had only two options: conceive a completely inert, stunned deity — but then what has that god to do with Christ, who is an offense to Jews by His teaching and to Marcion by His Jesus? — or admit that God possesses the full range of motion. But then what has he to do with Epicurus, who is necessary to neither him nor Christians? Look at the dilemma: this god, previously at rest, indifferent to making himself known by any act for eons, suddenly takes notice of human salvation. That shift can only come by an act of will. Was he not, then, shaken by a new will, proving himself subject to every other motion as well? What is a will without the goad of desire? [Who wills what he does not desire?] And desire inevitably drags care in its wake: who wills and desires a thing, yet takes no trouble for it? So once this god both willed and desired man's salvation, he created trouble for himself and others, Epicurus — Marcion's adviser — notwithstanding. He manufactured an adversary: the very thing he opposed by willing, desiring, and striving, whether sin or death. First and foremost, that adversary is the Judge and Lord of men, the Creator. Moreover, no contest runs its course without rivalry, and rivalry cannot exist without an opponent. Thus, by willing, desiring, and striving to liberate man, this god is already locked in rivalry — with the one from whom he liberates, against whom he must liberate himself, and with the things from which he liberates, into which he must liberate them. Consequently, the attendants of rivalry — anger, discord, hatred, contempt, indignation, bile, unwillingness, offense — must show up in the very arena where he rivals. If rivalry brings these in its train, and rivalry, by liberating man, achieves the work of goodness, then that goodness cannot exist without its own endowments — that is, without the senses and affections through which it operates against the Creator — lest it be exposed as irrational for lacking the very faculties it owes. We will defend all this far more fully in the case for the Creator, where these charges are also answered.

latin: Quod adtinet ad bonitatis quaestionem, his lineis deduximus eam minime deo adaequare, ut neque ingenitam neque rationalem neque perfectam, sed et improbam et iniustam et ipso iam bonitatis nomine indignam, quod scilicet in quantum deo congruat, in tantum deum non esse conueniat qui de tali bonitate etiam praeferatur, nec de tali modo uerum et sola. iam enim et hoc discuti par est, an deus de sola bonitate censendus sit, negatis ceteris adpendicibus sensibus et adfectibus. quos Marcionitae quidem a deo suo abigunt in creatorem. nos uero [et] agnoscimus in creatore ut deo dignos, et ex hoc quoque negabimus deum in quo non omnia, quae deo digna sint, constent. si aliquem de Epicuri schola deum adfectauit Christi nomine titulare, ut quod beatum et incorruptibile sit neque sibi neque alii molestias praestet — hanc enim sententiam ruminans Marcion remouit ab illo seueritates et iudiciarias uires —: aut in totum inmobilem et stupentem deum concepisse debuerat — et quid illi cum Christo, molesto et Iudaeis per doctrinam et sibi per Iesum? — aut et de ceteris motibus eum agnouisse. — et quid illi cum Epicuro, nec sibi nec Christianis necessario? ecce enim hoc ipso, quod retro quietus, qui nec notitiam sui aliquo interim opere curauerit, post tantum aeui senserit in hominis salutem, utique per uoluntatem, nonne concussibilis tunc fuit nouae uoluntati, ut et ceteris motibus uideatur obnoxius? quae enim uoluntas sine concupiscentiae stimulo est? [quis uolet quod non concupiscet?] sed et cura accedet uoluntati. quis enim uolet quid et concupiscet, et non curabit? igitur cum et uoluit et concupiit in hominis salutem, iam et sibi et aliis negotium fecit, Epicuro nolente, consiliario Marcionis. nam et aduersarium sibi constituit: ipsum illud, aduersus quod et uoluit et concupiit et curauit, siue delictum siue mortem. inprimis ipsum arbitrum eorum et dominum hominis, creatorem. porro nihil sine aemulatione decurret, quod sine aduersario non erit. denique uolens et concupiscens et curans hominem liberare, hoc ipso iam aemulatur et eum, a quo liberat, aduersus eum scilicet sibi liberaturus, et ea, de quibus liberat, in alia liberaturus. proinde autem aemulationi occurrant necesse est officiales suae in ea, quae aemulatur: ira discordia odium dedignatio indignatio bilis nolentia offensa. haec omnia si aemulationi adsistunt, aemulatio autem liberando homini procurat, liberatio autem hominis operatio bonitatis est, non poterit ea bonitas sine suis dotibus, id est sine sensibus et adfectibus, per quos administratur aduersus creatorem, ne sic quoque inrationalis praescribatur, si careat et sensibus et adfectibus debitis. haec multo plenius defendemus in causa creatoris, in qua et exprobrantur.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: But it is enough here to show the most perverse God in the very proclamation of solitary goodness, which they refuse to ascribe to Him the kinds of emotions they condemn in the Creator. For if He neither emulates nor becomes angry nor condemns nor harasses—since He does not even provide a judge—I cannot see how their system of discipline can hold together, let alone be more complete. What sort of thing is it to lay down precepts He will not enforce, to forbid offenses He will not avenge because He will not judge, a stranger to every sense of severity and reproof? Why does He forbid what He will not defend when it would be far more consistent not to forbid what He will not defend than to forbid what He will not defend? He should have simply permitted it, without any reason to forbid, so that He would not have to defend it. As it stands, what is forbidden without punishment is silently permitted. And surely He forbids only what He does not love to happen. Therefore the one who is not offended by a deed He does not love to happen is utterly foolish, since offense is the companion of a frustrated will.

Or if He is offended, He ought to become angry; if He becomes angry, He ought to avenge. For vengeance is the fruit of anger, and anger is the debt of offense, and offense, as I said, is the companion of a frustrated will. But He does not avenge; therefore He is not offended. If He is not offended, then His will is not harmed when what He did not want to happen occurs, and the offense now happens according to His will. Because what does not harm the will is not done against the will.

Or if this were the mark of divine virtue or goodness—to not want something to happen and to forbid it, yet not be moved when it does happen—we would say He is already moved, since He did not want it; and it is pointless to claim He is unmoved by the deed when He is moved to prevent it. When He did not want it to happen, He forbade it by that very unwillingness. Did He not also judge by not wanting it and therefore forbidding it? For He judged it not to be done and pronounced that judgment by forbidding it. Hence He does judge. If it is unworthy of God to judge, or if it is worthy only to the extent that He merely does not want and forbids but does not also defend what is admitted, then nothing is more unworthy of God than to fail to execute what He did not want and forbade: first, because any sentence or law of His deserves vindication by authority and the necessity of obedience; second, because the good must emulate what He did not want and forbade, while sparing the evil is more unworthy of God than to punish, and indeed of the best God, who is not good in any other way unless He opposes evil, so that He exercises the love of good through hatred of evil and fulfills the protection of good by expelling evil.

latin: At hic sufficit peruersissimum deum ostendi in ipso praeconio solitariae bonitatis, qua nolunt ei adscribere eiusmodi motus animi, quos in creatore reprehendunt. si enim neque aemulatur neque irascitur neque damnat neque uexat. utpote qui nec iudicem praestat, non inuenio, quomodo illi disciplinarum ratio consistat, et quidem plenior. quale est enim. ut praecepta constituat non executurus, ut delicta prohibeat non uindicaturus, quia non iudicaturus, extraneus scilicet ab omnibus sensibus seueritatis et animaduersionis? cur enim prohibet admitti quod non defendit admissum, cum multo rectius non prohibuisset quod defensurus non esset quam ut non defenderet quod prohibuisset? immo et permisisse directo debuit, sine causa prohibiturus, ut non defensurus. nam et nunc tacite permissum est quod sine ultione prohibetur. et utique non aliud prohibet admitti quam quod non amat fieri. stupidissimus ergo qui non offenditur facto quod non amat fieri, quando offensa comes sit frustratae uoluntatis. aut si offenditur, debet irasci; si irascitur, debet ulcisci. nam et ultio fructus est irae et ira debitum offensae et offensa, ut dixi, comes frustratae uoluntatis. sed non ulciscitur; ergo nec offenditur, si non offenditur, ergo nec laeditur uoluntas eius, cum fit quod noluit fieri: et fit iam delictum secundum uoluntatem eius. quia non fit aduersus uoluntatem quod non laedit uoluntatem. aut si hoc erit diuinae uirtutis siue bonitatis, nolle quidem fieri et prohibere fieri, non moueri tamen, si fiat, dicimus iam motum esse illum, qui noluit, et uane non moueri ad factum qui motus sit ad non faciendum. I quando noluit fieri; nolendo enim prohibuit. non autem et iudicauit nolendo fieri et idcirco prohibendo? non faciendum enim iudicauit et prohibendo pronuntiauit. ergo et ille iam iudicat. si indignum est deum iudicare, aut si eatenus dignum est deum iudicare, qua tantummodo nolit et prohibeat non etiam defendat admissum, atquin nihil deo tam indignum quam non exequi quod noluit et prohibuit admitti: primo, quod qualicunque sententiae suae et legi debeat uindictam in auctoritatem et obsequii necessitatem, secundo, quia (boni) aemulum sit necesse est quod noluit admitti et nolendo prohibuit, malo autem parcere deum indignius sit quam animaduertere, et quidem deo optimo, qui non alias plane bonus sit, nisi mali aemulus, uti boni amorem odio mali exerceat et boni tutelam expugnatione mali impleat.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: God judges evil outright by refusing to will it, condemns it by forbidding it — yet He dismisses the charge by refusing to avenge, and acquits by refusing to punish. Oh, God the truth-breaker, the self-imposed limiter of His own sentence! He shrinks from condemning what He condemns. He shrinks from hating what He does not love. He permits the very deed He forbids, preferring to display what He rejects rather than prove His case. The result: a make-believe goodness, a phantom discipline, precepts that expire, offenses left perfectly safe.

Listen, sinners — and you who have not yet become such, so that you may stay that way: a 'better' God has been discovered. He takes no offense, feels no anger, exacts no vengeance. No fire awaits in Gehenna for Him, no gnashing of teeth in outer darkness. He is simply good. He forbids sin, yes — but only on paper. Whether you enlist in His service is entirely up to you, so you can appear to honor God; He does not want your fear. That is why the Marcionites boast they do not fear their God at all.

They say, 'The evil one is feared, the good one is loved' — foolishly denying that the Lord they name is to be feared, when that very title means power, power that demands fear. How can you love unless you fear failing to love? Clearly He is not your Father, in whom both love from piety and fear from power belong together. Nor is He a legitimate Lord, so that you love Him for His humanity and fear Him for His discipline. In the end, favorites are loved but not feared. Only a just and orderly rule commands fear. Even an adulteress can be loved — she wins by seduction, not authority; by flattery, not power. What is more adulterous, finally, than leaving offenses unpunished?

So go ahead — you who do not fear God because He is 'good' — what lust will you not plunge into, the supreme fruit of life, as I know it, for all who do not fear God? What pleasure will you not frequent: the raging circus, the savage arena, the lascivious stage? In persecution, will you not instantly offer incense and buy your life by denying your soul? 'God forbid!' you cry. Then you already fear sin, and by fearing you have proved that the One who forbids sin is to be feared. Unless, of course, you follow the same perversity of your God — the one you do not fear — who forbids what He refuses to avenge.

Even more vainly, when asked what will become of each sinner on that day, they answer: he will be cast away. Cast away how? From sight? Is that not itself a judgment? He is judged worthy of being cast away — and surely by a judgment of condemnation — unless the sinner is cast away for salvation, so that this too might suit the 'best' God. What does 'cast away' mean, if not losing what he was about to gain? If he is not cast away, that is salvation? Then he is cast away to salvation's loss, and such a decree can come only from an angry, offended, avenging judge — that is, a judge.

latin: Sed iudicat plane malum nolendo et damnat prohibendo, dimittit autem non uindicando et absoluit non puniendo. o deum ueritatis praeuaricatorem, sententiae suae circumscriptorem! timet damnare quod damnat. timet odisse quod non amat, factum sinit quod fieri non sinit, mauult ostendere quid nolit quam probare. hoc erit bonitas imaginaria, disciplina phantasma et ipsa, transfunctoria praecepta, secura delicta. audite, peccatores, quique nondum hoc estis, ut esse possitis:\' deus melior inuentus est, qui nec offenditur nec irascitur nec ulciscitur, cui nullus ignis coquitur in gehenna, cui nullus dentium frendor horret in exterioribus tenebris: bonus tantum est. denique prohibet delinquere, sed litteris solis. in uobis est, si uelitis illi obsequium subsignare. ut honorem deo habuisse uideamini; timorem enim non uult atque adeo prae se ferunt Marcionitae, quod deum suum omnino non timeant. \'malus enim\', inquiunt, \'timebitur, bonus autem diligetur\', stulte, quem dominum appellas negas timendum, cum hoc nomen potestatis sit, etiam timendae? at quomodo diliges, nisi timeas non diligere? plane nec pater tuus est, in quem competat et amor propter pietatem et timor propter potestatem, nec legitimus dominus, ut diligas propter humanitatem et timeas propter disciplinam. sic denique plagiarii diliguntur, non etiam timentur. non enim timebitur nisi iusta et ordinaria dominatio. diligi autem potest etiam adultera; sollicitatione enim con-, stat, non auctoritate, et adulatione. non potestate. quid denique adulantius quam delicta non exequi? age itaque, qui deum non times quasi bonum, quid non in omnem libidinem ebullis, summum, quod sciam, fructum uitae omnibus, qui deum non timent? quid non frequentas tam sollemnes uoluptates circi furentis et caueae saeuientis et scaenae lasciuientis? quid non et in persecutionibus statim oblata acerra animam negatione lucraris? absit, inquis, absit! ergo iam times delictum et timendo probasti illum timeri, qui prohibet delictum. aliud est, si eadem dei tui peruersitate quae non times obseruas, qua et ille quod non uindicat prohibet. — multo adhuc uanius, cum interrogati: quid fiet peccatori cuique die illo? respondent abici illum. qua? si ab oculis, nonne et hoc iudicio agitur? iudicatur enim abiciendus, et utique iudicio damnationis; nisi si in salutem abicitur peccator, ut et hoc deo optimo competat. et quid erit abici, nisi amittere id, quod erat consecuturus. si non abiceretur, id est salutem? ergo salutis in detrimentum abicietur, et hoc decerni non poterit nisi ab irato et offenso et executore delicti, id est iudice.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: What end awaits the one cast out? 'The creator's fire will seize him,' they say. Has that god no element, no provision for this very purpose, by which he could release his own sinners without cruelty, so as not to hand them over to the creator? And what of the creator then? I suppose he will prepare a sulphurous Gehenna for them — obviously for his blasphemers — unless, perhaps, a zealous God chooses to spare those who desert his adversary. O God, perverse in every way, irrational at every turn, empty in all things, and therefore utterly nonexistent! I see no status, condition, nature, or order of his that holds together — not even the sacrament of his own faith.

Why is baptism even required among them? If it is for the remission of sins, how can he appear to forgive sins when he does not appear to retain them? After all, if he retained them, he would have to judge. If it is for release from death, how can he release from death the one he never bound to death in the first place? He would have condemned humanity if he had bound it to death from the beginning. If it is for the regeneration of man, how can he regenerate what he never generated? Repetition does not suit a being from whom nothing was ever done even once. If it is for the bestowal of the Holy Spirit, how can he confer the Spirit when he never granted the soul to begin with? The Spirit will, in a sense, supply what the soul lacks. So he marks a man who was never marked by him; he washes a man who was never defiled by him.

And in all this, does he plunge the entire sacrament of salvation into flesh that has arisen from salvation? Not even a peasant waters ground that will bear no fruit — unless he is as vain as Marcion's god. Therefore, when he imposes such great sanctity, without burden or glory, on the weakest or most unworthy flesh, what does he burden the weak flesh with, or adorn the unworthy flesh with? What does he not reward with salvation, the very flesh he burdens or adorns? What does he cheat of its labor's wage by not repaying the flesh with salvation? And what does he allow the honor of sanctity to die in that flesh?

latin: Exitus autem illi abiecto quis? \'ab igni\', inquiunt, \'creatoris deprehendetur\'. adeone nullum habet elemeutum uel in hanc causam prouisum, quo peccatores suos uel sine saeuitia releget, ne illos dedat creatori? quid tunc creator? credo. sulphuratiorem eis gehennam praeparabit, ut blasphemis suis scilicet; nisi quod deus zelotes fortassean desertoribus aduersarii sui parcat. o deum usquequaque peruersum, ubique inrationalem, in omnibus uanum, atque ita neminem! cuius non statum, non condicionem, non naturam, non ullum ordinem uideo consistere, iam nec ipsum fidei eius sacramentum. cui enim rei baptisma quoque apud eum exigitur? si remissio delictorum est, quomodo uidebitur delicta dimittere qui non uidebitur retinere, quia, si retineret, iudicaret? si absolutio mortis est, quomodo absoluet a morte qui non deuinxit ad mortem? damnasset enim, si a primordio deuinxisset. si regeneratio est hominis, quomodo regenerat qui non generauit? iteratio enim non competit ei, a quo quid nec semel factum est. si consecutio est spiritus sancti, quomodo spiritum adtribuet qui animam non prius contulit? quia suffectura est quodammodo spiritus animae. signat igitur hominem numquam apud se resignatum, lauat hominem numquam apud se coinquinatum. et in hoc totum salutis sacramentum carnem mergit exortem salutis? nec rusticus terram rigabit fructum non relaturam. nisi tam uanus quam deus Marcionis. proinde. cum tantam sine sarcinam siue gloriam infirmissimae aut indignissimae carni imponit sanctitatem, quid aut onerat infirmam aut exornat indignam? quid non salute remunerat quam onerat uel exornat? quid fraudat mercedem operis, non rependens carni salutem? quid et honorem sanctitatis in illa mori patitur?

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: What can I say about the vanity of a discipline that claims to sanctify what is already holy? In his system, flesh gets no stain — unless you are a virgin, a widow, celibate, or have bought your baptism with a divorce, as if eunuchs born of marriage do not even exist. This institution, beyond doubt, is built on the condemnation of marriage. Let us test whether it is just — not as those who would wreck the joy of holiness, like certain Nicolaitans, apologists for lust and luxury, but as those who know, follow, and prefer holiness without damning marriage, not treating the good as evil but the good as better. We do not throw marriage away; we set it aside. We do not command; we commend holiness, preserving both the good and the better as each person's strength allows, and only then stepping up to defend marriage when the enemy attacks it as filth in order to destroy the Creator, who blessed marriage for the integrity of the thing, for the increase of the human race (Genesis 1:28), just as he ordained the whole created order for sound and good uses.

Foods are not condemned because gluttons work harder to stuff their throats, nor is clothing accused because the ambitious swell with pride over costly garments. So marriage is not to be spat upon because intemperance pours it out into luxury. There is a vast gulf between cause and fault, between state and excess. Therefore it is not the institution but the transgression that deserves reproof, according to the judgment of the Institutor himself, whose words are both "increase and multiply" (Genesis 1:28) and "you shall not commit adultery, you shall not covet your neighbor's wife," punishing with death the incestuous, sacrilegious, monstrous madness of lust in men and beasts.

Even if a rule for marrying is now laid down — which spiritual reason, with the Paraclete as author, defends, prescribing one marriage in faith — it will be the same One who once loosened the reins who now tightens them; the One who scattered will gather; the One who planted will cut down the forest. The One who sowed will say: "It remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none," whose end is the same as its beginning: "increase and multiply." But the forest is not felled to be accused, nor the crop harvested to be condemned, but to obey its season. So marriage does not submit to the axe and sickle of holiness as something evil, but as something ripe, to be fulfilled and reserved for holiness itself, to which it yields pride of place.

From here I turn to the god of Marcion. When he rejects marriage as evil and the business of shame, he acts against the very holiness he pretends to cultivate. He eradicates its raw material: if there are no marriages, there is no holiness. The testimony of abstinence is empty when liberty is removed, because certain virtues are proven only in their opposites. Just as virtue is perfected in weakness, so abstinence from marriage is recognized only where the ability to marry exists. Who will be called abstinent when the thing to abstain from is gone? What temperance of appetite in hunger? What rejection of ambition in poverty? What restraint of lust in castration? And does it even suit the "best god" to choke off the entire seed of the human race? How can he want to save a man he forbids to be born? From whom is he taken away by being born? How will he have anyone in whom to stamp his goodness, if he refuses to let them exist? How will he love those whose origin he does not love? Perhaps he fears a surplus of offspring — lest he labor to liberate more, lest he make many heretics, lest he breed nobler Marcionites from Marcionites. Is not Pharaoh's hardness, slaughtering newborns, more humane? Pharaoh takes souls; this god does not give them. Pharaoh takes from life; this god refuses admission to life. There is no difference between them in homicide. Man is killed under both: under one, already born; under the other, waiting to be born. You would be grateful, O heretic god, if you were in the Creator's disposition, who joined male and female — for even your own Marcion was born of marriage.

Enough on the god of Marcion, whom neither the definitions of unique divinity nor the conditions of his states confirm in the least. But the whole sequence of this work will follow the same course. So if anyone thinks we have done too little, let him hope the rest is reserved for its proper time — just as the examination of the scriptures which Marcion uses is also reserved.

latin: Quid dicam autem de disciplinae uanitate, qua sanctificat substantiam sanctam? non tingitur apud illum caro. nisi uirgo, nisi uidua, nisi caeleps, nisi diuortio baptisma mercata, quasi non etiam spadonibus ex nuptiis nata. sine dubio ex damnatione coniugii institutio ista constabit. uideamus, an iusta, non quasi destructuri felicitatem sanctitatis, ut aliqui Nicolaitae, adsertores libidinis atque luxuriae, sed qui sanctitatem sine nuptiarum damnatione nouerimus et sectemur et praeferamus, non ut malo bonum, sed ut bono melius. non enim proicimus, sed deponimus nuptias, nec praescribimus. sed suademus sanctitatem, seruantes et bonum et melius pro uiribus cuiusque sectando, tunc denique coniugium exerte defendentes, cum inimice accusatur spurcitiae nomine in destructionem creatoris, qui proinde coniugium pro rei honestate benedixit in crementum generis humani, quemadmodum et uniuersum conditionis in integros et bonos usus. non ideo autem et cibi damnabuntur, quia operosius exquisiti in gulam committunt, [tunc] nec uestitus ideo accusabuntur, quia pretiosius comparati in ambitionem tumescunt. sic nec matrimonii res ideo despuentur, quia intemperantius diffusae in luxuriam inardescunt. multum differt inter causam et culpam, inter statum et excessum. ita huiusmodi non institutio, sed exorbitatio reprobanda est, secundum censuram institutoris ipsius, cuius est tam: crescite et multiplicamini, quam et: non adulterabis et uxorem proximi tui non concupisces, morte punientis et incestam, sacrilegam atque monstrosam in masculos et in pecudes libidinum insaniam. sed et si nubendi iam modus ponitur, quem quidem apud nos spiritalis ratio paracleto auctore defendit, unum in fide matrimonium praescribens, eiusdem erit modum figere, qui modum aliquando diffuderat; is colliget, qui sparsit; is caedet siluam. qui plantauit: is metet segetem, qui seminauit; is dicet: superest, ut et qui uxores habent sic sint atque si non habeant, cuius et retro fuit: crescite et multiplicamini: eiusdem finis, cuius et initium. non tamen ut accusanda caeditur silua, nec ut damnanda secatur seges, sed ut tempori suo parens. sic et conubii res non ut mala securem et falcem admittit sanctitatis, sed ut matura defungi, ut ipsi sanctitati reseruata, cui cedendo praestaret esse. unde iam dicam deum Marcionis, cum matrimonium ut malum et impudicitiae negotium reprobat, aduersus ipsam facere sanctitatem, cui uidetur studere. materiam enim eius eradit, quia si nuptiae non erunt, sanctitas nulla est. uacat enim abstinentiae testimonium, cum licentia eripitur, quoniam ita quaedam in diuersis probantur. sicut et uirtus in infirmitate perficitur, sic et abstinentia nubendi in facultate dinoscitur. quis denique abstinens dicetur sublato eo, a quo abstinendum est? quae temperantia gulae in fame? quae ambitionis repudiatio in egestate? quae libidinis infrenatio in castratione? iam uero sementem generis humani compescere totum nescio an hoc quoque optimo deo congruat. quomodo enim saluum hominem uolet quem uetat nasci. de quo nascitur auferendo? quomodo habebit in quo bonitatem suam signet, quem esse non patitur? quomodo diliget cuius originem non amat? timet forsitan redundantiam subolis, ne laboret plures liberando, ne multos faciat haereticos, ne generosiores habeat Marcionitas ex Marcionitis. non erit humanior duritia Pharaonis nascentium enecatrix? nam ille animas adimit, hic non dat; ille aufert de uita, hic non admittit in uitam. nihil apud ambos de homicidio differt. sub utroque homo interficitur: sub altero iam editus, sub altero edendus. gratus esses. o dee haeretice. si esses, in dispositionem creatoris, quod marem et feminam miscuit: utique enim et Marcion tuus ex nuptiis natus est. Satis haec de deo Marcionis, quem et definitiones unicae diuinitatis et condiciones statuum eius omnino non esse confirmant. sed et totius opusculi series in hoc utique succedet. proinde. si cui minus quid uidemur egisse, speret reseruatum suo tempori. sicut et ipsarum scripturarum examinationem, quibus Marcion utitur.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: So the whole debate comes down to numbers: whether we're allowed to posit two gods — maybe by poetic license, maybe by artistic license, and now, heretical license too. But Christian truth calls it straight: if God isn't one, God isn't. Period. Because we hold it more fitting that nothing exists at all than that something exists in a way it shouldn't.

Want to know why God has to be one? Ask what God is. You won't find any other answer. As far as human language can stretch, here's the definition — and every conscience will back me up: God is the supreme greatness, fixed in eternity, unborn, unending. That's what eternity means: the very condition that makes God supremely great, because that condition *is* God. And from that flows everything else — God is supreme in form, in reason, in power.

Everyone agrees on this — no one denies God is the supreme greatness, unless they're ready to call God the lowest trifle instead, which is just denying God by stripping away what makes God God. So what defines the supreme greatness? Simple: nothing equals it. Which means there *can't* be another supreme greatness. Because if there were, they'd be equals. And if they're equals, neither is supreme. The whole definition collapses — the law, if you will, that lets nothing stand alongside the supreme.

So the supreme greatness *must* be unique — no equal, or it stops being supreme. It exists *as* unique; that's the only way it exists at all. And since God *is* the supreme greatness, our truth got it right: if God isn't one, God isn't. Not that we're hedging — 'maybe God doesn't exist if not one.' No. We're defining the God we trust: this is what God *is*. If that's not true, God isn't.

So if the supreme greatness has to be unique, God has to be unique. God isn't God unless supreme; supreme isn't supreme unless peerless; peerless isn't peerless unless unique. Try smuggling in another god — you'll have to give him every divine attribute: eternal, supreme, the works. Then you've got two supreme greatnesses. How does that work? The definition of supreme is *having no peer*. That's a singular property. Two things can't both have no peer. They'd be each other's peer. Contradiction. Game over.

latin: Principalis itaque et exinde tota congressio de numero, an duos deos liceat induci, si forte, poetica et pictoria licentia, et tertia iam, haeretica. sed ueritas Christiana destricte pronuntiauit: deus si non unus est, non est, quia dignius credimus non esse quodcumque non ita fuerit, ut esse debebit. deum autem ut scias unum esse debere, quaere quid sit deus, et non aliter inuenies. quantum humana condicio de deo definire potest, id definio, quod et omnium conscientia agnoscet: deum summum esse magnum in aeternitate constitutum, [innatum, infectum, sine initio, sine-fine] — hunc enim statum aeternitati t censendum, quae summum magnum deum efficiat, dum hoc est in deo ipsa — atque ita et cetera, ut sit deus summum magnum et forma et ratione et ui et potestate. cum de isto conuenit apud omnes, — nemo enim negabit deum summum magnum quid esse, nisi qui potuerit deum imum modicum quid e contrario pronuntiare, ut deum neget auferendo quod dei est - quae erit iam condicio ipsius summi magni? nempe, ut nihil illi adaequetur, id est, ut non sit aliud summum magnum, quia, si fuerit, adaequabitur, et si adaequabitur, non erit iam summum magnum, euersa condicione et, ut ita dixerim, lege, quae summo magno nihil sinit adaequari. ergo unicum sit necesse est summum magnum, — quod fuerit par non habendo — ne non sit summum magnum. ergo non aliter erit quam per quod habet esse, id est unicum omnino. proinde deus cum summum magnum sit, recte ueritas nostra pronuntiauit: deus, si non. unus est, non est, non quasi dubitemus esse deum dicendo: si non unus, non est, sed quia quem confidimus esse, id eum definiamus esse, quod si non est, deus non est. [et summum scilicet magnum] porro (si) summum magnum unicum sit necesse est, ergo et deus unicus erit, non aliter deus, nisi summum magnum, nec aliter summum magnum, nisi parem non habens, nec aliter parem non habens, nisi unicus fuerit. certe quemcumque alium deum induxeris, non alia poteris eum forma tueri deum quam ut et illi proprium diuinitatis adscripseris, sicut aeternum ita et summum magnum. duo ergo summa magna quomodo consistent, cum hoc sit summum magnum, par non habere, par autem non habere uni competat, in duobus esse nullo modo possit?

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: How did he handle the question about healing on the Sabbath? "Doesn't each of you on the Sabbath untie his donkey or ox from the manger and lead it to water?" (Luke 13:15). So, acting in line with the law's own condition, he upheld the law; he did not dissolve it. The law commands that no work be done except what is done for the sake of any soul, how much more a human one? I see that the coherence of parables is required everywhere. "The kingdom of God is like a mustard seed, which a man took and sowed in his garden" (Luke 13:19). Who is meant by the man? Obviously Christ, who, even on Marcion's terms, is called the Son of Man. He received the seed of the kingdom from the Father — that is, the gospel message — and sowed it in his garden, which is this world. Suppose the 'man' is a human being; but since he said 'in his garden,' and neither the world nor the man belongs to the alien god but to the Creator, the one who sows in his own domain is shown to be the Creator's agent. Or if, to escape this trap, they shift the 'man' from Christ to a believer receiving the seed of the kingdom and sowing it in the garden of his heart, even that soil suits no one but the Creator.

I dread the next plain similitude, lest it betray the kingdom of another god. He compared it to leaven, not to unleavened bread, which is more familiar to the Creator. This conjecture suits those begging for arguments just fine. So I will drive out vanity with vanity and say fermentation fits the Creator's kingdom too, because after it comes the oven or furnace of Gehenna. What kind of kingdom belonging to a supremely mild god is followed by the fury of judgment with tearful severity? How often does he still show himself as a judge, and in the judge reveal the Creator? How often does he reject and condemn by rejecting? Just like here: "When the master of the house rises" — where? Nowhere but where Isaiah said: "When he rises to shake the earth" — "and shuts the door" (Luke 13:25), certainly to exclude the wicked. When they knock, he will answer, "I don't know where you're from," and again, when they list what they ate and drank in his presence and taught in their streets, he will add: "Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity" (Luke 13:27; Matthew 24:51). There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth — where? Outside, obviously, where they are excluded by the shut door. So the punishment comes from the one who executes the exclusion into punishment. "When they see the righteous entering the kingdom of God, but themselves thrown outside" (Luke 13:28). From whom? If from the Creator, who then is inside receiving the righteous into the kingdom? The 'good' god? What is the Creator doing there, then? Detaining in punishment outside those whom his adversary excluded? They would be received by him, if anything, rather in the adversary's spite. But the one who is about to exclude the wicked must surely know that the Creator will detain them in punishment — or he ought not to know. Therefore either they are detained against his will, and the one who detains is inferior to him, yielding to him unwillingly, or if he wants it that way, he himself has judged it so. And he will be no better than the Creator, since he becomes the author of the Creator's infamy. If these things hold together by no logic at all, so that one is supposed to punish and another to liberate, then both the judgment and the kingdom belong to one God. And since both belong to one, the one who judges is the Creator's.

latin: Quaestionem rursus de curatione sabbatis facta quomodo discussit? unusquisque uestrum sabbatis non soluits asinum aut bouem suum a praesepi et ducit ad potum? ergo secundum condicionem legis operatus legem confirmauit, non dissoluit, iubentem nullum opus fieri, nisi quod fieret omni animae, quanto potius humanae? Parabolarum congruentiam ubique recognoscor exigere. simile est regnum dei, inquit, grano sinapis, quod accepit homo et seminauit in horto suo. quis in persona hominis intellegendus? utique Christus, qui, licet Marcionis, filius hominis est dictus, qui accepit a patre semen regni, sermonem scilicet euangelii, et seminauit in horto, isto utique in mundo. puta nunc in homine, sed cum in (suo) horto dixerit nec mundus autem nec homo illius sit, sed creatoris, ergo qui in suum seminarit creatoris ostenditur. aut si, ut hunc laqueum euadant, conuerterint hominis personam a Christo in hominem accipientem semen regni et seminantem in horto cordis sui, nec ipsa materia alii conueniet quam creatori. De sequenti plane similitudine uereor, ne forte alterius dei regnum portendat. fermento enim comparauit illud, non azymis, quae familiariora sunt creatori. congruit et haec coniectura mendicantibus argumenta. itaque et ego uanitatem uanitate depellam, fermentationem quoque congruere dicens regno creatoris, quia post illam clibanus uel furnus gehennae sequatur. quale est enim, ut (sit) lenissimi dei regnum quod etiam iudicii feruor lacrimosa austeritate subsequitur? Quotiens adhuc se iudicem ostendit et in iudice creatorem! quotiens utique reicit et damnat reiciendo! sicut hic quoque: cum surrexerit, inquit, pater familiae — quo? nisi quo dixit Esaias: cum surrexerit comminuere terram - et cluserit ostium — utique excludendis iniquis, quibus pulsantibus respondebit: nescio unde sitis, et rursus, enumerantibus quod coram illo ederint et biberint et in plateis eorum docuerit [adiciet]: recedite a me omnes, operarii iniquitatis —, illic erit fletus et dentium frendor, — ubi? foris scilicet, ubi erunt exclusi ostio cluso; ab eo ergo erit poena, a quo fit exclusio in poenam — \'cum uidebunt iustos introeuntes in regnum dei, se uero detineri foris\'. a quo? si a creatore, quis ergo erit intus recipiens iustos in regnum? deus bonus? quid ergo illic creatori? ut foris detineat in poenam quos aduersarius eius exclusit? suscipiendos a se, si utique, magis in aduersarii bilem. sed et ille, exclusurus iniquos, sciat utique creatorem illos detenturum in poenam aut non sciat oportet. ergo aut nolente eo detinebuntur, et minor est illo, qui detinet, cedens ei nolens, aut si uult ita fieri, ipse ita faciendum iudicauit. et non erit melior creatore ipse auctor infamiae creatoris. haec si nulla ratione consistunt, ut alius punire alius liberare credatur, unius erit tam iudicium quam et regnum, et dum unius est utrumque, qui et iudicat, creatoris est.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: What kind of people does He command to be invited to lunch or dinner? He showed us through Isaiah: break your bread for the hungry, and bring the poor and the homeless into your house — people who, obviously, cannot repay this kindness. If Christ forbids angling for that repayment here, promising it instead in the resurrection, that is the Creator's signature: He takes no pleasure in those who love gifts, but in those who pursue recompense. (Isaiah 58:7)

Now weigh the parable of the host: to whom does it more properly belong? A certain man prepared a great dinner and invited many. That dinner's preparation plainly figures the satisfaction of eternal life. First point: strangers and those with no claim are not the ones usually summoned to a feast; it is household members and family. Therefore the invitation belongs to the Creator, to whom the invitees belonged — through Adam as human beings, and through the patriarchs as Jews — not to a god to whom they belonged neither by nature nor by privilege.

Next, if the one who prepared the dinner sends a summons to the guests, the dinner is the Creator's as well: He sent word to those already called through the patriarchs, now to be admonished through the prophets. This is not a god who sent no one to warn them and did nothing beforehand to call them, only to descend suddenly — merely making Himself known as inviter, merely inviting as He already compels them into the banquet, collapsing the hour of dining and the hour of invitation into one.

The invited make excuses. If they were summoned by some other god, their refusal is justified, because the call came suddenly; if not justified, then the call was not sudden. But if not sudden, then it came from the Creator, from whom they received the call long ago — and whose call they then rejected, first saying to Aaron, 'Make us gods to go before us,' and from then on hearing with their ears but not hearing, the call of the God who fits this parable most precisely through Jeremiah: 'Listen to my voice, and I will be your God and you shall be my people; walk in all the ways I command you' — there is the invitation — 'but they did not listen, nor did they turn their ear' — there is the people's refusal — 'but they walked in the stubbornness of their evil hearts: I bought a field, I bought oxen, I took a wife.' (Jeremiah 7:23)

And still He presses: 'I sent all my servants the prophets to you, rising early and sending them' — here is the Holy Spirit, the guests' admonisher — 'but my people did not listen, did not incline their ears, and stiffened their necks.' This was reported to the householder, who was then moved — and well that He was moved, since Marcion denies his god can be moved; so this one is mine. He then orders a roundup from the streets and alleys of the city.

Let us test whether this fits the sense of Jeremiah again: 'Have I become a wilderness to the house of Israel, or a land left desolate?' — that is: 'Do I lack people to call, or places to call them from?' — because my people said, 'We will not come to you.' So He sent to call others from the same city. Then, with room still to spare, He commanded gathering from the roads and hedges — that is, us from the foreign nations — by that very jealousy with which Deuteronomy says: 'I will hide my face from them and see what becomes of them in the end' — meaning others will take their place — 'for they are a perverse generation, children in whom there is no faith. They provoked me with a no-god, angered me with their idols; so I will provoke them with a no-people, anger them with a foolish nation' — in us, that is, whose hope the Jews groan over, and from whose taste the Lord says they will be barred, once Zion is abandoned like a watchtower in a vineyard, like a hut in a cucumber field, after they also rejected the final invitation in Christ. (Deuteronomy 32:21)

What in this sequence — according to the Creator's own dispositions and proclamations — can possibly suit the rival god, who has neither order nor disposition to match the parable's plot, who made the whole work at once? What would be his first call, and what his second act of admonition? Others must excuse themselves first; only then are others summoned. But now he comes inviting both groups at once — from the city, from the hedges — flatly contradicting the parable's mirror. Nor can he judge as haughty those he never invited before, whom he now confronts most aggressively. Or if he judges them for a future contempt of the call, then he also signals a future roundup from the nations to take their place. Clearly he must come a second time: [to preach to the nations. And if] he comes, I suspect it will not be to call guests again, but to seat them.

Meanwhile, you who read this dinner's invitation as the heavenly banquet of spiritual satisfaction and joy, remember that the Creator equally figures the earthly promises of wine, oil, grain, and the city itself into spiritual realities.

latin: Ad prandium uel ad cenam quales uocari iubet? quales ostenderat per Esaiam: confringe panem tuum esurienti. et mendicos et qui sine tecto sunt induc in domum tuam, qui scilicet humanitatis istius uicem retribuere non possint. hanc si Christus captari uetat, in resurrectione eam repromittens, creatoris est forma, cui non placent amantes munera, sectantes retributionem. Etiam inuitatoris parabola cui magis parti occurrat, expende. homo quidam fecit cenam et uocauit multos. utique cenae paratura uitae aeterna saturitatem figurat. dico primo extraneos et nullius iuris adfines inuitari ad cenam non solere, certe facilius solere domesticos et familiares. ergo creatoris est inuitasse, ad quem pertinebant qui inuitabantur, et per Adam, qua homines, et (per) patres, qua Iudaici, non eius, ad quem neque natura pertinebant neque praerogatiua. dehinc si is mittit ad conuiuas, qui cenam parauit, sic quoque creatoris est cena, qui misit ad conuiuas admonendos, ante iam uocatos per patres, admonendos autem per prophetas, non, qui neminem miserit ad monendum nec qui nihil prius egerit ad uocandum, sed ipse descenderit subito, tantum quod innotescens iam inuitans, tantum quod inuitans iam in conuiuium cogens, eandem faciens horam cenandi et ad cenam inuitandi. excusant se inuitati. si ab alio deo, merito, quia subito inuitati; si non merito, ergo nec subito; si autem non subito inuitati, ergo a creatore, a quo olim, cuius denique declinauerant uocationem tunc, primo dicentes ad Aaronem: fac nobis deos, qui praeeant nobis, atque exinde aure audientes et non audientes, uocationem scilicet dei, qui pertinentissime ad hanc parabolam per Hieremiam: audite, inquit, uocem meam, et ero uobis in deum et uos mihi in populum, et ibitis in omnibus uiis meis, quascumque mandauero uobis — ecce inuitatio dei — et non audierunt, inquit, et non aduerterunt aurem suam m, - ecce recuaatio populi - 8 e sed i e abieruntin his, quae concupiuerunt corde suo malo: \'agrum emi\' et \'boues mercatus sum\' et \'uxorem duxi ? . et adhuc ingerit: et emisi omnes ad uos famulos meos, prophetas, — hic erit spiritus sanctus, admonitor conuiuarum — die et ante lucem, et non audiit populus meus et non intendit auribus suis et obdurauit collum suum. hoc ut patri familiae renuntiatum est, motus tunc — bene quod et motus; negat enim Marcion moueri deum suum; ita et hoc meus est — mandat de plateis et uicis ciuitatis facere sublectionem. uideamus an eo sensu, quo rursus per Hieremiam: numquid solitudo factus sum domui Israhelis aut terra in incultum derelicta? — id est: numquid non habeo quos adlegam aut unde adlegam? — quoniam dixit populus meus: non uenimus ad te. itaque misit ad alios uocandos ex eadem adhuc ciuitate. dehinc loco abundante praecepit etiam de uiis et sepibus colligi, id est nos iam de extraneis gentibus, illa scilicet aemulatione, qua in Deuteronomio: auertam meam faciemab eis et monstrabo, quid illis in nouissimis, — id est alios possessuros locum eorum — . quoniam genitura peruersa est, filii in quibus fides non est. illi obaemulati sunt me in non deo et prouocauerunt me in iram in idolis suis, e t ego obaemulabor eos in non natione, (in natione) insipienti prouocabo eos in iram, in nobis scilicet, quorum spem Iudaei gemunt, de qua illos gustaturos negat dominus, derelicta Sione tamquam specula in uinea et in cucumerario casula, posteaquam et nouissimam in Christo inuitationem recusauit. quid ex hoc ordine, secundum dispositiones et praedicationes creatoris recensendo, competere potest illi, cuius nec ordo habet nec dispositio ad parabolae conspirationem, qui totum opus semel fecit? aut quae erit prima uocatio eius, et quae secundo actu admonitio? ante debent alii excusare, postea alii conuenisse. nunc autem pariter utramque partem inuitare uenit, de ciuitate, de sepibus, aduersus speculum parabolae. nec potest iam fastidiosos iudicare quos numquam retro inuitauit, quos cum maxime adgreditur. aut si de futuro eos iudicat contempturos uocationem, ergo et sublectionem loco eorum ex gentibus de futuro portendit. plane adhuc secundo uenturus est: [ut gentibus praedicet. et si] uenturus est autem, puto, non quasi uocaturus adhuc conuiuas, sed iam collocaturus. interea qui cenae istius uocationem in caeleste conuiuium interpretaris spiritalis saturitatis et iocunditatis, memento et terrenas promissiones uini et olei et frumenti et ipsius ciuitatis aeque in spiritalia figurari a creatore.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Who looks for the lost sheep and the lost coin? Is it not the one who lost them? Who lost them? Is it not the one who had them? Who, indeed, had them? Is it not the one to whom they belonged? If, therefore, the man is not anyone else's property except the Creator's, then the one to whom they belonged had them, the one who had them lost them, the one who lost them looked for them, the one who looked for them found them, the one who found them rejoiced. So the argument of both parables is empty concerning the one whose are neither the sheep nor the coin, that is, the man. For he did not lose, because he did not have, nor did he look, because he did not lose, nor did he find, because he did not look, nor did he rejoice, because he did not find. And therefore it is his to rejoice over the sinner's repentance—that is, over the recovery of the lost one—who once declared that he preferred the sinner's repentance to death.

latin: Ouem et drachmam perditam quis requirit? nonne qui perdidit? quis autem perdidit? nonne qui habuit? quis uero habuit? nonne cuius fuit? si igitur homo non alterius est res quam creatoris, is eum habuit, cuius fuit, is perdidit, qui habuit, is requisiuit, qui perdidit, is inuenit, qui quaesiuit, is exultauit, qui inuenit. ita utriusque parabolae argumentum uacat circa eum, cuius non est ouis neque drachma, id est homo. non enim perdidit, quia non habuit, nec requisiuit, quia non perdidit, nec inuenit, quia nec requisiuit, nec exultauit, quia non inuenit. atque adeo exultare illius est de paenitentia peccatoris, id est de perditi recuperatione, qui se professus est olim malle peccatoris paenitentiam quam mortem.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: What the two masters are who, He says, cannot be served, Luke 16:13 on the ground that while one is pleased the other must needs be displeased, He Himself makes clear, when He mentions God and mammon . Then, if you have no interpreter by you, you may learn again from Himself what He would have understood by mammon . For when advising us to provide for ourselves the help of friends in worldly affairs, after the example of that steward who, when removed from his office, relieves his lord's debtors by lessening their debts with a view to their recompensing him with their help, He said, And I say unto you, Make to yourselves friends of the mammon of unrighteousness, that is to say, of money, even as the steward had done. Now we are all of us aware that money is the instigator of unrighteousness, and the lord of the whole world.

Therefore, when he saw the covetousness of the Pharisees doing servile worship to it, He hurled this sentence against them, You cannot serve God and mammon . Luke 16:13 Then the Pharisees , who were covetous of riches, derided Him, when they understood that by mammon He meant money. Let no one think that under the word mammon the Creator was meant, and that Christ called them off from the service of the Creator. What folly ! Rather learn therefrom that one God was pointed out by Christ. For they were two masters whom He named, God and mammon — the Creator and money. You cannot indeed serve God — Him, of course whom they seemed to serve — and mammon to whom they preferred to devote themselves. If, however, he was giving himself out as another god , it would not be two masters, but three, that he had pointed out.

For the Creator was a master, and much more of a master, to be sure, than mammon , and more to be adored, as being more truly our Master. Now, how was it likely that He who had called mammon a master, and had associated him with God , should say nothing of Him who was really the Master of even these, that is, the Creator? Or else, by this silence respecting Him did He concede that service might be rendered to Him , since it was to Himself alone and to mammon that He said service could not be (simultaneously) rendered? When, therefore, He lays down the position that God is one, since He would have been sure to mention the Creator if He were Himself a rival to Him, He did (virtually) name the Creator, when He refrained from insisting that He was Master alone, without a rival god.

Accordingly, this will throw light upon the sense in which it was said, If you have not been faithful in the unrighteous mammon , who will commit to your trust the true riches? Luke 16:11 In the unrighteous mammon , that is to say, in unrighteous riches, not in the Creator; for even Marcion allows Him to be righteous: And if you have not been faithful in that which is another man's, who will give to you that which is mine? For whatever is unrighteous ought to be foreign to the servants of God . But in what way was the Creator foreign to the Pharisees , seeing that He was the proper God of the Jewish nation? Forasmuch then as the words, Who will entrust to you the truer riches? and, Who will give you that which is mine?

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Christ forbids divorce, saying that anyone who dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery, and that anyone who marries a woman dismissed by her husband is equally an adulterer—so that He also forbids divorce by making the marriage of a repudiated woman unlawful. Moses, however, permits repudiation in Deuteronomy: if a man takes a wife, lives with her, and then finds no favor in her because he discovers an indecent deed in her, he is to write a certificate of divorce, hand it to her, and send her out of his house (Deuteronomy).
