excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Then, turning to His disciples , He says: Woe unto him through whom offenses come! It were better for him if he had not been born, or if a millstone were hanged about his neck and he were cast into the sea, than that he should offend one of these little ones, Luke 17:1-2 that is, one of His disciples . Judge, then, what the sort of punishment is which He so severely threatens. For it is no stranger who is to avenge the offense done to His disciples . Recognise also in Him the Judge, and one too, who expresses Himself on the safety of His followers with the same tenderness as that which the Creator long ago exhibited: He that touches you touches the apple of my eye. Zechariah 2:8 Such identity of care proceeds from one and the same Being. A trespassing brother He will have rebuked.

Luke 17:3 If one failed in this duty of reproof, he in fact sinned , either because out of hatred he wished his brother to continue in sin , or else spared him from mistaken friendship, although possessing the injunction in Leviticus: You shall not hate your brother in your heart; your neighbor you shall seriously rebuke, and on his account shall not contract sin . Nor is it to be wondered at, if He thus teaches who forbids your refusing to bring back even your brother's cattle, if you find them astray in the road; much more should you bring back your erring brother to himself. He commands you to forgive your brother, should he trespass against you even seven times.

Luke 17:4 But that surely, is a small matter; for with the Creator there is a larger grace , when He sets no limits to forgiveness, indefinitely charging you not to bear any malice against your brother, Leviticus 19:18 and to give not merely to him who asks, but even to him who does not ask. For His will is, not that you should forgive an offense, but forget it. The law about lepers had a profound meaning as respects the forms of the disease itself, and of the inspection by the high priest . The interpretation of this sense it will be our task to ascertain. Marcion's labour, however, is to object to us the strictness of the law, with the view of maintaining that here also Christ is its enemy — forestalling its enactments even in His cure of the ten lepers .

These He simply commanded to show themselves to the priest ; and as they went, He cleansed them Luke 17:11-19 — without a touch, and without a word, by His silent power and simple will. Well, but what necessity was there for Christ , who had been once for all announced as the healer of our sicknesses and sins , and had proved Himself such by His acts, to busy Himself with inquiries into the qualities and details of cures; or for the Creator to be summoned to the scrutiny of the law in the person of Christ?

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: When He recommends perseverance and earnestness in prayer , He sets before us the parable of the judge who was compelled to listen to the widow , owing to the earnestness and importunity of her requests. Luke 18:1-8 He show us that it is God the judge whom we must importune with prayer , and not Himself, if He is not Himself the judge. But He added, that God would avenge His own elect. Luke 18:7-8 Since, then, He who judges will also Himself be the avenger, He proved that the Creator is on that account the specially good God , whom He represented as the avenger of His own elect, who cry day and night to Him.

And yet, when He introduces to our view the Creator's temple, and describes two men worshipping therein with diverse feelings — the Pharisee in pride , the publican in humility — and shows us how they accordingly went down to their homes, one rejected, the other justified, Luke 18:10-14 He surely, by thus teaching us the proper discipline of prayer , has determined that that God must be prayed to from whom men were to receive this discipline of prayer — whether condemnatory of pride , or justifying in humility. I do not find from Christ any temple, any suppliants, any sentence (of approval or condemnation) belonging to any other god than the Creator. Him does He enjoin us to worship in humility, as the lifter-up of the humble , not in pride , because He brings down the proud .

What other god has He manifested to me to receive my supplications? With what formula of worship, with what hope (shall I approach him?) I trow, none. For the prayer which He has taught us suits, as we have proved , none but the Creator. It is, of course, another matter if He does not wish to be prayed to, because He is the supremely and spontaneously good God! But who is this good God? There is, He says, none but one. Luke 18:19 It is not as if He had shown us that one of two gods was the supremely good; but He expressly asserts that there is one only good God , who is the only good, because He is the only God. Now, undoubtedly, He is the good God who sends rain on the just and on the unjust , and makes His sun to rise on the evil and on the good; Matthew 5:45 sustaining and nourishing and assisting even Marcionites themselves!

When afterwards a certain man asked him, 'Good Master, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?' (Jesus) inquired whether he knew (that is, in other words, whether he kept ) the commandments of the Creator, in order to testify that it was by the Creator's precepts that eternal life is acquired. Luke 18:18-20 Then, when he affirmed that from his youth up he had kept all the principal commandments, (Jesus) said to him: One thing you yet lack: sell all that you have, and give to the poor , and you shall have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me. Luke 18:21-22 Well now, Marcion , and all you who are companions in misery, and associates in hatred with that heretic , what will you dare say to this?

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Salvation comes to Zacchaeus' house as well. On what grounds? Had he perhaps believed that Christ came from Marcion's god? But the blind man's cry still rang in everyone's ears: 'Have mercy on me, Jesus, Son of David,' and the whole crowd was giving praise to God — not Marcion's god, but David's. (Luke 19:9-10) Zacchaeus, for all his foreign blood, may have picked up some scriptural knowledge through Jewish trade connections — more impressively, he fulfilled the prophet's commands even if he never read Isaiah: 'Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house' — which he did above all by welcoming the Lord into his home and feeding him — 'and when you see the naked, clothe them' — which he pledged above all by offering half his estate for every work of mercy, tearing up the bonds of predatory contracts, releasing the oppressed, canceling every unjust levy, and declaring, 'If I have extorted anything from anyone, I repay it fourfold.' (Luke 19:9-10) So the Lord says: 'Today salvation has come to this house.' He testified that the Creator's prophet had commanded what brings salvation. (Luke 19:9-10)

When he adds, 'For the Son of Man came to save what was lost,' I no longer waste time arguing that he came to save what was lost, whose it was, and to whom it was lost, since he came to save it. (Luke 19:10; Matthew 18:11) I move the debate to the next level. No one doubts we are talking about a human being. Since a human being consists of two substances — body and soul — the question is: from which substance did the loss occur? If from the body, then the body perished, not the soul. The Son of Man saves what perished: therefore the flesh has salvation too. If the loss came from the soul, the soul's loss is destined for salvation; the flesh, which did not perish, is already safe. If the whole human being perished from both substances, then the whole human being must be saved — and the heretics' verdict denying the flesh's salvation collapses. Now the Christ of the Creator stands confirmed, the one who promised the salvation of the whole human being according to the Creator. (Luke 19:10; Matthew 18:11)

The parable of the servants, judged according to the accounting of the Lord's entrusted money, shows God as judge even on the side of severity — not only demanding a return but taking away what someone merely seemed to have. (Luke 19:9-10) Or if the Creator fabricated this severity too — 'a harsh man, taking what he did not deposit and reaping what he did not sow' — that very line instructs me, since it is his money he teaches me to invest. (Luke 19:9-10)

latin: Consequitur et Zacchei domus salutem. quo merito? numquid uel ille crediderat Christum a (deo) Marcionis uenisse? atquin adhuc in auribus erat omnium uox illa caeci: miserere mei, Iesu, fili Dauid, et: omnis populus laudes referebant deo, non Marcionis, sed Dauid. enimuero Zaccheus, etsi allophylus, fortasse tamen aliqua notitia scripturarum ex commercio Iudaico adflatus, — plus est autem, (si) et ignorans Esaiam — praecepta eius impleuerat: confringito, inquit, panem tuum esurienti et non habentes tectum in domum tuam inducito — hoc cum maxime agebat, exceptum domo sua pascens dominum — et nudum si uideris, contegito; hoc cum maxime promittebat, in omnia misericordiae opera dimidium substantiae offerens, dissoluens uiolentiorum contractuum obnexus et dimittens conflictatos in laxamentum et omnem conscriptionem iniquam dissipans dicendo: et si cui quid per calumniam eripui, quadruplum reddo. itaque dominus: hodie, inquit, salus huic domui. testimonium dixit salutaria esse quae praeceperat prophetes creatoris. cum uero dicit: uenit enim filius hominis saluum facere quod periit, iam non contendo eum uenisse, ut saluum faceret quod perierat cuius fuerat et cui perierat quod saluum uenerat facere, sed in alterius quaestionis gradum dirigo. de homine agi nulla dubitatio est. hic cum ex duabus substantiis constet, ex corpore et anima, quaerendum est, ex qua substantiae specie perisse uideatur. si ex corpore, ergo corpus perierat, anima non. quod perierat saluum facit filius hominis: habet igitur et caro salutem, si ex anima perierat, animae perditio saluti destinatur: caro, quae non periit, salua est. si totus homo perierat ex utraque substantia, totus homo saluus fiat necesse est, et elisa est sententia haereticorum negantium carnis salutem. iam et Christus creatoris confirmatur, qui secundum creatorem totius hominis salutem pollicebatur. Seruorum quoque parabola, qui secundum rationem feneratae pecuniae dominicae diiudicantur, iudicem ostendit deum (tuum) etiam ex parte seueritatis, non tantum onerantem uerum et auferentem quod quis uideatur habuisse. aut si et haec creatorem finxerit, (austerum, tollentem quod non posuerit et metentem quod non seuerit,' hic quoque me ille instruit, cuius pecuniam ut fenerem edocet.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Christ knew exactly where John's baptism came from, so why did He ask as if He didn't? He knew the Pharisees would not answer Him; so why ask in vain? Was it so He could condemn them by their own mouths, or by their hearts? Refer this, then, to the defense of the Creator and to the comparison with Christ, and consider what would have happened if the Pharisees had actually answered. Suppose they had declared John's baptism merely human: they would have been stoned on the spot. Some anti-Marcion Marcion would have cried out: 'Oh, best God! Oh, God different from the Creator's examples! Knowing men would rush headlong, He Himself shoved them over the precipice.' For that is exactly how the Creator is treated in the law of the tree. 'But John's baptism was from heaven,' Christ said, 'and why did you not believe him?' (Matthew 22:15-22; Mark 12:13-17; Luke 20:20-26). Therefore, the One who wanted John to be believed, and who was going to rebuke them for not believing, belonged to the One whose sacrament John administered. Naturally they refused to admit what they knew. When He countered in turn — 'And I will not tell you by what authority I do these things' — He repaid evil for evil. 'Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's.' What things belong to God that are comparable to Caesar's denarius? The image and likeness of God, of course. So He commands that man be rendered to the Creator, in whose image and likeness and name and substance he was fashioned. Let Marcion's god hunt for his own coin; Christ orders the denarius of man to be rendered to His Caesar — not to a foreign one, unless it is necessary for the man who does not have his own denarius.

It is a just and proper rule that in every question the sense of the answer must pertain to the question asked. To answer something other than what was asked is the mark of a madman, and that is all the more alien to Christ, since it does not even befit a mere human. The Sadducees, who denied the resurrection, put a question to the Lord drawn from the law: a woman who had married seven brothers in succession, according to the legal precept — whose wife would she be in the resurrection? That was the substance of the question, the heart of the consultation; Christ had to answer this. He feared no one, so that He would not appear to dodge the questions or to hint through them at something else He did not teach openly. So He answered: the sons of this age marry — you see how precisely this fits the case, because they were asking about the coming age, in which no one will marry, as He had already established that here they marry, where there is also death — but those whom God has deemed worthy of the possession and resurrection of that age neither marry nor are given in marriage, because they no longer die, being like the angels of God, made sons of the resurrection. Since the sense of the answer must not be directed anywhere but to the question posed, if the question is resolved by the sense of the answer, then the Lord's answer carries no other meaning than that which resolves the question. You have, then, the times of permitted and forbidden marriages, not from His own invention, but from the resurrection question; you have, also, the confirmation of the resurrection itself and everything the Sadducees were asking about — not asking about another god, not asking about marriage law on its own terms. But if you make Christ answer things He was not asked about, you deny that He could answer what He was asked — caught by the wisdom of the Sadducees.

Now, at length and after the rule, I will turn back against their connected arguments. For, having gotten hold of the scriptural text — 'those whom God has deemed worthy of that age' — they run the words together in reading, so that they attach 'of God' to 'of that age,' in order to make another god of that age, when it ought to be read like this: 'those whom God has deemed worthy,' so that, with the distinction made after 'God,' 'of that age' attaches to what follows: that is, 'those whom God has deemed worthy of the possession and resurrection of that age.' For they were not consulting about God, but about the condition of that age — whose wife she would be after the resurrection in that age. And so they also twist the answer about marriages, so that 'the sons of this age marry and are given in marriage' is said of men as if the Creator permits marriages, but they themselves, whom the god of that age — that is, another god — has deemed worthy of the resurrection, do not marry even now, because they are not sons of this age. When He was consulted about the marriages of that age, not this one, He denied them — the very ones they were asking about. Therefore, those who caught the force of the voice and pronunciation and pause understood nothing other than what pertained to the matter of the consultation, and so the scribes said: 'Teacher, you have spoken well.' For He had confirmed the resurrection by giving it shape against the Sadducees' opinion. Finally, He did not refuse the testimony of those who presumed He had answered thus.

But if the scribes thought Christ was the son of David, and David calls Him Lord, what does this have to do with Christ, who is not David? Was He obscuring the scribes' error? No — He was securing honor for Christ, whom David calls Lord, confirming that Christ is more Lord than son of David, which does not suit the destroyer of the Creator. How fitting is this interpretation for our side! For the One who was once invoked as 'son of David' by that blind man — which He then let pass in silence, not having the scribes present — now, on the contrary, brought it forward before them on purpose, so that He might show Himself, whom the blind man had proclaimed as only the son of David according to the scribes' teaching, to be also his Lord — rewarding the blind man's faith, who had believed in Him as the son of David, and striking down the scribes' tradition, who did not know Him as Lord. Whatever pertains to the glory of Christ the Creator, Christ the Creator does not defend in any other way.

latin: Sciebat Christus, baptisma Iohannis unde esset. et cur quasi nesciens interrogabat? sciebat non responsuros sibi Pharisaeos. et cur frustra interrogabat? an. ut ex ore ipsorum iudicaret illos uel ex corde? refer ergo et haec ad excusati. onem creatoris et ad comparationem Christi, et considera iam, quid secuturum esset, si quid Pharisaei ad interrogationem renuntiassent. puta illos renuntiasse humanum Iohannis baptisma: statim lapidibus elisi- fuissent. existeret aliqui Marcion aduersus Marcionem, qui diceret: o deum optimum, o deum diuersum a creatoris exemplis! sciens praeceps ituros homines ipse illos in praerupium imposuit. sic enim et de creatore in arboris lege tractatur. \'sed de caelis fuit baptisma Iohannis). et quare, inquit Christus, non credidistis ei? ergo qui credi uoluerat Iohanni, increpaturus quod non credidissent, eius erat, cuius sacramentum Iohannes administrabat. certe nolentibus renuntiare, quid saperent. cum et ipse uicem opponit: et ego non dico uobis, in qua uirtute haec facio, malum malo reddidit. Reddite quae Caesaris Caesari, et quae sunt dei deo. quae erunt dei, quae similia sint denario Caesaris? imago scilicet et similitudo eius. hominem igitur reddi iubet creatori, in cuius imagine et similitudine et nomine et materia expressus est. quaerat sibi monetam deus Marcionis, Christus denarium hominis suo Caesari iubet reddi. non alieno; nisi quod necesse est, *** qui suum denarium non habet. Iusta et digna praescriptio est in omni quaestione ad propositum interrogationis pertinere debere sensum responsionis. ceterum aliud consulenti aliud respondere dementis est, quo magis absit a Christo quod ne homini quidem conuenit Saducaei, resurrectionis negatores, de ea habentes interrogationem proposuerant domino ex lege materiam mulieris, quae septem fratribus ex ordine defunctis secundum praeceptum legale nupsisset, cuius uiri deputanda esset in resurrectione. haec fuit materia quaestionis, haec substantia consultationis; ad hoc respondisse Christum necesse est. neminem timuit, ut (non.) sed honorem Christo Dauid procurabat, quem Christum dominum magis quam filium Dauid confirmabat, quod non congrueret destructori creatoris. at ei nostra parte quam conueniens interpretatio! nam qui olim a caeco illo (filius Dauid\' fuerat inuocatus, quod tunc reticuit non habens in praesentia scribas, nunc ultro coram eis de industria protulit, ut se, quem caecus secundum scribarum doctrinam filium tantum Dauid praedicarat, dominum quoque eius ostenderet, remunerata quidem fide caeci, qua filium Dauid crediderat [in] illum, pulsata uero traditione scribarum, qua non et dominum eum norant. quodcumque ad gloriam spectaret Christi creatoris sic non alius tueretur, quam Christus creatoris..

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: It was once settled that the authority over names belongs to the One who first announced His Christ to humanity and renamed the laws. So it will also be settled that the one who claims many will come in His name — a name that is not his if Christ and Jesus are not the Creator's, to whom the authority over names belongs — acts with sheer impudence. He should bar the reception of those whose equal he himself is, so that the one who comes in a borrowed name finds no welcome; otherwise, it was his duty to shield his disciples from the lie of that name, he who held the truth of the name by its very authority. In the end, men will come declaring, 'I am the Christ,' and you will receive them, since you have already accepted their counterpart; after all, this claimant does not come in his own name. What then? When the Lord of names Himself arrives — Christ and Jesus of the Creator — will you reject Him? How unjust, how wicked, and how unworthy of the best God, that you refuse to welcome Him coming in His own name, when you have welcomed another in that same name! Let us also examine the signs He assigns to the times: wars, I suspect, and kingdom rising against kingdom, nation against nation, pestilence, famine, earthquakes, terrors, and portents from heaven — all of which befit a severe and cruel God. Since He insists these things must happen, what sort of God does He reveal Himself to be: a destroyer or an approver of the Creator? He confirms that the Creator's own decrees must be fulfilled, decrees which the best God would have removed rather than established, if they were not His own. Yet He predicts these persecutions and sufferings for them, ordeals that lead to martyrdom and salvation. Take the prophecy in Zechariah: 'The Lord Almighty will protect them and consume them; they will stone them with slingstones and drink their blood like wine and fill the bowls like the corners of the altar, and the Lord will save them on that day like sheep, His people, because the holy stones are rolled.' Do not imagine these words forecast the sufferings they endured in so-called wars at the hands of foreigners; look at the details. No prophecy of wars fought with legitimate weapons lists stoning by popular mobs and unarmed tumults; no one measures rivers of blood by the capacity of bowls or equates the slaughter to a single altar's staining; no one calls those who fall armed in battle, fighting with equal ferocity, 'sheep' — but those who surrender themselves rather than retaliate, and are slaughtered in their innocence and patience. Finally: 'because the holy stones are rolled,' He says, not 'because soldiers fight.' For the stones are also the foundations on which we are built, constructed, as Paul says, on the foundation of the apostles — those holy stones, opposed to every offense, rolling on. And here, therefore, He forbids anxiety over what to answer before tribunals, He who suggested to Balaam what he had not thought — indeed, contrary to what he had thought — and who, because of Moses' slow tongue, promised him a mouth.

latin: Olim constitit de nominum proprietate, ei illam *, qui prior et Christum suum in homines adnuntiarit et legum transnominarit. constabit itaque et de impudentia eius, qui multos dicat uenturos in nomine ipsius, quod non sit ipsius, si non Christus et Iesus creatoris est, ad quem proprietas nominum pertinet. amplius et prohibeat eos recipi, quorum et ipse par sit, ut qui proinde in nomine uenit alieno: si non, ipsius erat a mendacio nominis praeuenire discipulos, qui per proprietatem nominis possidebat ueritatem eius. uenient denique illi dicentes: ego sum Christus: recipies eos, qui consimilem recepisti; nec hic enim in nomine suo uenit. quid nunc? quando et ipse ueniet nominum dominus, Christus et Iesus creatoris, reicies illum P et quam iniquum, quam iniustum et optimo deo indignum, ut non recipias eum in suo nomine uenientem, qui alium in nomine eius recepisti! Videamus et quae signa temporibus imponat: bella, opinor., et regnum super regnum et gentem super gentem et pestem et fames terraeque motus et formidines et prodigia de caelo, quae omnia seuero et atroci deo congruunt. haec cum adicit etiam oportere fieri, quem se praestat? destructorem an probatorem creatoris? cuius dispositiones confirmat impleri oportere, quas ut optimus tam tristes quam atroces abstulisset potius quam constituisset, si non ipsius fuissent ante haec autem persecutiones eis praedicat et passiones euenturas, in martyrium utique et in salutem. accipe praedicatum in Zacharia: dominus, inquit, omnipotens proteget eos et consument illos, et lapidabunt lapidibus fundae et bibent sanguinem illorum uelut uinum et replebunt pateras quasi altaris, et saluos eos faciet dominus illo die uelut oues, populum suum, quia lapides sancti uolutant. et ne putes haec in passiones praedicari, quae illos tot bellorum nomine ab allophylis manebant, respice ad species. nemo in praedicatione bellorum legitimis armis debellandorum lapidationem enumerat popularibus coetibus magis et inermi tumultui familiarem; nemo, tanta in bello sanguinis flumina paterarum capacitate metitur aut unius altaris cruentationi adaequat; nemo oues appellat eos, qui in bello armati et ipsi ex eadem feritate certantes cadunt, sed qui in sua proprietate atque patientia dedentes potius semetipsos quam uindicantes trucidantur. denique: quia lapides, inquit, sancti uolutant, non \'quia milites pugnant\'. lapides enim sunt et fundamenta, super quae nos aedificamur, exstructi secundum Paulum super fundamenta apostolorum, qui lapides sancti oppositi omnium offensui uolutant. et hic igitur ipse cogitari uetat, quid responderi oporteat apud tribunalia, qui et Balaae quod non cogitauerat, immo contra quam cogitauerat suggessit et Moysi causato linguae tarditatem os repromisit.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Someone will argue that two supreme beings can coexist, distinct and separate within their own boundaries. They will cite the example of earthly kingdoms, many in number yet each supreme in its own region, and they will think human things can be compared with divine things.

If that argument is allowed, what stops us from introducing not just a third and fourth god, but as many gods as there are kings of nations? The issue concerns God, whose defining property is that he admits no comparison with any example. Nature itself declares this — if not Isaiah, then God speaking through Isaiah: "To whom will you liken me?" (Isaiah 40:18). Human things may be compared with divine things, but not with God. For God is one thing; the things of God are another.

Finally, whoever uses a king as an example of a supreme being should see that the example collapses. A king may be supreme on his own throne up to God, yet he remains beneath God; once compared to God, he ceases to be supreme, having been transferred to God. If that is so, how can you use that thing as an analogy for God when the analogy vanishes the moment it approaches the comparison? What if even among kings the supreme is not multiple but unique and singular — namely the King of kings, who, by the summit of greatness and the subjection of all other ranks, stands as the culmination of dominion?

Even kings of another sort, singular in the union of empire and presiding over what we might call minute kingdoms, if examined from every side to determine who excels in the substance and power of their realms, will inevitably yield a single summit of greatness, all lower degrees gradually excluded by the process of comparison. Thus, even when the supreme appears multiple in dispersion, it is unique in its powers, nature, and state. Accordingly, when two gods are compared as two supreme beings, the union of the supreme must concede to the other by the verdict of comparison, because the supreme consists in its own victory — having overcome another great being, not supreme — and from that defeat it possesses a solitude of singular excellence, making it unique. This inescapable logic forces the conclusion: either deny that God is the supreme being, which no wise person will accept, or refuse to share that supremacy with anyone else.

latin: Sed argumentabitur quilibet posse et duo summa magna consistere, distincta atque disiuncta in suis finibus, et utique aduocabit exemplum regna terrarum, tanta numero et tamen summa magna in suis quibusque regionibus, et putabit ubique humana diuinis conferenda. iam ergo si huic argumentationi locus dabitur, quid prohibet, non dico et tertium et quartum deum inducere, uerum tot iam numero quot et gentium reges? de deo agitur, cuius hoc principaliter proprium est, nullius exempli capere comparationem. hoc natura ipsa, si non aliquis Esaias, uel ipse per Esaiam deus, contionabitur: cui mesimilabitis? diuinis forsitan comparabuntur humana, deo non ita. aliud enim deus, aliud quae dei. denique qui exemplo uteris regis quasi summi magni, uide ne iam non possis eo uti. rei enim, etsi summum magnum est in suo solio usque ad deum, tamen infra deum; comparatus autem ad deum excidet iam de summo magno, translato in deum. hoc si ita, quomodo uteris eius rei exemplo ad dei comparationem quae, dum ad comparationem accedit, amittitur? quid nunc, si nec inter reges plurifarium uideri potest summum magnum, sed unicum et singulare, apud eum scilicet, qui rex regum ob summitatem magnitudinis et subiectionem ceterorum graduum quasi culmen dominationis excipitur\'? sed etiam [alterius formae] reges, qui singulares in unione imperii praesunt si(militer) minutalibus, ut ita dixerim, regnis, (si) undique conferantur in examinationem, qua constet, quis eorum praecellat in substantiis et uiribus regni, in unum necesse est summitas magnitudinis eliquetur, omnibus gradatim per comparationis exitum de magnitudinis summa expressis et exclusis. I adeo etsi in disperso multifarium uidetur summum magnum, suis uiribus et sua natura et suo statu unicum est. proinde cum duo dii conferuntur ut duo [reges et duo] summa magna, in alterum concedat necesse est unio summi magni ex sententia comparationis, quia summum uictoria sua constat, superato aemulo alio magno, non tamen summo, atque ex defectione, aemuli solitudinem quandam de singularitate praestantiae suae possidens unicum est. ineluctabilis iste complexus in hoc sententiam constringit: aut negandum deum esse summum magnum, quod nemo patietur sapiens, aut nulli alii communicandum.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: He knew exactly what He was doing, and He knew precisely when He had to suffer, since the Law had already sketched out His passion in advance. Out of every Jewish festival, He picked the Passover, because Moses had already declared the mystery: the Passover belongs to the Lord. That is why He let His desire show: 'I have earnestly wanted to eat this Passover with you before I suffer' (Luke 22:15). Oh, you destroyer of the Law, who still wanted to keep the Passover! No doubt the fresh green rites of Judaism had charmed Him. Or was it that He Himself — led like a sheep to slaughter, silent like a sheep before its shearer — was aching to fulfill the figure of His saving blood (Isaiah 53:7)? He could have been handed over by any random stranger, so I would not even have to say this psalm was fulfilled: 'The one who eats my bread has lifted his heel against me' (Psalm 41:9). He could have been betrayed for nothing. After all, what great effort did the betrayer expend on a man who, by offending the people to their faces, could not have been seized more easily than invaded? But that scenario would have suited some other Christ, not the One who actually fulfilled the prophecies. Scripture says: 'Because they sold the Righteous One' (Zechariah 11:12-13). And the exact amount and final disposition of the price — later, when Judas repented and the silver was returned and used to buy the potter's field, as Matthew's Gospel records (Matthew 27:3-10) — Jeremiah had already foretold: 'They took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of the One they valued — or honored — and gave them for the potter's field' (Jeremiah 32:9).

So, having confessed that He had longed to eat the Passover with His own — for it would have been unfitting for God to long for something alien — He took bread, distributed it to the disciples, and made it His body by saying, 'This is My body,' that is, the figure of My body (Luke 22:19). But a figure cannot exist unless the reality exists. A phantom, an empty thing, cannot take on a figure. Or if He called bread His body because He lacked a body, then He should have given bread for us — making a mockery of Marcion's fantasy, so that bread might be crucified. But why call bread His body and not a gourd, which Marcion kept in place of a heart? He fails to grasp that this was an ancient figure of Christ's body, spoken through Jeremiah: 'They plotted against me, saying, Come, let us put wood into his bread' — that is, the cross into His body (Jeremiah 11:19). Therefore the Illuminator of ancient things has made it perfectly clear what He meant by bread: by calling His body bread, and by establishing the covenant in the cup, sealed with His blood, He confirmed the substance of the body (Luke 22:20). No body can have blood except a fleshly one. Even if someone posits a non-fleshly quality of body, it still would not have blood except as flesh. So the proof of the body rests on the testimony of the flesh, and the proof of the flesh rests on the testimony of the blood.

And so that you may also recognize the ancient figure of blood in wine, Isaiah steps forward: 'Who is this coming from Edom, with crimsoned garments from Bozrah? Who is this, glorious in His apparel, marching in the greatness of His strength? Why are Your garments red, and Your clothes like one who treads in the winepress?' (Isaiah 63:1-3). The prophetic Spirit, as if already gazing on the Lord coming to His passion, clothed in flesh so that He might suffer in it, marks the blood-stained condition of the flesh by the redness of the garments — trampled and pressed by the violence of the passion, as in a winepress, because from there men descend as if bloodied by the redness of wine. Even more plainly, Genesis in the blessing of Judah — from whose tribe the lineage of Christ's flesh would arise — was already sketching Christ in Judah: 'He will wash His robe in wine and His garment in the blood of the grape' (Genesis 49:11), identifying the robe and garment as flesh, and the wine as blood. So now He has consecrated His blood in wine, He who then prefigured wine as blood.

latin: Proinde sciit, et quando pati oporteret eum, cuius passionem lex figura(ra)t. nam ex tot festis Iudaeorum paschae diem elegit in hoc enim sacramentum pronuntiarat Moyses: pascha est domini. ideo et adfectum suum ostendit: concupiscentia concupii pascha edere uobiscum, antequam patiar. o legis destructorem, qui concupierat etiam pascha seruare! nimirum uerbecina illum [in] Iudaica delectarat. an ipse erat, qui, tamquam ouis ad uictimam adduci habens et tamquam ouis coram tondente sic os non aperturus, figuram sanguinis sui salutaris implere concupiscebat? poterat et ab extraneo quolibet tradi, ne dicerem et in hoc psalmum expunctum: qui mecum panem edit leuauit in me plantam. poterat et sine praemio tradi. quanta enim opera traditoris circa eum, qui populum coram offendens nec tradi magis potuisset quam inuadi? sed hoc alii competisset Christo, non qui prophetias adimplebat. scriptum est enim: pro eo quod uenumdederunt iustum. nam et quantitatem et exitum pretii postea Iuda paenitente reuocati et in emptionem dati agri figuli, sicut in euangelio Mathei continetur, Hieremias praecanit: et acceperunt triginta argentea pretium adpretiati — uel honorati - et dederunt ea in agrum figuli. professus itaque se concupiscentia concupisse edere pascha ut suum, — indignum enim, ut quid alienum concupisceret deus — acceptum panem et distributum discipulis corpus suum illum fecit hoc est corpus meum dicendo, id est (figura. corporis mei\'. figura autem non fuisset nisi ueritatis esset corpus. ceterum uacua res, quod est phantasma, figuram capere non posset. aut si propterea panem corpus sibi finxit, quia corporis carebat uanitatem, ergo panem debuit tradere pro nobis. faciebat ad uanitatem Marcionis, ut panis crucifigeretur. cur autem panem corpus suum appellat et non magis peponem, quem Marcion cordis loco habuit, non intellegens ueterem fuisse istam figuram corporis Christi dicentis per Hieremiam: aduersus me cogitauerunt cogitatum dicentes: uenite. coiciamus lignum in panem eius, scilicet crucem in corpus eius? itaque inluminator antiquitatum, quid tunc uoluerit significasse panem, satis declarauit corpus suum uocans panemsic et in calicis mentione testamentum constituens sanguine suo obsignatum substantiam corporis confirmauit. nullius enim corporis sanguis potest esse nisi carnis. nam et si qua corporis qualitas non carnea opponetur nobis, certe sanguinem nisi carnea non habebit. ita consistet probatio corporis de testimonio carnis, probatio carnis de testimonio sanguinis. ut autem et sanguinis ueterem figuram in uino recognoseas. aderit Esaias: quis, inquit, qui aduenit ex Edom, rubor uestimentorum eius ex Bosor? sic decorus in stola uiolentia cum fortitudine? quare rubra uestimenta tua, et indumenta sicut de foro torcularis, pleno conculcato? spiritus enim propheticus, uelut iam contemplabundus dominum ad passionem uenientem, carne scilicet uestitum ut in ea passum, cruentum habitum carnis in uestimentorum rubore designat, conculcatae et expressae ui passionis tamquam in foro torcularis, quia et inde quasi cruentati homines de uini rubore descendunt. multo manifestius Genesis in benedictione Iudae, ex cuius tribu carnis census Christi processurus, iam tunc Christum in Iuda deliniabat: lauabit, inquit, in uino stolam suam et in sanguine uuae amictum suum, stolam et amictum carnem demonstrans et uinum sanguinem. ita et nunc sanguinem suum in uino consecrauit qui tunc uinum in sanguinem figurauit.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Woe, says He, to that man by whom the Son of man is betrayed! Luke 22:22 Now it is certain that in this woe must be understood the imprecation and threat of an angry and incensed Master, unless Judas was to escape with impunity after so vast a sin . If he were meant to escape with impunity, the woe was an idle word; if not, he was of course to be punished by Him against whom he had committed the sin of treachery.

Now, if He knowingly permitted the man, whom He deliberately elected to be one of His companions, to plunge into so great a crime, you must no longer use an argument against the Creator in Adam's case, which may now recoil on your own God: either that he was ignorant , and had no foresight to hinder the future sinner; or that he was unable to hinder him, even if he was ignorant ; or else that he was unwilling , even if he had the foreknowledge and the ability; and so deserved the stigma of maliciousness, in having permitted the man of his own choice to perish in his sin . I advise you therefore (willingly) to acknowledge the Creator in that god of yours, rather than against your will to be assimilating your excellent god to Him.

For in the case of Peter, too, he gives you proof that he is a jealous God , when he destined the apostle, after his presumptuous protestations of zeal , to a flat denial of him, rather than prevent his fall . The Christ of the prophets was destined, moreover, to be betrayed with a kiss , Luke 22:47-49 for He was the Son indeed of Him who was honoured with the lips by the people. Isaiah 29:13 When led before the council, He is asked whether He is the Christ. Luke 22:66-67 Of what Christ could the Jews have inquired but their own? Why, therefore, did He not, even at that moment, declare to them the rival (Christ)? You reply, In order that He might be able to suffer. In other words, that this most excellent god might plunge men into crime, whom he was still keeping in ignorance . But even if he had told them, he would yet have to suffer.

For he said, If I tell you, you will not believe . Luke 22:67 And refusing to believe , they would have continued to insist on his death. And would he not even more probably still have had to suffer, if had announced himself as sent by the rival god, and as being, therefore, the enemy of the Creator? It was not, then, in order that He might suffer, that He at that critical moment refrained from proclaiming Himself the other Christ , but because they wanted to extort a confession from His mouth, which they did not mean to believe even if He had given it to them, whereas it was their bounden duty to have acknowledged Him in consequence of His works, which were fulfilling their Scriptures. It was thus plainly His course to keep Himself at that moment unrevealed, because a spontaneous recognition was due to Him.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: They began to heap charges on him once he was brought before Pilate, because he claimed to be the Christ, the King — and, beyond doubt, the Son of God, who will sit at God's right hand. They would have saddled him with a different title, unsure whether he had actually said he was the Son of God, unless, as you put it, he had declared that he is exactly what they were accusing him of being. When Pilate questioned him, 'Are you the Christ?' he answered, 'You say so,' so that he would not appear to have said more out of fear of authority. The Lord was therefore installed in judgment — and he takes his stand to judge his people; the Lord himself comes into judgment with the elders and rulers of his people, according to Isaiah (Isaiah) — and from that point on every scripture of his passion was fulfilled: the nations were in an uproar and the peoples plotted in vain; the kings of the earth took their stand and the rulers gathered as one against the Lord and against his Christ (Psalm). 'Nations' means the Romans who were with Pilate; 'peoples' means the tribes of Israel; 'kings' points to Herod; 'rulers' points to the chief priests.

Even Herod, sent by Pilate as if he were a gift, bore witness in the words of Hosea (Hosea). For the prophet had foretold about Christ: 'And they will lead him bound as a gift to the king.' Herod was delighted to see Jesus, yet he heard not a single word from him. Like a lamb before its shearer, he did not open his mouth, because the Lord had given him a tongue of discipline, so that he would know when he ought to speak — that tongue, I mean, which in the psalm he proved was stuck to his throat by not speaking (Psalm). Barabbas, a thoroughly guilty man, was granted life as if he were good, while Christ, the most righteous, was demanded for death as if he were a murderer. Two criminals were crucified alongside him, so that he would be counted among the wicked. His clothing was divided by the soldiers, partly by lot, but Marcion has stripped away the fact of the division, looking back at the psalm's prophecy: 'They divided my garments among themselves and cast lots for my clothing' (Psalm). So take away the cross itself as well, for the same psalm does not keep silent about it: 'They pierced my hands and my feet' (Psalm). The whole outcome is read there: 'Dogs surrounded me, a gang of evildoers encircled me' (Psalm). All who stared at me mocked me with their noses; they curled their lips and shook their heads: 'He trusted in God, let him rescue him' (Psalm). What testimony do the garments offer now? Take the spoils of your false ones: the entire psalm is Christ's garments.

Look, even the elements were shaken, for the Lord was suffering. But if the adversary had been wounded, heaven would have draped itself in shadows, the sun would have insulted with its rays, the day would have stood still, gladly watching Marcion's Christ hanging on the gibbet. These arguments would have sufficed for me even if they had not been foretold: 'The heavens,' says Isaiah, 'will become a garment of darkness' (Isaiah); this will be the day of which Amos also says: 'And on that day, says the Lord, the sun will set at noon' — you have the significance of the sixth hour as well — 'and it will grow dark over the land' (Amos). The temple veil was torn, and the angels, abandoning the daughter of Zion, left her like a watchtower in a vineyard and like a hut in a cucumber field (Isaiah). Oh, how thoroughly Christ himself fulfilled the thirtieth psalm! He cries out to the Father, so that even in dying he might fulfill the prophets with his last voice (Psalm 30). With those words he breathed his last. Who breathed his last? The Spirit himself, or the flesh the Spirit? But the Spirit could not breathe his last on his own. There is one who expires and another who is expired. If the Spirit is expired, he must be expired by another. And if he were only Spirit, it would be said that he departed rather than expired. Who, then, expires the Spirit, if not the flesh, which also breathes while it has him and so expires him when it loses him? Finally, if there was no flesh but a phantom of flesh, and the phantom was Spirit, and the Spirit expired himself and departed by expiring, then beyond doubt the phantom departed, since the Spirit, which was the phantom, departed, and the phantom appeared nowhere with the Spirit. So nothing remained on the wood, nothing hung even after the expiration, nothing was asked of Pilate, nothing was taken down from the cross, nothing was wrapped in a shroud, nothing was laid in a new tomb? But indeed, something did. What was it, then? If it was a phantom, then the Spirit was still in it. If the Spirit had departed, then he had taken the phantom away. All that remains for the heretic's impudence is to say that a phantom of a phantom remained there; but Joseph certainly knew it was a body, which he handled with all reverence — that Joseph, who did not consent to the crime of the Jews, a blessed man, who did not walk in the counsel of the impious, did not stand in the way of sinners, and did not sit in the seat of the pestilential (Psalm).

Constitutus est igitur dominus in iudicio — et statuit in iudicio populum suum; ipse dominus in iudicium uenit cum presbyteris et archontibuspopuli, secundum Esaiam — atque exinde omne scriptum passionis suae impleuit: tumultuatae suntibidem nationes et populi meditati suntinania; adstiterunt reges terrae etarchontes congregati sunt in unum aduersus dominum et aduersus Christum eius: \'nationes\' Romani qui cum Pilato fuerant; \'populi\' tribus Israhelis; (reges) in Herode, (archontes) in summis sacerdotibus. nam et Herodi uelut munus a Pilato missus Osee uocibus fidem reddidit. de Christo enim prophetauerat: et uinctum eum ducent xenium regi. delectatus est denique Herodes uiso Iesu nec uocem ullam ab eo audiuit. tamquam agnus enim ante tondentem sic non aperuit os suum, quia dominus dederat illi linguam disciplinae, ut sciret, quando eum oporteret proferre sermonem, illam scilicet linguam, quam in psalmo adglutinatam gutturi suo tunc probabat non loquendo. Et Barrabas quidem nocentissimus uita ut bonus donatur, Christus uero iustissimus ut homicida morti expostulatur. sed et duo scelesti circumfiguntur illi, ut inter iniquos scilicet deputaretur. uestitum plane eius a militibus diuisum partim, (partim) sorti concessum Marcion abstulit respiciens psalmi prophetiam: dispertiti sunt sibi uestimenta mea et in uestitum meum sortem miserunt. aufer igitur et crucem ipsam. idem enim psalmus de ea non tacet: foderunt manus meas et pedes. totus in illo exitus legitur: circumdederunt me canes, synagoga maleficorum circumuallauit me. omnes, qui spectabant me, naso inridebant me; locuti sunt labiis et capita mouerunt: sperauit in deum, liberet eum. quo iam testimonium uestimentorum? habe falsi tui praedam: totus psalmus uestimenta sunt Christi. Ecce autem et elementa concutiuntur. dominus enim patiebatur ipsorum. ceterum aduersario laeso caelum luminibus loruisset, magis sol radiis insultasset, magis dies stetisset, libenter spectans pendentem in patibulo Christum Marcionis. haec argumentata quoque mihi competissent, et si non fuissent praedicata: caelum, inquit Esaias, uestiam tenebris; hic erit dies, de quo et Amos: et erit die illa, dicit dominus, occidet sol meridie — habes et horae sextae significationem — et contenebrabit super terram. scissum est et templi uelum, angeli eruptione derelinquentis filiam Sionis tamquam in uinea speculam et in cucumerario casulam.s o quantum perseuerauit etiam tricesimo psalmo Christus ipsum reddere! uociferatur ad patrem: ***, ut et moriens ultima uoce prophetas adimpleret. hoc dicto expirauit. quis? spiritus semetipsum an caro spiritum? sed spiritus semetipsum expirare non potuit. alius est qui expirat, alius qui expiratur. si spiritus expiratur, ab alio expiretur necesse est. quodsi solus spiritus fuisset, discessisse potius diceretur quam expirasse. quis igitur expirat spiritum nisi caro, quae et spirat quando illum habet et ita eum cum amittit expirat? denique si caro non fuit, sed phantasma carnis, phantasma autem spiritus fuit, spiritus autem semetipsum expirauit et expirando discessit, sine dubio phantasma discessit, cum spiritus, qui erat phantasma, discessit, et nusquam comparuit phantasma cum spiritu. nihil ergo remansit in ligno, nihil pependit etiam post expirationem, nihil de Pilato postulatum, nihil de patibulo detractum, nihil sindone inuolutum, nihil sepulcro nouo conditum? atquin non nihil. quid ergo illud fuit? si phantasma, adhuc ergo inerat et spiritus. si discesserat spiritus, ergo abstulerat phantasma. superest impudentiae haereticae dicere phantasma illic phantasmatis remansisse; sed scilicet Ioseph corpus fuisse nouerat quod tota pietate tractauit, ille Ioseph, qui non consenserat in scelere Iudaeis, beatus uir, qui non abiit in consilio impiorum et in uia peccatorum non stetit et in cathedra pestium non sedit.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: It was also fitting that the Lord's burial be prophesied and that it already then deserved a blessing, since prophecy did not overlook the service of those women who gathered at the tomb before dawn with spices prepared. For Hosea speaks of this: they will seek my face; before dawn they will keep vigil toward me, saying, 'Let us go and turn back to the Lord, for he has torn and will heal us; he has struck and will have mercy on us; he will heal us after two days, and on the third day we will rise again' (Hosea). Who could refuse to believe this when considering those women, tossed between the pain of their present destitution, in which they seemed struck by the Lord, and the hope of his resurrection, by which they expected to be restored? But once his body was not found, his burial was removed from the midst, according to Isaiah (Isaiah). And two angels appeared there as well. Almost all of God's word, as was his custom, stands on two witnesses. Isaiah also foresaw the women returning from the tomb and from that vision of the angels: 'Come, women coming from the vision; come to announce the Lord's resurrection' (Isaiah).

It is a good thing, indeed, that the disciples' incredulity persisted to the very end, so that our defense would stand firm: Christ taught the disciples the Law, but he presented himself to them as no other than the prophets. For when two of them were traveling and the Lord joined them, not appearing as he truly was, but even disguising himself from their knowledge of what had happened, they said, 'We thought he was the redeemer of Israel, certainly his Christ -- that is, the Creator's.' So completely had he not presented another to them. Yet they did not think him to be of the Creator; and when he was thought to be the Creator's, he would not have endured that opinion about himself if he were not the one they thought he was. Otherwise, he would be the author of error and a falsifier of the truth against the title of the best God. But not even after the resurrection did he show himself to them as anyone other than the one they had thought him to be. Clearly he reproached them: 'O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe all that he spoke to you' (Luke 24:25). What had he spoken? That he was of another God? Prove it, and I will concede the point. Or did the angels say the same to the women: 'Remember what he told you in Galilee, that the Son of Man must be delivered and crucified and rise on the third day' (Luke 24:6-7)? And why was it necessary, unless it was so written by God the Creator? Therefore he rebuked them as those scandalized by the passion alone and doubtful of the resurrection faith announced to them by women, through whom they had not believed him to be the one they had thought. So, what they had thought -- that is what he, wanting to be believed, confirmed himself to be: the Christ of the Creator, the Redeemer of Israel.

What could be clearer about the truth of the body? When they were hesitating, lest it be a phantom -- indeed, believing it to be a phantom -- he said, 'Why are you troubled, and why do doubts arise in your hearts? See my hands and my feet, that I myself am he; for a spirit does not have bones, as you see me having' (Luke 24:38-39). And Marcion, I believe, did not want to erase certain things contrary to himself from his gospel, so that from those he could erase but did not, those he did erase might either be denied or said to have been rightly erased; and he spares only those things which, by interpreting them differently rather than deleting them, he subverts. He wants the text to read: 'A spirit does not have bones, as you see me having' -- that is, not having bones, just as a spirit does not. What is the reason for this twisting, since he could have spoken simply: 'Because a spirit does not have bones, as you see me not having'? Why does he offer his hands and feet for inspection, limbs consisting of bones, if he had no bones? Why does he add, 'Know that I am he' -- whom, namely, they had known bodily before? Or if he was a phantom through and through, why did he rebuke them for believing it to be a phantom? Yet while they still did not believe, he asked for food, to show that he even had teeth. We have fulfilled, I think, the wager. We have shown the Christ of the Law -- in teachings, judgments, affections, senses, virtues, passions, and even resurrection -- to be none other than the Creator's. For by sending the apostles to preach to all nations, to go out into all the earth, he commanded their sound to go out into all the earth and their words to the ends of the world, fulfilling the Psalm (Psalm 19:4). I pity you, Marcion; you have labored in vain. For Christ Jesus in your gospel is mine.

latin: Oportuerat etiam sepultorem domini prophetari ac iam tunc merito benedici, si nec mulierum illarum officium praeterit prophetia, quae ante lucem conuenerunt ad sepulcrum cum odorum paratura. de hoc enim per Osee: et quaerent, inquit, faciem meam; ante lucem uigilabunt ad me dicentes: eamus et conuertamur ad dominum, quia ipse eripuit [dixit] et curabit nos, percussit et miserebitur nostri, sanabit nos post biduum, in die tertia resurgemus. quis enim haec non credat in recogitatu mulierum illarum uolutata inter dolorem praesentis destitutionis, qua percussae sibi uidebantur a domino, et spem resurrectionis ipsius, qua restitutuiri se arbitrabantur? corpore autem non inuento sublata erat sepultura eius de medio secundum Esaiam. sed et duo ibidem angeli apparuerunt. tot fere laterensibus uti solebat in duobus testibus consistens dei sermo. reuertentes quoque a sepulcro mulieres et ab illa angelorum uisione prospiciebatEsaias: mulieres, inquit, [uenite] uenientes a uisione, uenite, ad renuntiandam scilicet domini resurrectionem. Bene autem,I quod incredulitas discipulorum perseuerabat, ut in finem usque defensio nostra consisteret Christum legum non alium se discipulis edidisse quam prophetarum. nam cum duo ex illis iter agerent et dominus eis adhaesisset, non comparens quod ipse esset, etiam dissimulans de conscientia rei gestae: nos autem putabamus, inquiunt, ipsum esse redemptorem Israhelis, utique suum Christum, id est creatoris. adeo nec alium se ediderat illis. ceterum non existimarent eum creatoris,I et cum creatoris existimaretur, non sustinuisset hanc de se existimationem, si non is esset, qui existimabatur. aut ipse! erit auctor erroris et praeuaricator ueritatis aduersus dei optimi titulum. sed nec post resurrectionem alium se eis ostendit quam quem existimatum sibi dixerant. plane inuectus est in illos: o insensati et tardi corde in non credendo omnibus, \'quae locutus est ad uos.\' quaenam locutus? alterius se dei esse? proba, et manus dedo. an eadem et angeli ad mulieres: rememoramini, quae locutus sit uobis in Galilaea dicens, quod oportet tradi filium hominis et crucifigi et tertia die resurgere? et quare oportebat, nisi quia ita a deo creatore scriptum? igitur increpuit illos ut de sola passione scandalizatos et ut dubios de fide resurrectionis adnuntiatae sibi a feminis, per quae non crediderant ipsum fuisse, quem existimauerant. itaque quod existimauerant, id uolens credi se eum se confirmabat, quem existimauerant, creatoris scilicet Christum, redemptorem Israhelis. De corporis autem ueritate quid potest clarius? cum haesitantibus eis, ne phantasma esset, immo phantasma credentibus: quid turbati estis? (in quit,) et quid cogitationes subeunt in corda uestra? uidete manus meas et pedes, quia ipse ego sum, quoniam spiritus ossa non habet, sicut me habentem uidetis. et Marcion quaedam contraria sibi illa, credo, industria eradere de euangelio suo noluit, ut ex his, quae eradere potuit nec erasit, illa, quae erasit, aut negetur erasisse aut merito erasisse dicatur; nec parcit nisi eis, quae non minus aliter interpretando quam delendo subuertit. uult itaque sic dictum: spiritus ossa non habet, sicut me uidetis habentem, quasi ad spiritum referatur sicut me uidetis habentem, id est non habentem ossa, sicut et spiritus. et quae ratio tortuositatis istius, cum simpliciter pronuntiare potuisset:. \'quia spiritus ossa non habet, sicut me uidetis non habentem\'? cur autem inspectui eorum manus et pedes suos offert, quae membra ex ossibus constant, si ossa non habebat? cur adicit: et scitote, quia ego sum, quem scilicet corporeum retro nouerant? aut si phantasma erat usquequaque, cur illos phantasma credentes increpabat? atquin adhuc eis non credentibus propterea cibum desiderauit, ut se ostenderet etiam dentes habere. Impleuimus, ut opinor, sponsionem. exhibuimus legum Christum prophetarum doctrinis sententiis adfectibus sensibus uirtutibus passionibus etiam resun-ectione non alium quam creatoris, siquidem et apostolos mittens ad praedicandum uniuersis nationibus in omnem terram exire sonum eorum et in terminos terrae uoces eorum psalmum adimplendo praecepit. misereor tui, Marcion; frustra laborasti. Christus enim Iesus in euangelio tuo meus est.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: What reason could possibly justify composing two supreme, supreme beings? First, I demand to know: why stop at two? If number suited the divine substance, it would be far more fitting to believe that substance is abundant. Valentinus was at least more honorable and generous in his invention: he dared to posit two primal principles, Bythos and Sigen, and then, like the sow of Aeneas, farrowed a litter of thirty Aeons, pouring out a whole swarm of divinity. But any logic that refuses to admit more than one supreme being also refuses to admit two, because it thereby admits a plurality. Once you pass one, you have entered the realm of number; one is, after all, a number. Whatever rationale could admit two could just as easily admit more. Two is already a multitude, unity already breached.

In our view, the force of this reasoning does not permit belief in many gods, and the very rule that establishes one God excludes two. For what must God be? A being to whom nothing is equal, so that He is supreme and greatest—yes, unique, because nothing equals Him. Now, if there are two supreme, supreme beings, two equals, to what task or profit would they be assigned? What difference does the number make when two equals are indistinguishable from one? The reality present in both is a single thing. Even if there were many equals, they would all amount to the same as one; they would effectively be one, since they do not differ from each other insofar as they are equals. Furthermore, if neither of the two surpasses the other—so that both are supreme, both are God, neither offers more than the other—they demonstrate no rationale for their own number. Lacking superiority, they fail the test: the number of the divine ought to rest on the highest reason, or else the very worship owed to it is dragged into uncertainty.

Consider the dilemma: faced with two gods as perfectly matched as two supreme beings, what am I to do? If I worship both, I fear the sheer volume of service would be judged superstition rather than religion, because I could earn the favor of both by honoring just one—a fact that itself testifies to their equality and unity, since in reverencing one I revere the other, and in the one I possess two. If I worship only one, I face the same scruple: I would seem to be pouring out the empty vanity of number without distinction, pointlessly. The safer conclusion: it is better to worship neither than to worship one with a divided heart or both in vain.

latin: Aut quae ratio duo summa magna composuit? primo enim exigam, cur non plura, si duo, quando locupletiorem oporteret credi substantiam diuinitatis, si competeret ei numerus. honestior et liberalior Valentinus, qui simul ausus est duos concipere, Bython et Sigen, tum usque ad triginta Aeonum fetus, tamquam Aeneiae scrofae, examen diuinitatis effudit. quaecumque ratio plura summa magna non patitur admitti, eadem nec duo, ut (et) ipsa plura. [post unum] post ; unum enim numerus. quae potuit duo admittere, eadem potuit et plura. et duo enim multitudo, unione iam excessa. denique apud nos uis rationis istius ipso termino plures deos credi non sinit, quo nec duos illa regula unum deum sistens. i qua deum id esse oporteat, cui nihil adaequetur, ut summo i magno, unicum autem sit, cui nihil adaequetur. iam nunc i duo summa magna, duo paria, cui operae pretio, cui emolumento deputarentur? quid interfuit numeri, cum duo paria non differant uno? una enim res est, quae eadem in duobus est. etiamsi plura essent paria, tantundem omnia (quantum) ; unum fuissent, nullo inter se differendo, qua paria. porro si i neutrum ex duobus altero distat, ut ambo summa magna, qua dei ambo, neutrum plus altero praestat, nullam iam rationem numeri sui ostendunt, praestantiam non habentes, numerus autem diuinitatis summa ratione constare deberet, uel quoniam et cultura eius in anceps deduceretur. ecce enim duos intuens deos tam pares quam duo summa magna, quid facerem? si ambos colerem, uererer, ne abundantia officii superstitio potius quam religio existimaretur, quia duos tam pares et in altero ambos possem in uno demereri, hoc ipsum testimonio praestans parilitati et unitati eorum, dum alterum in altero uenerarer, dum in uno mihi duo sunt. si alterum colerem, aeque recogitarem, ne suffundere uiderer numeri uanitatem sine differentia superuacui, hoc est: tutius censerem neutrum colendum quam alterum cum scrupulo [colendum ] aut ambos uane.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: We still seem to be arguing as if Marcion had established two equals. While we insist that the one true God must be believed to be the Supreme, the Great, excluding any equal from Him, it is as though we have retreated from the issue of two equals; nevertheless, by teaching that equals cannot exist according to the form of the Supreme and Great, we have sufficiently confirmed that two cannot exist. Otherwise, we would certainly be conceding that Marcion constitutes unequal gods: one a Judge, fierce and warlike, the other mild, placid, and merely good and optimal. Let us examine this alternative just as closely: whether diversity can at least accommodate two, since equality could not. Furthermore, the same rule of the Supreme and Great will defend us here too, since it vindicates the entire state of divinity. It is fitting and, in a sense, seizing the adversary's meaning by the throat—he who does not deny the Creator God—to justly prescribe that diversity has no place between those whom, having confessed them equally as gods, he cannot make diverse. Not because men cannot be utterly diverse under the same title, but because God will not be called—indeed, cannot be believed—unless He is the Supreme and Great. Therefore, when the Supreme and Great is compelled to acknowledge the God he does not deny, he cannot admit that he ascribes any diminution to the Supreme and Great by which He would be subjected to another Supreme and Great. For He ceases to be if He is subjected. But it is not in God's nature to cease from His state—that is, from being the Supreme and Great. For even in that supposedly superior god, the Supreme and Great would be endangered if it were captured in the Creator. Thus, when two gods are pronounced, two Supreme and Great Ones, it is necessary that neither is greater or lesser than the other, neither more sublime nor more cast down. Deny the God whom you call worse; deny the Supreme and Great whom you believe to be lesser. Having confessed God, you have confessed both as two Supreme and Great Ones. You take nothing away from one nor ascribe anything to the other. In recognizing the divinity, you have denied the diversity.

latin: Sic adhuc uidemur disputare, quasi Marcion duos pares constituat. nam dum defendimus deum, summum magnum, unicum credi oportere, excludentes ab eo parilitatem, tamquam de duobus paribus de his retractauimus, nihilominus tamen docendo pares esse non posse secundum summi magni formam satis confirmauimus duos esse non posse, alioquin certi Marcionem dispares deos constituere, alterum iudicem, ferum, bellipotentem, alterum mitem, placidum et tantummodo bonum atque optimum. dispiciamus aeque et hanc partem, an diuersitas saltim duos capiat, si parilitas capere non potuit. porro et hic eadem regula summi magni patrocinabitur nobis, utpote quae totum statum uindicet diuinitatis. conueniens enim et quodammodo iniecta manu detinens aduersarii sensum non negantis creatorem deum, iustissime praescribo illi diuersitati locum non esse inter eos, quos ex aequo deos confessus non potest facere diuersos. non quia non et homines licet sub eadem appellatione diuersissimos esse, sed quia deus non erit dicendus, quia nec credendus, nisi summum magnum. cum ergo summum magnum cogatur agnoscere quem deum non negat, non potest admitti, ut summo magno aliquam adscribat diminutionem, qua subiciatur alii summo magno. desinit enim, si subiciatur. non est autem dei desinere de statu suo, id est de summo magno. nam et in illo deo potiore periclitari poterit summum magnum, si depretiari capit in creatore. ita cum duo dii pronuntiantur duo summa magna, necesse est neutrum altero aut maius sit aut minus, neutrum altero aut sublimius aut deiectius. nega deum quem dicis deteriorem; nega summum magnum quem credis minorem. deum uero confessus utrumque duo summa magna confessus es. nihil alteri adimes aut alteri adscribes. agnoscens diuinitatem negasti diuersitatem.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: You will try to shake the retracted name of God with these arguments; the move is passive, and you allow others to use it too, because Scripture says: "God takes his stand in the divine council; in the midst of the gods he holds judgment" (Ps 82:1), and again: "I said, 'You are gods'" (Ps 82:6). Yet that does not grant them possession of the Supreme Great One simply because they bear the title "gods"; the same holds for the Creator.

I will answer the fool who has not considered this, lest the same retort be turned against Marcion's God: that he too is called God, yet not thereby proven to be the Supreme Great One, any more than the Creator's angels or humans. If the sharing of names prejudges natures, how many wicked slaves insult kings by usurping the names of Alexander, Darius, and Holofernes? Yet the kings lose nothing of what they are. The nations' idols are commonly called gods, but no one is God by the very fact of being so called.

Therefore I do not defend the Supreme Great One in the Creator by the name of God, nor by its sound, nor by the mere label of this name, but by the substance itself to which this name belongs. Finding that substance alone innate, uncorrupted, alone eternal, and the maker of the universe, I ascribe and vindicate the Supreme Great One not to the name but to the reality, not to the appellation but to the condition.

And because the substance to which I ascribe it already bears the name God, you think I ascribe it to the name, since I must use the name to indicate which substance I mean—namely, the one by which it is consistent that he is called God. But the Supreme Great One is reckoned from the substance, not from the name. Even Marcion, vindicating his God, vindicates according to the reality, not the word.

So we contend that the Supreme Great One, which we ascribe to God from the law of substance, not from the lottery of the name, must be equal in the two who consist of that substance which is called God. Insofar as they are called gods—that is, Supreme Great Ones, the substance innate and eternal, and therefore great and supreme—to that extent one Supreme Great One cannot be less and worse than another.

If the happiness, sublimity, and integrity of the Supreme Great One stand in Marcion's God, they will stand equally in ours; if not in ours either, then equally not in Marcion's. Therefore the two Supreme Great Ones will not be equal, because the already established rule of the Supreme Great One does not sustain comparison, nor unequal, because another rule of the Supreme Great One arises, not admitting diminution.

You have stalled, Marcion, in the middle of your Pontic storm. The waves of truth envelop you on both sides. You cannot establish gods as equal or unequal, for there are not two. What pertains properly to the retracted number—although the whole dispute is fought over two gods—we have enclosed him within these lines, within which we will now engage on the singular properties.

nec tamen ideo regibus id quod sunt detrahetur. nam et ipsa idola gentium dei uulgo, sed deus nemo ea re, qua deus dicitur. ita ego non nomini dei nec sono nec notae nominis huius summum magnum in creatore defendo, sed ipsi substantiae, cui nomen hoc contigit. hanc inueniens solam innatam infectam, solam aeternam et uniuersitatis conditricem, non nomini, sed statui, nec appellationi, sed condicioni eius summum magnum et adscribo et uindico. et ideo. quia deus iam uocari obtinuit substantia cui adscribo, nomini me adscribere putas, quia necesse est per nomen ostendam cui adscribam substantiae, scilicet qua constat qui deus dicitur. at summum magnum ex substantia, non ex nomine, deputatur. denique hoc et Marcion suo deo uindicans, secundum statum, non secundum uocabulum uindicat. id ergo summum magnum, quod deo adscribimus ex substantiae lege, non ex nominis sorte, contendimus ex pari esse debere in duobus, qui ea substantia constant, quae deus dicitur, quia in quantum dii uocantur, id est summa magna, substantiae scilicet mento innatae et aeternae ac per hoc magnae et summae, in tantum non possit summum magnum minus et deterius alio summo magno haberi. si summi magni felicitas et sublimitas et integritas stabit in deo Marcionis, stabit aeque et in nostro, si non et in nostro, aeque nec in Marcionis. ergo nec paria erunt duo summa magna, quia prohibet disposita iam regula summi magni comparationem non sustinens, nec disparia, quia et alia summi magni regula occurrit, diminutionem non admittens. haesisti, Marcion, in medio Ponti tui aestu. utrimque te fluctus ueritatis inuoluunt. nec pares nec dispares deos sistere potes. duo enim non sunt. quod pertineat proprie ad numeri retractatum, quamquam tota materia de duobus deis dimicetur, his interim lineis eum clusimus, intra quas de singularibus iam proprietatibus congrediemur.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: The Marcionites open their case with a flourish: they parade a 'new God' as if we should be embarrassed by the old one. Children puff themselves up over new shoes, too, but an old schoolmaster soon makes them pay for their empty pride. So they announce a new God—unknown, unheard of in the old world, the old age, under the old God—whom no one knew, not even ignorance itself, as ancient, until a certain Jesus Christ revealed him. And he did it in old names, yet made them new. No one else had done it before. I thank them for this boast; it is the greatest help I could ask for in proving their heresy—the claim of a new divinity. That is the kind of novelty that even spawned new gods for the pagans, each consecrated with a brand-new, ever-new title. What is a new god but a false one? Not even Saturn’s vast antiquity makes him a god today, because novelty once produced him, back when he was first consecrated. Living, genuine divinity is measured not by novelty or antiquity, but by its own truth. Eternity has no time; it is all time. What it does, it cannot undergo. It has no age, because it cannot be born. If God is old, he will cease to be; if he is new, he never was. Novelty testifies to a beginning; antiquity threatens an end. But God is as far removed from beginning and end as he is from time itself—the arbiter and measurer of both.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: I know exactly what sense they mean when they boast of a "new God"—knowledge, of course. But I wanted to strike back at the very novelty of that knowledge as it strikes untrained souls, and at the natural charm novelty itself exerts, and from there drag the whole discussion onto the terrain of the unknown God. After all, the one they set up as new by knowledge they thereby prove was unknown before that knowledge. So then, back to the starting line and the first step! Prove that an unknown God could have existed. I find, plainly enough, altars prostituted to unknown gods—but that is Attic idolatry. Likewise, to uncertain gods—but that is Roman superstition. Moreover, uncertain gods are less known precisely because they are less certain, and therefore unknown to the degree they are less certain. What title shall we carve out for Marcion's two gods? Both, I think: now uncertain, and previously unknown. For just as the known God, the Creator, made Him unknown, so the certain God made Him uncertain. But I will not wander off to say: if God was unknown and hidden, the region of hiding places overshadowed Him—new, indeed, and itself unknown, and similarly uncertain even now—certainly something immense and greater, without doubt, than the one He hid. Instead I will briefly propose and most fully carry out my case, laying down the rule that God could not have been unknown by reason of magnitude nor ought to have been by reason of benignity, especially since in both respects our Creator is superior. But since I see that in certain quarters it is deemed necessary to demand proof of every new and previously unknown God according to the form of the Creator, I must first commend this very procedure by reason, so that I may more steadily rely on the patronage of reasoned argument. First of all, what sense does it make that someone who acknowledges the Creator God and confesses Him prior in knowledge should not know another God by the same methods by which he already learned to know God in the other case? Every prior thing supplies a norm for the posterior. Two gods are now on the table: the unknown and the known. The question about the known God is settled. His existence is certain, because He would not have been known if He did not exist. The dispute presses hard on the unknown God. For He can both exist and not exist, because if He existed, He would have been known. Therefore, what is sought, as long as it is ignored, remains in doubt as long as it is sought, and can fail to exist as long as it remains in doubt. You have a certain God insofar as He is known, and an uncertain God insofar as He is unknown. If that is so, does it strike you as defensible by just reason that uncertain things should be proved according to the norm, form, and rule of certain things? Besides, if for this cause—which is itself still uncertain—arguments drawn from uncertain things are also adduced, a chain of questions will be implicated, endangered by the re-examination of their own equally uncertain arguments, perilous to faith through the uncertain, and we will be driven into those already indeterminable questions the apostle does not love; but if the argument proceeds from certain, indubitable, and absolute parts of the rule, the uncertain, doubtful, and unexplored things will be prejudged. Plainly, when a diversity of status is found, perhaps uncertain things will not be summoned to the form of certain things, so that, freed from the rest of the comparative summons, they might stand on the diversity of the principal status. But when two gods are proposed, their principal status is common. For what it means to be God, both are: innate, unaltered, eternal. This will be the principal status; let Marcion look to the rest, if he has arranged them in diversity. For posterior things are not in the re-examination—nor will they be admitted—if the principal status is established. Moreover, it is established, because both are gods: and thus their status is common. When they are summoned to proof under that status, if they are uncertain, they will be summoned according to the form of certain things, with whom they are judged to share communion of principal status, so that they may also share in proof. Hence, therefore, I shall most constantly maintain that a God who is today uncertain, because previously unknown, does not exist—since it is established that the one who exists is established by this very fact never to have been unknown, and therefore not uncertain.
