latin: Igitur per haec omnia ostendit, cuius dei sapientiam loquatur inter perfectos, eius scilicet, qui sapientiam sapientium abstulerit et prudentiam prudentium inritam fecerit, qui infatuauerit sapientia mundi, stulta eligens eius et disponens in salutem. hanc dicit sapientiam in occulto fuisse, quae fuerit in stultis et in pusillis et (in) inhonestis, quae latuerit etiam sub figuris, allegoriis et aenigmatibus. reuelanda postmodum in Christo, posito in lumen nationum a creatore promittente per Esaiae uocem patefacturum se thesauros inuisibiles et occultos. nam ut absconderit aliquid is deus, qui nihil egit omnino, in quod aliquid abscondisse existimaretur, satis incredibile. ipse si esset, latere non posset, nedum aliqua eius sacramenta. creator autem tam ipse notus quam et sacramenta eius, palam scilicet decurrentia apud Israhel, sed de significantiis obumbrata, in quibus sapientia dei delitiscebat. inter perfectos narranda suo in tempore, proposita uero in proposito dei ante saecula. cuius et saecula, nisi creatoris? si enim et saecula temporibus structa sunt, tempora autem diebus et mensibus et annis compinguntur, dies porro et menses et anni solibus et lunis et sideribus creatoris signantur in hoc ab eo positis, — et erunt enim, inquit, in signa mensium et annorum — apparet et saecula creatoris esse et omne, quod ante saecula propositum dicatur, non alterius esse, quam cuius et saecula. aut probet dei sui saecula Marcion; ostendat et mundum ipsum, in quo saecula deputentur, uas quodammodo temporum, et signa aliqua uel organa eorum. si nihil demonstrat, reuertor, ut et illud dicam: cur autem ante saecula creatoris proposuit gloriam nostram? posset uideri eam ante saecula proposuisse, quam introductione saeculi reuelasset. at cum id facit paene iam totis saeculis creatoris prodactis, uane ante saecula proposuit et non magis intra saecula quod reuelaturus erat paene post saecula. non enim eius est festinasse in proponendo, cuius est retardasse in reuelando. creatori autem competit utrumque: et ante saecula proposuisse et in fine saeculorum reuelasse, quia et quod proposuit et reuelauit medio spatio saeculorum in figuris et aenigmatibus et allegoriis praeministrauit.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: God himself will illuminate the hidden things of darkness, and he will do it through Christ, who promised Christ as a light to the nations and declared himself a lamp that examines kidneys and hearts. Praise will come from him to each person, and so will the opposite of praise, since he acts as a judge. You say, 'Surely he here interprets the God of the world by saying: We have become a spectacle to the world, and to angels, and to men.' But if he had meant 'world' as 'men of the world,' he would not have named men again afterwards. On the contrary, to keep you from arguing that way, the providence of the Holy Spirit demonstrated how he spoke: we have become a spectacle to the world, while angels, who minister to the world, and men, to whom they minister, look on. The man of such great constancy—or rather the Holy Spirit himself—feared to name the God of the world freely, especially when writing to sons he had generated in the Gospel; against that God he could not be seen to preach unless he did so openly. I am not defending the idea that, according to the Creator's law, it was displeasing to the one who had his father's wife—he was following the discipline of the common and public religion. But when he condemns that man to be handed over to Satan, he acts as a herald of the God who condemns. Let him explain how he says it: 'hand this man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord' (1 Cor 5:5). While he judges both the destruction of the flesh and the salvation of the spirit, and commands 'take away the evil from your midst,' he recalls the Creator's most frequent sentence. 'Purge the old leaven, that you may be a new lump, as you really are unleavened' (1 Cor 5:7). Therefore, the unleavened bread was a figure of ours with the Creator. So also our Passover, Christ, has been sacrificed. Why is Christ our Passover, if not because the Passover was a figure of Christ through the likeness of the saving blood of the victim and of Christ? What do the Creator's festival images mean to us and to Christ, if they were not ours? But by turning us away from fornication, he manifests the resurrection of the flesh. 'The body is not for fornication, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body' (1 Cor 6:13)—'so that it may be a temple of God and God a temple' (1 Cor 6:19). Will the temple of God then perish, and God the temple? But you see: the one whom God raised, and will raise us, he also raised in the body, because the body is for the Lord and the Lord for the body. And he rightly adds: 'Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?' (1 Cor 6:15).

latin: Et occulta tenebrarum ipse inluminabit, utique per Christum, qui Christum in lumen nationum repromisit quique se lucernam pronuntiauit scrutantem renes et corda. ab illo erit et laus unicuique, a quo et contrarium laudis, ut a iudice. certe, inquis, uel hic mundum deum mundi interpretatur dicendo: spectaculum facti sumus mundo, et angelis et hominibus, quia, si mundum homines mundi significasset, non etiam homines postmodum nominasset. immo, ne ita argumentareris, prouidentia spiritus sancti demonstrauit, quomodo dixisset: spectaculum facti sumus mundo, dum angelis, qui mundo ministrant, et hominibus, quibus ministrant. uerebatur nimirum tantae constantiae uir, ne dicam spiritus sanctus, praesertim ad filios scribens, quos in euangelio generauerat, libere deum mundi nominare, aduersus <quem) nisi exerte non posset uideri praedicare. non defendo secundum legem creatoris displicuisse illum, qui mulierem patris sui habuit — communis et publicae religionis secutus sit disciplinam —: sed cum eum damnat dedendum satanae, damnatoris dei praeco, est. uiderit et quomodo dixerit: in interitum carnis, ut spiritus saluus sit in die domini, dum et de carnis interitu et de salute spiritus iudicarit et \'auferri\' iubens \'malum de medio\' creatoris frequentissimam sententiam commemorauerit. Expurgate uetus fermentum, ut sitis noua consparsio, sicut estis azymi. ergo azymi figurae erant nostrae apud creatorem. sic et pascha nostrum immolatus est Christus. quare pascha Christus, si non pascha figura Christi per similitudinem sanguinis salutaris pecoris et Christi? quid nobis et Christo imagines induit sollemnium creatoris, si non erant nostrae? Auertens autem nos a fornicatione manifestat carnis resurrectionem. corpus, inquit, non fornicationi, sed domino, et dominus corpori, 'ut templum deo et deus templo\'. templum ergo deo peribit et deus templo? atquin uides: quem deus suscitauit et nos suscitabit, in corpore quoque suscitauit, quia corpus domino et dominus corpori. et bene quod aggerat: nescitis corpora uestra membra esse Christi?

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Why on earth did He zero in on fishing as the trade from which to draft Simon and the sons of Zebedee as apostles? The incident is hardly trivial; it sets up His entire argument. He tells a trembling Peter, shaken by the massive haul, 'Do not fear; from now on you will be catching men' (Jeremiah). That declaration planted the realization that the prophecy was fulfilled: He is the very one Jeremiah announced when he said, 'Behold, I will send many fishermen, and they will fish for them — namely, men.' At once they abandoned their boats and followed Him, recognizing the One who had begun to act on His own words. It would be a different matter if He had simply tried to recruit from the guild of boatmen, destined to have Marcion as an apostle and a shipmaster somewhere down the line. We have already demonstrated against the antithesis that nothing advances Marcion's proposal — at least as he imagines it — regarding the supposed diversity between law and gospel. That diversity itself was arranged by the Creator, finally proclaimed in the promise of a new law, a new word, and a new testament. But since he argues his case more closely with his so-called 'commiseronem' and 'coodibilem' in the cleansing of the leper, I am not reluctant to engage and, first of all, to display the force of the figurative law. In the case of the leper — not to be touched, indeed to be cut off from all intercourse — that law forbade contact with a man stained by sins, and the apostle even forbids eating with such a person; for anyone who mingles with a sinner shares the marks of sins as if by contagion. Therefore the Lord, desiring the law to be understood more deeply — since it signifies spiritual realities through physical ones — and not abolishing it but rather building it up so that it might be acknowledged as more relevant, touched the leper. From that leper, even if a human being could be defiled, God certainly would not be, being by nature uncontaminable; thus it will not be prescribed for Him that He ought to observe the law and avoid touching the unclean, when the touch of the unclean could not defile Him. I teach that this fits my Christ all the more, while I prove it does not fit yours.

latin: De tot generibus operum quid utique ad piscaturam respexit, ut ab illa in apostolos sumeret Simonem et filios Zebedaei — non enim simplex factum uideri potest de quo argumentum processurum erat — dicens Petro trepidanti de copiosa indagine piscium: ne time, abhinc enim homines eris capiens? hoc enim dicto intellectum illis suggerebat adimpletae prophetiae, se eum esse, qui per Hieremiam pronuntiarat: ecce ego mittam piscatores multos, et piscabuntur illos, homines scilicet. denique relictis nauclis secuti sunt eum, ipsum intellegentes, qui coeperat facere quod edixerat. aliud est, si adfectauit de nauiculariorum collegio adlegere, habiturus apostolum quandoque nauclerum Marcionem. excerpts.author: Origen
english: Let us now briefly consider what we should think about the promises as well. It is certain that no living creature can be completely idle and immobile; by nature it must always be in motion, acting, and desiring something. I regard it as clear that this impulse belongs to every living thing. Therefore, the rational animal — that is, human nature — must all the more always be moving or acting in some way. If a person is forgetful of himself and ignores what befits him, his whole intention is directed toward bodily needs, and through all his movements he is occupied with bodily pleasures and desires. But if he is the sort who strives to care for or provide something for the common good — whether consulting for the state, obeying magistrates, or practicing whatever else seems certainly useful in common — he exercises himself in that. Now if someone understands something better than these bodily things and devotes himself to wisdom and knowledge, he will without doubt direct all his industry toward such studies, so that he may come to know the investigated truth of things and their reason. Just as in this life one person judges the body's greatest good to be pleasure, another seeks the common good, and another devotes himself to study and intelligence, so we ask whether in that true life — the life "hidden with Christ in God" (Col 3:3), that is, eternal life — there might be some such order or status of living for us.

Some people, in a way rejecting the labor of intelligence and clinging to the surface of the letter of the law while indulging their own pleasure and desire, disciples of the letter alone, think that the future promises are to be expected in bodily pleasure and luxury. Because of this they especially desire to have flesh again after the resurrection — flesh that would never lack the ability to eat and drink and do all things that belong to flesh and blood — not following the apostle Paul's teaching about the "spiritual body" of the resurrection (1 Cor 15:44). Consequently they also add that marriages and the procreation of children will continue after the resurrection. They imagine for themselves the earthly city of Jerusalem rebuilt with precious stones laid in its foundations, its walls raised from jasper, its battlements adorned with crystal, and its surrounding wall made of chosen and varied stones: jasper, sapphire, chalcedony, emerald, sardius, onyx, chrysolite, chrysoprase, hyacinth, and amethyst (Rev 21:19–20). They also think that foreign ministers of their delights will be given to them — tillers, vineyard cultivators, builders of walls — from whom their ruined and collapsed city will be rebuilt. They think they will receive the riches of the nations to eat and will dominate in their wealth, so that even the camels of Midian and Ephah will come and bring them gold, frankincense, and precious stones (Isa 60:6). They try to confirm this from prophetic authority, from what is written about the promises to Jerusalem: that those who serve God will eat and drink, but sinners will hunger and thirst, and that the just will rejoice but the impious will be possessed by confusion (Isa 65:13–14). They also bring forward the Savior's voice from the New Testament, where he promises his disciples the joy of wine, saying he will not drink from this cup until he drinks it new with them in his Father's kingdom (Matt 26:29; Mark 14:25; Luke 22:18). They add, too, that the Savior called blessed those who now hunger and thirst, promising they will be satisfied (Matt 5:6; Luke 6:21), and they cite many other scriptural examples whose force they do not think should be understood figuratively or spiritually. Then, following the form of this life and the dispositions of this world — its dignities, orders, and eminent powers — they think they will be kings and princes, just like these earthly ones, because of what is said in the gospel: "You will have authority over five cities" (Luke 19:19; cf. Matt 25:21, 23). To put it briefly, according to the conduct of this life they want everything expected from the promises to be similar in all respects — that is, for what is to be again. These are the thoughts of those who believe in Christ but understand the divine scriptures in a certain Jewish sense, presuming nothing worthy of the divine promises.

But those who receive the theory of the scriptures according to the apostles' sense hope that the saints will indeed eat — but the bread of life, which nourishes the soul with the foods of truth and wisdom, illuminates the mind, and intoxicates it with the cups of divine wisdom. This is just as divine scripture says: "Wisdom has prepared her table, has killed her victims, has mixed her wine in the cup, and cries out with a loud voice: 'Turn to me and eat the bread I have prepared for you, and drink the wine I have mixed for you'" (Prov 9:2, 5). Nourished by these foods of wisdom, the mind is restored to integrity and perfection, just as man was made from the beginning in the image and likeness of God (Gen 1:26). So even if someone departs this life less educated but has brought forth probable works, he may be instructed in that city of Jerusalem of the saints — that is, taught, formed, and made a living stone, a precious and chosen stone, because he has borne the struggles of life and the contests of piety strongly and constantly (1 Pet 2:5). There he will know more truly and clearly what has already been predicted here: that man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God (Deut 8:3; Matt 4:4; Luke 4:4). The princes and rulers, too, are to be understood as those who rule, teach, instruct, and establish the inferiors in divine things.

Now if these things seem less worthy to those who hope for them, let us inquire — repeating a little — how natural and innate to the soul is the desire for the thing itself, so that we may finally describe the species themselves of the bread of life, the quality of its wine, and the property of the principalities through the consequence of theory. Just as in those arts usually fulfilled by hand, the reason — what or how or for what use something is made — resides in the mind, while the effectiveness of the work is carried out by the ministry of the hands, so in the works of God, which he has made, we must understand that the reason and intelligence of those things we see made by him remain hidden. And just as when our eye sees things made by an artisan, if it perceives something especially well made, the soul immediately burns to investigate how or in what way or for what use it was made: much more, and beyond all comparison, the soul burns with ineffable desire to know the reason of those things made by God which we see. We certainly believe this desire — this love — has been implanted in us by God. Just as the eye naturally requires light and sight, and our body desires food and drink by nature, so our mind has its own natural desire to know the truth of God and the causes of things. We have received this desire from God not so that it may never be fulfilled, lest the love of truth seem to have been inserted in our mind by the Creator God in vain if it is never satisfied.

Multo ergo magis rationabile animal, id est hominis naturam necesse est semper aliquid movere vel agere. Et si quidem immemor sui sit eb quid se deceat ignoret, circa usus corporales omnis sua movetur intentio et per omnes motus suos erga voluptates ac libidines corporis oecupatur; si vero talis sit, qui in commune aliquid curare vel providere studeat, aut rei publicae consulens aut magistratibus parens aut quidquid illud est, quod in commune certe prodesse videatur, exercet. excerpts.author: Origen
english: But since human senses and common understanding are not sufficient to commit the whole matter to them and, so to speak, to pronounce visibly on invisible things, we must also take up the testimonies of divine Scripture as proof of the things we say. So that these testimonies may have a certain and undoubted faith, either in the things that must be said by us or in those already said, it seems necessary first to show that the Scriptures themselves are divine, that is, inspired by the Spirit of God. Therefore, we will briefly set forth this point also from the divine Scriptures themselves, which have competently moved us, bringing them forward — that is, from Moses, the first lawgiver of the Hebrew nation, and from the words of Jesus Christ, the author and principle of the Christian religion and doctrine.

For although many lawgivers have existed among the Greeks and barbarians, and innumerable teachers or philosophers have promised to assert the truth, we do not recall any lawgiver who could have implanted a certain affection and zeal even in the minds of foreign nations, so that they would willingly receive his laws or defend them with their whole heart. No one, therefore, could have insinuated the truth that seemed true to him, not only to many other foreign nations, but not even to a single nation, so that their knowledge or credulity would reach everyone. And indeed, it cannot be doubted that lawgivers wished their laws to be observed by all men, if it could be done, and that masters wished the truth that seemed true to them to become known to all. But knowing that they could not do this at all, nor did such great virtue subsist in them as could provoke foreign nations to the observance of their laws or assertions, they did not even dare to try or begin this, lest they be marked as imprudent and ineffective in this undertaking. But in the whole world, in all Greece and in all foreign nations, there are innumerable and immense multitudes who, having abandoned the laws of their fathers and those whom they thought were gods, have handed themselves over to the observance of Moses' law and to the discipleship and worship of Christ. And this has happened not without great hatred stirred up against them by those who venerate idols, so that they are often afflicted with torments and sometimes even led to death; yet they embrace and guard the word of Christ's doctrine with all affection. And it is evident how the religion itself has grown in a short time, profiting from the punishments and deaths of its cultivators, and also from the plundering of goods and every kind of suffering tolerated by them. And it is all the more wonderful that not even the teachers themselves are sufficiently suitable or numerous: yet 'the word is preached' (Psalm 19:4) 'in the whole world', so that 'Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish' (Romans 1:14) receive the religion of Christian doctrine. From this there is no doubt that 'these things are not done by human strength or resources', so that the word of Christ Jesus may grow strong with all power and credibility in the minds and souls of all. For it is manifest that these things were predicted by him and confirmed by divine responses, when he says, 'You will be brought before governors and kings for my sake, as a testimony to them and to the Gentiles' (Matthew 10:18); and again, 'This gospel will be preached in all nations' (Matthew 24:14); and again, 'Many will say to me on that day: Lord, Lord, did we not eat and drink in your name, and did we not cast out demons in your name? And I will say to them: Depart from me, workers of lawlessness, for I never knew you' (Matthew 7:22-23). If these things had been said by him but had not nonetheless come to pass, perhaps they would seem less true and would not have any authority. But now, since the things that were predicted by him have come to pass, and have been predicted with such great power and authority, it is most clearly declared that God truly exists, who, having become man, handed down salutary precepts to men.

What then must be said from the fact that the prophets had foretold beforehand concerning him, 'The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler's staff from between his feet, until he comes to whom it belongs, and until the expectation of the nations comes'? For it is manifestly apparent from history itself and from what is seen today that since the time of Christ no kings have existed among the Jews. And all those Jewish ambitions, in which they carried their boasting to the highest degree and in which they exulted — that is, whether concerning the beauty of the temple or the distinction of the altar and all those priestly miters, garments, and vestments of the high priests — have been simultaneously and utterly destroyed. For the prophecy has been fulfilled which said, 'For many days the children of Israel shall sit without a king, without a prince, without sacrifice, without altar, without priesthood, and without oracle' (Hosea 3:4). We therefore use these testimonies against those who seem to assert concerning the things said by Jacob in Genesis that they were spoken about Judah, and that a prince from the tribe of Judah still remains — namely, this one whom they call the patriarch, the prince of their nation — and that there cannot fail to be from his seed those who remain until the coming of that Christ whom they describe for themselves. But if it is true that the prophet says, 'For many days the children of Israel shall sit without a king, without a prince; there shall be no sacrifice, no altar, no priesthood,' and assuredly since the temple was overthrown — sacrifices are not offered, an altar is not found, a priesthood does not exist — it is most certain that 'princes have failed from Judah,' just as it is written, and 'a ruler from between his feet, until he comes to whom it belongs.' It is established, therefore, that 'he has come to whom it belongs, in whom also the expectation of the nations is.' Which is manifestly seen fulfilled in the multitude of those who through Christ have believed in God from diverse nations.

But also in the song of Deuteronomy, through prophecy, the election of a foolish nation is designated for the sins of the prior people — none other, surely, than this one which has been made through Christ. For thus it says: 'They provoked me to jealousy with their idols; and I will provoke them to jealousy with a nation that is not a nation, I will anger them with a foolish nation' (Deuteronomy 32:21). It is therefore sufficiently evident to recognize how the Hebrews, who are said to have 'provoked God' in those who are not gods, and to have 'angered him with their idols,' have themselves been provoked to jealousy by a 'foolish nation,' which God chose through the coming of Christ Jesus and his disciples. For thus says the apostle: 'Consider your calling, brothers, that not many wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble are called; but God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise, and God chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong, and God chose the low and despised things of the world, even things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are' (1 Corinthians 1:26-28). Therefore 'carnal Israel' must 'not boast'; for so he is called by the apostle: 'that no flesh should boast in the presence of God' (1 Corinthians 1:29).

latin: Verum quoniam de tantis et talibus rebus disserentibus non suffieit humanis sensibus et communi intellectui summam rei committere et, ut ita dixerim, visibiliter de invisibilibus pronuntiare, assumenda sunt nobis ad probationem horum, quae dicimus, etiam divinarum scripturarum testimonia. Quae testimonia ut certam et indubitatam "tree d o habeant fidem sive in his, quae dicenda a nobis, sive quae iam dicta sunt, necessarium prius videtur ostendere quod ipsae scripturae divinae sint, id est dei spiritu inspiratae. lgitur quam poterimus breviter etiam de hoc adsignabimus ex ipsis divinis scripturis quae nos conpetenter moverint proferentes, id est de Moyseo primo, legislatore gentis Hebraeae, et ex verbis lesu Christi, auctoris et principis Christianorum religionis et dogmatis. Cum enim permulti legislatores extiterint apud Graecos et barbaros, innumeri quoque doctores vel philosophi veritatem se pollicentes adserere, nullum meminimus legislatorem adfectum quendam et studium etiam exterarum gentium animis inicere potuisse, ut leges suas vel susciperent libenter vel cum omni animi intentione defenderent. Nemo ergo eam quae sibi visa est veritatem non solum pluribus aliis exteris nationibus, ‚sed ne uni quidem genti ita insinuare atque inolescere potuit, ut ad omnes eius scientia vel credulitas perveniret. Et quidem dubitari non potest quod et legislatores optaverint observari ab omnibus, si fieri posset, hominibus leges suas, et magistri, omnibus innotescere eam quae sibi visa fuerat veritatem. Sed scientes quia id omnino non possent, nee virtus in eis aliqua tanta subsisteret, quae etiam exteras nationes ad legum suarum vel adsertionum observantiam provocaret, ne conari quidem hoc aut incipere omnino ausi sunt, ne inprudentes eos etiam in hoc inefficax et inexplebile notaret inceptum. At vero in omni orbe terrarum, in omni Graecia atque universis exteris nationibus innumeri sunt et inmensi, qui relictis patris legibus et his, quos putabant deos, ad observantiam Moysi legis et discipulatum se Christi ceultumque tradiderunt, et hoc non sine ingenti odio adversum se commoto eorum, qui simulacra venerantur, ita ut ab his frequenter et cruciatibus adfligantur, nonnumquam etiam agantur in mortem; amplectuntur tamen et cum omni affectu custodiunt doctrinae Christi sermonem. Et est videre quomodo brevi tempore ipsa religio creverit, poenis eultorum mortibusque proficiens, sed et bonorum direptionibus atque omni ab his suppliciorum genere tolerato; et eo maxime mirum est quod ne doctores quidem ipsi vel satis idonei sunt vel satis plures: “praedicatur’ tamen sermo iste -in omni orbe terrarum”, ita ut ‘Graeci ac barbari, sapientes et insipientes’ religionem Christianae doctrinae suscipiant. Ex quo dubium non est “non haec humanis’ viribus aut ‘opibus” agi, ut cum omni potestate et creduhtate sermo Christi lesu apud omnium mentes atque animos convalescat. Nam et praedicta esse ab eo haec ipsa et divinis ab eo responsis confirmata, manifestum est cum dicit quia “apud praesides et iudices adducemini propter me, in testimonium ipsis et gentibuse; et rursum: “Praedieabitur hoe evangelium in omnibus gentibus”; et iterum: “Multi mihi dicent in illa die: Domine, domine, nonne in tuo nomine mandueavimus et bibimus, et in tuo nomine daemonia eiecimus? et dicam eis: Discedite a me, operarii iniquitatis s numquam cognovi vosc”. Quae si ita quidem dicta ab eo fuissent nee tamen ad finem ea, quae praedicta sunt, pervenissent, fortassis minus esse vera viderentur nec habere aliquid auctoritatis. Nune vero cum in effectum res, quae fuerant ab eo praedictae, perveniant, cum tanta autem potestate atque auctoritate praedictae sint, manifestissime declaratur deum vere esse, qui homo factus salutaria praecepta hominibus tradidit. 3. Quid vero inde dicendum est quod prophetae de ipso antea praedixerant ‘non cessaturos principes ex luda neque duces ex femoribus eius, usquequo veniat ille, cui repositum este regnum scilicet, et "usquequo veniat expectatio gentium-? Manifestissime enim ex ipsa bistoria apparet et ex his, quae hodie pervidentur, quia ex temporibus Christi ultra reges apud ludaeos non extiterunt. Sed et omnes illae ambitiones Iudaicae, in quibus iactantiae quam plurimum gerebant et in quibus exultabant, id est vel de templi decore vel de altaris insignibus atque omnibus illis sacerdotalibus infulis indumentisque pontificum, simul universa destructa sunt. Completa est enim prophetia, quae dixerat: “Per dies multos sedebunt fili Israhel sine rege, sine principe; non erit hostia nec altare nec sacerdotium nec responsa”. His ergo testimonis utimur adversum eos, qui videntur adse rere de his, quae in Genesi ab lacob dicta sunt, quod de luda dieta sint et dicunt permanere adhue principem ex genere ludae, istum videlicet, qui est gentis ipsorum princeps, quem nominant patriarcham, nec deficere posse de semine eius qui permaneant usque ad adventum eius Christi, quem sibi ipsi describunt. Sed si verum est quod ait propheta, quia “dies multos sedebunt fili Israhel sine rege, sine principe; nec erit hostia nec altare nec sacerdotium”, et utique ex quo subversum est templum -nec hostiae- offeruntur “nec altare- invenitur “nec sacerdotiumconstat: certissimum est defecisse “principes ex luda-, sieut scriptum est, et -ducem ex femoribus eius, usquequo venit ille, eui repositum est Constat ergo quia ‘venit ille, cui repositum este, in quo et ‘expectatio gentium- est. Quod manifeste videtur impletum de multitudine eorum, qui per Christum deo ex diversis gentibus crediderunt. 4. Sed et in Deuteronomii cantico per prophetiam designatur pro peccatis prioris populi futura esse insensatae gentis electio, non alia utique quam haec, quae per Christum facta est. Sie enim ait: “Exacerbaverunt me in simulacris suis, et ego in zelo concitabo eos, in gente insipiente inritabo eos”. Est ergo satis evidenter agnoscere, quemammodum Hebraei, qui deum ‘exacerbasse’ dieuntur in his, qui non sunt du, et inritasse eum ‘in simulacris suis. inritati sunt et ipsi in zelotypia per ‘gentem insipientem”, quam deus -elegit- per adventum Christi lesu et discipulos eius. Sie enim dicit apostolus: “Videte enim vocationem vestram, fratres, quoniam non multi sapientes inter vos secundum carnem, non multi potentes, non multi nobiles; sed quae stulta sunt mundi elegit deus et ea, quae non sunt, ut ea, quae erant prius, destrueret”. excerpts.author: Origen
english: The time has come, now that we have passed through these matters, to return to the incarnation of our Lord and Savior—how he became man and lived among us. We consider this according to our very limited powers, drawing more from the contemplation of his works than from our own understanding. We have observed his visible creatures and, by faith, contemplated the invisible ones as well, since human frailty cannot see everything with the eyes or grasp everything by reason. We human beings are, after all, the weakest and most fragile of all rational animals, for those beings that exist in heaven or above the heavens are far more excellent. Therefore we must seek the mediator between all these creatures and God, the very one whom the apostle Paul calls the firstborn of all creation (Colossians 1:15). We see what the holy scriptures say of his majesty: that he is the image of the invisible God and the firstborn of all creation (Colossians 1:15); that in him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities (Colossians 1:16); that he is before all things and in him all things hold together (Colossians 1:17); that he is the head of all things, having God the Father alone as his head, as it is written: "The head of Christ is God" (1 Corinthians 11:3). We also perceive that no one knows the Father except the Son, and no one knows the Son except the Father (Matthew 11:27; Luke 10:22). For who can know what wisdom is except the one who begot it? Who can know what truth is except the Father of truth? Who could explore the nature of the Word that is from God except God alone, in whom the Word was? (John 1:1) We must therefore hold it certain that this Word—or Reason, if you prefer—knows this wisdom and this truth, and that no one but the Father knows them. As it is written: "I do not think the world itself could contain the books that would be written" (John 21:25), concerning the glory and majesty of the Son of God. It is impossible to commit to writing what pertains to the Savior's glory. Having considered these great and stupendous things about the nature of the Son of God, we stand astonished with the utmost wonder that this supreme nature emptied itself, becoming man and living among men. The grace poured upon his lips testifies to this (Psalm 45:2), the heavenly Father bears witness to him (Matthew 3:17; 17:5), and it is confirmed by the signs, diverse wonders, and mighty works he performed. He also sent prophets as forerunners and heralds of his coming before he appeared in the body. After his ascension into the heavens, he filled holy apostles with the power of his divinity—men who were formerly tax collectors or fishermen, unskilled and uneducated—and sent them around the whole earth so that from every nation and all peoples they might gather a community of the godly who believe in him.

Yet of all his miracles and mighty deeds, this one utterly surpasses the wonder of the human mind; the frailty of mortal intelligence cannot find how to conceive it: that the very Word of the Father and the Wisdom of God, in whom all visible and invisible things were created (Colossians 1:16), is believed to have been enclosed within the bodily limits of the man who appeared in Judea. Not only that, but that the Wisdom of God entered a woman's womb, was born as an infant, and cried like any other child. Then, too, he is said to have been troubled even to the point of death, as he himself declared: "My soul is sorrowful even to death" (Matthew 26:38). Finally, he was brought to the most shameful death known among men, even though he rose again on the third day. When we see certain things in him that are so human they seem no different from the common frailty of mortals, and other things so divine that they belong only to that first, ineffable divine nature, the narrowness of human intellect is stopped short, overwhelmed by the stupor of such wonder. It does not know what to hold, where to turn, or what to do. If it senses God, it sees a mortal; if it thinks him a man, it sees one who, having conquered the kingdom of death, returns from the dead bearing spoils (Ephesians 4:8; Colossians 2:15). Therefore he must be contemplated with all fear and reverence, so that in one and the same person the truth of both natures may be shown—so that nothing unworthy or unseemly is attributed to that divine and ineffable substance, nor, on the other hand, are the things he did dismissed as false or imaginary. To set these things forth to human ears and explain them in words far exceeds our powers, our merits, our genius, or our speech. I suspect it even surpasses the minds of the holy apostles; indeed, perhaps the explanation of this mystery is more excellent than that of all the heavenly powers. Concerning this, we will set forth only a few things, not out of rashness, but because the order of our subject demands it—drawing from what our faith contains rather than what human reason usually defends, offering our conjectures rather than dogmatic assertions.

The only-begotten Son of God, through whom all visible and invisible things were made (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16), as scripture teaches, made all things and loves what he made. Since he is himself the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15), he invisibly gave a share of himself to all rational creatures, so that each might participate in him to the degree that it clung to him with love. But because of the faculty of free will, a variety and diversity of souls arose: some held fast to their Creator with more ardent love, others with a thinner, weaker love. That soul about which Jesus said, "No one takes my soul from me" (John 10:18), from the beginning of creation and ever after, clung to him inseparably and indissolubly—as to the Wisdom, the Word, the Truth, and the true Light of God—receiving everything from him entirely and yielding itself wholly to his light and splendor. It became one spirit with him principally, just as the apostle promises to those who should imitate it: "He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit" (1 Corinthians 6:17). By this substance of the soul, then, serving as mediator between God and flesh (for it was not possible for the divine nature to unite with a body without a mediator), the God-man is born, as we said, with this mediating substance in place—a substance for which assuming a body was not contrary to nature. Nor was it contrary to the nature of that rational soul to receive God, into whom, as we said above, it had already surrendered itself completely, as it were to the Word of Wisdom. Therefore, because it was wholly in the Son of God, or had received all of God within itself, the Son of God, together with the flesh he assumed, is called Christ, the Power of God, and the Wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24). Again, the Son of God, through whom all things were created, is called Jesus Christ; and he is called the Son of Man. For the Son of God is said to have died, on account of that nature which could undergo death; and the Son of Man is the one who is to come in the glory of God the Father with the holy angels (Matthew 16:27; 25:31). Throughout all scripture, the divine nature is spoken of with human words, and the human nature is adorned with the titles of divinity. One can say more about this than about anything else: what is written, "The two shall become one flesh, and they are no longer two but one flesh" (Genesis 2:24; Ephesians 5:31), is more truly realized in the Word of God being one with the soul in the flesh than in a man and his wife. And to be one spirit with God is fitting for the human soul that has joined itself to God through love, so that it may be said to be one spirit by merit of love. What is the merit of love? It has forged an inseparable unity with God, so that the assumption of the soul was not by a mixture of persons but by the reception of virtues—as the prophet says to him: "You have loved justice and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions" (Psalm 45:7). By merit of love, then, the soul is anointed with the oil of gladness—that is, the soul with the Word of God becomes Christ. To be anointed with the oil of gladness means to be filled with the Holy Spirit. The phrase "beyond your companions" shows that this was not the grace of the Spirit as given to the prophets, but the fullness of the Word of God dwelling substantially in him, as the apostle said: "In him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily" (Colossians 2:9). Finally, for this reason it says not only "You have loved justice" but adds "and hated iniquity." To hate iniquity is what scripture says of him: he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth (1 Peter 2:22; Isaiah 53:9), and he was tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). The Lord himself says: "Which of you convicts me of sin?" (John 8:46), and again: "Behold, the ruler of this world comes, and he has nothing in me" (John 14:30). All these things show that no sense of sin ever existed in him. To make this even clearer, the prophet says: "Before the child knows how to call father or mother, he turns away from iniquity" (Isaiah 7:16).

Qui etiam ante praesentiam suam hane, quam ostendit in corpore, praecursores et nuntios adventus sui misit prophetas; post ascensionem vero suam in caelos sanctos apostolos divinitatis suae virtute repletos homines vel ex publicanis vel ex piseatoribus imperitos et indoctos ceircumire fecit orbem terrarum, ut ex omni gente atque ex omnibus populis piorum plebem in se credentium congregarent. 2. Verum ex omnibus de eo miraculis et magnificis illud. penitus ammirationem humanae mentis excedit, nec invenit mortalis intellegentiae fragilitas, quomodo sentire vel intellegere possit quod tanta illa potentia divinae maiestatis, ipsum illud patris verbum atque ipsa sapientia dei, in qua “creata sunt omnia visibilia et invisibilia, intra eireumseriptionem eius hominis, qui apparuit in Iudaea, fuisse credenda sit, sed et ingressa esse dei sapientia vulvam feminae et nasci parvulus et vagitum emittere ad similitudinem plorantium parvulorum; tum deinde quod et in morte conturbari refertur, ut ipse etiam profitetur dicens: “Tristis est anima mea usque ad mortem”; et ad ultimum quod usque ad eam quae inter homines indignissima habetur adductus est mortem, licet post tertiam surrexerit diem. Cum ergo quaedam in eo ita videamus humana, ut nihil a communi mortalium fragihtate distare videantur, quaedam ita divina, quae nulli alii nisi illi primae et ineffabili naturae conveniant deitatis, haeret humani intellectus angustia et tantae ammirationis stupore pereulsa, quo declinet, quid teneat, quo se convertat, ignorat. Si deum sentiat, mortalem videt; si hominem putet, devicto "mortis regno cum spoliüs redeuntem a mortuis cernit. Propter quod cum omni metu et reverentia contemplandum est, ut in uno eodemque ita utriusque naturae veritas demonstretur, ut neque aliquid indignum et indecens in divina illa et ineffabili substantia sentiatur, neque rursum quae gesta sunt falsis inlusa imaginibus aestimentur. Quae quidem in aures humanas proferre et sermonibus explicare, longe vires vel meriti nostri vel ingenii ac sermonis excedit. Arbitror autem quia etiam sanctorum apostolorum supergrediatur mensuram; quin immo fortassis etiam totius creaturae caelestium virtutum eminentior est saeramenti istius explanatio. De quo nos non temeritate aliqua, sed quoniam ordo loci poposcit, ea magis quae fides nostra continet, quam quae humanae rationis adsertio vindicare solet, quam paucissimis proferemus, suspiciones potius nostras quam manifestas aliquas adfirmationes in medium proferentes. 3. lgitur unigenitus filius dei, per quem ‘omnia facta esse visibilia et invisibilia- in superioribus sermo disputationis edocuit, secundum seripturae sententiam et fecit omnia et “quae fecit diligit. Hac ergo substantia animae inter deum carnemque mediante (mon enim possibile erat dei naturam corpori sine mediatore misceri) nascitur, ut diximus, deus-homo, illa substantia media existente, cui utique contra naturam non erat corpus assumere. Dilectionis igitur merito unguitur ‘oleo laetitiae, id est anima cum verbo dei Christus efficitur. -Unginamque ‘oleo laetitiae- non aliud intellegitur quam spiritu sancto repleri. Quod autem “prae participibus- dixit, indicat quia non gratia spiritus sicut prophetis ei data est, sed ipsius verbi dei in ea substantialis inerat “plenitudo”, sicut et apostolus dixit: “In quo inhabitat omnis plenitudo deitatis corporahter”. Denique propter hoe non solum dixit: “Dilexisti iustitiam”, sed addidit “et odisti iniquitatem”. ‘Odisse- enim ‘iniquitatem- illud est, quod scriptura dicit de eo quia “peccatum non fecit, nec inventus est dolus in ore eius”, et quod ait: “Temptatus per omnia pro similitudine absque peccato”. Sed et ipse dominus dicit: “Quis vestrum me arguit de peccato?” Et iterum ipse dicit de se: “Eece venit mundi huius princeps et in me non invenit quidquam”. Quae omnia nullum in eo peccati sensum indicant extitisse. Quod ut propheta evidentius designaret, quia numquam eum -iniquitatis- sensus intrasset, ait: “Priusquam sciret puer vocare patrem aut matrem, avertit se ab iniquitate”.

excerpts.author: Origen
english: In what follows, Celsus, assailing the Mosaic history, finds fault with those who give it a tropical and allegorical signification.

And here one might say to this great man, who inscribed upon his own work the title of a True Discourse , Why, good sir, do you make it a boast to have it recorded that the gods should engage in such adventures as are described by your learned poets and philosophers , and be guilty of abominable intrigues, and of engaging in wars against their own fathers, and of cutting off their secret parts, and should dare to commit and to suffer such enormities; while Moses , who gives no such accounts respecting God , nor even regarding the holy angels , and who relates deeds of far less atrocity regarding men (for in his writings no one ever ventured to commit such crimes as Kronos did against Uranus, or Zeus against his father, or that of the father of men and gods, who had intercourse with his own daughter), should be considered as having deceived those who were placed under his laws , and to have led them into error ?

And here Celsus seems to me to act somewhat as Thrasymachus the Platonic philosopher did, when he would not allow Socrates to answer regarding justice , as he wished, but said, Take care not to say that utility is justice , or duty, or anything of that kind. For in like manner Celsus assails (as he thinks) the Mosaic histories, and finds fault with those who understand them allegorically, at the same time bestowing also some praise upon those who do so, to the effect that they are more impartial (than those who do not); and thus, as it were, he prevents by his cavils those who are able to show the true state of the case from offering such a defense as they would wish to offer.

excerpts.author: Origen
english: Celsus also brings up the warning given to them that, by not obeying the law, they will suffer the same fate as those who were enemies. And before Celsus invokes what he considers opposing passages from Christ's teaching against the law, we must address the points already raised. We say, then, that the law is twofold: one part pertains to the literal wording, the other to the underlying meaning, as some of our predecessors have taught. The part pertaining to the literal wording comes not so much from us as from one of the prophets who, speaking on behalf of God, declared it to be 'judgments not good' and 'commandments not good' (Ezekiel 20:25-26). But the part pertaining to the meaning is said by the same prophet, speaking on behalf of God, to be 'judgments good' and 'commandments good'; for the prophet does not plainly contradict himself in the same passage. Accordingly, Paul also said that the 'letter' kills, which corresponds to the part pertaining to the literal wording, while 'the Spirit' gives life, which corresponds to the part pertaining to the meaning (2 Corinthians 3:7-8). There is, therefore, something analogous to be found in Paul to the supposed contradictions according to the prophet. For just as Ezekiel says, 'I gave them judgments not good and commandments not good, in which they will not live,' and elsewhere, 'I gave them judgments good and commandments good, in which they will live' (Ezekiel 20:25-26), these are equivalent in force; so also Paul, where he wishes to criticize the literal letter of the law, says: 'If the ministry of death, engraved in letters on stone, came in glory, so that the sons of Israel could not gaze at Moses' face because of the glory of his face, which was being brought to an end, will not the ministry of the Spirit be attended with even greater glory?' (2 Corinthians 3:7-8). But where he marvels at the law and accepts it, he calls it spiritual, saying, 'We know that the law is spiritual' (Romans 7:14), and he accepts it in the passage: 'So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good' (Romans 7:12).

greek: Φέρει δ ὁ Κέλσος καὶ τὸ προειρῆσθαι αὐτοῖς μὴ πειθομένοις τῷ νόμῳ τὰ αὐτὰ πείσεσθαι, ἅπερ ἔδρων τοὺς πολεμίους. καὶ πρὶν ἄν τι παρατιθεὶς τούτοις ὁ Κέλσος χρήσηται οἷς νομίζει ἐναντιώμασι πρὸς τὸν νόμον ἀπὸ τῆς Χριστοῦ διδασκαλίας, λεκτέον περὶ τῶν προειρημένων. φαμὲν τοίνυν ὅτι ὁ νόμος διττός ἐστιν, ὁ μέν τις πρὸς ῥητὸν ὁ δὲ πρὸς διάνοιαν, ὡς καὶ τῶν πρὸ ἡμῶν τινες ἐδίδαξαν. καὶ ὁ μὲν πρὸς τὸ ῥητὸν οὐ τοσοῦτον ὑφ᾿ ἡμῶν ὅσον ὑπὸ τοῦ ἔν τινι τῶν προφητῶν λέγοντος θεοῦ εἴρηται εἶναι „δικαιώματα οὐ καλὰ“ καὶ „προστάγματα οὐ καλά“· ὁ δὲ πρὸς διάνοιαν κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν προφήτην ἐκ προσώπου τοῦ θεοῦ λέγεται εἶναι „δικαιώματα καλὰ“ καὶ „προστάγματα καλά“· οὐ γὰρ προφανῶς ἐναντία λέγει ὁ προφήτης ἐν ταὐτῷ. ᾧ ἀκολούθως καὶ ὁ Παῦλος τὸ μὲν „γράμμα“ εἶπεν ἀποκτέννειν, ὅπερ ἴσον ἐστὶ τῷ (πρὸς) τὸ ῥητόν· „τὸ δὲ πνεῦμα“ ζῳοποιεῖν, ὅπερ ἰσοδυναμεῖ τῷ πρὸς διάνοιαν. ἔστι γοῦν παρὰ τῷ Παύλῳ ἀνάλογόν τι εὑρεῖν τοῖς νομισθεῖσιν ἂν ἐναντιώμασι κατὰ τὸν προφήτην. ὡς γὰρ ὅπου μὲν Ἰεζεκιὴλ λέγει· „ἔδωκα αὐτοῖς δικαιώματα οὐ καλὰ καὶ προστάγματα οὐ καλὰ, ἐν οἷς οὐ ζήσονται ἐν αὐτοῖς“ ὅπου δέ· „ἔδωκα αὐτοῖς δικαιώματα καλὰ καὶ προστάγματα καλὰ, ἐν οἷς ζήσονται ἐν αὐτοῖς,“ ἤτοι ἰσοδυναμοῦν γε τούτοις· οὕτω καὶ ὁ Παῦλος, ὅπου μὲν τὸ τοῦ νομικοῦ γράμματος διαβαλεῖν θέλει, φησίν· „εἰ δὲ ἡ διακονία τοῦ θανάτου (ἐν) γράμμασιν ἐντετυπωμένη λίθοις ἐγενήθη ἐν δόξῃ, ὥστε μὴ δύνασθαι ἀτενίσαι τοὺς υἱοὺς Ἰσραὴλ εἰς τὸ πρόσωπον Μωϋσέως διὰ τὴν δόξαν τοῦ προσώπου αὐτοῦ τὴν καταργουμένην, πῶς οὐχὶ μᾶλλον ἡ διακονία τοῦ πνεύματος ἔσται ἐν δόξῃ;“ ὅπου δὲ θαυμάζει τὸν νόμον καὶ ἀποδέχεται, πνευματικὸν αὐτὸν ὀνομάζει λέγων· „οἴδαμεν δὲ ὅτι ὁ νόμος πνευματικός ἐστιν,“ ἀποδέχεται δὲ ἐν τῷ· „ὥστε ὁ μὲν νόμος ἅγιος, καὶ ἡ ἐντολὴ ἁγία καὶ δικαία καὶ ἀγαθή.“

excerpts.author: Origen
english: He goes on to claim that we mock those who worship Zeus, because a tomb of his is displayed in Crete, and that we show no less reverence for the one who came from that tomb — all without understanding how or why the Cretans act as they do. In these remarks he is actually defending the Cretans, Zeus, and the tomb itself, appealing to allegorical meanings by which the myth about Zeus is said to have been invented; at the same time he accuses us, even though we acknowledge that our Jesus was buried and also affirm that he rose from the tomb — a claim the Cretans no longer make about Zeus.

Since he appears to be arguing for the Cretan tomb of Zeus on the grounds that we do not know how or that the Cretans do such things, we will point out that even the Cyrenaean Callimachus, who read countless poems and examined nearly all of Greek history, found no allegorical interpretation in the traditions concerning Zeus and his tomb. Consequently, he also rebukes the Cretans in the hymn he wrote to Zeus, declaring: "Cretans are always liars; for they built a tomb for you, Lord, but you did not die, for you are eternal." The one who said "you did not die, for you are eternal" thereby denied the burial of Zeus in Crete and asserted that the beginning of death occurred with Zeus. But the beginning of death is earthly birth; he puts it this way: "On Parrhasia, Rhea bore you, having lain with him." He ought to have seen that, since he denied the birth of Zeus in Crete because of the tomb there, it followed from the Arcadian birth that the one born must also die. Callimachus says the same sort of thing on these matters: "Zeus, they say you were born in the mountains of Ida, Zeus, and they say you were born in Arcadia; which ones, Father, lied? Cretans are always liars" — and so on.

It was Celsus who brought us to these points. He is ignorant about Jesus, and while he accepts the written accounts that Jesus died and was buried, he treats the resurrection as a fabrication — despite myriads of prophets who foretold it and many signs of his appearance after death.

greek: Μετὰ ταῦτα λέγει περὶ ἡμῶν ὅτι καταγελῶμεν τῶν προσκυνούντων τὸν Δία, ἐπεὶ τάφος αὐτοῦ ἐν Κρήτῃ δείκνυται, καὶ οὐδὲν ἧττον σέβομεν τὸν ἀπὸ τοῦ τάφου. οὐκ εἰδότες, πῶς καὶ καθὸ Κρῆτες τὸ τοιοῦτον ποιοῦσιν. ὅρα οὖν ὅτι ἐν τούτοις ἀπολογεῖται μὲν περὶ Κρητῶν καὶ τοῦ Διὸς καὶ τοῦ τάφου αὐτοῦ. αἰνιττόμενος τροπικὰς ὑπονοίας, καθ᾿ ἃς πεπλάσθαι λέγεται ὁ περὶ τοῦ Διὸς μῦθος· ἡμῶν δὲ κατηγορεῖ, ὁμολογούντων μὲν τετάφθαι τὸν ἡμέτερον Ἰησοῦν φασκόντων δὲ καὶ ἐγηγέρθαι αὐτὸν ἀπὸ τοῦ τάφου, ὅπερ Κρῆτες οὐκέτι περὶ τοῦ Διὸς ἱστοροῦσιν. ἐπεὶ δὲ δοκεῖ συναγορεύειν τῷ ἐν Κρήτῃ τάφῳ τοῦ Διὸς λέγων· ὅπως μὲν καὶ καθότι Κρῆτες τοῦτο ποιοῦσιν, οὐκ εἰδότες, φήσομεν ὅτι καὶ ὁ Κυρηναῖος Καλλίμαχος, πλεῖστα ὅσα ἀναγνοὺς ποιήματα καὶ ἱστορίαν σχεδὸν πᾶσαν ἀναλεξάμενος Ἑλληνικὴν, οὐδεμίαν οἶδε τροπολογίαν ἐν τοῖς περὶ Διὸς καὶ τοῦ τάφου αὐτοῦ. διὸ καὶ ἐγκαλεῖ τοῖς Κρησὶν ἐν τῷ εἰς τὸν Δία γραφέντι αὐτῷ ὕμνῳ λέγων· Κρῆτες ἀεὶ ψεῦσται· καὶ γὰρ τάφον, ὦ ἄνα. σεῖο Κρῆτες ἐτεκτήναντο· σὺ δ᾿ οὐ θάνες. ἐσσὶ γὰρ αἰεί. καὶ ὁ εἰπὼν „σὺ δ᾿ οὐ θάνες, ἐσσὶ γὰρ αἰεὶ.“ ἀρνησάμενος τὴν ἐν Κρήτῃ ταφὴν τοῦ Διὸς, τὴν ἀρχὴν τοῦ θανάτου ἱστορεῖ γεγονέναι περὶ τὸν Δία. ἀρχὴ δὲ θανάτου ἡ ἐπὶ γῆς γένεσις· λέγει δὲ οὕτως· ἐν δέ σε Παῤῥασίοις Ῥείη τέκεν εὐνηθεῖσα. ἐχρῆν δ᾿ αὐτὸν, ὡς ἠρνήσατο τὴν ἐν Κρήτῃ γένεσιν τοῦ Διὸς διὰ τὸν τάφον αὐτοῦ, ὁρᾶν ὅτι ἠκολούθει τῇ ἐν Ἀρκαδίᾳ γενέσει αὐτοῦ τὸ καὶ ἀποθανεῖν τὸν γεγεννημένον. τοιαῦτα δὲ καὶ περὶ τούτων λέγει ὁ Καλλίμαχος· Ζεῦ. σὲ μὲν Ἰδαίοισιν ἐν οὔρεσί φασι γενέσθαι, Ζεῦ, σὲ δ᾿ ἐν Ἀρκαδίῃ· πότεροι, πάτερ, ἐψεύσαντο; Κρῆτες ἀεὶ ψεῦσται· καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς. εἰς ταῦτα δ᾿ ἡμᾶς ἤγαγεν ὁ Κέλσος. ἀγνωμονῶν περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ καὶ συγκατατιθέμενος μὲν τοῖς γεγραμμένοις, ὅτι ἀπέθανε καὶ ἐτάφη, πλάσμα δ᾿ ἡγούμενος εἶναι ὅτι καὶ ἀνέστη ἀπὸ τῶν νεκρῶν, καὶ ταῦτα μυρίων προφητῶν καὶ τοῦτο προειρηκότων καὶ πολλῶν ὄντων σημείων τῆς μετὰ θάνατον ἐπιφανείας αὐτοῦ.

excerpts.author: Hippolytus
english: First fragment (Preface) As I wish to give an accurate account of the times of the captivity of the children of Israel in Babylon , and to discuss the prophecies contained in the visions of the blessed Daniel, (as well as) his manner of life from his boyhood in Babylon , I too shall proceed to bear my testimony to that holy and righteous man, a prophet and witness of Christ , who not only declared the visions of Nebuchadnezzar the king in those times, but also trained youths of like mind with himself, and raised up faithful witnesses in the world. He is horn, then, in the time of the prophetic ministry of the blessed Jeremiah, and in the reign of Jehoiakim or Eliakim. Along with the other captives, he is carried off a prisoner to Babylon . Now there are born to the blessed Josiah these five sons — Jehoahaz, Eliakim, Johanan, Zedekiah, or Jeconiah, and Sadum. And on his father's death, Jehoahaz is anointed as king by the people at the age of twenty-three years. Against him comes up Pharaoh -Necho, in the third month of his reign; and he takes him (Jehoahaz) prisoner, and carries him into Egypt , and imposes tribute on the land to the extent of one hundred talents of silver and ten talents of gold. And in his stead he sets up his brother Eliakim as king over the land, whose name also he changed to Jehoiakim, and who was then eleven years old. Against him came up Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon , and carries him off prisoner to Babylon , taking with him also some of the vessels…

1. In speaking of a lioness from the sea, he meant the rising of the kingdom of Babylon , and that this was the golden head of the image. And in speaking of its eagle wings, be meant that king Nebuchadnezzar was exalted and that his glory was lifted up against God. Then he says its wings were plucked off, i.e., that his glory was destroyed; for he was driven out of his kingdom. And the words, A man's heart was given it, and it was made stand upon the feet of a man , mean that he came to himself again, and recognised that he was but a man , and gave the glory to God . Then after the lioness he sees a second beast, like a bear, which signified the Persians. For after the Babylonians the Persians obtained the power. And in saying that it had three ribs in its mouth, he pointed to the three nations, Persians , Medes, and Babylonians , which were expressed in the image by the silver after the gold. Then comes the third beast, a leopard, which means the Greeks; for after the Persians , Alexander of Macedon had the power, when Darius was overthrown, which was also indicated by the brass in the image. And in saying that the beast had four wings of a fowl, and four heads, he showed most clearly how the kingdom of Alexander was parted into four divisions. For in speaking of four heads, he meant the four kings that arose out of it. For Alexander, when dying, divided his kingdom into four parts. Then he says, The fourth beast (was) dreadful and terrible: it had iron teeth, and claws of…

2. After this, then, what remains, beloved, but the toes of the feet of the image, in which part shall be of iron and part of clay mixed together? By the toes of the feet he meant, mystically , the ten kings that rise out of that kingdom. As Daniel says, I considered the beast; and, lo, (there were) ten horns behind, among which shall come up another little horn springing from them; by which none other is meant than the antichrist that is to rise; and he shall set up the kingdom of Judah. And in saying that three horns were plucked up by the roots by this one, he indicates the three kings of Egypt , Libya, and Ethiopia , whom this one will slay in the array of war . And when he has conquered all, he will prove himself a terrible and savage tyrant, and will cause tribulation and persecution to the saints , exalting himself against them. And after him, it remains that the stone shall come from heaven which smote the image and shivered it, and subverted all the kingdoms, and gave the kingdom to the saints of the Most High. This became a great mountain, and filled the whole earth.

3. As these things, then, are destined to come to pass, and as the toes of the image turn out to be democracies, and the ten horns of the beast are distributed among ten kings, let us look at what is before us more carefully, and scan it, as it were, with open eye. The golden head of the image is identical with the lioness, by which the Babylonians were represented. The golden shoulders and the arms of silver are the same with the bear, by which the Persians and Medes are meant. The belly and thighs of brass are the leopard, by which the Greeks who ruled from Alexander onwards are intended. The legs of iron are the dreadful and terrible beast, by which the Romans who hold the empire now are meant. The toes of clay and iron are the ten horns which are to be. The one other little horn springing up in their midst is the antichrist. The stone that smites the image and breaks it in pieces, and that filled the whole earth, is Christ, who comes from heaven and brings judgment on the world.

english: He did not say "first day." If He had said "first day," He would have been compelled to say "second day" as it came into being. Instead, He had to say not "first" but "one," so that by using "one" He could show this day as cyclical, and the week as completed, yet still a single unit.

excerpts.author: Hippolytus
english: Therefore the Proverbs are exhortative words, useful along every path of life. For those who make their way to God, a guide arises, much like the example of refreshing those wearied by the length of the journey. These, then, are the Proverbs of Solomon — that is, of the Peaceful One, or rather the Savior Christ. Since we know the Lord's words without error, lest anyone snatch us away by the homonymy, the text tells us who wrote these things and whose king he was, so that the speaker's credibility may make the word acceptable and the hearers attentive. They belong to that Solomon to whom the Lord said, 'I will give you a wise and understanding heart; none like you has arisen before you, nor will one arise after you' (1 Kings 3:12), together with the rest written about him. He was wise, born of a wise father; therefore his line is joined to David, from whom Solomon came, 'taught the sacred writings from childhood,' and he did not receive the kingdom by lot or by violence, but by the anointing of the Spirit and the vote of God.

excerpts.author: Hippolytus
english: The iron horns now trample the very tracks of the feet and the toes that have taken their place in line with the sign of the terrifying beast, just as was indicated in former times. From the heavens a stone will come to strike the image and crush it; it will remove every kingdom and give the kingdom to the saints of the Most High. This stone has become a great boundary and has filled the earth. Scripture speaks of it: “I was watching in a vision of the night, and behold, one like a son of man was coming with the clouds of heaven. He approached the Ancient of Days and was presented before him. To him were given dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion that shall not pass away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed” (Daniel 7:13-14).

greek: Τῶν γὰρ σιδηρῶν κνημῶν τῶν νῦν ἐπικρωτουσῶν ἐπὶ τὼ ἴχνη τῶν ποδῶν καὶ τοὺς δακτύλους χωρησάντων κατὼ τὴν τοῦ φοβεροῦ θηρίου δεῖξζιν, καθὼς ἐν τοῖς ἔμ.- προσθεν καιροῖς σεσήμανται, ἥξει ἀπ᾿ οὐρανῶν ὁ λίθος ὁ πατάξας τὴν εἰκόνα καὶ συντρίψας αὐτὴν καὶ μεταστήσει πάσας τὰς βασιλείας καὶ δώσει τὴν βασιλείαν ἁγίοις ὑψίστου. οὗτος ὁ γενηθεὶς ὅρος μέγα καὶ πληρώσας τὴν γῆν, περὶ οὗ εἴρηται “ ἐθεώρουν ἐν ὁραΐ-- ματι τῆς νυκτὸς καὶ ἰδοὺ μετὰ τῶν νεφελῶν τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ἐρχό-- μενος ὡς υἱὸς ἀνθρώπου καὶ ἕως τοῦ παλαιοῦ τῶν ἡμερῶν ἔφθα-- σεν καὶ αὐτῷ ἐδύθη ἡ ἀρχὴ καὶ ἡ τιμὴ καὶ ἡ βασιλεία καὶ πάν- τες λαοί, φυλαὶ καὶ γλῶσσαι δουλεύσουσιν αὐτῷ. ἐξουσία αὐτοῦ ἐξουσία αἰώνιος ἥτις οὐ παρελεύσεται καὶ βασιλεία αὐτοῦ οὐ διαφθαρήσεται."

excerpts.author: Cyprian
english: Brothers, the Gospel's commands are nothing less than God's own teaching. They lay the foundation for our hope, strengthen our faith, feed our hearts, steer our course, and guard our salvation. By instructing willing minds here on earth, they lead us into the kingdom of heaven. God chose to speak many things through his servants the prophets, yet the Son's words are far greater. The Word of God — who once spoke in the prophets — now testifies with his own voice. He no longer merely commands that a way be prepared for the One who comes; he comes himself, opens the way, and shows it to us. We once wandered blind and unprepared in death's darkness, but now, lit by grace's light, we walk the path of life with the Lord as our guide.

Among his saving counsels and divine precepts given for his people's welfare, he also gave us the very form of prayer. The One who gave us life taught us how to pray, marking what we should ask for — an act of the same kindness by which he bestows every other gift. He did this so that when we speak to the Father in the prayer the Son taught, we may be heard more readily. He had already foretold the hour when true worshipers would worship the Father in spirit and truth (John 4:23), and he fulfilled that promise. Because we have received the Spirit and truth through his sanctification, we can now worship him truly and spiritually, following his own tradition.

What prayer could be more spiritual than the one Christ gave us — Christ, from whom the Holy Spirit was sent to us? What prayer could be truer before the Father than the one spoken by the Son, who is Truth itself? To pray differently from his teaching is therefore not merely ignorance; it is fault. He himself said: 'You reject God's commandment to keep your own tradition.' So let us pray, brothers, as God our Teacher taught. It is a friendly, intimate prayer to ask God for what is his own, letting Christ's prayer carry our words to the Father's ears. When we pray, let the Father recognize his Son's voice. The One who dwells within our hearts should also dwell in our words. And since we have him as our Advocate with the Father for our sins, let us sinners plead our case in the Advocate's own words when we ask forgiveness. He promised that whatever we ask the Father in his name will be granted; how much more effectively, then, do we receive what we seek when we ask in Christ's name using Christ's own prayer?

Multa et per Prophetas servos suos dici Deus voluit et audiri; sed quanto majora quae Filius loquitur, quae Dei sermo qui in Prophetis fuit propria voce testatur, non jam mandans ut paretur venienti via, sed ipse veniens, et viam nobis aperiens et ostendens; ut qui, in tenebris mortis errantes, improvidi et caeci prius fuimus, luce gratiae luminati, iter vitae duce et rectore Domino teneremus. Qui inter caetera salutaria sua monita et praecepta divina quibus populo suo consulit ad salutem, etiam orandi ipse formam dedit, ipse quid precaremur monuit et instruxit. Qui fecit vivere, docuit et orare, benignitate ea scilicet qua et caetera dare et conferre dignatus est; ut, dum prece et oratione quam Filius docuit apud Patrem loquimur, facilius audiamur. Jam praedixerat horam venire quando veri adoratores adorarent Patrem in spiritu et veritate, et implevit quod ante promisit; ut qui spiritum et veritatem de ejus sanctificatione percepimus, de traditione quoque ejus vere et spiritaliter adoremus. Quae enim potest esse magis spiritalis oratio quam quae a Christo nobis data est, a quo nobis et Spiritus sanctus missus est? Quae vera magis apud Patrem precatio quam quae a Filio, qui est Veritas, de ejus ore prolata est? ut aliter orare quam docuit non ignorantia sola sit, sed et culpa, quando ipse posuerit et dixerit: Rejicitis mandatum Dei, ut traditionem vestram statuatis. Oremus itaque, fratres dilectissimi, sicut magister Deus docuit. Amica et familiaris oratio est Deum de suo rogare, ad aures ejus ascendere Christi oratione. Agnoscat Pater Filii sui verba cum precem facimus. Qui habitat intus in pectore, ipse sit et in voce. Et cum ipsum habeamus apud Patrem advocatum pro peccatis nostris, quando peccatores pro delictis nostris petimus, advocati nostri verba promamus. Nam, cum dicat quia quodcumque petierimus a Patre in nomine ejus dabit nobis,, quanto efficacius impetramus quod petimus in Christi nomine, si petamus ipsius oratione?

excerpts.author: Novatian
english: Consider another passage where Scripture calls God an angel. When Jacob complained to his wives, Leah and Rachel, about their father's injustice and told them he wished to return to his own land, he backed his words with the authority of a dream. He told them the angel of God had spoken to him in that dream: 'Jacob.' Jacob answered, 'Here I am.' The angel said, 'Look up and see: the he-goats and rams mounting the ewes and she-goats are striped, speckled, and mottled. I have seen everything Laban has done to you. I am the God who appeared to you at Bethel, where you anointed a standing stone for me and vowed a vow to me. Now arise, leave this land, and return to the land of your birth, and I will be with you' (Genesis 31:11–13). The angel of God speaks these words to Jacob, and the angel himself declares, 'I am the God who appeared to you in the place of God.' We therefore see not only an angel but God himself, without any hesitation. The angel refers to the vow Jacob made to him at the place of God, and he does not say 'in my place.' There is a place of God, and here God is present. At Bethel the text simply says 'the place of God'; it does not say 'the place of an angel and God,' but only 'of God.' Yet the one who makes these promises is called both God and angel. A proper distinction exists between the one called simply God and the one called not simply God but also angel. If no other angel can claim such authority — to confess he is God and to testify a vow was made to him — except Christ, to whom a vow can be made not because he is an angel but because he is God, then clearly the figure here cannot be the Father but the Son, God and angel.

Since Christ is that one, anyone who calls Christ merely a man or only an angel runs a grave risk. Such a claim strips away the power of the divine name that Christ has frequently received from the faith of the heavenly Scriptures, which call him both angel and God. To these points another is added: just as divine Scripture frequently calls him angel and God, so it also calls him man and God. It expresses what he was going to be and depicts in image what he already possessed in the truth of his substance. Jacob was left alone, and a man wrestled with him until daybreak. When the man saw he could not prevail, he touched Jacob's hip socket, and said, 'Let me go, for the dawn is rising.' Jacob replied, 'I will not let you go unless you bless me.' The man said, 'Your name shall no longer be Jacob, but Israel, for you have striven with God and with men and have prevailed.' Then Jacob named the place Peniel, saying, 'For I have seen God face to face, and yet my life is preserved' (Genesis 32:24–33). The sun rose as he passed Peniel, and he limped on his hip. The text says, 'A man wrestled with Jacob.' If he is only a solitary man, who is he? Where is he from? Why does he contend and wrestle with Jacob? What occasioned it? What had happened? What is the reason for so great a struggle? Why, moreover, does Jacob — who proves strong enough to hold the man he wrestles — demand a blessing from him because dawn is breaking, unless this struggle prefigures the conflict between Christ and the sons of Jacob, which the Gospel says is fulfilled? Against this man the people of Jacob have wrestled. In that wrestling the people prevailed, because they won a victory of iniquity over Christ. At that time, because of the crime they committed, they began to limp severely and uncertainly in their own faith and salvation. Though they were found superior in condemning Christ, they still need his mercy; they still need his blessing. The man who wrestled with Jacob said, 'Your name shall no longer be Jacob, but Israel.' Since Israel means a man who sees God, the Lord elegantly showed that the one who wrestled with Jacob was not only a man but also God. Jacob saw God face to face, even while he held a man in his grip. To leave no doubt, the man himself gave the interpretation: 'You have striven with God and with men, and have prevailed.' Jacob, understanding the power of the mystery and perceiving the authority of the one he had wrestled, named the place 'Vision of God.' He added the reason: 'I have seen God face to face, and my soul is saved.' He saw God, with whom he wrestled as with a man; yet he held a man as victor, and asked a blessing as from God, as an inferior. Thus he wrestled with God and with man. If this wrestling was prefigured there but fulfilled in the Gospel between Christ and the people of Jacob — where the people, though found superior, are found inferior because proven guilty — who will doubt that Christ, in whom the figure of this wrestling is completed, is not only a man but also God? The figure itself proves he is both man and God.

Even after all this, divine Scripture does not cease to call the angel God and God an angel. When Jacob was about to bless Manasseh and Ephraim, Joseph's sons, he crossed his hands over their heads and said, 'The God who has fed me from my youth until this day, the angel who has redeemed me from all evil, bless these boys' (Genesis 48:15–16). He identifies the same angel he called God so closely that at the end of his prayer he uses the singular: 'bless these boys.' If he had meant two distinct persons — one God, one angel — he would have used the plural. Instead he places the singular number of one person in the blessing, showing he intends the same one to be understood as both God and angel. The Father cannot be that one; but Christ, who is God and angel, can be. Jacob signified Christ as the author of this blessing by laying his crossed hands on the boys, as if Christ were their father, and by that gesture he showed the figure and form of the future passion. No one should therefore doubt that Christ is an angel, and likewise should not hesitate to confess him God. For he understands that the same one is invoked as both God and angel in the blessing of these boys, through the sacrament of the passion, embodied in the figure of the hands.

excerpts.author: Commodian
english: Look at Leah: she was a type of the Synagogue, with eyes as weak as Jacob found her by sign; yet she served again for the less-loved wife (Genesis 29:17-18). It is a true mystery and type of our Church. Listen fully to the word spoken to Rebecca from heaven: from that source you imitate strangers, so that you may believe in Christ. Then consider Tamar's twin birth: look at Cain, the first tiller of the soil, and at Abel the shepherd, who was blameless, slain and offered up in his brother's murder by his own brother (Genesis 4:1-16). So then, you younger ones approved by Christ, understand this.

excerpts.author: Methodius of Olympus
english: I. From the Discourse on the Resurrection. I. Read the Book on the Resurrection by St. Methodius, Bishop and Martyr, of which that which follows is a selection, that the body is not the fetter of the soul , as Origen thought, nor are souls called by the prophet Jeremiah fettered on account of their being within bodies. For he lays down the principle that the body does not hinder the energies of the soul , but that rather the body is carried about with it, and cooperates in whatever the soul commits to it. But how are we to understand the opinion of Gregory the theologian, and many Others? II. That Origen said that the body was given to the soul as a fetter after the fall, and that previously it lived without a body; but that this body which we wear is the cause of our sins ; wherefore also he called it a fetter, as it can hinder the soul from good works. III. That if the body was given to the soul after the fall as a fetter, it must have been given as a fetter upon the evil or the good. Now it is impossible that it should be upon the good; for no physician or artificer gives to that which has gone wrong a remedy to cause further error , much less would God do so. It remains, then, that it was a fetter upon evil . But surely we see that, at the beginning, Cain, clad in this body, committed murder ; and it is evident into what wickedness those who succeeded him ran. excerpts.author: Justin Martyr
english: Notice how God promises the same things to Isaac and to Jacob. To Isaac He says, "All the nations of the earth will be blessed in your seed" (Gen 28:14); to Jacob, "All the tribes of the earth will be blessed in you and in your seed" (Gen 28:14). He no longer says this to Esau, or to Reuben, or to anyone else, but only to those from whom the Christ was to come according to the plan worked through the virgin Mary. If you would only examine the blessing of Judah, you would see what I mean. The line of descent divides from Jacob and runs through Judah, Perez, Jesse, and David. These genealogies were symbols showing that some of your race will be found to be true children of Abraham, standing in the portion of the Christ, while others, though children of Abraham, are like the sand on the seashore: barren and unfruitful, vast and innumerable, yet producing nothing at all — only drinking the seawater. That is exactly what condemns the vast multitude of your people: you drink the teachings of bitterness and atheism, and spit out the word of God.

Scripture indeed says in Judah: "A ruler will not fail from Judah, and a leader from his loins, until he comes to whom it belongs, and he will be the expectation of the nations" (Gen 49:10). It is clear this was spoken not of Judah but of the Christ. We from all nations do not wait for Judah; we wait for Jesus, the one who led your fathers out of Egypt. Until the Christ's coming the prophecy was proclaimed: "Until he comes to whom it belongs, and he will be the expectation of the nations." He has come, as we have shown in many ways, and He is expected to come again on the clouds — Jesus, whose name you profane and strive to profane throughout the earth. I could dispute the phrase with you — you read it, "Until what is reserved for him comes" — but the Seventy did not translate it that way; they rendered it, "Until he comes to whom it is reserved." Since the following words — "And he will be the expectation of the nations" — show the passage concerns the Christ, I will not wrangle over a single phrase, nor appeal to writings you reject (Jeremiah, Ezra, David), from which I have also drawn proof. I argue from the Scriptures you yourselves acknowledge up to this day. If your teachers had understood them, you know they would have suppressed them, just as they did the account of Isaiah's death — you sawed him in half with a wooden saw — which is itself a mystery of the Christ who will divide your race in two: some He will deem worthy to recline with the holy patriarchs and prophets in the eternal kingdom; others He will send to the judgment of unquenchable fire alongside the disobedient and unrepentant from every nation, as He has already declared: "They will come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven, but the sons of the kingdom will be cast into the outer darkness." I say these things because I care for nothing but the truth; I will not flatter anyone, even if you hate me for it this very moment. I am not defending my own race — I mean the Samaritans — for in a written address to Caesar I charged them with being deceived by the magician Simon of their own people, whom they call a god above all authority, power, and might.
