greek: Τίνι οὖν, φημί, ἔτι τις χρήσαιτο διδασκάλῳ (??) πόθεν ὠφεληθείη τις. εἰ μηδὲ ἐν τούτοις τὸ ἀληθές ἐστιν; Ἐγένοντό τινες πρὸ πολλοῦ χρόνου πάντων τούτων τῶν νομιζομένων φιλοσόφων παλαιότεροι, μακάριοι καὶ δίκαιοι καὶ θεοφιλεῖς, θείῳ πνεύματι λαλήσαντες καὶ τὰ μέλλοντα θεσπίσαντες, ἃ δὴ νῦν γίνεται· προφήτας δὲ αὐτοὺς καλοῦσιν. Οὗτοι μόνοι τὸ ἀληθὲς καὶ εἶδον καὶ ἐξεῖπον ἀνθρώποις, μήτ᾿ εὐλαβηθέντες μήτε δυσωπηθέντες τινά. μὴ ἡττημένοι δόξης. ἀλλὰ μόνα ταῦτα εἰπόντες ἃ ἤκουσαν καὶ ἃ εἶδον ἁγίῳ πληρωθέντες πνεύματι. Συγγράμματα δὲ αὐτῶν ἔτι καὶ νῦν διαμένει, καὶ ἔστιν ἐντυχόντα τούτοις πλεῖστον ὠφεληθῆναι καὶ περὶ ἀρχῶν καὶ περὶ τέλους καὶ ὧν χρὴ εἰδέναι τὸν φιλόσοφον, πιστεύσαντα ἐκείνοις. Οὐ γὰρ μετὰ ἀποδείξεως πεποίηνται τότε τοὺς λόγους, ἃτε ἀνωτέρω πάσης ἀποδείξεως ὄντες ἀξιόπιστοι μάρτυρες τῆς ἀληθείας· τὰ δὲ ἀποβάντα καὶ ἀποβαίνοντα ἐξαναγκάζει συντίθεσθαι τοῖς λελαλημένοις δι᾿ αὐτῶν. Καίτοι γε καὶ διὰ τὰς δυνάμεις, ἃς ἐπετέλουν, πιστεύεσθαι δίκαιοι ἦσαν, ἐπειδὴ καὶ τὸν ποιητὴν τῶν ὅλων θεὸν καὶ πατέρα ἐδόξαζον καὶ τὸν παρ᾿ αὐτοῦ Χριστὸν υἱὸν αὐτοῦ κατήγγελλον· ὅπερ οἱ ἀπὸ τοῦ πλάνου καὶ ἀκαθάρτου πνεύματος ἐμπιπλάμενοι ψευδοπροφῆται οὕτε ἐποίησαν οὔτε ποιοῦσιν, ἀλλὰ δυνάμεις τινὰς ἐνεργεῖν εἰς κατάπληξιν τῶν ἀνθρώπων τολμῶσι καὶ τὰ τῆς πλάνης πνεύματα καὶ δαιμόνια δοξολογοῦσιν. Εὔχου δέ σοι πρὸ πάντων φωτὸς ἀνοιχθῆναι πύλας· οὐ γὰρ συνοπτὰ οὐδὲ συννοητὰ πᾶσίν ἐστιν, εἰ μή τῳ θεὸς δῷ συνιέναι καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς αὐτοῦ.

excerpts.author: Athenagoras
english: I have adequately demonstrated that we are not atheists, since we acknowledge one God — ungenerated, eternal, invisible, impassible, incomprehensible, and uncircumscribed — who is apprehended only by mind and reason and encompassed by light, beauty, spirit, and indescribable power, under whom all things came to be through his Word and are ordered and held together. We also recognize the Son of God. Let no one suppose it laughable that God has a Son. Our conception differs entirely from the poets who invent myths, portraying their gods as no better than human beings; we have not thought that way about the Father or the Son. Rather, the Son of God is the Father's Reason in idea and in energy, for through him and by him all things were made, the Father and the Son being one. Since the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son, united by the unity and power of the Spirit, the Son of God is the Mind and Reason of the Father. If the force of this reasoning compels you to ask what the Son desires, I will answer concisely: he is the Father's firstborn, not as one who came into existence (for God, as eternal Mind, possessed his Reason within himself from the beginning, being eternally rational), but as Idea and Energy that proceeded before all material things, when formless matter and useless earth lay subjected, the denser mingled with the lighter upon it. The prophetic Spirit concurs with this Reason, declaring, "The Lord created me the beginning of his ways for his works" (Proverbs 8:22). We also affirm that the Holy Spirit, who inspires prophetic utterance, is an efflux of God, flowing forth and returning like a ray of the sun. Who would not be perplexed to hear us called atheists when we confess God the Father, God the Son, and the Holy Spirit, displaying both their power in unity and their distinction in order? Our theology does not rest on these points alone; we also teach a multitude of angels and ministers, whom the Creator and Maker of the world, God, distributed and ordered through his Word to govern the elements, the heavens, the world, all that is in it, and their harmonious arrangement.

greek: Τὸ μὲν οὖν ἄθεοι μὴ εἶναι, ἕνα τὸν ἀγένητον καὶ ἀΐδιον καὶ ἀόρατον καὶ ἀπαθῆ καὶ ἀκατάληπτον καὶ ἀχώρητον, νῷ μόνῳ καὶ λόγῳ καταλαμβανόμενον, φωτὶ καὶ κάλλει καὶ πνεύματι καὶ δυνάμει ἀνεκδιηγήτῳ περιεχόμενον, ὑφ᾿ οὗ γεγένηται τὸ πᾶν διὰ τοῦ αὐτοῦ λόγου καὶ διακεκόσμηται καὶ συγκρατεῖται, θεὸν ἄγοντες, ἱκανῶς μοι δέδεικται. Νοοῦμεν γὰρ καὶ υἱὸν τοῦ θεοῦ. Καὶ μή μοι γελοῖόν τις νομίσῃ τὸ υἱὸν εἶναι τῷ θεῷ. Οὐ γὰρ ὡς ποιηταὶ μυθοποιοῦσιν, οὐδὲν βελτίους τῶν ἀνθρώπων δεικνῦντες τοὺς θεούς, ἢ περὶ τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ πατρὸς ἢ περὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ πεφρονήκαμεν. Ἀλλ᾿ ἔστιν ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ λόγος τοῦ πατρὸς ἐν ἰδέᾳ καὶ ἐνεργείᾳ· πρὸς αὐτοῦ γὰρ καὶ δι᾿ αὐτοῦ πάντα ἐγένετο, ἑνὸς ὄντος τοῦ πατρὸς καὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ. Ὄντος δὲ τοῦ υἱοῦ ἐν πατρὶ καὶ πατρὸς ἐν υἱῷ, ἑνότητι καὶ δυνάμει πνεύματος, νοῦς καὶ λόγος τοῦ πατρὸς ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ. Εἰ δὲ δι᾿ ὑπερβολὴν συνέσεως σκοπεῖν ὑμῖν ἔπεισιν, ὁ παῖς τί βούλεται, ἐρῶ διὰ βραχέων πρῶτον γέννημα εἶναι τῷ πατρί, οὐχ ὡς γενόμενον (ἐξ ἀρχῆς γὰρ ὁ θεός, νοῦς ἀΐδιος ὤν, εἶχεν αὐτὸς ἐν ἑαυτῷ τὸν λόγον, ἀϊδίως λογικὸς ὤν), ἀλλ᾿ ὡς τῶν ὑλικῶν ξυμπάντων, ἀποίου φύσεως καὶ γῆς ἀχρείας ὑποκειμένων δίκην, μεμιγμένων τῶν παχυμερεστέρων πρὸς τὰ κουφότερα ἐπ᾿ αὐτοῖς, ἰδέα καὶ ἐνέργεια εἶναι προελθών. Συνᾴδει δὲ τῷ λόγῳ καὶ τὸ προφητικὸν πνεῦμα· Κύριος γάρ, φησίν, ἔκτισέ με ἀρχὴν ὁδῶν αὐτοῦ εἰς ἔργα αὐτοῦ. Καίτοι καὶ αὐτὸ τὸ ἐνεργοῦν τοῖς ἐκφωνοῦσι προφητικῶς ἅγιον πνεῦμα ἀπόῤῥοιαν εἶναί φαμεν τοῦ θεοῦ, ἀποῤῥέον καὶ ἐπαναφερόμενον ὡς ἀκτῖνα ἡλίου.Τίς οὖν οὐκ ἂν ἀπορήσαι, λέγοντας θεὸν πατέρα καὶ υἱὸν θεὸν καὶ πνεῦμα ἅγιον, δεικνύντας αὐτῶν καὶ τὴν ἐν τῇ ἑνώσει δύναμιν καὶ τὴν ἐν τῇ τάξει διαίρεσιν, ἀκούσας ἀθέους καλουμένους; Καὶ οὐκ ἐπὶ τούτοις τὸ θεολογικὸν ἡμῶν ἵσταται μέρος· ἀλλὰ καὶ πλῆθος ἀγγέλων καὶ λειτουργῶν φαμεν, οὓς ὁ ποιητὴς καὶ δημιουργὸς κόσμου θεὸς διὰ τοῦ παρ᾿ αὐτοῦ λόγου διένειμε καὶ διέταξε περί τε τὰ στοιχεῖα εἶναι καὶ τοὺς οὐρανοὺς καὶ τὸν κόσμον καὶ τὰ ἐν αὐτῷ καὶ τὴν τούτων εὐταξίαν.

excerpts.author: Athenagoras
english: Nearly everyone agrees, even against their will, that a single divine principle underlies the origins of all things; we insist that the One who ordered the whole world is this God. Why, then, are others free to speak and write about the divine as they please, while we who both understand and rightly believe are bound by a law to demonstrate by signs of truth and reason that one God exists? Poets and philosophers, like everyone else, approached these matters thoughtfully. Moved by a kinship with the breath from God, each one's own soul stirred them to seek and, if possible, find and grasp the truth. Yet they only managed to speculate; they never found it, because they did not ask to learn about God from God but from themselves. Consequently, each one dogmatized differently about God, matter, forms, and the world. We, however, have prophets as witnesses to what we understand and believe. Inspired by the divine Spirit, they proclaimed the truth about God and the things of God. You yourselves would say the same: surpassing others in understanding and in reverence for the truly divine, you would call it irrational to abandon faith in the Spirit from God, who moved the prophets' mouths like instruments, and instead pay attention to human opinions.

greek: Ὅταν οὖν τὸ μὲν εἷναι ἓν τὸ θεῖον ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πλεῖστον κἂν μὴ θέλωσι τοῖς πᾶσι συμφωνῆται ἐπὶ τὰς ἀρχὰς τῶν ὅλων παραγινομένοις, ἡμεῖς δὲ κρατύνωμεν τὸν διακοσμήσαντα τὸ πᾶν τοῦτο τοῦτον εἶναι τὸν θεόν, τίς ἡ αἰτία τοῖς μὲν ἐπ᾿ ἀδείας ἐξεῖναι καὶ λέγειν καὶ γράφειν περὶ τοῦ θείου ἃ θέλουσιν, ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν δὲ κεῖσθαι νόμον, οἵ ἔχομεν ὅ τι καὶ νοοῦμεν καὶ ὀρθῶς πεπιστεύκαμεν, ἕνα θεὸν εἶναι, ἀληθείας σημείοις καὶ λόγοις παραστῆσαι; Ποιηταὶ μὲν γὰρ καὶ φιλόσοφοι, ὡς καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις, ἐπέβαλον στοχαστικῶς, κινηθέντες μὲν κατὰ συμπάθειαν τῆς παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ πνοῆς ὑπὸ τῆς αὐτὸς αὐτοῦ ψυχῆς ἕκαστος ζητῆσαι, εἰ δυνατὸς εὑρεῖν καὶ νοῆσαι τὴν ἀλήθειαν· τοσοῦτον δὲ δυνηθέντες ὅσον περινοῆσαι οὐχ εὕρηνται, ὡς οὐ παρὰ θεοῦ περὶ θεοῦ ἀξιώσαντες μαθεῖν ἀλλὰ παρ᾿ αὐτοῦ ἕκαστος· διὸ καὶ ἄλλος ἄλλως ἐδογμάτισεν αὐτῶν καὶ περὶ θεοῦ καὶ περὶ ὕλης καὶ περὶ εἰδῶν καὶ περὶ κόσμου. Ἡμεῖς δὲ ὧν νοοῦμεν καὶ πεπιστεύκαμεν ἔχομεν προφήτας μάρτυρας, οἵ πνεύματι ἐνθέῳ ἐκπεφωνήκασι καὶ περὶ τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ περὶ τῶν τοῦ θεοῦ. Εἴποιτε δ᾿ ἂν καὶ ὑμεῖς, συνέσει καὶ τῇ περὶ τὸ ὄντως θεῖον εὐσεβείᾳ τοὺς ἄλλους προὔχοντες, ὡς ἔστιν ἄλογον παραλιπόντας πιστεύειν τῷ παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ πνεύματι, ὡς ὄργανα κεκινηκότι τὰ τῶν προφητῶν στόματα, προσέχειν δόξαις ἀνθρωπίναις.

excerpts.author: Athenagoras
english: If we had rested content with such thoughts, anyone would take our reasoning for merely human. But the voices of the prophets confirm our thoughts—and I assume even you, so devoted to learning and knowledge, are not unacquainted with Moses, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the other prophets. Driven by the divine Spirit moving their minds, they uttered what the Spirit wrought in them, using them as a flutist breathes into an instrument. So what do they say? "The Lord our God; another will not be reckoned besides Him" (Isaiah 44:6). And again: "I am God first and after these things, and besides me there is no God" (Isaiah 46:9-10). Similarly: "Before me another God was not generated and after me there will not be one; I am God and there is no one besides me" (Isaiah 43:10-11). And concerning greatness: "The heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool of my feet. What kind of house will you build for me, or what is the place of my rest?" (Isaiah 66:1-2). I leave it to you, now that you have these books, to examine those prophecies more carefully, so that with proper reasoning you may set aside the prejudice against us.

greek: Εἰ μὲν οὖν ταῖς τοιαύταις ἐννοίαις ἀπηρκούμεθα, ἀνθρωπικὸν ἄν τις εἶναι τὸν καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς ἐνόμισε λόγον. Ἐπεὶ δὲ αἱ φωναὶ τῶν προφητῶν πιστοῦσιν ἡμῶν τοὺς λογισμούς (νομίζω καὶ ὑμᾶς, φιλομαθεστάτους καὶ ἐπιστημονεστάτους ὄντας, οὐκ ἀνοήτους γεγονέναι οὔτε τῶν Μωσέως οὔτε τῶν Ἠσαΐου καὶ Ἱερεμίου καὶ τῶν λοιπῶν προφητῶν, οἳ κατ᾿ ἔκστασιν τῶν ἐν αὐτοῖς λογισμῶν κινήσαντος αὐτοὺς τοῦ θείου πνεύματος ἃ ἐνηργοῦντο ἐξεφώνησαν, συγχρησαμένου τοῦ πνεύματος ὡσεὶ καὶ αὐλητὴς αὐτὸν ἐμπνεύσαι), τί οὖν οὗτοι; Κύριος ὁ θεὸς ἡμῶν· οὐ λογισθήσεται ἕτερος πρὸς αὐτόν. Καὶ πάλιν· Ἐγὼ θεὸς πρῶτος καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα, καὶ πλὴν ἐμοῦ οὐκ ἔστι θεός. Ὁμοίως· Ἔμπροσθεν ἐμοῦ οὐκ ἐγένετο ἄλλος θεὸς καὶ μετ᾿ ἐμὲ οὐκ ἔσται· ἐγὼ ὁ θεὸς καὶ οὐκ ἔστι πάρεξ ἐμοῦ. Καὶ περὶ τοῦ μεγέθους· Ὁ οὐρανός μοι θρόνος, ἡ δὲ γῆ ὑποπόδιον τῶν ποδῶν μου. Ποῖον οἶκον οἰκοδομήσετέ μοι, ἢ τίς τόπος τῆς καταπαύσεώς μου; Καταλείπω δὲ ὑμῖν, ἐπ᾿ αὐτῶν τῶν βιβλίων γενομένοις, ἀκριβέστερον τὰς ἐκείνων ἐξετάσαι προφητείας, ὅπως μετὰ τοῦ προσήκοντος λογισμοῦ τὴν καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς ἐπήρειαν ἀποσκευάσησθε.

excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english: The true spiritual disciple receives the Spirit of God. From the beginning the Spirit was present to humanity in every arrangement of God. He announced the future, revealed the present, and narrated the past. He judges all things, yet no one judges him.

For he judges the nations—creatures who serve the creature rather than the Creator, consuming their entire effort in vain with a depraved mind (Rom 1:25). He also judges the Jews, who do not perceive the word of liberty nor wish to go free, even though their Liberator stands present among them. They pretend to serve outside the law at the wrong time, as if God needed anything, and they refuse to recognize or understand Christ's advent, which he accomplished for human salvation. All the prophets foretold two advents of his (Acts 3:18).

In the first, he was made flesh, knowing how to bear weakness. He sat upon a donkey's colt (Zech 9:9). He became the stone the builders rejected (Ps 118:22). He was led like a sheep to slaughter. By stretching out his hands he dissolved Amalek. He gathered the scattered children from the ends of the earth into the Father's fold. He remembered his dead who slept, and descended to them so that he might raise them.

But the second advent will be different: he will come upon the clouds, bringing a day that burns like a furnace. He will strike the earth with the word of his mouth and slay the wicked with the breath of his lips (Isa 11:4). He will hold a winnowing fork in his hand, clear his threshing floor, gather the wheat into his barn, and burn the chaff with unquenchable fire (Matt 3:12).

Nam judicat gentes, creature magis quam Oreatori servientes, et reprobabili mente universam suam operationem in vanum consumentes. Judicat autem etiam Judos, non percipientes verbum libertatis, neque volentes abire liberos, cum habeant preesentem liberatorem ; sed intempestive extra legem servire simulantes nihil indigenti Deo, et Christi adventum, quem propter salutem hominum fecit, non cognoseentes, neque intelligere volentes, quoniam duos adventus ejus omnes annuntiaverunt prophetee: unum quidem, in homo in plaga factus est, sciens ferre imbecillitatem, et in pullo asinee sedens, et reprobatus lapis ab eedificantibus, et sicut ovis ad victimam adductus, et per extensionem manuum dissolvens quidem Amalech; congregans autem dispersos filios a terminis terre in ovile Patris, et recommemoratus mortuorum suorum qui dormierant, et descendens ad eos, uti erueret eos®; secundum autem, in quo super nubes veniet, superducens diem que est sicut clibanus ardens, et percutiens terram verbo oris sui, et spiritu per labia sua interficiens impios, et ventilabrum in manu habens, et’ emundans aream suam, et triticum quidem in horreum comburens autem paleas igne inexstinguibili.

excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english: We have come to know the plan of our salvation through those who brought the Gospel to us. At first they proclaimed it by word of mouth; later, by God's will, they handed it down to us in the Scriptures, which were to become the foundation and pillar of our faith. It is not right to claim that they preached before they possessed full knowledge, as some dare to assert, boasting that they are correctors of the Apostles. After our Lord rose from the dead and they were clothed with the power of the Holy Spirit coming from on high, they were filled with all things and gained perfect knowledge. They went out to the ends of the earth, preaching the good things that come from God to us and announcing heavenly peace to humanity—each of them equally possessing the Gospel of God. Thus Matthew, writing in the Hebrews' own language, published his Gospel while Peter and Paul were evangelizing in Rome and founding the Church. After their departure, Mark, the disciple and interpreter of Peter, handed down to us in writing what Peter had proclaimed. Luke, a follower of Paul, set down in a book the Gospel that Paul preached. Later, John, the disciple of the Lord who had reclined on His breast, published his Gospel while living at Ephesus in Asia. All of them proclaimed to us one God, the Maker of heaven and earth, announced by the Law and the Prophets, and one Christ, the Son of God. Anyone who refuses to assent to them despises the Lord's own companions, despises Christ the Lord, despises the Father, and stands self-condemned by resisting and opposing his own salvation—exactly what all heretics do.

Et omnes isti unum Deum factorem cceli et terre a lege et prophetis annuntiatum, et unum Christum filium Dei tradiderunt nobis: quibus si quis non assentit, spernit quidem participes Domini, spernit autem et ipsum Christum Dominum, spernit vero et Patrem, et est a semetipso damnatus, resistens et repugnans saluti suze: quod faciunt omnes heeretici.

excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english: John, the Lord's disciple, proclaims this faith in order to uproot the error that Cerinthus sowed among people, and earlier still the error of the so-called Nicolaitans—a counterfeit offshoot that confuses them. He writes to persuade them that one God made all things through His Word, not one Creator and another Father of the Lord, as they claim (John 1:1). They teach two sons: one begotten of the Creator, another Christ from above who remained impassible, descended into Jesus the Creator's son, and then returned to His Pleroma. They distinguish the Only-begotten from the true Word, the only-begotten Son, and insist that our material condition was fashioned not by the first God but by a lower power severed from the invisible, unnameable realm. To fence off all such teachings and fix the rule of truth in the Church, John grounds everything in the one Almighty God who created all things, visible and invisible, through His Word (John 1:1). He also shows that through the very Word by which God perfected creation, He provided salvation for those who live in that creation. So John opens his Gospel doctrine: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was with God in the beginning. All things were made through Him, and without Him nothing was made. What was made in Him was life, and the life was the light of men. The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it" (John 1:1). John insists, "All things were made through Him"; therefore this condition of ours also falls within "all things." The heretics cannot restrict "all things" to what lies inside their Pleroma. If their Pleroma contains these things, then our condition is not outside it—as the previous book demonstrated. If our condition lies outside their Pleroma, then their Pleroma is not "all things," which is impossible. Hence our condition is not outside. John himself removes every dispute: "He was in the world, and the world was made through Him, yet the world did not know Him. He came to His own, and His own people did not receive Him" (John 1:10–11). Marcion and his followers deny both that the world was made through Him and that He came to His own; they say He came to another's realm. Some Gnostics claim angels made the world, not God's Word. Valentinians say the Demiurge made it, not the Word. They teach that the Demiurge fashioned creation as a likeness of the things above, but the Gospel declares plainly that all things were made through the Word who was with God in the beginning, and that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). In their systems, however, neither the Word, nor Christ, nor the Savior composed of all things became flesh. They refuse to admit that the Word and Christ entered this world. The Savior, they say, did not become incarnate or suffer, but descended like a dove into Jesus—who sprang from their lower condition—announced the unknown Father, and then ascended back to the Pleroma. Some say Jesus of that lower condition was incarnate and suffered, passing through Mary like water through a pipe. Others say the Demiurge's son received the Jesus from that condition. Others say Jesus was born of Joseph and Mary, and the impassible, fleshless Christ from above descended into Him. But by no heretical opinion did the Word of God become flesh. Examine all their rules and you will find that every one presents God's Word as fleshless and impassible, and the Christ above as likewise. Some imagine He appeared only as a transfigured man, yet deny He was born or incarnate. Others deny He took human form at all, saying He descended like a dove into Jesus born of Mary. Thus the Lord's disciple exposes them all as false witnesses and declares: "The Word became flesh and dwelt among us" (John 1:14). Lest anyone ask whose Word became flesh, John himself answers: "There was a man sent from God, whose name was John. He came as a witness to testify concerning the light, so that through him all might believe. He himself was not the light, but came to testify about the light" (John 1:6–8). The forerunner John, who testifies to the light—by which God was he sent? Surely by the God whose angel is Gabriel, who announced John's own birth and promised through the prophets to send His messenger before His Son's face to prepare His way—that is, to testify to the light in the spirit and power of Elijah (Luke 1:17). And Elijah—servant and prophet of which God? Of the One who made heaven and earth, as Elijah himself confesses (1 Kings 18:36). Therefore John was sent by the Founder and Creator of this world. How else could he bear witness to the light that descended from the invisible, unnameable realm? All heretics decree that the Demiurge is ignorant of the power above him, yet John is found to be that power's witness and revealer. For this reason the Lord said John was more than a prophet (Luke 7:26). All the other prophets announced the coming of the Father's light and longed to see the One they preached. John not only announced Him like the rest, but saw Him coming, pointed Him out, and persuaded many to believe in Him—so that he holds the office of both prophet and apostle.

latin: Hane fidem annuntians Johannes Domini discipulus, volens per Evangelii annuntiationem auferre eum, qui a Cerintho inseminatus erat hominibus errorem, et multo prius ab his qui dicuntur Nicolaite, qui sunt vulsio ejus quee falso cognominatur ut confunderet eos, et suaderet quoniam unus Deus qui omnia fecit per Verbum suum ; et non, quemadmodum illi dicunt, alterum quidem fabricatorem, alium autem Patrem Domini: et alium quidem fabricatoris filium, alterum vero ®de superioribus Christum, quem et impassibilem perseverasse, descendentem in Jesum filium fabricatoris, et iterum revolasse in suum Pleroma: et Tinitium quidem esse monogenem; Logon autem verum filium unigeniti: et eam conditionem quze est secundum nos, non a primo Deo factam, sed a virtute aliqua valde deorsum subjecta, et abscissa ab eorum communicatione quze sunt invisibilia et innominabilia. Omnia igitur talia cireumscribere volens discipulus Domini, et ' regulam veritatis constituere in Ecclesia, quia est unus Deus omnipotens, qui per Verbum suum omnia fecit, et visibilia et invisibilia; significans quoque, quoniam per Verbum, per quod Deus perfecit conditionem, in hoe et salutem his qui in conditione sunt preestitit hominibus; sic inchoavit in ea que est secundum Evangelium doctrina: Jn principio erat Verbum, et Verbum erat apud Deum, et Deus erat Verbum: hoc erat in principio apud Deum. Omnia per ipsum facta sunt, et sine ipso factum est nihil. Quod factum est, in ipso vita erat, et vita erat lua hominum, et lux in tenebris lucet, et tenebre eam non comprehenderunt. Omnia, inquit, per ipsum facta sunt ; in omnibus ergo est et hzee quae secundum nos est conditio: non enim concedetur eis, omnia dici ea que sunt infra Pleroma ipsorum. Si enim et hee Pleroma ipsorum continet, non extra est tanta ista conditio, quemadmodum ostendimus in eo libro qui ante hune est ; si autem extra Pleroma sunt heec, quod quidem impossibile visum est, jam non est omnia Pleroma ipsorum: non est ergo extra heee tanta conditio. Abstulit autem a nobis dissensiones omnes ipse Johannes, dicens: In hoc mundo erat, et mundus per ipsum factus est, et mundus eum non cognovit. In sua propria venit, et sui eum non receperunt. Secundum autem Marcionem et eos qui similes sunt ei, neque mundus per eum factus est ; neque in sua venit, sed in aliena, Secundum autem quosdam Gnosticorum, ¢ab angelis factus est iste mundus, et non per Verbum Dei. Secundum autem eos qui sunt a Valentino, iterum non per eum factus est, sed per Demiurgum. Hic enim operabatur similitudines tales fieri, ad imitationem eorum que sunt sursum, quemadmodum dicunt: Demiurgus autem perficiebat fabricationem conditionis. Emissum enim dicunt eum a matre Dominum et Demiurgum ejus dispositionis quee est secundum conditionem, per quem hune mundum factum volunt: cum Evangelium manifeste dicat, quoniam per Verbum, quod in principio erat apud Deum, omnia sunt facta: quod Verbum, inquit, caro factum est, et habitavit in nobis. 8. Secundum autem illos, neque Verbum caro factum est, neque Christus, neque qui ex omnibus factus est Salvator. Htenim Verbum et Christum nec advenisse in hune mundum volunt: Salvatorem vero non incarnatum neque passum; descendisse autem quasi columbam in eum Jesum qui factus est ex dispositione, et cum annuntiasset incognitum Patrem, iterum ascendisse in Pleroma. Incarnatum autem et passum quidam quidem eum qui ex dispositione sit dicunt Jesum, quem per Mariam dicunt pertransisse, quasi aquam per tubum: alii vero ° Demiurgi filium, in quem descendisse eum Jesum qui ex dispositione sit: alii rursum Jesum quidem ex Joseph et Maria natum dicunt, et in hune descendisse Christum qui de superioribus sit, sine carne et impassibilem exsistentem. Secundum autem nullam sententiam heereticorum, Verbum Dei caro factum est. Si enim quis regulas ipsorum omnium perscrutetur, inveniet quoniam sine carne et impassibilis ab omnibus illis inducitur Dei Verbum, et qui est in superioribus Christus. Alii enim putant manifestatum eum, quemadmodum hominem transfiguratum; neque autem natum, neque incarnatum dicunt illum: alii vero neque figuram eum assumsisse hominis; sed quemadmodum columbam descendisse in eum Jesum, qui natus est ex Maria. Omnes igitur illos falsos testes ostendens discipulus Domini, ait: Ht Verbum caro factum est, et habitavit in nobis. Et ut non inquiramus, cujus Dei Verbum caro factum est, ipse insuper docet, dicens : Fuit homo missus a Deo, erat ei nomen Johannes: hic venit in testimonium, ut testaretur de lumine. Non erat ipse lumen, sed ut testaretur de lumine. Preecursor igitur Johannes, qui testatur de lumine, a quo Deo missus est? Utique ab eo cujus Gabriel est angelus, qui etiam evangelisavit generationem ejus; qui et per prophetas promisit angelum suum missurum ante faciem Filii sui, et preeparaturum viam ejus, hoc est, testificaturum de lumine, i spiritw et virtute Helie. Helias autem rursus cujus Dei servus et propheta fuit? Ejus qui fecit coelum et terram, quemadmodum et ipse confitetur. A conditore igitur et fabricatore hujus mundi missus Johannes, quemadmodum poterat testificari de eo lumine, quod ex his que sunt innominabilia et invisibilia descenderit ? Omnes enim heeretici decreverunt, Demiurgum ignorare eam que sit super eum virtutem, cujus testis et ostensor invenitur Johannes. Propter hoc Dominus plus quam prophetam dixit eum habuisse. Reliqui enim omnes prophetze annuntiaverunt adventum paterni luminis; concupierunt autem digni esse videre eum quem preedicabant: Johannes autem et preenuntiavit similiter sicut alii, et advenientem vidit et demonstravit, et credere in eum suasit multis, ita ut ipse et prophete et apostoli locum habuerit.

excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english: We cannot know God by measuring his magnitude, for it is impossible to measure the Father; but we are led to God through his love, which works by his Word. As we obey him, we always learn how great God is, and that he himself is the one who establishes, chooses, and adorns all things, doing so in a way that relates to us. Consequently, we have been formed together with everything he contains. This is precisely what Scripture declares: "God formed man from the dust of the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life" (Genesis 2:7). Therefore, angels did not make us, nor did they form us, nor could angels fashion the image of God, nor could any other power remote from the Father — only the Word of the Lord could do so. God did not need such helpers to accomplish what he had predetermined, as if he lacked his own hands. The Word and Wisdom, the Son and Spirit, are always present with him; through them and in them he freely and willingly made all things, and to them he speaks, saying, "Let us make man in our image and likeness," himself drawing from his own being the substance of creatures, the pattern of his works, and the form of the world's ornaments.

Scripture has rightly proclaimed: "First of all, believe that there is one God, who established and consummated and made all things from what did not exist, so that all things might be; capable of all things, and not capable of being grasped by anyone." The prophet Malachi likewise says: "Is there not one God who established us? Is there not one Father of us all?" (Malachi 2:10). The Apostle confirms this: "There is one God, the Father, who is over all and in us all" (Ephesians 4:6). And the Lord himself declares: "All things have been handed over to me by my Father" — clearly by the one who made all things, for nothing has been taken away. Because of this, he is the Judge of the living and the dead, holding the key of David: "he will open, and no one will shut; he will shut, and no one will open." No one else could open the Father's book, whether in heaven, on earth, or under the earth, nor even see it — except the Lamb who was slain and redeemed us with his blood. He received all authority from the one who made all things by the Word and adorned them by Wisdom, when the Word became flesh, so that just as the Word of God held primacy in heaven, he might also hold primacy on earth, because he is the just man who committed no sin and in whose mouth no deceit was found. And he might hold primacy over the things under the earth, having become the firstborn of the dead, so that all things might see their King, as we have said before, and so that the paternal light might shine upon the flesh of the Lord, and its radiant glow might come to us from his flesh, and thus humanity might become incorruptible, wrapped in the Father's light.

We have demonstrated through many passages that the Word, that is, the Son, was always with the Father. And that Wisdom — that is, the Spirit — was with him before all creation, Solomon testifies: "God founded the earth by Wisdom; by his understanding the deeps burst forth, and the clouds dropped down dew." And again: "The Lord created me at the beginning of his work, the first of his acts of old. Ages ago I was set up, at the first, before the beginning of the earth. When there were no depths I was brought forth, when there were no springs abounding with water. Before the mountains had been shaped, before the hills, I was brought forth." And again: "When he established the heavens, I was there; when he made firm the fountains of the deep, when he made strong the foundations of the earth, I was beside him, like a master workman; and I was daily his delight, rejoicing before him always, rejoicing in his inhabited world and delighting in the children of man."

Therefore, there is one God who made and ordered all things by the Word and Wisdom; this is the Demiurge, who gave this world to the human race. According to his magnitude he is unknown to all who have been made by him — no one has plumbed his height, neither the ancients who have rested nor those who live now. But according to his love, he is always known through the one by whom he established all things: our Lord Jesus Christ. In the last times he became man among men, to join the end to the beginning. For this reason the prophets, receiving the prophetic gift from the same Word, foretold his coming in the flesh, through which the mingling and communion of God and man was accomplished according to the Father's good pleasure. From the beginning the Word of God had foretold that God would be seen by human beings, would converse with them on earth, and would be present with his creature, saving it, making himself perceptible to it, and liberating us from the hands of all who hate us — that is, from the spirit of all transgression — and making us serve him in holiness and justice all our days, so that humanity, having received the Spirit of God, might give glory to the Father.

Et nos igitur cum his que continentur ab eo, factisumus. Et hic est de quo Scriptura ait; Ht plasmavit Deus hominem, limum terre accipiens, et insufflavit in faciem ejus Jjlatum vite. Non ergo angeli fecerunt, nos, nec nos plasmaverunt, nec angeli potuerunt imaginem facere Dei, nec alius quis preter Verbum Domini, nec virtus longe absistens a Patre uniNec enim indigebat horum Deus ad faciendum quie ipse apud se preefinierat fieri, quasi ipse suas non haberet manus. Adest enim ei semper Verbum et Sapientia, Filius et Spiritus, per quos, et in quibus omnia libere et sponte fecit, ad quos et loquitur, dicens: Faciamus hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram; ipse a semetipso substantiam creaturarum, et exemplum factorum, et figuram in mundo ornamentorum accipiens. 2. Bene autem et in prophetis Malachias ait: Nonne unus Deus qui constituit nos? Nonne Pater unus est omnium nostrum ? Consequenter autem et Apostolus ait: nus Deus, inquit, Pater, qui super omnes, et in omnibus nobis. Similiter autem et Dominus: Omnia mihi, inquit, tradita sunt a Patre meo; manifeste ab eo qui omnia fecit: non enim aliena, sed In omnibus autem nihil subtractum est: et propter hoe idem est Judex viventium et mortuorum, habens clavem David: ' aperiet, et nemo claudet : claudet, et nemo aperiet. Nemo enim alius poterat nec in ccelo, nec in terra, nec sub terra aperire paternum librum, nec videre eum, nisi agnus qui occisus est, et sanguine suo redemit nos, ab eodem, qui omnia Verbo fecit et Sapientia adornavit, accipiens omnium potestatem, quando Verbum caro factum est, ut quemadmodum in ccelis principatum habuit Verbum Dei, sic et in terra haberet principatum, quoniam homo justus, gui peccatum non fecit, nec inventus est dolus in ore ejus; principatum autem habeat eorum que sunt sub terra, ipse primogenitus mortuorum factus, et ut videant omnia, quemadmodum preediximus, suum Regem: et ut in carnem Domini occurrat paterna lux, et a carne ejus rutila veniat in nos, et sic homo deveniat in incorruptelam, circumdatus paterno lumine. 3. Et quoniam Verbum, id est Filius, semper cum Patre erat, per multa demonstravimus. Et rursus autem: Dominus creavit me principium viarum suarum in opera sua, ante swcula fundavit me, initio antequam terram faceret, priusqguam abyssos constitueret, et priusquam procederent fontes aquarum, antequam montes confirmarentur: ante omnes autem colles genuit me. excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english: The spiritual disciple truly receives the Spirit of God, who from the beginning was present in all of God's arrangements with humanity, announcing future things, revealing present things, and explaining past things. He judges all, yet is judged by no one. For he judges the nations, creatures who serve the Creator more than the created order, consuming their entire effort in vain with a reprobate mind. He also judges the Jews, who do not perceive the word of liberty and refuse to go free even though their Liberator is present. Instead, they pretend to serve God outside the Law at the wrong time, as if He needed anything, and they neither know nor wish to understand Christ's advent, which He accomplished for human salvation, even though all the prophets announced His two advents. In the first, He was made man in affliction, knowing how to bear infirmity, and sat upon a colt, the foal of a donkey (Zech 9:9); He was the stone rejected by the builders (Psalm 118:22), and like a lamb led to the slaughter (Isaiah 53:7), dissolving Amalek by the extension of His hands; gathering the scattered children from the ends of the earth into the Father's fold, remembering His dead who slept, and descending to them to raise them up. In the second advent, He will come upon the clouds, bringing a day like a burning furnace, striking the earth with the word of His mouth, and slaying the impious with the breath of His lips. He will hold a winnowing fork in His hand, clear His threshing floor, gather the wheat into His barn, but burn the chaff with unquenchable fire.

Let us examine, then, the doctrine of Marcion: how does he accept that there are two gods, infinitely separated from one another? How can he be good if he draws alien men away from the One who made them and calls them into his own kingdom? Why does his goodness fail by not saving all? Why does he appear good toward men but most unjust toward the One who made men, taking away what belongs to Him? How can the Lord be just if He proceeds from another Father, yet accepts this human condition, confessing the bread to be His body and confirming the cup's mixture to be His blood? Why did He confess Himself to be the Son of Man if He did not undergo the generation that comes from man? How could He forgive us the sins we owe to our Maker and God? How could He be crucified when He was not flesh but only appeared as a man, and blood and water flowed from His side? What was that body which the buriers buried? And what was it that rose from the dead?

He will also judge all those who follow Valentinus, because with their tongues they confess one God the Father, from whom are all things, yet they say the One who made all things is the fruit of defection or lapse. They likewise confess one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, with their tongues, but according to their opinion they assign their own 'emission' to the Only-begotten, another to the Word, another to Christ, and another to the Savior. Thus they claim all things are virtually one, yet each is understood separately with its own emission according to their system. Their tongues alone have fallen into unity, but their opinion and deep sense, falling away from unity, will be scrutinized and incur the multiform judgment of God when they are questioned by Christ about the things they devised for themselves. Their own prophet Homer will accuse them, from whom they learned such things, saying: 'For he is an enemy to me, even as the gates of Hades, who hides one thing in his heart but declares another.' He will also judge the empty talk of the wicked Gnostics, showing them to be disciples of Simon Magus. How will they be judged who presumptuously say they are gods?

Let us also examine the Ebionites: how can they be saved unless God is the One who worked their salvation on earth? How can man pass into God unless God first passed into man? How can he escape the generation of death unless he enters a new generation, wonderfully and unexpectedly given by God as a sign of salvation—that regeneration from the Virgin through faith? What adoption will they receive from God while remaining in this generation according to man in this world? How did the Lord have 'more than Solomon' and 'more than Jonah' if He was merely David, who shared the same substance with them? How did He conquer the one strong against men, who alone conquered man and held him under his power—conquering the conqueror and releasing the conquered man—unless He was superior to the man who was conquered? Who is better than the man made in the likeness of God, and who is more excellent than the Son of God, after whose likeness man was made? For this reason, in the end He revealed the likeness: the Son of God became man, taking the ancient formation upon Himself, as we demonstrated in the preceding book.

Judicat autem etiam Judos, non percipientes verbum libertatis, neque volentes abire liberos, cum habeant preesentem liberatorem ; sed intempestive extra legem servire simulantes nihil indigenti Deo, et Christi adventum, quem propter salutem hominum fecit, non cognoseentes, neque intelligere volentes, quoniam duos adventus ejus omnes annuntiaverunt prophetee: unum quidem, in homo in plaga factus est, sciens ferre imbecillitatem, et in pullo asinee sedens, et reprobatus lapis ab eedificantibus, et sicut ovis ad victimam adductus, et per extensionem manuum dissolvens quidem Amalech; congregans autem dispersos filios a terminis terre in ovile Patris, et recommemoratus mortuorum suorum qui dormierant, et descendens ad eos, uti erueret eos®; secundum autem, in quo super nubes veniet, superducens diem que est sicut clibanus ardens, et percutiens terram verbo oris sui, et spiritu per labia sua interficiens impios, et ventilabrum in manu habens, et’ emundans aream suam, et triticum quidem in horreum comburens autem paleas igne inexstinguibili. 1. excerpts.author: Irenaeus
english: God indeed fashions within his own formation, and what follows is adapted to his child. For through the hands of the Father — that is, through the Son and the Spirit — the human person is made according to the likeness of God, yet not as a mere part. The soul and the spirit can be parts of a human being, but the human being is not a part; the perfect human is a blending and union of the soul that takes on the Spirit of the Father and is interwoven with the flesh, which is formed according to the image. That is why the Apostle also says: 'We speak wisdom among the perfect' — calling perfect those who have received the Spirit of God and speak in tongues through the Spirit of God, just as we have heard many brothers speaking in the Church, possessing prophetic gifts, speaking in every language through the Spirit, bringing the hidden things of people into the light for their benefit, and declaring the mysteries of God. The Apostle calls these people 'spiritual' (1 Corinthians 12–14). They exist as spiritual by participation in the Spirit, not by deprivation or interception of the flesh, and not by that alone.

For if someone takes away the substance of the flesh — that is, the formation — and understands only the spirit, he is no longer a spiritual human being but merely the spirit of a human, or the Spirit of God. But when the spirit, blended with the soul, is united to the formation, then, by the outpouring of the Spirit, the perfect human is made; and this is the one who is made according to the image and likeness of God. But if the Spirit is lacking to the soul, that person is truly animal — such a one is carnal, abandoned, imperfect, possessing the image indeed in the formation, yet not taking on the likeness through the Spirit; just as this one is imperfect. So again, if someone removes the image and despises the formation, he can no longer understand the human being, but only some part of a human, as we said before, or something else besides a human. For the formation of the flesh itself, by itself, is not the perfect human; it is the body of a human, and a part. Nor is the soul itself, by itself, the human; it is the soul of a human, and a part. Nor is the Spirit the human; he is called Spirit, not human. But the blending and union of all these things makes the perfect human.

And because of this, the Apostle, explaining himself, set forth the perfect and spiritual human of salvation, saying in the first letter to the Thessalonians: 'May the God of peace sanctify you completely, and may your spirit and soul and body be kept blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ' (1 Thessalonians 5:23). And what cause did he have to pray for the integrity and perfection of these three — soul, body, and spirit — except that he knew the salvation of the three, their reunification, to be one and the same? That is why he also says that those are perfect who present these three blameless to the Lord. Therefore, the perfect are those who have the Spirit of God persevering in them, and who have kept their souls and bodies blameless, preserving the faith toward God and keeping the justice toward the neighbor.

And from this he also says that the temple of God is the formation: 'Do you not know that you are God's temple and that God's Spirit dwells in you? If anyone destroys God's temple, God will destroy him. For God's temple is holy, and you are that temple' (1 Corinthians 3:16–17) — clearly calling the body the temple in which the Spirit dwells. Just as the Lord also said of himself: 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up' — but he spoke of the temple of his body. And not only is it a temple, but also the temple of Christ, as he says to the Corinthians: 'Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute?' (1 Corinthians 6:15). He is not saying this about some other spiritual man; for that one does not embrace a prostitute. But our body — that is, the flesh which perseveres in holiness and purity — he said are members of Christ; when, however, it embraces a prostitute, the members become those of a prostitute. And because of this he said: 'If anyone destroys God's temple, God will destroy him.' Therefore, to say that the temple of God, in which the Spirit of the Father dwells, and the members of Christ, do not share in salvation but are led to perdition — is that not the utmost blasphemy? For since our bodies are raised not from their own substance but from the power of God, he says to the Corinthians: 'The body is not meant for sexual immorality, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body. And God raised the Lord and will also raise us up by his power' (1 Corinthians 6:13–14).

Ecclesia, prophetica habentes charismata, et per Spiritum universis linguis loquentes, et absconsa hominum in manifestum producentes ad utilitatem, et mysteria Dei enarrantes, quos et spiritales” Apostolus vocat; secundum participationem Spiritus exsistentes spiritales, sed non secundum defraudationem et interceptionem carnis, et nude hoc ipsum solum. Si enim substantiam tollat aliquis carnis, id est plasmatis, et nude ipsum solum spiritum intelligat, jam non spiritalis homo est quod est tale, sed spiritus hominis, aut Spiritus Dei. Cum autem spiritus hic commixtus anime unitur plasmati, propter effusionem Spiritus spiritalis et perfectus homo factus est : et hic est qui secundum imaginem et similitudinem factus est Dei. Si autem defuerit anime Spiritus, animalis est vere, qui est talis, et carnalis derelictus imperfectus imaginem quidem habens in plasmate, similitudinem vero non assumens per Spiritum; sicut autem hic imperfectus est. Sic iterum si quis tollat imaginem, et spernat plasma, jam non hominem intelligere potest, sed aut partem aliquam hominis, quemadmodum preediximus, vel aliud aliquid preter hominem. Neque enim plasmatio carnis ipsa secundum se homo perfectus est ; sed corpus hominis, et pars hominis. Neque enim et anima ipsa secundum se homo; sed anima hominis, et pars hominis. Neque Spiritus homo: spiritus enim, et non homo vocatur. Commixtio autem et unitio horum omnium perfectum hominem efficit. Et propter hoc Apostolus seipsum exponens, explanavit perfectum et spiritalem salutis hominem, in prima epistola ad Thessalonicenses dicens sic: Deus autem pacis sanctificet vos perfectos, et integer vester spiritus, et anima, et corpus sine querela in adventum Domini Jesu Christi servetur. Hoc autem, inquit, dicebat de corpare suo. Et non tantum templum, sed et templum Christi scit corpora nostra, Corinthiis dicens sic: Nescitis quoniam corpora vestra membra Christi sunt? Tollens ergo membra Christi, faciam membra meretricis? excerpts.author: Theophilus of Antioch
english: God's people, as bearers of the Holy Spirit and having become prophets, were inspired and made wise by God Himself, and so became God-taught, holy, and righteous. For this reason they were deemed worthy to receive this reward, having become instruments of God and having received wisdom from Him; through that wisdom they spoke about the creation of the world and everything else. They also foretold plagues, famines, and wars. Not merely one or two, but many were raised up at various times and seasons—not only among the Hebrews but also among the Greeks, a Sibyl—and all have spoken in friendly accord with one another, covering both the events before them, those in their own day, and those now being fulfilled among us. Therefore we too are convinced that the things to come will be so, just as the first things were fulfilled.

greek: Οἱ δὲ τοῦ θεοῦ ἄνθρωποι, πνευματοφόροι πνεύματος ἁγίου καὶ προφῆται γενόμενοι, ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ ἐμπνευσθέντες καὶ σοφισθέντες, ἐγένοντο θεοδίδακτοι καὶ ὅσιοι καὶ δίκαιοι. Διὸ καὶ κατηξιώθησαν τὴν ἀντιμισθίαν ταύτην λαβεῖν, ὄργανα θεοῦ γενόμενοι καὶ χωρήσαντες σοφίαν τὴν παρ᾿ αὐτοῦ, δι᾿ ἧς σοφίας εἶπον καὶ τὰ περὶ τῆς κτίσεως τοῦ κόσμου καὶ τῶν λοιπῶν ἁπάντων. Καὶ γὰρ περὶ λοιμῶν καὶ λιμῶν καὶ πολέμων προεῖπον. Καὶ οὐχ εἷς ἢ δύο ἀλλὰ πλείονες κατὰ χρόνους καὶ καιροὺς ἐγενήθησαν παρὰ Ἑβραίοις, ἀλλὰ καὶ παρὰ Ἕλλησιν Σίβυλλα· καὶ πάντες φίλα ἀλλήλοις καὶ σύμφωνα εἰρήκασιν, τά τε πρὸ αὐτῶν γεγενημένα καὶ τὰ κατ᾿ αὐτοὺς γεγονότα καὶ τὰ καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς νυνὶ τελειούμενα· διὸ καὶ πεπείσμεθα καὶ περὶ τῶν μελλόντων οὕτως ἔσεσθαι, καθὼς καὶ τὰ πρῶτα ἀπήρτισται.

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: The sacrifice acceptable to God is the separation of the body and its passions without regret, and this is true reverence for the living God. It is not without reason that Socrates calls philosophy a study of death; for the person who neither relies on sight in thinking nor is drawn by any of the other senses, but encounters reality with a pure mind, shares in true philosophy. This is also what Pythagoras intends by the five‑year silence that he prescribes for his followers, so that, turning away from sensible things, they may contemplate the divine with a pure mind. The leading Greek thinkers who philosophized in this way were following Moses. For Moses commands that whole burnt offerings be flayed and divided into parts, since the cognitive soul, once it has been stripped of its material covering and has shed bodily chatter and all the passions that empty, false assumptions generate, and has put off fleshly desires, must be consecrated to the light. Most people, however, clothe themselves in mortality like snails, and curl up around their own excesses like hedgehogs; they conceive of the blessed, immortal God in the same way they think of themselves. It has escaped their notice—even if they live close to us—that God has given us countless gifts of which He Himself has no share: being unbegotten, He has no birth; needing nothing, He requires no nourishment; abiding in equality, He knows no growth; being immortal and ageless, He enjoys a good old age and a good death. Therefore no one should suppose that hands, feet, mouth, eyes, entrances, exits, organs, or threats are passions of God, as they are spoken of among the Hebrews; by no means. It is more proper to allegorize some of these names, which we will clarify in due course as our discussion proceeds.

"Wisdom is the panacea for all things," Callimachus writes in his epigrams; "one wise man springs from another, both in the past and in the present," says Bacchylides in his Paeans, for it is not easy to find the gates of unspoken words. Isocrates, in his Panathenaic Oration, asks what kind of people he calls well‑educated, and he answers: first, those who deal well with the circumstances that confront them each day and possess a good reputation in their times, able to aim for the most part at what is advantageous; then, those who always converse properly and justly with those who approach them, and who bear the unpleasantness and heaviness of others easily and readily, while presenting themselves to their companions as light and moderate as possible; also, those who master their pleasures and are not overly defeated by misfortunes, but conduct themselves bravely in them, proving worthy of the nature in which we share; and fourth, which is most important, those who are not corrupted by good fortune, nor become arrogant, but remain in the order of those who think rightly. He then adds the conclusion of his speech: those who possess a disposition of soul well‑suited not to only one of these things but to all of them—I call these people wise, perfect men, and possessors of every virtue. Do you see how the Greeks, even though they do not know how to know, extol the cognitive life? They do not even dream of what knowledge is. If, then, it has been agreed that knowledge is our rational food, blessed are those who hunger and thirst for truth, for they will be filled with eternal food (Matthew 5:6). The philosopher Euripides, on the stage, is found to harmonize with what has been said, not knowing how to indicate the Father and the Son simultaneously: "To you who care for all things I bring a drink‑offering and a mixing bowl, Zeus—whether you are called Hades or by another name—you who accept a bloodless sacrifice, full of all fruitfulness." For Christ is a bloodless, whole sacrifice for us. And that he speaks without knowing the Savior, he will make clear by adding: "For you wield the scepter of Zeus among the heavenly gods, and you share the rule of Hades among the earthly ones." Then he says outright: "Send the souls of the dead to the light, so that those who wish to learn may know from what source they sprang, what is the root of evils, and what they must seek, having sacrificed, to find rest from their labors." It is not without reason, then, that purifications are the beginning of the mysteries among the Greeks, just as the bath is among the barbarians.

greek: Θυσία δὲ ἡ τῷ θεῷ δεκτὴ σώματός τε καὶ τῶν τούτου παθῶν ἀμετανόητος χωρισμός. ἡ ἀληθὴς τῷ ὄντι θεοσέβεια αὕτη. καὶ μή τι εἰκότως μελέτη θανάτου διὰ τοῦτο εἴρηται τῷ Σωκράτει ἡ φιλοσοφία· ὁ γὰρ μήτε τὴν ὄψιν παρατιθέμενος ἐν τῷ διανοεῖσθαι μήτε τινὰ τῶν ἄλλων αἰσθήσεων ἐφελκόμενος, ἀλλ’ αὐτῷ καθαρῷ τῷ νῷ τοῖς πράγμασιν ἐντυγχάνων τὴν ἀληθῆ φιλοσοφίαν μέτεισιν. τοῦτο ἄρα βούλεται καὶ τῷ Πυθαγόρᾳ ἡ τῆς πενταετίας σιωπή, ἣν τοῖς γνωρίμοις παρεγγυᾷ, ὡς δὴ ἀποστραφέντες τῶν αἰσθητῶν ψιλῷ τῷ νῷ τὸ θεῖον ἐποπτεύοιεν. παρὰ Μωυσέως τοιαῦτα φιλοσοφήσαντες οἱ τῶν Ἑλλήνων ἄκροι. προστάσσει γὰρ τὰ ὁλοκαυτώματα δείραντας εἰς μέλη διανεῖμαι, ἐπειδὴ γυμνὴν τῆς ὑλικῆς δορᾶς γενομένην τὴν γνωστικὴν ψυχὴν ἄνευ τῆς σωματικῆς φλυαρίας καὶ τῶν παθῶν πάντων, ὅσα περιποιοῦσιν αἱ κεναὶ καὶ ψευδεῖς ὑπολήψεις, ἀποδυσαμένην τὰς σαρκικὰς ἐπιθυμίας, τῷ φωτὶ καθιερωθῆναι ἀνάγκη. οἱ δὲ πλεῖστοι τῶν ἀνθρώπων τὸ θνητὸν ἐνδυόμενοι καθάπερ οἱ κοχλίαι καὶ περὶ τὰς αὑτῶν ἀκρασίας ὥσπερ οἱ ἐχῖνοι σφαιρηδὸν εἱλούμενοι περὶ τοῦ μακαρίου καὶ ἀφθάρτου θεοῦ τοιαῦτα οἷα καὶ περὶ αὑτῶν δοξάζουσιν. λέληθεν δ’ αὐτούς, κἂν πλησίον ἡμῶν τύχωσιν, ὡς μυρία ὅσα δεδώρηται ἡμῖν ὁ θεός, ὧν αὐτὸς ἀμέτοχος, γένεσιν μὲν ἀγένητος ὤν, τροφὴν δὲ ἀνενδεὴς ὤν, καὶ αὔξησιν ἐν ἰσότητι ὤν, εὐγηρίαν τε καὶ εὐθανασίαν ἀθάνατός τε καὶ ἀγήρως ὑπάρχων. διὸ καὶ χεῖρας καὶ πόδας καὶ στόμα καὶ ὀφθαλμοὺς καὶ εἰσόδους καὶ ἐξόδους καὶ ὀργὰς καὶ ἀπειλὰς μὴ πάθη θεοῦ τις ὑπολάβῃ παρὰ Ἑβραίοις λέγεσθαι, μηδαμῶς, ἀλληγορεῖσθαι δέ τινα ἐκ τούτων τῶν ὀνομάτων ὁσιώτερον, ἃ δὴ καὶ προϊόντος τοῦ λόγου κατὰ τὸν οἰκεῖον καιρὸν διασαφήσομεν. ἦ πανακὲς πάντων φάρμακον ἁ σοφία, Καλλίμαχος ἐν τοῖς ἐπιγράμμασι γράφει· ἕτερος (δὲ) ἐξ ἑτέρου σοφὸς τό τε πάλαι τό τε νῦν, φησὶ Βακχυλίδης ἐν τοῖς Παιᾶσιν· οὐδὲ γὰρ ῥᾷστον ἀρρήτων ἐπέων πύλας ἐξευρεῖν· καλῶς ἄρα Ἰσοκράτης ἐν τῷ Παναθηναϊκῷ τίνας οὖν καλῶ πεπαιδευμένους; προθεὶς ἐπιφέρει· πρῶτον μὲν τοὺς καλῶς χρωμένους τοῖς πράγμασι τοῖς κατὰ τὴν ἡμέραν ἑκάστην προσπίπτουσι καὶ τὴν δόξαν ἐπιτυχῆ τῶν καιρῶν ἔχοντας καὶ δυναμένην ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ στοχάζεσθαι τοῦ συμφέροντος· ἔπειτα τοὺς πρεπόντως καὶ δικαίως ὁμιλοῦντας ἀεὶ τοῖς πλησιάζουσι καὶ τὰς μὲν τῶν ἄλλων ἀηδίας καὶ βαρύτητας εὐκόλως καὶ ῥᾳδίως φέροντας, σφᾶς δ’ αὐτοὺς ὡς δυνατὸν ἐλαφροτάτους καὶ μετριωτάτους τοῖς ξυνοῦσι παρέχοντας· ἔτι δὲ τοὺς τῶν μὲν ἡδονῶν κρατοῦντας, τῶν δὲ συμφορῶν μὴ λίαν ἡττωμένους, ἀλλ’ ἀνδρωδῶς ἐν αὐταῖς ἀναστρεφομένους καὶ τῆς φύσεως ἀξίως ἧς μετέχοντες τυγχάνομεν· τέταρτον, ὅπερ μέγιστόν ἐστι, τοὺς μὴ διαφθειρομένους ὑπὸ τῶν εὐπραγιῶν μηδ’ ἐξισταμένους αὑτῶν μηδὲ ὑπερηφάνους γινομένους, ἀλλ’ ἐμμένοντας τῇ τάξει τῶν εὖ φρονούντων. εἶτα ἐπιφέρει τὸν κολοφῶνα τοῦ λόγου· τοὺς δὲ μὴ μόνον πρὸς ἓν τούτων, ἀλλὰ πρὸς ἅπαντα ταῦτα τὴν ἕξιν τῆς ψυχῆς εὐάρμοστον ἔχοντας, τούτους φημὶ καὶ φρονίμους εἶναι καὶ τελείους ἄνδρας καὶ πάσας ἔχειν τὰς ἀρετάς. ὁρᾷς πῶς τὸν γνωστικὸν βίον καὶ Ἕλληνες, καίτοι μὴ εἰδότες ὡς ἐπίστασθαι χρή, ἐκθειάζουσι; τίς δ’ ἔστιν ἡ γνῶσις, οὐδὲ ὄναρ ἴσασιν. Εἰ τοίνυν λογικὸν ἡμῖν βρῶμα ἡ γνῶσις εἶναι συμπεφώνηται, μακάριοι τῷ ὄντι κατὰ τὴν γραφὴν οἱ πεινῶντες καὶ διψῶντες τὴν ἀλήθειαν, ὅτι πλησθήσονται τροφῆς ἀιδίου. πάνυ θαυμαστῶς ὁ ἐπὶ τῆς σκηνῆς φιλόσοφος Εὐριπίδης τοῖς προειρημένοις ἡμῖν συνῳδὸς διὰ τούτων εὑρίσκεται, πατέρα καὶ υἱὸν ἅμα οὐκ οἶδ’ ὅπως αἰνισσόμενος· σοὶ τῷ πάντων μεδέοντι χοὴν πέλανόν τε φέρω, Ζεὺς εἴτ’ Ἀίδης ὀνομαζόμενος στέργεις· σὺ δέ μοι θυσίαν ἄπυρον παγκαρπείας δέξαι πλήρη προχυτίαν. ὁλοκάρπωμα γὰρ ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἄπυρον θῦμα ὁ Χριστός. καὶ ὅτι τὸν σωτῆρα αὐτὸν οὐκ εἰδὼς λέγει, σαφὲς ποιήσει ἐπάγων· σὺ γὰρ ἔν τε θεοῖς τοῖς οὐρανίδαις σκῆπτρον τὸ Διὸς μεταχειρίζεις χθονίων τ’ Ἀίδῃ μετέχεις ἀρχῆς. ἔπειτα ἄντικρυς λέγει· πέμψον δ’ ἐς φῶς ψυχὰς ἐνέρων τοῖς βουλομένοις ἄθλους προμαθεῖν πόθεν ἔβλαστον, τίς ῥίζα κακῶν, τίνα δεῖ μακάρων ἐκθυσαμένους εὑρεῖν μοχθῶν ἀνάπαυλαν. οὐκ ἀπεικότως ἄρα καὶ τῶν μυστηρίων τῶν παρ’ Ἕλλησιν ἄρχει μὲν τὰ καθάρσια, καθάπερ καὶ τοῖς βαρβάροις τὸ λουτρόν.

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: We will address a little later the question of whether the philosophers' doctrines were found among the Hebrews, but first, as is fitting, we must speak of the times of Moses, through which it will be demonstrated beyond dispute that the Hebrew philosophy is the most ancient of all wisdom. Tatian has already treated these matters accurately in his *Against the Greeks*, and Cassian has also done so in the first of his *Exegetical Works*; nevertheless, this memorandum requires us to run through the relevant statements in their proper place. Apion the grammarian, surnamed Plistonicus, in the fourth book of his *Egyptian Histories* — though hostile toward the Hebrews, being Egyptian by birth, and having even composed a book against the Jews — mentions Amosis, king of the Egyptians, and the events of his reign, and cites Ptolemaeus of Mendes as a witness. Ptolemaeus writes: "Amosis, who became Inachus in the Argive reckoning, dug up Avaris," as recorded in his *Chronicles*. This Ptolemaeus was a priest; having set forth the deeds of the Egyptian kings in three complete books, he states that under Amosis, king of Egypt, the Jews made their exodus from Egypt under the leadership of Moses, from which it follows that Moses flourished in the time of Inachus. The most ancient of the Greek traditions are the Argolic ones, those stemming from Inachus, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus teaches in his *Chronicles*; and of these, the Attic traditions, which derive from Cecrops — who was two-natured and autochthonous, as Tatian says word for word — are forty generations later, while the Arcadian traditions, which derive from Pelasgus, are nine generations later.

greek: Καὶ περὶ μὲν τοῦ παρ’ Ἑβραίων τὰ τῶν φιλοσόφων ἐσκευωρῆσθαι δόγματα μικρὸν ὕστερον διαληψόμεθα, πρότερον δέ, ὅπερ ἀκόλουθον ἦν, περὶ τῶν κατὰ Μωυσέα χρόνων ἤδη λεκτέον, δἰ ὧν δειχθήσεται ἀναμφηρίστως πάσης σοφίας ἀρχαιοτάτη ἡ κατὰ Ἑβραίους φιλοσοφία. εἴρηται μὲν οὖν περὶ τούτων ἀκριβῶς Τατιανῷ ἐν τῷ Πρὸς Ἕλληνας, εἴρηται δὲ καὶ Κασσιανῷ ἐν τῷ πρώτῳ τῶν Ἐξηγητικῶν· ἀπαιτεῖ δὲ ὅμως τὸ ὑπόμνημα καὶ ἡμᾶς ἐπιδραμεῖν τὰ κατὰ τὸν τόπον εἰρημένα. Ἀπίων τοίνυν ὁ γραμματικός, ὁ Πλειστονίκης ἐπικληθείς, ἐν τῇ τετάρτῃ τῶν Αἰγυπτιακῶν ἱστοριῶν, καίτοι φιλαπεχθημόνως πρὸς Ἑβραίους διακείμενος, ἅτε Αἰγύπτιος τὸ γένος, ὡς καὶ κατὰ Ἰουδαίων συντάξασθαι βιβλίον, Ἀμώσιος τοῦ Αἰγυπτίων βασιλέως μεμνημένος καὶ τῶν κατ’ αὐτὸν πράξεων, μάρτυρα παρατίθεται Πτολεμαῖον τὸν Μενδήσιον. καὶ τὰ τῆς λέξεως αὐτοῦ ὧδε ἔχει· κατέσκαψε δὲ τὴν Ἀουαρίαν Ἄμωσις κατὰ τὸν Ἀργεῖον γενόμενος Ἴναχον, ὡς ἐν τοῖς Χρόνοις ἀνέγραφεν ὁ Μενδήσιος Πτολεμαῖος. ὁ δὲ Πτολεμαῖος οὗτος ἱερεὺς μὲν ἦν, τὰς δὲ τῶν Αἰγυπτίων βασιλέων πράξεις ἐν τρισὶν ὅλαις ἐκθέμενος βίβλοις κατὰ Ἄμωσίν φησιν Αἰγύπτου βασιλέα Μωυσέως ἡγουμένου γεγονέναι Ἰουδαίοις τὴν ἐξ Αἰγύπτου πορείαν, ἐξ ὧν συνῶπται κατὰ Ἴναχον ἠκμακέναι τὸν Μωσέα. παλαίτατα δὲ τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν τὰ Ἀργολικά, τὰ ἀπὸ Ἰνάχου λέγω, ὡς Διονύσιος ὁ Ἁλικαρνασσεὺς ἐν τοῖς Χρόνοις διδάσκει, τούτων δὲ † τεσσαράκοντα μὲν γενεαῖς νεώτερα τὰ Ἀττικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Κέκροπος τοῦ διφυοῦς δὴ καὶ αὐτόχθονος, ὥς φησι κατὰ λέξιν ὁ Τατιανός, ἐννέα δὲ τὰ Ἀρκαδικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Πελασγοῦ·

excerpts.author: Clement of Alexandria
english: That the word "pedagogy" literally means the leading of children is clear from the name itself; next we must examine the children whom Scripture praises, and then set the Pedagogue before them. We are those children; yet Scripture celebrates us in many ways and allegorizes us through a variety of names, transmuting the simplicity of faith. In the Gospel the Lord stood on the shore and called to his disciples, who were fishing, "Children, do you have any fish?" (John 21:5), addressing men already in a state of knowledge as children. Again, people brought children to him for a blessing through the laying on of hands, but the disciples tried to stop them. Jesus said, "Let the children come to me and do not hinder them, for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these" (Matthew 19:14). What this means the Lord himself explains: "Unless you turn and become like these children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven" (Matthew 18:3). He is not allegorizing regeneration here, but holding up the simplicity found in children as a pattern for us to imitate. The prophetic Spirit also singles out children: "The children went out to meet the Lord with palm and olive branches, crying, ‘Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!’" (Matthew 21:9). That cry is light, glory, and praise mingled with supplication to the Lord; for "Hosanna," when rendered into Greek, means exactly that. It seems to me that Scripture, by allegorizing this prophecy, reproaches the faint-hearted in the words, "Have you never read, ‘From the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise’?" (Matthew 21:16; Psalm 8:2). In the Gospel the Lord likewise opens the disciples’ eyes, urging them to attend to him as one already hastening to the Father. He makes his hearers more eager, foretelling that he will soon be taken from them, and shows how diligently they must grasp the truth while the Word has not yet been taken up into heaven. Once more, therefore, he calls them children: "Children, I am with you only a little longer" (John 13:33). And again he likens the kingdom of heaven to children sitting in the marketplaces who call out, ‘We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not mourn’ (Matthew 11:16–17), along with whatever else fits that picture. Not only does the Gospel think this way; prophecy agrees with it. David says, "Praise the Lord, you children; praise the name of the Lord" (Psalm 148:12–13). And Isaiah says, "Behold, I and the children whom God has given me" (Isaiah 8:18). Do you marvel, then, to hear that men among the nations are children to the Lord?

greek: Ὅτι μὲν οὖν ἡ παιδαγωγία παίδων ἐστὶν ἀγωγή, σαφὲς ἐκ τοῦ ὀνόματος· λοιπὸν δέ ἐστι τοὺς παῖδας ἐπιθεωρῆσαι, οὓς αἰνίττεται ἡ γραφή, εἶτα τὸν παιδαγωγὸν αὐτοῖς ἐπιστῆσαι. οἱ παῖδες ἡμεῖς· πολλαχῶς δὲ ἡμᾶς ἐξυμνεῖ πολυτρόπως τε ἀλληγορεῖ ὀνόμασι ποικίλοις τὸ ἀφελὲς τῆς πίστεως ἐξαλλάττουσα ἡ γραφή. ἐν γοῦν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ· »σταθείς«, φησίν, »ὁ κύριος ἐπὶ τῷ αἰγιαλῷ πρὸς τοὺς μαθητάς (ἁλιεύοντες δὲ ἔτυχον) ἐνεφώνησέν [τε], παιδία, μή τι ὄψον ἔχετε;« τοὺς ἤδη ἐν ἕξει τῶν γνωρίμων παῖδας προσειπών. »προσήνεγκάν τε αὐτῷ«, φησί, »παιδία« εἰς χειροθεσίαν εὐλογίας, κωλυόντων δὲ τῶν γνωρίμων, εἶπεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς »ἄφετε τὰ παιδία καὶ μὴ κωλύετε αὐτὰ ἐλθεῖν πρός με· τῶν γὰρ τοιούτων ἐστὶν ἡ βασιλεία τῶν οὐρανῶν.« τί βούλεται τὸ λεχθέν, αὐτὸς διασαφήσει ὁ κύριος λέγων »ἐὰν μὴ στραφῆτε καὶ γένησθε ὡς τὰ παιδία ταῦτα, οὐ μὴ εἰσέλθητε εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρανῶν,« οὐ τὴν ἀναγέννησιν ἐνταῦθα ἀλληγορῶν, ἀλλὰ τὴν ἐν παισὶν ἁπλότητα εἰς ἐξομοίωσιν παρακατατιθέμενος ἡμῖν. τοὺς παῖδας [ἡμᾶς] καὶ τὸ προφητικὸν ἐκλέγεται πνεῦμα· »δρεψάμενοι«, φησί, »κλάδους ἐλαίας ἢ φοινίκων οἱ παῖδες ἐξῆλθον εἰς ὑπάντησιν κυρίῳ καὶ ἐκέκραγον λέγοντες, ὡσαννὰ τῷ υἱῷ Δαβίδ, εὐλογημένος ὁ ἐρχόμενος ἐν ὀνόματι κυρίου,« φῶς καὶ δόξα καὶ αἶνος μεθ᾿ ἱκετηρίας τῷ κυρίῳ· τουτὶ γὰρ ἐμφαίνει ἑρμηνευόμενον Ἑλλάδι φωνῇ τὸ ὡσαννά. καί μοι δοκεῖ ἡ γραφὴ ταύτην αἰνιττομένη τὴν προφητείαν τὴν προειρημένην ἐν ὀνείδους μέρει τοῖς ῥᾳθύμοις ἐγκαλεῖν· »οὐδέποτε ἀνέγνωτε ὅτι ἐκ στόματος νηπίων καὶ θηλαζόντων κατηρτίσω αἶνον;« τοῦτό τοι καὶ ὁ κύριος ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ μυωπίζει τοὺς γνωρίμους, προσέχειν αὐτῷ παρορμῶν ὡς ἤδη σπεύδων πρὸς τὸν πατέρα, ὀρεκτικωτέρους παρασκευάζων τοὺς ἀκροατὰς μετ᾿ ὀλίγον ἀπεῖναι προμηνύων, ὡς δέον αὐτοῖς ἀποκαρπίζεσθαι τῆς ἀληθείας ἀφειδέστερον δηλῶν ὅσον οὐδέπω ἀπαίροντος εἰς οὐρανὸν τοῦ λόγου. πάλιν οὖν αὐτοὺς παιδία καλεῖ· φησὶ γὰρ »παιδία, ἔτι μικρὸν μεθ᾿ ὑμῶν εἰμι.« αὖθίς τε παιδίοις ὁμοιοῖ τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρανῶν »ἐν ἀγοραῖς καθημένοις καὶ λέγουσιν, ηὐλήσαμεν ὑμῖν καὶ οὐκ ὠρχήσασθε, ἐθρηνήσαμεν καὶ οὐκ ἐκόψασθε,« καὶ ὅσα ἄλλα τούτοις οἰκείως ἐπήγαγεν. καὶ οὔτι γε μόνον τὸ εὐαγγέλιον ταύτῃ φρονεῖ, ὁμοδοξεῖ δὲ αὐτῷ καὶ ἡ προφητεία. λέγει γοῦν Δαβὶδ »αἰνεῖτε, παῖδες, κύριον, αἰνεῖτε τὸ ὄνομα κυρίου.« λέγει δὲ καὶ διὰ Ἡσαΐου »ἰδοὺ ἐγὼ καὶ τὰ παιδία, ἅ μοι ἔδωκεν ὁ θεός.« Θαυμάζεις ἀκούων τοὺς ἄνδρας τοὺς ἐν ἔθνεσι παῖδας παρὰ κυρίῳ;

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Christ is the head of the man. Who is Christ? Is he not the author of the man? 'Head' stands for authority, and authority belongs only to the author. So of which man is he head? Certainly of the one the text immediately names: the man must not be veiled, since he is God's image. If he is the Creator's image — for the Creator, looking at his own Word, was about to make a man: 'Let us make man in our image and likeness' (Genesis 1:26) — how could I have another head, not the one whose image I am? When I am the Creator's image, there is no room in me for a different head. Why, then, should the woman have authority over the head? If it is because she was made from the man and for the man by the Creator's institution, then the apostle also enforced her discipline, deriving the reasons for it from that same institution. He adds, 'because of the angels.' Which angels? That is, whose angels? If they are the Creator's apostate angels, rightly so, that the face which scandalized them might bear a mark of humility and the veiling of beauty. But if they are angels of another god, why would he fear them, when even the Marcionites themselves do not desire women? We have often shown that the apostle ranks heresies among evils as an evil, and that those who flee heresies as evil are to be approved. Therefore we have already proven in the Gospel the truth of the Lord's body and blood against Marcion's phantom, and that every mention of judgment belongs to the Creator as the judging God — a point that runs through nearly the whole work. Now for spiritual gifts. I say this too: these things were promised by the Creator in Christ, under that rule — most just, I think — by which no one's revelation is to be believed except his whose promise has been proven. Isaiah declared: 'A shoot will come forth from the stump of Jesse, and a branch will grow from his roots, and the Spirit of the Lord will rest on him' (Isaiah 11:1-2). Then he lists the Spirit's qualities: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and piety; the spirit will fill him with the fear of the Lord. He portrays Christ as the flower, rising from the branch sprung from Jesse's root — that is, from the virgin of David's line, Jesse's son — in whom Christ was to possess the full substance of the Spirit, not as a later addition to one who had always been the Spirit of God even before the flesh. Otherwise you might argue the prophecy refers to that Christ who, as a mere man by David's lineage alone, would only later receive his God's Spirit. Rather, from the moment he flourished in flesh taken from David's stock, every operation of spiritual grace was to rest in him and cease for the Jews. The fact itself testifies: from then on nothing breathed the Creator's Spirit among them, once the wise architect, the prudent counselor, and the prophet were taken from Judea — so that it became: 'the law and the prophets until John.' Now see how he also foretold the charisms that would come after Christ was taken up into heaven: 'He ascended on high; he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men.' He says elegantly 'to the sons of men,' not to humanity at large, pointing us to the true sons of men, the apostles. For in the Gospel he says: 'I have begotten you,' and: 'My children, whom I am again in labor with' — and already now that promise of the Spirit is fulfilled, the one made through Joel: 'In the last days I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; your sons and daughters will prophesy, and on my male and female servants I will pour out my Spirit' (Joel 2:28-29). Certainly, if the Creator promised the grace of his Spirit for the last days, and Christ the dispenser of spiritual things appeared in the last days, as the apostle says: 'When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son,' and again: 'The appointed time has grown short' — it follows that this grace of the Spirit belongs to Christ the preacher, from the preaching of the last times. Finally, compare the apostle's list with Isaiah's. 'To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom' — Isaiah immediately places the spirit of wisdom. 'To another the word of knowledge' — here is the spirit of understanding and counsel. 'To another faith by the same Spirit' — here is the spirit of piety and fear of God. 'To another gifts of healing, to another miracles' — here is the spirit of might. 'To another prophecy, to another discernment of spirits, to another kinds of tongues, to another interpretation of tongues' — here is the spirit of knowledge. See the apostle conspiring with the prophet both in distributing the one Spirit and in specifying its operations. I can say: the same one who fitted the unity of diverse charisms to the many and varied members of our body shows himself Lord both of the human body and of the Holy Spirit. He did not want the merits of charisms to reside in the Spirit, any more than he placed them in the human body. He also taught the apostle to set love above all charisms by a chief commandment that Christ himself endorsed: 'You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your strength, and with all your soul, and your neighbor as yourself.' And when he recalls something written in the law — that the Creator would speak in other tongues and through other lips — that very recollection confirms the charism of tongues; nor can it appear here that an alien charism was confirmed by the Creator's preaching. Likewise, when he prescribes silence for women in the church so they do not speak even to learn — though he has already shown they have the right to prophesy, since he puts a veil on a prophesying woman — he takes the authority for the woman's subjection from the law, which, as I said once, he ought not to have known except to destroy it. But so we may move on from spiritual things, the facts themselves must prove which of us rashly claims his God and whether this can be opposed to our side. If the Creator promised in his Christ, not yet revealed, as destined only for the Jews, that he would have his operations in his Christ and his people in his time — then let Marcion produce the gifts of his god: some prophets who spoke not from human sense but from God's Spirit, who foretold the future and exposed the heart's secrets; let him produce a psalm, a vision, a spiritual prayer, at least in ecstasy, that is, in madness, if any interpretation of tongues accompanies it. Let him also prove that a woman prophesied among his own holier women. I say: if all these things come more easily from me and certainly align with the Creator's rules, dispositions, and disciplines, then beyond doubt Christ and the Spirit and the apostle belong to my God. My profession stands for whoever wishes to demand it.

latin: Caput uiri Christus est. quis Christus? qui non est uiri auctor? \'caput\' enim ad auctoritatem posuit, auctoritas autem non alterius erit quam auctoris. cuius denique uiri caput est? certe de quo subicit: uir enim non debet caput uelari, cum sit dei imago. igitur si creatoris est imago — ille enim Christum sermonem suum intuens, hominem futurum: faciamus, inquit, hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram — quomodo possum alterum habere caput, non eum, cuius imago sum? cum enim imago sim creatoris, non est in me locus capitis alterius. sed et quare mulier potestatem super caput habere debebit? si quia ex uiro et propter uirum facta est secundum institutionem creatoris, sic quoque eius disciplinam apostolus curauit, de cuius institutione causas disciplinae interpretatur. adicit etiam: propter angelos. quos? id est cuius? si creatoris apostatas, merito, ut illa facies, quae eos\' scandalizauit, notam quandam referat de habitu humilitatis et obscuratione decoris; si uero propter angelos dei alterius, quid ueretur, si nec ipsi Marcionitae feminas adpetunt? Saepe iam ostendimus haereses apud apostolum inter mala ut malum poni et eos probabiles intellegendos, qui haereses ut malum fugiant. Proinde panis et calicis sacramento iam in euangelio probauimus corporis et sanguinis dominici ueritatem aduersus phantasma Marcionis, sed et omnem iudicii mentionem creatori competere, ut deo iudici, toto paene opere tractatum est. Nunc de spiritalibus. dico haec quoque, in Christum a creatore promissa ***, sub illa praescriptione, iustissima opinor, qua non alterius credenda sit exhibitio, quam cuius probata fuerit repromissio. pronuntiauit Esaias: prodibit uirga de radice Iesse, et flos [de radice] ascendet de uirga, et requiescet super eum spiritus dei. dehinc species eius enumerat: spiritus sapientiae et intellegentiae, spiritus consilii et ualentiae, spiritus agnitionis et religionis, spiritus eum replebit timoris dei. Christum enim in floris figura ostendit, oriturum ei uirga profecta de radice Iesse, id est uirgine generis Dauid, filii Iesse, in quo Christo consistere haberet tota substantia spiritus, non quasi postea obueutura illi, qui semper spiritus dei fuerit, ante carnem quoque, - ne ex hoc argumenteris prophetiam ad eum Christum pertinere, qui ut homo tantum ex solo censu Dauid postea consecuturus sit dei sui spiritum, — sed quoniam exinde, quo floruisset in carne sumpta ex stirpe Dauid, requiescere in illo haberet omnis operatio gratiae spiritalis et concessare et finem facere, quantum ad Iudaeos; sicut et res ipsa testatur, nihil exinde spirante penes illos spiritu creatoris, ablato a Iudaea sapiente et prudente architecto et consiliario et propheta, ut hoc sit: lex et prophetae usque ad Iohannem. accipe nunc, quomodo et a Christo in caelum recepto charismata obuentura pronuntiarit: ascendit in sublimitatem, id est in caelum; captiuam duxit captiuitatem, id est mortem uel humanam seruitutem; data dedit filiis hominum, id est donatiua, quae charismata dicimus. eleganter \'filiis hominum\' ait, non passim (hominibus\\ nos ostendens filios hominum, id est uere hominum, apostolorum. in euangelio enim, inquit, ego uos generaui, et: filii mei, quos parturio rursus, iam nunc et illa promissio spiritus absoluta, facta per Iohelem: in nouissimis temporibus effundam de meo spiritu in omnem carnem, et prophetabunt filii filiaeque eorum, et super seruos et ancillas meas de meo spiritu -effundam. et utique si in nouissimos dies gratiam spiritus creator repromisit, Christus autem spiritalium dispensator in nouissimis diebus apparuit dicente apostolo: at ubi tempus expletum est, misit deus filium suum, et rursus: quia tempus iam in collecto est, apparet et de temporum ultimorum praedicatione hanc gratiam spiritus ad Christum praedicatoris pertinere. compara denique species apostoli et Esaiae. alii, inquit, datur per spiritum sermo sapientiae: statim et Esaias sapientiae spiritum posuit; alii sermo scientiae: hic erit sermo intellegentiae et consilii; alii fides in eodem spiritu: hic erit spiritus religionis et timoris dei; alii donum curationum, alii uirtutum: hic erit ualentiae spiritus; alii prophetia, alii distinctio spirituum, alii genera linguarum, alii interpretatio linguarum: hic erit agnitionis spiritus. uide apostolum et in distributione facienda unius spiritus et in specialitate interpretanda prophetae conspirantem. possum dicere: ipsum quod corporis nostri per multa et diuersa membra unitatem charismatum uariorum compagini adaequauit, eundem et corporis humani et spiritus sancti dominum ostendit, qui merita charismatum noluerit esse in corpore spiritus, quae nec (membrorum) in corpore humano collocauit, qui de dilectione quoque omnibus charismatibus praeponenda apostolum instruxerit principali praecepto quod probauit et Christus: diliges dominum de totis praecordiis et totis uiribus et tota anima et proximum tibi tamquam te. et si quod in lege scriptum esset commemorat in aliis linguis et in aliis labiis locuturum creatorem, cum hac commemoratione charisma linguarum confirmat, nec hic potest uideri alienum charisma creatoris praedicatione confirmasse. aeque praescribens silentium mulieribus in ecclesia, ne quid discendi dumtaxat gratia loquantur, — ceterum prophetandi ius et illas habere iam ostendit, cum mulieri etiam prophetanti uelamen imponit — ex lege accipit subiciendae feminae auctoritatem, quam, ut semel dixerim, nosse non debuit nisi in destructionem. Sed ut iam a spiritalibus recedamus, res ipsae probare debebunt, quis nostrum temere deo suo uindicet et an nostrae parti possit opponi haec, et si creator repromisit in suum Christum nondum reuelatum, ut Iudaeis tantum destinatum, suas habitura in suo tempore in suo Christo et in suo populo operationes. exhibeat itaque Marcion dei sui dona, aliquos prophetas, qui tamen non de humano sensu, sed de dei spiritu sint locuti, qui et futura praenuntiarint et cordis occulta traduxerint; edat aliquem psalmum, aliquam uisionem, aliquam orationem, dumtaxat spiritalem, in ecstasi, id est in amentia, si qua linguae interpretatio accessit; probet mihi etiam mulierem apud se prophetasse ex illis suis sanctioribus feminis magnis, dicam: si haec omnia facilius a me proferuntur et utique conspirantia regulis et dispositionibus et disciplinis creatoris, sine dubio dei mei erit et Christus et spiritus et apostolus. habet professionem meam qui uoluerit eam exigere.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: The sacrament of our water is a blessed thing: through it we are washed clean of the sins that sprang from our original blindness and set free for eternal life. This treatise will not sit idle; it instructs both those undergoing the most rigorous formation and those who rest content with simple belief, never having probed the rationale behind the traditions, and who therefore carry a probable faith that remains untested through their own ignorance. And so, just recently, a certain viper of the Caian heresy, armed with its most poisonous doctrine, has seized many people, above all by destroying Baptism. This follows nature perfectly: for vipers, asps, and even king snakes habitually haunt dry, waterless places. But we are little fish, born in our ΙΧΘΥΣ Jesus Christ, and we survive only by staying in the water. Thus the monstrous Quintilla—who did not even possess a legitimate right to teach—knew exactly how to kill the little fish: by dragging them out of the water.
