latin: Felix sacramentum aquae nostrae qua abluti delictis pristinae caecitatis, in vitam aeternam liberamur. Non erit otiosum digestum istud, instruens tam eos qui cum maxime formantur, quam et illos qui simpliciter credidisse contenti, non exploratis rationibus traditionum, intentatam probabilem fidem per imperitiam portant: atque adeo nuper conversata istic quaedam de Caiana haeresi vipera venenatissima doctrina sua plerosque rapuit, imprimis Baptismum destruens. Plane secundum naturam: nam fere viperae, et aspides, ipsique reguli serpentes arida et inaquosa sectantur. Sed nos pisciculi secundum ΙΧΘΥΝ nostrum Jesum Christum in qua nascimur, nec aliter quam in aqua permanendo salvi sumus. Ita Quintillia monstrosissima, cui nec integre quidem docendi jus erat, optime norat pisciculos necare, de aqua auferens.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: We have said what our modest abilities allowed about everything that constitutes the religion of Baptism; now I will move on, as best I can, to its remaining aspect, dealing with certain minor questions. The Baptism announced by John already faced a question posed by the Lord himself to the Pharisees: was that Baptism heavenly, or truly earthly? They could not give a consistent answer, because they did not understand, because they did not believe. We, furthermore, can assess it with only as much understanding as we have faith: that Baptism was indeed divine, but by command, not by power. We read that John was sent by the Lord into this office, yet human in condition. For he exhibited nothing heavenly, but served heavenly things—specifically, he was put in charge of repentance, which lies within human power. Finally, the teachers of the law and the Pharisees, who refused to believe, did not even practice repentance. Now, if repentance is human, then Baptism of the same nature had to be human as well; otherwise it would have granted both the Holy Spirit and the remission of sins, if it were heavenly. But it forgives neither sin nor grants the Spirit—God alone does that. Even the Lord himself, unless he had first ascended to the Father, denied in another way that the Spirit would descend. What the Lord was not yet conferring, a servant certainly could not provide. So much so that later we find in the Acts of the Apostles that those who had John's Baptism had not received the Holy Spirit, whom they did not even know by hearing; therefore it was not heavenly, because it did not exhibit heavenly things. Since the very thing that was heavenly in John, the spirit of prophecy, failed after the transfer of the whole Spirit into the Lord—so much so that he who had predicted, he who had designated the Coming One, afterwards inquired whether he himself had sent him. Therefore, Baptism was administered for repentance, as a candidate for the remission and sanctification in Christ that would follow. For what he preached—a Baptism of repentance for the remission of sins—was announced for a future remission. Indeed, repentance precedes, remission follows, and this is to prepare the way: he who prepares does not himself perfect, but procures perfection for another. He himself professes that his things are not heavenly, but Christ's, saying: 'He who is from the earth speaks from the earth; he who comes from above is above all' (John 3:31). Also, to baptize only in repentance; soon to come is the one who will baptize in Spirit and fire. Clearly, because the true and stable faith of water by which one is baptized for salvation; but the simulated and weak faith is baptized in fire for judgment.

latin: Diximus, quantum mediocritati nostrae licuit, de universis quae Baptismi religionem struunt; nunc ad reliquum statum ejus, aeque ut potero, progrediar de quaestiunculis quibusdam. Baptismus ab Joanne denuntiatus jam tunc habuit quaestionem ab ipso quidem Domino propositam Pharisaeis, coelestisne is Baptismus esset, an vero terrenus? De quo illi non valuerunt constanter respondere, utpote non intelligentes, quia non credentes. Nos porro quantula fide sumus, tantulo et intellectu possumus aestimare, divinum quidem eum Baptismum fuisse, mandatu tamen, non et potestate, quod et Joannem a Domino missum legimus in hoc munus caeterum humanum conditione. Nihil enim coeleste praestabat, sed coelestibus praeministrabat, poenitentiae scilicet praepositus, quae est in hominis potestate. Denique legis doctores et Pharisaei, qui credere noluerunt, nec poenitentiam egere. Quod si poenitentia humanum est, et Baptismus ipsius ejusdem conditionis fuerit necesse est; aut daret et Spiritum Sanctum et remissionem delictorum, si coelestis fuisset. Sed neque peccatum dimittit, neque Spiritum indulget, nisi Deus solus. Etiam ipse Dominus, nisi ipse prius ascenderet ad Patrem, aliter negavit, Spiritum descensurum. Id quod Dominus nondum conferebat, servus utique praestare non posset. Adeo postea in Actis apostolorum invenimus, quoniam qui Joannis Baptismum habebant, non accepissent Spiritum sanctum, quem ne auditu quidem noverant: ergo non erat coeleste, quod coelestia non exhibebat: cum ipsum quod coeleste in Joanne fuerat, spiritus prophetiae, post totius spiritus in Dominum translationem usque adeo defecerit, ut quem praedicaverat, quem advenientem designaverat, postmodum, an ipse esset miserit sciscitatum. Agebatur itaque Baptismus poenitentiae, quasi canditatus remissionis et sanctificationis in Christo subsecuturae. Nam quod praedicabat Baptismum poenitentiae in remissionem delictorum, in futuram remissionem enuntiatum est. Siquidem poenitentia antecedit, remissio subsequitur, et hoc est viam praeparare: qui autem praeparat, non idem ipse perficit, sed alii perficiendum procurat. Ipse profitetur sua non esse coelestia, sed Christi, dicendo: Qui de terra est, de terra loquitur: qui de supernis venit, super omnes est. Item, in sola poenitentia tinguere; venturum mox, qui tingueret in spiritu et igni. Scilicet, quia vera et stabilis aquae fides qua tinguitur in salutem; simulata autem et infirma, igni tinguitur in judicium.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: When the rule is laid down that no one attains salvation without Baptism, based on the Lord's own pronouncement—"Unless someone is born of water, he will not have life" (John 3:5)—some people raise scrupulous, or rather reckless, objections: how can the Apostles qualify for salvation under that rule, since we do not find them baptized in the Lord, except for Paul? Indeed, since Paul alone among them put on the Baptism of Christ, either the verdict on the danger facing the rest, who lack Christ's water, must be prejudged so the rule stands, or the rule itself must be scrapped if salvation is also established for the unbaptized. I have heard such arguments, with the Lord as my witness, so no one may think me so lost as to stir them up voluntarily out of a lust for writing that only sows scruples in others. And now I will answer, as best I can, those who deny the Apostles were baptized.

If the Apostles had undergone the human baptism of John and desired the Lord's baptism, since the Lord Himself had defined there is only one Baptism, saying to Peter when he refused to be washed: "He who has been washed once has no need to be washed again"—a statement He would never have made to someone who had never been baptized at all—then that is the evident proof against those who strip the Apostles even of John's Baptism, just to destroy the sacrament of water. Can it be believed that the way of the Lord was then being prepared in those persons, that is, the Baptism of John, who were destined to open the way of the Lord throughout the whole world? The Lord Himself, who owed no debt of repentance, was baptized; was it not necessary for sinners? So what? Were the others not baptized? But they were not Christ's companions; they were rivals of the faith, teachers of the law, and Pharisees. From this it is also suggested that, when those who opposed the Lord refused to be baptized, those who followed the Lord were baptized, and did not share the taste of their rivals—especially when the Lord to whom they clung extolled John in testimony, saying: "No one is greater among those born of women than John the Baptist."

Others forcibly argue that the Apostles then fulfilled the role of Baptism when they were sprinkled and covered by waves in the boat, and that Peter himself was sufficiently immersed when he walked on the sea. In my opinion, however, it is one thing to be sprinkled or overwhelmed by the violence of the sea, and another to be baptized by the discipline of religion. Moreover, that boat represented the figure of the Church, which is tossed in the sea—that is, the world—by waves—that is, persecutions and temptations—while the Lord sleeps, as it were, in patience, until He is roused by the prayers of the Saints in the last days, restrains the world, and grants tranquility to His own. Now, whether the Apostles were baptized in some way or remained unbaptized, and whether the Lord's saying about one washing, spoken through Peter's person, applies only to us, it is still far too reckless to speculate on the Apostles' salvation. For them, the privilege of the first calling, and from then on of intimate familiarity, could confer the compendium of Baptism. They followed the One who promised salvation to every believer: "Your faith has saved you," He said, and "Your sins are forgiven"—certainly to the believer, not to the baptized. If that was lacking to the Apostles, I do not know what faith they possessed; with a single word of the Lord, the tax collector rose and abandoned his post; he deserted his father, his boat, and the trade by which he sustained his life; he disregarded his father's funeral: he fulfilled that supreme commandment of the Lord—"Whoever prefers father or mother to me is not worthy of me"—before he had even heard it.

latin: Cum vero praescribitur nemini sine Baptismo competere salutem, ex illa maxime pronuntiatione Domini, qui ait: Nisi natus ex aqua quis erit, non habet vitam, suboriuntur scrupulosi, imo temerarii retractatus quorumdam, quomodo ex ista praescriptione Apostolis salus competat, quos tinctos non invenimus in Domino, praeter Paulum. Imo cum Paulus solus ex illis Baptismum Christi induerit, aut praejudicatum esse de caeterorum periculo, qui careant aqua Christi, ut praescriptio salva sit, aut rescindi praescriptionem, si etiam non tinctis salus statuta est. Audivi, Domino teste, ejusmodi, ne quis me tam perditum existimet, ut ultro exagitem libidine styli, quae aliis scrupulum incutiant. Et nunc illis, ut potero, respondebo, qui negant Apostolos tinctos. Nam si humanum Joannis Baptismum inierant, et dominicum desiderabant quatenus unum Baptismum definierat ipse Dominus, dicens Petro perfundi nolenti: Qui semel lavit, non habet necesse rursum: quod utique non tincto non omnino dixisset: et haec est probatio exserta adversus illos, qui adimunt Apostolis etiam Joannis Baptismum, ut destruant aquae sacramentum. An credibile videri potest, in his personis viam tunc Domini praeparatam, id est Baptismum Joannis, quae ad viam Domini per totum orbem aperiendam destinabantur? Ipse Dominus, nullius poenitentiae debitor, tinctus est, peccatoribus non fuit necesse? Quid ergo? alii tincti non sunt? non tamen comites Christi, sed aemuli fidei, legis doctores et Pharisaei. Unde et suggeritur, cum adversantes Domino tingui noluerint, eos qui Dominum sequebantur, tinctos fuisse, nec cum aemulis suis sapuisse, maxime quando Dominus cui adhaerebant, testimonio Joannem extulisset, nemo, dicens, major inter natos foeminarum Joanne baptizatore. Alii plane satis coacte injiciunt tunc apostolos Baptismi vicem implesse cum in navicula fluctibus aspersi operti sunt; ipsum quoque Petrum per mare ingredientem satis mersum. Ut opinor autem, aliud aspergi vel intercipi violentia maris, aliud tingui disciplina religionis. Caeterum navicula illa figuram Ecclesiae praeferebat, quod in mari, id est saeculo, fluctibus, id est persecutionibus et tentationibus inquietatur Domino per patientiam velut dormiente, donec orationibus Sanctorum in ultimis suscitatus, compescat saeculum et tranquillitatem suis reddat. Nunc sive tincti quoquo modo fuerunt, sive illoti perseveraverunt, ut et illud dictum Domini, de uno lavacro sub Petri persona ad nos tantummodo spectet, de salute tamen Apostolorum satis temerarium est aestimare, quia illis vel primae allectionis, et exinde individuae familiaritatis praerogativa compendium Baptismi conferre posset. Cum illo, opinor, sequebantur illum, qui credenti cuique salutem pollicebatur: Fides tua te, aiebat, salvum fecit, et: Remittuntur tibi peccata, credenti utique, nec tamen tincto. Id si Apostolis defuit, nescio quorum fides: uno verbo Domini suscitatus teloneum dereliquit; patrem, et navem, et artem qua vitam sustentabat, deseruit; patris exequias despexit: summum illud Domini praeceptum: Qui patrem aut matrem mihi praetulerit, non est me dignus, ante perfecit quam audivit.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Those most wicked characters raise these questions. They claim baptism isn't necessary for people who have faith, since Abraham pleased God through the sacrament of faith without any water at all. But in everything, the later revelation settles the matter, and what comes after overrides what came before. Salvation used to be possible through bare faith before the Lord's passion and resurrection. Once faith expanded to include belief in his birth, passion, and resurrection, the sacrament was amplified—baptism was added as a seal, a kind of garment for faith that had previously stood naked and lacked power without its own law. The law of baptism was imposed, and a form was prescribed: "Go, make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matt 28:19). To that law was appended the definition: "Unless someone is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God" (John 3:5), which bound faith to the necessity of baptism. From then on, all who believed were baptized. Even Paul, the moment he believed, was baptized. This is exactly what the Lord commanded in that stroke of blindness: "Get up and go into Damascus; there you will be told what you must do" (Acts 22:10)—namely, be baptized, the one thing he still lacked. He had already learned and believed thoroughly that the Nazarene is the Lord, the Son of God.

latin: Hic ergo scelestissimi illi provocant quaestiones. Adeo, dicunt, Baptismus non est necessarius, quibus fides satis est, nam et Abraham nullius aquae nisi fidei sacramento Deo placuit. Sed in omnibus posteriora concludunt, et sequentia antecedentibus praevalent. Fuerit salus retro per fidem nudam ante Domini passionem et resurrectionem. At ubi fides aucta est credendi in nativitatem, passionem, resurrectionemque ejus, addita est ampliatio sacramento, obsignatio Baptismi vestimentum quodammodo fidei, quae retro erat nuda, nec potentiam habuit sine sua lege. Lex enim tinguendi imposita est, et forma praescripta. Ite, inquit, docete nationes, tinguentes eas in nomine Patris et Filii et Spiritus sancti. Huic legi collata definitio illa: Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua et spiritu, non intrabit in regnum coelorum, obstrinxit fidem ad Baptismi necessitatem. Itaque omnes exinde credentes tinguebantur. Tunc et Paulus ubi credidit, tinctus est. Et hoc est quod Dominus in illa plaga orbationis praeceperat: Exsurge, dicens, et introi Damascum, illic tibi demonstrabitur quid debeas agere, scilicet tingui, quod solum ei deerat. Alioquin satis didicerat atque crediderat Nazarenum esse Dominum Dei Filium.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: They drag the Apostle's own words into court: "Christ did not send me to baptize" (1 Cor 1:17), as if that single line cancels baptism altogether. If the argument holds, why did he baptize Gaius, Crispus, and the whole household of Stephanas (1 Cor 1:14-16)? Even granting that Christ did not commission him personally to baptize, he had ordered the other Apostles to do exactly that. Paul wrote these words to Corinth under pressure; schisms and party spirit were tearing the church apart, some claiming Paul, others Apollos. To keep the peace and avoid looking like he was feathering his own nest, the Apostle says he was sent to preach, not to baptize. Preaching comes first, baptism follows; and I would argue that whoever is authorized to preach is also authorized to baptize.

latin: Sed de ipso Apostolo revolvunt, quod dixerit: Non enim me ad tinguendum Christus misit, quasi hoc argumento Baptismus adimatur. Cur enim tinxit Gaium et Crispum et Stephanae domum? Quanquam etsi non eum miserat Christus ad tinguendum, tamen aliis Apostolis praeceperat tinguere. Verum haec pro conditione tunc temporis ad Corinthios scripta sunt, quoniam schismata et dissensiones inter illos movebantur, dum alius Paulo deputat, alius Apollo. Propter quod pacificus Apostolus, ne sibi omnia defendere videretur, non ad tinguendum ait se missum, sed ad praedicandum. Nam et prius est praedicare, posterius tinguere. Si prius praedicatum: puto autem licuit et tinguere cui licuit praedicare.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: I'm not sure there's anything left to air in the baptism debate, but I'll backtrack and cover what I skipped earlier so I don't look like I'm ducking the implications. There is exactly one baptism for us — grounded in the Lord's Gospel and the apostles' letters — because there is one Lord, one baptism, and one Church in heaven. But what rules apply to heretics? That's a fair question, since the call was handed to us. Heretics have zero share in our discipline; the very fact that we've cut communion with them brands them as outsiders. I'm not about to recognize in them what was commanded to me, because they don't worship the same God we do, nor the same Christ — that is, the identical one. So their baptism isn't the same either, because the source isn't the same. Since they don't have it rightly, they flat-out don't have it; you can't count what isn't there, and they can't receive what they don't possess. We've already hashed this out at length in Greek. The bottom line: we go through the washing once, sins are washed away once, because repeating it is out of the question. Meanwhile, the Jewish Israelite scrubs up daily because he gets dirty daily. To keep that cycle from infecting us, the rule was locked in: one washing. Happy the water that cleanses once and for all — no joke to fishermen, not fouled by constant grime, never turning around and re-defiling the very people it just washed.

latin: Nescio si quid amplius ad controversiam Baptismi ventilatur. Sane retexam, quod supra omisi, ne imminentes sensus videar intercidere. Unus omnino baptismus est nobis, tam ex Domini Evangelio, quam ex Apostoli litteris; quoniam unus Dominus et unum Baptismum et una Ecclesia in coelis. Sed circa haereticos sane quid custodiendum sit, digne quis retractet; ad nos enim editum est. Haeretici autem nullum habent consortium nostrae disciplinae, quos extraneos utique testatur ipsa ademptio communicationis. Non debeo in illis agnoscere quod mihi est praeceptum, quia non idem Deus est nobis et illis, nec unus Christus, id est idem. Ideoque nec Baptismus unus, quia non idem. Quem cum rite non habeant, sine dubio non habent, nec capit numerari, quod non habetur: ita nec possunt accipere, quia non habent. Sed de isto plenius jam nobis in graeco digestum est. Semel ergo lavacrum inimus, semel delicta diluuntur, quia ea iterari non oportet. Caeterum Israel Judaeus quotidie lavat, quia quotidie inquinatur. Quod ne in nobis quoque factitaretur, propterea de uno lavacro definitum est. Felix aqua quae semel abluit, quae ludibrio pescatoribus non est, quae non assiduitate sordium infecta, rursus, quos diluit, inquinat.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: We also have a second washing, one and the same thing: the washing of blood. The Lord speaks of it: 'I have a baptism to be baptized with,' He says, even though He had already been baptized (Luke 12:50). He came through water and blood, just as John wrote, so that He might be baptized with water, glorified with blood, and thus make us called by water, chosen by blood (John 19:34-35; 1 John 5:6). He poured out these two baptisms from the wound in His pierced side, so that those who believe in His blood would be washed with water, and those who have been washed with water would also drink His blood. This is the Baptism that represents a washing not accepted and renders it lost.

latin: Est quidem nobis etiam secundum lavacrum, unum et ipsum, sanguinis scilicet: de quo Dominus: Habeo, inquit, Baptismo tingui, cum jam tinctus fuisset. Venerat enim per aquam et sanguinem, sicut Joannes scripsit, ut aqua tingueretur, sanguine glorificaretur, proinde nos faceret aqua vocatos, sanguine electos. Hos duos baptismos de vulnere perfossi lateris emisit, quia qui in sanguinem ejus crederent, aqua lavarentur: qui aqua lavissent, etiam sanguinem potarent. Hic est Baptismus, qui lavacrum et non acceptum repraesentat, et perditum reddit.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: We finish by addressing who may give and receive Baptism. The bishop, as the highest priest, holds that right. Presbyters and deacons come next, but only with the bishop's authority, for the honor of the Church. Keep that order, and you keep the peace. Abandon it, and even laypeople claim the right. Since Baptism is received equally by all, it can be given equally by all — provided no bishop, presbyter, or deacon is already on hand. Learners must not be kept from the Lord's word. Therefore Baptism, equally God's judgment, may be exercised by everyone; yet laypeople bear a heavier obligation to modesty and reverence, since those virtues belong to the greater orders, lest they usurp the bishop's consecrated office. Rivalry breeds schism. "All things are permitted," the most holy Apostle said, "but not all things are expedient" (1 Corinthians 6:12). It suffices to act in necessity, when place, time, or the person's condition compels. Then the constancy of the one who helps is credited, because the peril of the one in danger demands it. Otherwise he bears guilt for a lost soul if he withholds what he was free to give. The petulance of the woman who usurped teaching will not win her the right to baptize either — unless some new beast like the first arises, so that just as she took Baptism away, another woman might confer it on her own. If some writings falsely ascribed to Paul are used to defend Thecla's example as license for women to teach and baptize, let them know: in Asia the presbyter who forged that scripture, padding it with Paul's name, was convicted and confessed he did it out of love for Paul, and was deposed. What could be nearer to faith than this — that the man who would not even let a woman learn steadily would grant her power to teach and baptize? "Let them be silent, and at home consult their husbands."

latin: Superest ad concludendam materiolam de observatione quoque dandi et accipiendi Baptismum commonefacere. Dandi quidem habet jus summus sacerdos, qui est episcopus. Dehinc presbyteri et diaconi, non tamen sine episcopi auctoritate, propter Ecclesiae honorem. Quo salvo, salva pax est. Alioquin etiam laicis jus est. Quod enim ex aequo accipitur, ex aequo dari potest, nisi episcopi jam aut presbyteri, aut diaconi vocantur, discentes, Domini sermo non debet abscondi ab ullo. Proinde et Baptismus aeque Dei census ab omnibus exerceri potest: sed quanto magis laicis disciplina verecundiae et modestiae incumbit, cum ea majoribus competat, ne sibi assumant dicatum episcopi officium episcopatus. Aemulatio schismatum mater est. Omnia licere, dixit sanctissimus Apostolus, sed non omnia expedire. Sufficiat scilicet in necessitatibus ut utaris, sicubi aut loci, aut temporis, aut personae conditio compellit. Tunc enim constantia succurrentis excipitur, cum urget circumstantia periclitantis. Quoniam reus erit perditi hominis, si supersederit praestare, quod libere potuit. Petulantia autem mulieris quae usurpavit docere, utique non etiam tinguendi jus sibi pariet, nisi si quae nova bestia evenerit similis pristinae: ut quemadmodum illa Baptismum auferebat, ita aliqua per se eum conferat. Quod si quae Paulo perperam adscripta sunt, exemplum Theclae ad licentiam mulierum docendi tinguendique defendunt; sciant in Asia presbyterum, qui eam scripturam construxit, quasi titulo Pauli de suo cumulans, convictum atque confessum id se amore Pauli fecisse, loco decessisse. Quam enim fidei proximum videretur, ut is docendi et tinguendi daret foeminae potestatem, qui ne discere quidem constanter mulieri permisit: Taceant, et domi maritos suos consulant.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: People whose job it is know that Baptism must not be accepted rashly. You hand your own to every petitioner, and that gift carries a title that counts just the same as almsgiving. Rather, you must grasp this: do not give holy things to dogs, and do not cast your pearls before swine, and do not impose hands easily, lest you become partners in strangers' sins (Matthew 7:6). If Philip baptized the eunuch so easily, consider that the Lord's manifest and evident dignity intervened. The Spirit had ordered Philip to take that road; the eunuch was found neither idle nor suddenly craving baptism, but he had gone to the temple to pray, impressed by divine Scripture. So it had to happen that the man to whom God sent an Apostle on his own initiative was seized; the Spirit then commanded Philip to join the eunuch's chariot, the Scripture of his faith turned up at the right moment, he was exhorted and taken up, the Lord was revealed, faith did not wait, water was not delayed, and the Apostle was snatched away with the task finished. Paul, too, was baptized quickly. He had quickly recognized that his host Simon was a vessel of election constituted by God. The dignity of God sends out its own prerogatives; every petition can both deceive and be deceived. Therefore, according to the condition and disposition of each person — even their age — delaying Baptism is more useful, especially with young children. Why impose danger on sponsors as well? They themselves can fail their promises through death, and be deceived by the outcome of a bad character. The Lord says: Do not prohibit them from coming to me (Matthew 19:14). So let them come while they grow up, let them come while they learn, while they are taught where they are coming; let them become Christians when they can know Christ. Why does innocent age rush to the remission of sins? One acts more cautiously in worldly matters, so that to whom earthly substance is not entrusted, divine substance may be entrusted; let them know how to seek salvation, so that you may seem to have given to the one who asks. For no lesser reason the unmarried are also to be delayed, in whom temptation lies ready both for virgins through maturity and for widows through wandering, until they either marry or are strengthened in continence. If anyone understands the weight of Baptism, they will fear the consequence more than the delay: intact faith is secure concerning salvation.

latin: Caeterum Baptismum non temere credendum esse sciunt, quorum officium est. Omni petenti te dato, suum habet titulum perinde ad eleemosynam pertinentem. Imo illud potius perspiciendum: Nolite dare sanctum canibus, et porcis projicere margaritas vestras, et manus ne facile imposueris, ne participes aliena delicta. Si Philippus tam facile tinxit eunuchum, recogitemus manifestam et exsertam dignationem Domini intercessisse. Spiritus Philippo praeceperat in eam viam praetendere; spado et ipse inventus est non otiosus, nec qui subito tingui concupisceret: sed ad templum orandi gratia profectus Scripturae divinae impressus. Sic oportebat deprendi, cui ultro Deus Apostolum miserat, ad quem rursus Spiritus, ut se curriculo eunuchi adjungeret, jussit, Scriptura ipsius fidei occurrit in tempore, exhortatus assumitur, Dominus ostenditur, fides non moratur, aqua non exspectatur, Apostolus perfecto negotio eripitur. Sed et Paulus revera cito tinctus est. Cito enim cognoverat Simon hospes vas eum esse electionis constitutum. Dei dignatio suas praemittit praerogativas; omnis petitio et decipere et decipi potest. Itaque pro cujusque personae conditione ac dispositione, etiam aetate cunctatio Baptismi utilior est: praecipue tamen circa parvulos. Quid enim necesse est, sponsores etiam periculo ingeri? quia et ipsi per mortalitatem destituere promissiones suas possunt, et proventu malae indolis falli. Ait quidem Dominus: Nolite illos prohibere ad me venire. Veniant ergo dum adolescunt, veniant dum discunt, dum quo veniant, docentur; fiant Christiani, cum Christum nosse potuerint. Quid festinat innocens aetas ad remissionem peccatorum? Cautius agetur in saecularibus, ut cui substantia terrena non creditur, divina credatur; norint petere salutem, ut petenti dedisse videaris. Non minore de caussa innupti quoque procrastinandi, in quibus tentatio praeparata est tam virginibus per maturitatem, quam viduis per vagationem, donec aut nubant, aut continentiae corroborentur. Si qui pondus intelligant Baptismi, magis timebunt consecutionem quam dilationem: fides integra secura est de salute.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Easter outranks Passover as the day for baptism, because the Lord's passion -- the very death we are plunged into -- has been accomplished, and the typology fits without strain: when Jesus was about to eat his final Passover, he sent the disciples ahead with the sign, "You will find a man carrying a water jar," and that water pointed to the place where the feast would be kept (Mark 14:13-15; Luke 22:10-12).

From that moment Pentecost opens a broad field for scheduling baptisms, since the risen Lord appeared repeatedly to his disciples then, the Holy Spirit's grace was poured out, and the hope of his return was signaled when the angels told the apostles, "He will come back in the same way you saw him go into heaven" (Acts 1:11) -- a promise stamped with Pentecost's own date.
Jeremiah clinches the double reference: "I will gather them from the ends of the earth on a feast day" (Jeremiah 31:8), naming both Passover and Pentecost, the latter being the feast day proper.
Even so, every day belongs to the Lord, every hour, every moment is fit for baptism; if the only difference is solemnity, grace itself makes no distinction.

latin: Diem Baptismo solemniorem Pascha praestat, cum et passio Domini in qua tinguimur, adimpleta est, nec incongruenter ad figuram interpretabitur, quod cum ultimum Pascha Dominus esset acturus, missis discipulis ad praeparandum, Invenietis, inquit, hominem aquam bajulantem Paschae celebrandae locum de signo aquae ostendit. Exinde Pentecoste ordinandis lavacris latissimum spatium est, quo et Domini resurrectio inter discipulos frequentata est, et gratia Spiritus sancti dedicata, et spes adventus Domini subostensa, quod tunc in coelos recuperato eo, Angeli ad apostolos dixerunt, sic venturum quemadmodum et in coelos conscendit utique in Pentecoste. Sed enim Jeremias cum dicit: Et congregabo illos ab extremis terrae in die festo, Paschae diem significat et Pentecostes, qui est proprie dies festus. Caeterum omnis dies Domini est, omnis hora, omne tempus habile Baptismo: si de solemnitate interest, de gratia nihil refert.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: But consider the sheer force of perversity: it aims to undermine faith or reject it outright, turning the very evidence that establishes faith into weapons against it. Nothing hardens human minds like the simplicity of divine works seen in action, and the magnificence promised in their effect. Here, too, because a man is plunged into water with such stark simplicity — no pomp, no novel apparatus, ultimately no expense — dipped amid a few words, and rises no cleaner than before, the promise of eternity strikes people as incredible. I am lying if the solemnities and mysteries of idols do not, by contrast, build their own credibility and authority on spectacle, stagecraft, and expense. Away with it, this wretched unbelief that denies God his own properties: simplicity and power. So what? Is it not a wonder that death is washed away by washing? Yet all the more it must be believed precisely because it is wonderful enough to be disbelieved. What kind of works should divine works be, if not beyond all wonder? We ourselves wonder, but we wonder because we believe. Unbelief, on the other hand, wonders and refuses to believe. It treats simple things as empty, magnificent things as impossible. And let it stand as you suppose: the divine pronouncement has already raced ahead to cover both points. God chose the foolish things of the world to shame its wisdom (1 Cor. 1:27), and the weak things — what is easy for God. For if God is both wise and powerful, which even passersby do not deny, he rightly establishes the materials of his operation in the opponents of wisdom and power — that is, in foolishness and impossibility. Since all power draws its cause from the very things that provoke it.

latin: Sed enim quanta vis est perversitatis ad fidem labefactandam, vel in totum non recipiendam, ut ex his eam impugnet, ex quibus constat. Nihil adeo est quod tam obduret mentes hominum, quam simplicitas divinorum operum quae in actu videtur, et magnificentia quae in effectu repromittitur: ut hic quoque, quoniam tanta simplicitate sine pompa, sine apparatu novo aliquo, denique sine sumptu homo in aqua demissus, et inter pauca verba tinctus, non multo vel nihilo mundior resurgit, eo incredibilis existimetur consecutio aeternitatis. Mentior, si non e contrario idolorum solemnia vel arcana, de suggestu et apparatu, deque sumptu, fidem et auctoritatem sibi exstruunt. Pro! misera incredulitas, quae denegas Deo proprietates suas, simplicitatem et potestatem. Quid ergo? nonne mirandum et lavacro dilui mortem? Atquin eo magis credendum, si, quia mirandum est, idcirco non creditur. Qualia enim decet esse opera divina, nisi super omnem admirationem? Nos quoque ipsi miramur, sed quia credimus. Caeterum incredulitas miratur, non credit. Miratur enim simplicia quasi vana, magnifica quasi impossibilia. Et sit plane ut putas, satis ad utrumque divina pronuntiatio praecucurrit: Stulta mundi elegit Deus ut confundat sapientiam ejus, et Praedifficitia penes homines, facilia penes Deum. Nam si Deus et sapiens et potens, quod etiam praetereuntes eum non negant, merito in adversariis sapientiae potentiaeque, id est in stultitia et impossibilitate materias operationis suae instituit. Quoniam virtus omnis ex his caussam accipit, a quibus provocatur.

english: Candidates for baptism must pray with frequent prayers, fasts, kneeling, all-night vigils, and a confession of all past sins, so that they may also reenact John's baptism—Scripture says, "They were baptized, confessing their sins" (Mark 1:5). We should count it a gain if we do not have to confess our injustices or shameful deeds in public; in doing so we simultaneously settle the old conflicts between flesh and spirit and lay up defenses against the temptations that will follow. "Watch and pray, lest you fall into temptation" (Matthew 26:41). That, I think, is exactly why the disciples were tempted: they fell asleep, so that they abandoned the arrested Lord, and the one who stayed by him and even used a sword went on to deny him three times. After all, it had already been said: "No one untested will attain the heavenly kingdom." The Lord himself, immediately after his baptism, was hemmed in by temptations for forty days while he fasted. Someone will object, "Then we too ought to fast right after baptism." And who forbids it, except the necessity of joy and the celebration of salvation? But the Lord, as I see it, turned the reproach of the figure of Israel back on himself. The people crossed the sea and were driven into the wilderness for forty years; though they were fed with divine food, they still remembered their bellies and throats more than God. Then the Lord, led away from the water into the desert, spent forty days fasting and showed that man does not live on bread alone but on the word of God, and that temptations arising from gluttony and excess are cut down by abstinence. Therefore blessed are those whom the grace of God awaits: when you come up from that most holy washing of new birth and stretch out your first hands to the Mother together with the brothers, ask the Father, ask the Lord for your peculiar gifts, your thanksgivings, the distributions of charisms—since it is said, "Ask and you will receive." For you have sought and found; you have knocked, and it has been opened to you. I ask only this: that when you ask, you also remember the sinner Tertullian.

latin: Ingressuros Baptismum, orationibus crebris, jejuniis et geniculationibus, et pervigiliis orare oportet, et cum confessione omnium retro delictorum, ut exponant etiam Baptismum Joannis, Tinguebantur, inquit, confitentes delicta sua. Nobis gratulandum est, si non publice confitemur iniquitates aut turpitudines nostras. Simul enim et de pristinis satisfacimus conflictatione carnis et spiritus, et subsecuturis tentationibus munimenta praestruimus. Vigilate et orate, inquit, ne incidatis in tentationem. Et ideo, credo, tentati sunt, quoniam obdormierunt, ut apprehensum Dominum destituerint, et qui cum eo perstiterit, et gladio sit usus, ter etiam negaverit: nam et praecesserat dictum: Neminem intentatum regna coelestia consecuturum. Ipsum Dominum post lavacrum statim tentationes circumsteterunt quadraginta diebus jejuniis functum. Ergo et nos, dicet aliquis, a lavacro potius jejunare oportet. Et quis enim prohibet, nisi necessitas gaudii et gratulatio salutis? Sed Dominus, quantum existimo, de figura Israelis exprobrationem in ipsum retorsit. Namque populus mare transgressus, et in solitudine translatus per quadraginta annos, illic cum divinis aleretur, nihilominus ventris et gulae meminerat, quam Dei. Deinde Dominus post aquam segregatus in deserto quadraginta dierum jejunia emensus, ostendit non pane vivere hominem Dei, sed Dei verbo: tentationesque plenitudini et immoderantiae ventris appositas abstinentia elidi. Igitur benedicti quos gratia Dei expectat. cum de illo sanctissimo lavacro novi natalis ascenditis, et primas manus apud Matrem cum fratribus aperitis, petite de Patre, petite de Domino, peculia, gratias, distributiones charismatum, subjiciente, Petite et accipietis, inquit. Quaesistis enim et invenistis; pulsastis, et apertum est vobis. Tantum oro, ut cum petitis etiam Tertulliani peccatoris memineritis.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Mindful of that pronouncement as if it were a binding rule, we nevertheless address how foolish and impossible it is for water to be reformed. What, after all, has this substance done to merit so great an office of dignity? In my view, we must demand the credentials of the liquid element—and they are abundant, stretching back to the very beginning. One of them is this: before the world was even sketched out, while it still lay unpolished, water was already at rest with God. "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth." The earth was formless and empty, darkness covered the deep, and the Spirit of God hovered over the waters (Genesis 1:1-2). So take note, human being: first, venerate the antiquity of water, because it is an ancient substance; second, venerate its dignity, because it served as the seat of the divine Spirit—more pleasing to Him than any other element at that time. After all, the darkness was still starless and shapeless, the abyss was gloomy, the earth unready, the heavens crude. Water alone, always a perfect material—joyful, simple, pure in itself—offered itself as a worthy vehicle for God.

And from that point on, the whole ordering of the world was established by God, so to speak, through the moderating agency of water. To suspend the heavenly firmament, He separated the waters in the middle; to make the dry land appear, He gathered the waters apart. Once the world was ordered through the elements and inhabitants were assigned, the first waters received the command to bring forth living souls. Since the first liquid produced life, it is no wonder that in Baptism waters know how to animate. Even the fashioning of man was completed with water's assistance. The material came from earth, yet it was not workable unless moist and supple—clay that the separated waters, before the fourth day, had tempered with surviving moisture. If I were to go on listing all or most of the things that attest this element's authority—how great its power and grace, how many its talents and offices, how vast its service to the world—I fear I would seem to be compiling praises of water rather than reasons for Baptism. Yet I could teach more fully that there is no room for doubt: if God has arranged this material in all His works and operations, He has also made it serve in His own sacraments—since what governs earthly life also procures heavenly life.

latin: Hujus memores pronuntiationis, tanquam praescriptionis, nihilominus quam stultum et impossibile sit aqua reformari tractamus. Quid utique ista materia tantae dignationis meruerit officium? Ut opinor, auctoritas liquidi elementi exigenda est. Atquin plurima suppetit, et quidem a primordio. Nam unum ex his est quae ante omnem mundi suggestum impolita adhuc specie penes Deum quiescebant: In primordio, inquit, fecit Deus coelum et terram. Terra autem erat invisibilis et incomposita, et tenebrae erant super abyssum, et spiritus Dei super aquas ferebatur. Habes, homo, imprimis aetatem venerari aquarum, quod antiqua substantia; dehinc dignationem, quod divini spiritus sedes, gratior scilicet caeteris tunc elementis. Nam et tenebrae totae adhuc sine cultu siderum informes, et tristis abyssus, et terra imparata, et coelum rude: solus liquor, semper materia perfecta, laeta simplex, de suo pura, dignum vectaculum Deo subjiciebat. Quid quod exinde dispositio mundi modulatricibus quodammodo aquis Deo constitit. Nam, ut firmamentum coeleste suspenderet, in medietate distinctis aquis fecit; et, ut terram aridam suspenderet, segregatis aquis expediit. Ordinato dehinc per elementa mundo cum incolae darentur, primis aquis praeceptum est animas proferre. Primus liquor quod viveret edidit ne mirum sit, in Baptismo, si aquae animare, noverunt. Nam ipsius quoque hominis figurandi opus, sociantibus aquis absolutum est. De terra materia convenit, non tamen habilis nisi humecta et succida, quam scilicet ante quartum diem segregatae aquae in stationem suam, superstite humore, limo temperarant. Si exinde universa vel plura prosequar quae de elementi istius auctoritate commemorem, quanta vis ejus aut gratia, quot ingenia, quot officia, quantum instrumentum mundo ferat; vereor ne laudes aquae potius, quam Baptismi rationes videar congregasse. Licet eo plenius docerem non esse dubitandum, si materiam, quam in omnibus rebus et operibus suis Deus disposuit, etiam in sacramentis propriis parere fecit; si quae vitam terrenam gubernat, et in coelesti procurat.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: That is enough on the points where the rationale for Baptism first comes into focus—beginning with the very pattern that, even then, foreshadowed the rite. The Spirit of God, who from the beginning hovered over the waters, was destined to remake those who would be dipped. The Holy One was borne over the holy element; or, if you prefer, the waters drew their sanctity from the One who hovered above them. Since any subject matter inevitably absorbs the quality of what hangs over it—especially the physical drawing from the spiritual, because spirit penetrates and indwells so easily by its subtlety—the nature of the waters was sanctified by the Holy One, and the waters themselves acquired the power to sanctify.

No one should ask: Are we baptized in those very same waters that existed at the start? Of course not—except insofar as the genus is one, even if the species are many. What belongs to the genus overflows into every species. So it makes no difference whether a person is washed in sea or pool, river or spring, lake or trough; nothing distinguishes those John baptized in the Jordan from those Peter baptized in the Tiber—unless the eunuch Philip baptized with happenstance water on the road somehow received more or less salvation. Therefore, all waters, by virtue of their original privilege, obtain the sacrament of sanctification once God is invoked. The Spirit immediately comes from heaven and rests upon the waters, sanctifying them from himself; thus sanctified, they drink in the power to sanctify.

True, the analogy fits the simple act: because sins pollute us like filth, we are washed with water. But sins do not appear on the flesh—no one carries the stain of idolatry, adultery, or fraud on the skin; they defile the spirit, which is the author of the sin. The spirit commands, the flesh serves; yet both share the guilt, the spirit for giving the order, the flesh for carrying it out. So when the waters are medicated, as it were, by the Angel's intervention, the spirit is washed bodily in the waters, and the flesh is cleansed spiritually in the same bath.

latin: Sed ea satis erit praecerpsisse, in quibus et ratio Baptismi recognoscitur prima illa, qua jam tunc etiam ipso habitu praenotabatur ad Baptismi figuram, Dei spiritum, qui ab initio supervectabatur super aquas, intinctos reformaturum. Sanctum autem utique super sanctum ferebatur; aut ab eo quod superferebatur, id quod ferebat, sanctitatem mutuabatur. Quoniam subjecta quaeque materia, ejus quae desuper imminet, qualitatem rapiat necesse est, maxime corporalis spiritalem, et penetrare et insidere facilem per substantiae suae subtilitatem. Ita de Sancto sanctificata natura aquarum, et ipsa sanctificare concepit. Nemo dicat: Numquid ipsis enim aquis tinguimur quae tunc in primordio fuerunt? non utique ipsis nisi ex ea parte, qua genus quidem unum, species vero complures. Quod autem generi attributum est, etiam in specie redundat. Ideoque nulla distinctio est, mari quis an stagno, flumine an fonte, lacu an alveo diluatur, nec quidquam refert inter eos quos Joannes in Jordane, et quos Petrus in Tiberi tinxit. Nisi et ille spado, quem Philippus inter vias fortuita aqua tinxit, plus salutis aut minus retulit. Igitur omnes aquae de pristina originis praerogativa sacramentum sanctificationis consequuntur, invocato Deo. Supervenit enim statim spiritus de coelis, et aquis superest, sanctificans eas de semetipso, et ita sanctificatae vim sanctificandi combibunt. Quanquam ad simplicem actum competat similitudo, ut, quoniam vice sordium delictis inquinamur, aquis abluamur. Sed delicta, sicut non in carne comparent, quia nemo super cutem portat maculam idololatriae, aut stupri, aut fraudis; ita ejusmodi in spiritu sordent, qui est auctor delicti. Spiritus enim dominatur, caro famulatur; tamen utromque inter se communicant reatum, spiritus ob imperium, caro ob ministerium. Igitur medicatis quodammodo aquis per Angeli interventum, et spiritus in aquis corporaliter diluitur, et caro in eisdem spiritaliter mundatur.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Foreign nations, devoid of any spiritual understanding, ascribe the same power to their idols, but they delude themselves with empty water. They even undergo initiation through a bath—dedicated to some Isis or Mithras—and they actually wash their own gods. Moreover, they sprinkle villages, houses, temples, and entire cities with water; at the Apollinarian and Eleusinian games they drench themselves thoroughly. They presume this earns them rebirth and immunity from their perjuries. Among the ancients, anyone who had defiled himself with homicide would expiate his guilt with purifying water. So if they boast of water's natural property alone—claiming it is the proper material for cleansing in the rites of purification—how much more truly will water deliver that power through God's authority, since He established its very nature? If they think religion sanctifies water, what religion surpasses that of the living God? Once that is acknowledged, we recognize here the devil's mimicry, aping the works of God, because he too practices a baptism among his followers. What a resemblance: the unclean one cleanses, the destroyer liberates, the condemned one absolves. He will inevitably wreck his own work, washing away the very sins he inspires. These facts stand as testimony for those who reject the faith: if they refuse to believe the things of God, why do they credit their counterfeits in the devil's camp? Do not unclean spirits also, without any sacrament, brood over waters at other times, mimicking that primordial brooding of the divine Spirit? Everyone knows the dark springs, the remote streams, the pools in baths, the channels in houses or cisterns, and the wells said to be seized—surely by the force of a harmful spirit. They call the drowned, the frenzied, and the hydrophobic—those whom waters have killed or driven to madness and terror. Why recount all this? So that no one may find it harder to believe the holy Angel of God attends the waters to temper them for human salvation, when the evil angel habitually exploits the profane use of the same element for human destruction. If an angel's intervention in water seems novel, it anticipated a future pattern. An angel descending stirred the pool of Bethesda; those seeking healing watched for it. Whoever managed to step in first ceased his suffering after the washing (John 5:4). That figure of bodily cure foreshadowed spiritual cure, following the rule that carnal realities always prefigure spiritual ones. As God's grace advanced among humanity, something greater was added to the water and the angel: they once healed bodily ailments, now they heal the spirit; they once procured temporal safety, now they remake eternal salvation; they once freed a single person once a year, now they preserve multitudes daily, death having been abolished through the washing away of sins. With guilt removed, punishment is also removed. Thus man is restored to God in His likeness—he who was originally made in God's image; the image lies in the likeness, the likeness in eternity. For he receives the Spirit of God, which he first received from God's breath but later lost through sin.

Caeterum villas, domos, templa totasque urbes aspergine circumlatae aquae expiant passim, certe ludis Apollinaribus et Eleusiniis tinguntur. Idque se in regenerationem et impunitatem perjuriorum suorum agere praesumunt. Item penes veteres quisquis se homicidio infecerat, purgatrice aqua se expiebat. Igitur si de sola natura aquis, quod propria materia sit abluendi in auspicia emundationis, blandiuntur, quanto id verius aquae praestabunt per Dei auctoritatem, a quo omnis natura earum constituta est? Si religione aquam medicari putant, quae potior religio, quam Dei vivi? quo agnito, hic quoque studium diaboli recognoscimus res Dei aemulantis, cum et ipse Baptismum in suis exercet. Quid simile? Immundus emundat, perditor liberat, damnatus absolvit. Suam videlicet operam destruet, diluens delicta quae inspirat ipse. Haec quidem in testimonium posita sunt repellentibus fidem, si minime credant rebus Dei, quarum affectationibus apud aemulum Dei credunt. Annon et alias sine ullo sacramento immundi spiritus aquis incubant, adfectantes illam in primordio divini spiritus gestationem? Sciunt opaci quique fontes, et avii quique rivi, et in balneis piscinae, et euripi in domibus vel cisternae, et putei, qui rapere dicuntur, scilicet per vim spiritus nocentis. Nam et enectos et lymphatos et hydrophobos vocant, quos aquae necaverunt, aut amentia vel formidine exercuerunt. Quorsum ista retulimus? Ne quis durius credat Angelum Dei sanctum aquis in salutem hominis temperandis adesse, cum Angelus malus profanum commercium ejusdem elementi in perniciem hominis frequentet. Angelum aquis intervenire si novum videtur, exemplum futuri praecucurrit. Piscinam Bethsaidam Angelus interveniens commovebat; observabant qui valetudinem querebantur. Nam si quis praevenerat descendere illuc, queri post lavacrum desinebat. Figura ista medicinae corporalis spiritalem medicinam canebat, ea forma, qua semper carnalia in figura spiritalium antecedunt. Proficiente itaque in hominibus gratia Dei, plus aquis et Angelo accessit: qui vitia corporis remediabant, nunc spiritum medentur: qui temporalem operabantur salutem, nunc aeternam reformant: qui unum semel anno liberabant, nunc quotidie populos conservant, deleta morte per ablutionem delictorum. Exempto scilicet reatu, eximitur et poena. Ita restituitur homo Deo ad similitudinem ejus, qui retro ad imaginem Dei fuerat; imago in effigie, similitudo in aeternitate censetur. Recipit enim illum Dei spiritum, quem tunc de afflatu ejus acceperat, sed post amiserat per delictum.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: We do not receive the Holy Spirit in the waters; rather, once we have been cleansed in the water under the Angel, we are prepared for the Holy Spirit. This pattern also appeared earlier. Just as John went before the Lord as a forerunner to prepare his ways, so the Angel, the arbiter of Baptism, clears the way for the coming Holy Spirit through the washing away of sins—a washing that faith obtains, sealed in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. If every word stands on the testimony of three witnesses, how much more does the very number of the divine names guarantee our confident hope, now that we possess those same three as guarantors of our faith and sponsors of our salvation through the blessing? And when both the profession of faith and the pledge of salvation are made under those three, the mention of the Church becomes unavoidable; for where the three are—that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—there is the Church, which is the body of the three.

Sic enim Joannes ante praecursor Domini fuit, praeparans vias ejus: ita et Angelus Baptismi arbiter superventuro Spiritui sancto vias dirigit ablutione delictorum, quam fides impetrat, obsignata in Patre, et Filio, et Spiritu sancto. Nam si in tribus testibus stabit omne verbum, quanto magis, dum habemus per benedictionem eosdem arbitros fidei, quos et sponsores salutis, sufficit ad fiduciam spei nostrae etiam numerus nominum divinorum? Cum autem sub tribus, et testatio fidei, et sponsio salutis pignerentur, necessario adjicitur Ecclesiae mentio; quoniam ubi tres, id est Pater et Filius et Spiritus sanctus, ibi Ecclesia, quae trium corpus est.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Afterward, we step from the bath and are anointed with blessed oil, following the ancient rite by which priests were anointed with oil from a horn. This goes back to Aaron, whom Moses anointed. From that practice comes the very name ‘Christ,’ from ‘chrism’ meaning anointing—a title that fitted the Lord because He was made spiritual, anointed with the Spirit by God the Father, just as Acts says: ‘They were gathered together in this city against Your holy Son, whom You anointed’ (Acts 4:27). In the same way, the anointing runs on our bodies but works in our spirits, just as Baptism itself is a bodily act—we are plunged in water—whose spiritual effect is that we are freed from sins.

latin: Exinde, egressi de lavacro, perungimur benedicta unctione de pristina disciplina, qua ungi oleo de cornu in sacerdotium solebant. Ex quo Aaron a Moyse unctus est: unde Christus dicitur, a chrismate quod est unctio, quae Domino nomen accommodavit, facta spiritualis, quia spiritu unctus est a Deo Patre, sicut in Actis: Collecti sunt enim vere in ista civitate adversus sanctum Filium tuum, quem unxisti. Sic et in nobis carnaliter currit unctio, sed spiritaliter proficit: quomodo et ipsius Baptismi carnalis actus, quod in aqua mergimur; spiritalis effectus, quod delictis liberamur.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: Then the hand is laid on, calling and inviting the Holy Spirit through a blessing. Human ingenuity may claim the right to summon a spirit into the water and animate the union of the baptized by placing hands on them, using some other spirit of great clarity. So will God not be allowed to modulate spiritual sublimity through holy hands in His own instrument? This also comes from the old sacrament, by which Jacob blessed his grandchildren Ephraim and Manasseh, the sons of Joseph, by laying hands on their heads and crossing them over—turning them obliquely toward himself so that, in distorting the figure of Christ, they already foreshadowed the future blessing in Christ (Genesis 48:14). Then that most holy Spirit descends willingly from the Father upon the purified and blessed bodies, over the waters of Baptism, as if recognizing His former seat, and rests there, having come down in the form of a dove upon the Lord, so that the nature of the Holy Spirit might be declared through an animal of simplicity and innocence—a dove that even physically lacks bile. And therefore: 'Be simple as doves,' He says; not even this command is without support from the preceding figure. For just as after the waters of the flood, by which ancient iniquity was purged, after Baptism, so to speak, the dove—a herald of heavenly wrath—announced peace to the earth when sent out from the ark and returned with an olive branch, a sign still held out among nations as a pledge of peace: by the same arrangement, the dove of the Holy Spirit flies to the spiritual effect on the earth, that is, on our flesh emerging from the washing after former sins, bringing the peace of God, sent from heaven where the Church is figured as the ark. But the world sins again, which makes Baptism compare poorly with the flood. And so it is destined for fire, just as the man who restores his sins after Baptism is; this too must be taken as a sign of our warning.

latin: Dehinc manus imponitur, per benedictionem advocans et invitans Spiritum sanctum. Sane humano ingenio licebit spiritum in aquam arcessere et concorporationem eorum, accommodatis desuper manibus, alio spiritu tantae claritatis animare; Deo autem in suo organo non licebit per manus sanctas sublimitatem modulari spiritalem? Sed est hoc quoque de veteri sacramento, quo nepotes suos ex Joseph Ephraim et Manassem Jacob, capitibus impositis et intermutatis manibus, benedixerit, et quidem ita transversim obliquatis in se, ut Christum deformantes, jam tunc portenderent benedictionem in Christum futuram. Tunc ille sanctissimus Spiritus super emundata et benedicta corpora libens a Patre descendit, super Baptismi aquas, tanquam pristinam sedem recognoscens, conquiescit, columbae figura delapsus in Dominum, ut natura Spiritus sancti declararetur per animal simplicitatis et innocentiae, quod etiam corporaliter ipso felle careat columba. Ideoque: Estote, inquit, simplices sicut columbae, ne hoc quidem sine argumento praecedentis figurae. Quemadmodum enim post aquas diluvii, quibus iniquitas antiqua purgata est, post Baptismum (ut ita dixerim) mundi pacem coelestis irae praeco columba terris adnuntiavit dimissa ex arca, et cum olea reversa; quod signum etiam apud nationes paci praetenditur: eadem dispositione spiritalis effectus terrae, id est carni nostrae emergenti de lavacro post vetera delicta, columba sancti Spiritus advolat, pacem Dei afferens, emissa de coelis, ubi Ecclesia est arca figurata. Sed mundus rursus delinquit, quo male comparetur Baptismus diluvio. Itaque igni destinatur, sicut et homo qui post Baptismum delicta restaurat, ut hoc quoque in signum admonitionis nostrae debeat accipi.

excerpts.author: Tertullian
english: How many natural defenses, how many gracious privileges, how many ritual solemnities, how many figures, prefigurings, and prayers have established the sacrality of water? First, when the people marched out of Egypt and crossed the sea, the water let them escape Pharaoh's power, then turned and drowned him with his entire army (Exodus 14:28). What figure could more clearly prefigure the sacrament of Baptism? Nations are freed from the world through water, leaving the devil, their former master, crushed beneath the waves. Again, when bitterness poisoned the water, Moses' wood healed it, restoring sweetness (Exodus 15:25). That wood was Christ, who from himself cures the toxic, bitter veins of our fallen nature with the waters of Baptism. This is the water that flowed from the rock that accompanied the people (Exodus 17:6). If the rock is Christ, then beyond doubt the water in Christ is blessed for Baptism. How vast is water's grace before God and his Christ for confirming Baptism! Christ is never without water, since he himself was baptized. He inaugurated the first display of his power at a wedding by turning water into wine (John 2:1-11). When he speaks, he invites the thirsty to his eternal water (John 4:14). When he teaches on love, he counts a cup of water offered to a brother among the works of love. At the well he regains his strength; he walks gladly on the water, crosses it, serves water to his disciples. He maintains the testimony of Baptism all the way to his passion. When he is handed over to the cross, water intervenes — Pilate's hands know it. When he is pierced, water bursts from his side — the soldier's lance knows it (John 19:34).

latin: Quot igitur patrocinia naturae, quot privilegia gratiae, quot solemnia disciplinae, figurae, praestructiones, precationes religionem aquae ordinaverunt? Primo quidem, cum populus de Aegypto libere expeditus, vim regis Aegypti, per aquam transgressus, evadit, ipsum regem cum totis copiis aqua exstinxit. Quae figura manifestior in Baptimi sacramento? Liberantur de saeculo nationes per aquam scilicet, et diabolum, dominatorem pristinum, in aqua oppressum derelinquunt. Item aqua de amaritudinis vitio in suum commodum suavitatis Mosei ligno remediatur. Lignum illud erat Christus, venenatae et amarae retro naturae venas insaluberrimas, aquas Baptismi, scilicet, ex sese remedians. Haec est aqua, quae de comite petra populo defluebat. Si enim petra Christus, sine dubio aqua in Christo Baptismum videmus benedici. Quanta aquae gratia penes Deum et Christum ejus est ad Baptismi confirmationem. Nunquam sine aqua Christus, siquidem et ipse aqua tinguitur. Prima rudimenta potestatis suae, vocatus ad nuptias, aqua auspicatur. Cum sermonem facit, sitientes ad aquam suam invitat sempiternam. Cum de agape docet, aquae calicem, fratri oblatum, inter opera dilectionis probat. Apud puteum vires resumit; super aquam incedit libenter, transfretat; aquam discentibus ministrat; perseverat testimonium Baptismi usque ad passionem; cum deditur in crucem, aqua intervenit, sciunt Pilati manus; cum vulneratur, aqua de latere prorumpit, scit lancea militis.

excerpts.author: Origen
english: The descent of the holy fathers into Egypt—that is, into this world—can be seen to have been granted by God’s providence for the illumination of others and the instruction of the human race, so that through them the rest of souls, once enlightened, might be helped. For to these fathers first were entrusted the oracles of God, since this alone is the race that is said to ‘see’ God; for that is what the name Israel means when interpreted. It follows, then, that what is told of the ten plagues striking Egypt so that God’s people might be let go, or of the events in the desert with the people, or of the tabernacle built from the contribution of all the people, or of the priestly garment woven, or of the vessels of ministry—all these, as it is written, contain a shadow and form of the heavenly things. Paul states plainly of them that they ‘serve as a copy and shadow of the heavenly things’ (Hebrews 8:5).

This same law also contains the statutes and ordinances by which one must live in the holy land. Warnings are set for those who transgress the law; likewise, for those who need purification, various kinds of purifications are prescribed, so that through them they may finally arrive at that one purification after which it is no longer permitted to be defiled.

The people themselves are brought to a numbering, yet not all. Childish souls do not yet have the time to be numbered by divine command; neither are those souls numbered that cannot become the head of another but are themselves subject to another as to a head, whom Scripture calls ‘women.’ They certainly are not enrolled in the number God commands; only those called ‘men’ are numbered, thereby showing that the former cannot be counted from outside but are included within those who are called men.

Especially, however, those come to the true numbering who are ready to march out to the battles of Israel, who can fight against those enemies and adversaries that the Son, seated at the right hand of the Father, subjects so that He may ‘destroy every principality and power’. Through the number of His soldiers—those who serve God and do not entangle themselves in worldly affairs—the kingdoms of the adversaries are overthrown. Around them are carried the ‘shields of faith,’ the ‘darts of wisdom’ are brandished, the ‘helmet of the hope of salvation’ shines, and the ‘breastplate of love’ fully guards the heart. Such soldiers, I think, are the ones indicated and prepared for battles of this kind, those who are commanded to be numbered in the divine books by God’s command.

Far more glorious and perfect are those who are said to have their ‘heads’ numbered. Those punished for their sins, whose bodies ‘fell in the desert,’ seem to resemble those who indeed progressed, but could not reach the end of perfection for various reasons: they are said to have ‘murmured,’ ‘worshipped idols,’ ‘committed fornication,’ or to have conceived such thoughts as it was certainly not permitted to conceive.

Nor do I consider empty that sacrament by which some, possessing many flocks and herds, anticipate and seize a place suitable for the pastures and nourishment of their flocks—a place the Israelite first defended with his right hand. When they ask Moses for it, they are separated beyond the streams of the Jordan and cut off from possession of the holy land. The Jordan can be seen to water and inundate thirsting souls and the senses adjacent to them, according to the form of the heavenly things.

Nor does it seem idle that Moses hears from God the things described in the Levitical law, while the people become hearers of Moses in Deuteronomy and learn from him what they could not hear from God. For this reason Deuteronomy is called the second law, because it seems to signify that, with the first law—which seems to have been given through Moses—having ceased, a second legislation is formed, handed down especially by Moses to Jesus, his successor; he is believed to preserve the form of our Savior, whose second law, that is the gospel precepts, brings all things to perfection.

We must consider, though, whether it might indicate something more: just as in Deuteronomy a more evident and manifest legislation is declared than in the earlier writings, so also from the Savior’s advent—which He fulfilled in humility, having taken the form of a servant—a more glorious and clear second advent is indicated ‘in the glory of His Father’. In it the form of Deuteronomy is fulfilled, when in the kingdom of heaven all the saints live by the laws of that eternal gospel; and just as He now fulfilled the law that ‘has a shadow of the good things to come’ by His coming, so through that glorious advent the shadow of this advent will be fulfilled and brought to perfection. For thus the prophet said of Him: ‘The Spirit before our face is Christ the Lord, of whom we said, “In His shadow we shall live among the nations”’, when He will transfer all the saints from the temporal gospel to the ‘eternal gospel’, as John designated in the Apocalypse concerning the ‘eternal gospel’ (Revelation 14:6).

In all these things it suffices for us to conform our understanding to the rule of piety and to think of the Holy Spirit’s words such that our composed speech does not rely on the eloquence of human frailty, but, as it is written: ‘All the glory of the king is within’ (Psalm 45:13), and the treasure of divine meanings is contained and enclosed within the ‘fragile vessel’ of humble letter.

But if anyone seeks a more exact explanation of each point, let him come and hear with us how the apostle Paul, ‘through the Holy Spirit’ who ‘searches even the depths of God,’ scrutinizing the height of divine wisdom and knowledge, yet not prevailing to the end—nor, as I might say, to intimate knowledge—proclaims in desperation and amazement: ‘O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!’ And with the desperation of perfect comprehension he proclaimed this, hear him saying: ‘How inscrutable are His judgments and how unsearchable His ways!’ (Romans 11:33). For he did not say it is difficult to scrutinize the ‘judgments of God,’ but that it is altogether impossible; nor that it is difficult to investigate His ‘ways,’ but that they cannot be investigated.

However much one may advance in scrutiny and profit by more intent study, aided by the grace of God and illuminated in mind, he cannot reach the perfect end of the things sought. Nor does any created mind have the possibility of comprehending them in any way; but as it finds some portion of what is sought, it sees again other things that must be sought; and even if it reaches those, it will perceive much more, again, of what ought to be sought.

Et qua desperatione perfectae conpraehensionis haec proclamaverit, audi ipsum dicentem: “Quam inscrutabilia sunt iudicia dei, et quam investigabiles viae eius”. Non enim dixit difficile posse scrutari “udicia dei, sed omnino non posse; nec dixit difficile investigari posse ‘vias’ elus, sed non posse investigar. Quantumcumque enim quis in scrutando promoveat et studio intentiore proficiat, gratia quoque dei adiutus sensumque -inluminatus, ad perfectum finem eorum, quae requiruntur, pervenire non poterit. excerpts.author: Origen
english: 1. As, then, after those first discussions which, according to the requirements of the case, we held at the beginning regarding the Father , Son, and Holy Spirit , it seemed right that we should retrace our steps, and show that the same God was the creator and founder of the world, and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ , i.e., that the God of the law and of the prophets and of the Gospel was one and the same; and that, in the next place, it ought to be shown, with respect to Christ , in what manner He who had formerly been demonstrated to be the Word and Wisdom of God became man; it remains that we now return with all possible brevity to the subject of the Holy Spirit . It is time, then, that we say a few words to the best of our ability regarding the Holy Spirit , whom our Lord and Saviour in the Gospel according to John has named the Paraclete. For as it is the same God Himself, and the same Christ, so also is it the same Holy Spirit who was in the prophets and apostles , i.e., either in those who believed in God before the advent of Christ , or in those who by means of Christ have sought refuge in God . We have heard, indeed, that certain heretics have dared to say that there are two Gods and two Christs, but we have never known of the doctrine of two Holy Spirits being preached by any one. For how could they maintain this out of Scripture, or what distinction could they lay down between Holy Spirit and Holy Spirit , if indeed any definition or description of Holy…

2. Now we are of opinion that every rational creature, without any distinction, receives a share of Him in the same way as of the Wisdom and of the Word of God . I observe, however, that the chief advent of the Holy Spirit is declared to men , after the ascension of Christ to heaven, rather than before His coming into the world. For, before that, it was upon the prophets alone, and upon a few individuals — if there happened to be any among the people deserving of it — that the gift of the Holy Spirit was conferred; but after the advent of the Saviour , it is written that the prediction of the prophet Joel was fulfilled, In the last days it shall come to pass, and I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh, and they shall prophesy, which is similar to the well-known statement, All nations shall serve Him. By the grace , then, of the Holy Spirit , along with numerous other results, this most glorious consequence is clearly demonstrated, that with regard to those things which were written in the prophets or in the law of Moses , it was only a few persons at that time, viz., the prophets themselves, and scarcely another individual out of the whole nation, who were able to look beyond the mere corporeal meaning and discover something greater, i.e., something spiritual, in the law or in the prophets ; but now there are countless multitudes of believers who, although unable to unfold methodically and clearly the results of their spiritual understanding, are nevertheless most firmly…

3. And as there are many ways of apprehending Christ, who, although He is wisdom, does not act the part or possess the power of wisdom in all men , but only in those who give themselves to the study of wisdom in Him; and who, although called a physician, does not act as one towards all, but only towards those who understand their feeble and sickly condition, and flee to His compassion that they may obtain health; so also I think is it with the Holy Spirit , in whom is contained every kind of gifts. For on some is bestowed by the Spirit the word of wisdom, on others the word of knowledge , on others faith ; and so to each individual of those who are capable of receiving Him, is the Spirit Himself made to be that quality, or understood to be that which is needed by the individual who has deserved to participate. These divisions and differences not being perceived by those who hear Him called Paraclete in the Gospel , and not duly considering in consequence of what work or act He is named the Paraclete, they have compared Him to some common spirits or other, and by this means have tried to disturb the Churches of Christ , and so excite dissensions of no small extent among brethren; whereas the Gospel shows Him to be of such power and majesty, that it says the apostles could not yet receive those things which the Saviour wished to teach them until the advent of the Holy Spirit , who, pouring Himself into their souls , might enlighten them regarding the nature and faith of the…

4. We must therefore know that the Paraclete is the Holy Spirit , who teaches truths which cannot be uttered in words, and which are, so to speak, unutterable, and which it is not lawful for a man to utter, i.e., which cannot be indicated by human language. The phrase it is not lawful is, we think, used by the apostle instead of it is not possible; as also is the case in the passage where he says, All things are lawful for me, but all things are not expedient: all things are lawful for me; but all things edify not. For those things which are in our power because we may have them, he says are lawful for us. But the Paraclete, who is called the Holy Spirit , is so called from His work of consolation, para clesis being termed in Latin consolatio . For if any one has deserved to participate in the Holy Spirit by the knowledge of His ineffable mysteries , he undoubtedly obtains comfort and joy of heart. For since he comes by the teaching of the Spirit to the knowledge of the reasons of all things which happen — how or why they occur — his soul can in no respect be troubled, or admit any feeling of sorrow; nor is he alarmed by anything, since, clinging to the Word of God and His wisdom, he through the Holy Spirit calls Jesus Lord. excerpts.author: Origen
english: He goes on to say that the pronouncements uttered by the Pythia, the Dodonian priests, the Clarian oracle, the shrine at Branchidae, the oracle of Ammon, and by thousands of other prophets — through whom the whole earth was gently settled — are not given any credence at all. Yet the things spoken by those in Judea in the same fashion, or even things that were never spoken, and the sort of utterances still customary today among the peoples of Phoenicia and Palestine, these they regard as marvelous and unalterable.

Let us then address the oracles that have been cited. We can collect from Aristotle and the philosophers of the Peripatetic school plenty of arguments to overturn the case for the Pythia and the other oracles. We can also adduce the statements of Epicurus and his followers on the same subject to show that even some Greeks reject the prophetic claims that are revered and wondered at throughout Greece.

But suppose we grant that the phenomena surrounding the Pythia and the other oracles are not fabrications or human pretenses of divine inspiration. Let us see whether, even on that concession, one can demonstrate to those who investigate honestly that accepting these utterances as genuine oracles does not compel us to acknowledge the presence of gods. On the contrary, they point to evil demons and spirits hostile to the human race, beings that obstruct the soul's ascent, the path of virtue, and the restoration of true piety toward God.

The Pythia is reported to be the most renowned of the oracles. She sits over the mouth of the Castalian spring, and the prophetess of Apollo receives a spirit through her female organs; filled with it, she delivers what are taken to be solemn and divine prophecies. Consider whether this does not reveal the unclean and profane character of that spirit. It does not enter the prophetess's soul through pure, invisible channels — channels far cleaner than the female organs — but through parts that it is not even lawful for a sane person to look at or touch. And this happens not merely once or twice (for perhaps that might seem more tolerable), but as often as she is believed to prophesy from Apollo.

Moreover, driving the supposed prophetess into an ecstatic, manic state in which she loses all self-possession is not the work of a divine spirit. The one indwelt by the divine Spirit ought to have been benefited long before by everything taught through the oracles, and to have become more discerning — most of all at the very moment when the divine is present to him.
